en: Before verse 1, Ś₁ and B₃ insert, followed by *1–4: oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya.
Before stanza 1, Ś₂ inserts:
*oṃ śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya oṃ*. Before stanza 1, Ñ₁ inserts:
Followed by *1–4:
oṃ namo kṛṣṇāya / Before verse 1, V1 inserts:
Followed by *1–4:
oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya / Before verse 1, B1 inserts:
Followed by *1–4:
*namo gaṇapataye*. Before verse 1, B2 inserts:
Followed by *1–4:
Oṃ Śrīkṛṣṇaḥ! Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One!
May that Viṣṇu— who is the six-syllabled Brahman, the Lord, the Supreme Person, the source of the waves of the qualities (guṇas), of creation, maintenance, time,
and dissolution, and the progenitor of the manifold universe beginning with primordial matter (pradhāna) and the intellect (buddhi)— grant us the prosperity of intelligence and liberation.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, and having bowed down to Brahmā and the others,
and having saluted my Guru, I shall proclaim this Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas.
He was a knower of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, one who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas),
an expert in the true principles of the Dharmaśāstras and other treatises, and the son of Vasiṣṭha’s daughter.
Before verse 1, D₂ inserts, followed by *5–6:
"May there be well-being! Salutations to the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, whose very nature is that of the Guru, Gaṇeśa, and Bhāratī."
I bow to that pure-minded Lord of the Gaṇas, who is praised even by the hosts of gods for the accomplishment of all desires cherished by the mind, and who is a fire to the fuel of every obstacle.
I bow eternally to that Grandfather, who sits upon a lotus throne, whose face is like a lotus, whose source is the lotus, and whose four faces are adorned with the six-limbed Vedas.
Before verse 1, D₄ inserts *16, followed by *7–8: .... .... .... .tātmane [lacuna] /
Salutations again and again to the original author of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

May that Lord Keśava bring you joy—he who, having assumed that incomparable form of Narasiṃha which pervades the three worlds, beautiful in appearance with its mass of thick, lovely, and radiant manes; he by whom the broad chest of the enemy of the gods, as hard as a heap of diamond-stone, was rent asunder with his claws.
Before verse 1, D5 inserts [text], followed by *9–10,
and thereafter by *1–4.

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī. Victorious is Brahmā, whose body is the interior of a lotus, whose face is a lotus, who was born from the womb of a lotus, whose lotus-feet are bowed to by the gods, and who is seated upon a lotus-throne.
Victorious is the Lord, whose body is as dark blue as a cloud filled with heavy rain,
and who is marked by the jagged rocks from his tossing of Mount Mandara;
victorious is he whose broad forehead is crowded by a crown of matted locks adorned with the crescent moon.
The four lotus-faces of Śambhu, blossoming with the rays of his gleaming teeth.
Oṃ. Salutation to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Oṃ. Salutation to the Blessed One, Śrī Vāsudeva.
[Before verse 1, D₇ inserts: Oṃ.
Before verse 1, D₈ inserts:]
Followed by *1–4:
oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya śrīgaṇeśasarasvatībhyāṃ namaḥ / Before verse 1, T1 inserts:
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, who has four arms, and whose face is serene, for the pacification of all obstacles. (ViP 1.1.0) *12*
We worship Gajanana, the sun to the lotus-face of the unborn one, who possesses many tusks yet appears as single-tusked to his devotees, day and night.

May that blessed Sarasvatī protect me—she who is as white as the kunda flower, the moon, snow, or a string of pearls; she who is draped in radiant white garments; she whose hands are adorned with a lute and a staff; she who sits upon a white lotus; she who is eternally worshipped by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; she who removes every trace of dullness.
Before verse 1, T1 inserts,
followed by *15–17: oṃ / From whom this world was born, in whom it stands, and into whom all this finally goes to its setting.

Salutation to that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), whose form is pure consciousness alone and who is devoid of conceptual constructions such as "existent" and "non-existent. Salutation to that best of sages, Parāśara, who, being noble and possessing the very nature of the Lord, truly established the paths of worldly enjoyment and liberation along with their means, and who, revealing these, composed this jewel of a Purāṇa.
I bow to that Parāśara, who composed the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, which is filled with six parts like another Veda consisting of its limbs (aṅgas).
Before verse 1, T3 inserts: *oṃ śrīviṣṇave namaḥ*. Before verse 1, G1 inserts:
Followed by *8:
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati!
May there be no obstacle!
Before verse 1, G₂ inserts:
Salutation to the Supreme One, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is the medicine for worldly existence, who destroys the suffering of his devotees,
who is higher than the highest, who is mounted upon Garuḍa, who bestows happiness, and who is the boon-granting Boar.
Before verse 1, G₃ inserts:
Hariḥ Oṃ. May the Viṣṇupurāṇa, together with its commentary, be auspicious at its commencement; may there be no obstacle. Salutation to Śrī for the sake of Śrī.
Salutation to Śrī Hayagrīva. Salutation to Śrī Rāmacandra, the Supreme Brahman.
Hariḥ oṃ. May there be no obstacle.
Before verse 1, M₂ inserts [the following], followed by *1 and *8, then *19:
Having prostrated and offered salutations to Parāśara, the best of sages, who had completed his morning rites, Maitreya questioned him.
For from you, O Guru, the study of the Vedas has been mastered in its entirety,
as well as all the Dharmaśāstras and the Vedāṅgas in their proper order.
O best of sages, through your grace, even those who are generally my enemies will say of me that I have not exerted myself in any of the scriptures.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, I desire to hear from you how the world came into being and,
O illustrious one, how it will come to be again.
O Brahman, tell me of what this world consists, from whence this world of moving and unmoving beings arises,
how it was dissolved, where it remained latent, and where it will go to its dissolution.
The dimensions of the elements, the origin of the gods and others,
and the configuration of the oceans, mountains, and the earth as it is.
O best of sages, [tell us] the configuration and dimensions of the sun and other celestial bodies,
as well as the lineages of the gods and others, the Manus, and the Manvantaras.
The kalpas and the various divisions of kalpas as conceived within the four ages,
the essential nature of the end of a kalpa, and the characteristics of each age in their entirety.
O great sage, [I wish to hear] the life-stories of the gods, sages, and kings,
as well as the proper compilation of the Vedic branches performed by Vyāsa.
O delight of the Vasiṣṭhas, I desire to hear from you everything regarding the duties of the Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as those of the residents of the various stages of life (āśramas).
O Brahman, direct your mind toward showing me favor,
so that by your grace, O great sage, I may understand this.
Parāśara said: Well said, Maitreya, knower of dharma! I have been reminded of that which my father’s father, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, spoke in the past.
O Maitreya, I heard that my father had been devoured by a Rākṣasa instigated by Viśvāmitra; consequently, an incomparable anger arose within me.
Then I commenced a sacrificial session (satra) for the destruction of the Rākṣasas;
in that sacrifice, hundreds of night-stalkers were reduced to ashes.
Then, as those Rākṣasas were being completely destroyed,
the illustrious Vasiṣṭha, our grandfather, spoke to me.
"Enough with this excessive anger, my dear; abandon this resentment. The Rākṣasas are not at fault; it was so ordained for your father."
This anger belongs to the deluded; how could it belong to those possessed of knowledge?
For whom, my dear, can anyone be slain by whom? Since a person experiences the fruits of his own actions.
O child, even for fame and ascetic merit that have been accumulated by men with great effort, anger is the supreme destroyer.
O dear one, the supreme sages always avoid anger, which is the cause that obstructs both heaven and liberation; do not fall under its power.
Enough with these wretched, innocent night-stalkers who have been consumed by fire;
let this sacrifice of yours cease, for the virtuous have forgiveness as their very essence.
Thus, having been thus entreated by that high-souled father,
I immediately brought the sacrificial session to a close out of respect for his words.
Then the blessed Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was pleased;
and at that time Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, arrived there.
Having been offered water for his hands by my grandfather and having accepted a seat,
the illustrious Maitreya, the elder brother of Pulaha, spoke to me.
§ Pulastya said:
Since you have resorted to forgiveness toward this teacher despite his great enmity because of his words,
therefore you shall know all the scriptures.
"Since you, O illustrious one, have ensured that there shall be no severance of my lineage even when you were angry,
I therefore grant you another great boon."
"O child, you shall become the compiler of the Purāṇa-saṃhitās;
and you shall come to know the ultimate reality of the deities exactly as it is."
And regarding both active and ceased karma, O child, your intellect shall become free from stain and free from doubt through my grace.
Then the Blessed One said: "O Vasiṣṭha, my grandfather, everything that was told to you by Pulastya shall come to pass."
Thus, all that was previously spoken by Vasiṣṭha and the wise Pulastya has come to my memory in its entirety because of your question.
Therefore, O Maitreya, as you inquire, I shall tell you this Purāṇa-saṃhitā in its entirety; understand it correctly, exactly as it is.
The universe has arisen from Viṣṇu and is situated in him alone;
he is the agent of the sustenance and withdrawal of this universe, and the universe is he.
Having heard the words of his friend’s son and recalled that boon of his own, that highly fortunate one became a savior by preventing the sacrifice;
he then instructed the excellent sage Maitreya in the supreme Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa], which establishes the true meaning for those who speak it and bestows all goals upon those who hear it.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: To the immutable, pure, eternal Supreme Self;
Salutation to Viṣṇu, who is of one and the same form at all times, the conqueror of all.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Hari, and to Śaṅkara;
to Vāsudeva, the Savior, who brings about the creation, maintenance, and end of the world.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause of liberation, whose nature is both one and many, whose essence is both gross and subtle, and whose form is both unmanifest and manifest.
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is the source of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and who is himself composed of the world.
Having prostrated before the Imperishable One, the Supreme Person, who is the support of the universe, subtler than the subtlest, and who dwells within all beings; ViP_1,2.5.
In ultimate reality, he is the very nature of knowledge, absolutely pure;
yet, due to erroneous perception, he appears to abide in the form of an object.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu, the devourer of the universe, the Lord who presides over its maintenance and creation, the sovereign of the worlds, unborn, undecaying, and immutable;
I shall relate it just as it was told in the past when the Blessed One, the lotus-born Grandfather, was questioned by Dakṣa and other most excellent sages.
They told it to King Purukutsa on the bank of the Narmadā;
he told it to Sārasvata, and by him, to me, Sārasvata.
He is the highest of the high, the supreme Self abiding within the self;
He is devoid of all specific designations and qualifiers such as form, color, and the like.
He who is devoid of diminution and destruction, as well as transformation, growth, and birth,
can be described simply as "always existing."
Since he dwells everywhere and everything dwells within him,
for that reason he is recited by the wise as Vāsudeva.
That Brahman is supreme, eternal, unborn, undecaying, and immutable;
it is always of a single nature and stainless because of the absence of anything to be discarded.
All this is indeed that very same [reality], existing in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
as well as in the form of the Person (puruṣa) and in the form of Time (kāla).
O twice-born one, the first form of the supreme Brahman is Puruṣa;
likewise, there are two other forms, the manifest and the unmanifest, and Time is yet another.
That which is indeed the supreme among primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), the manifest (vyakta), and time (kāla)—
the pure reality that the wise perceive— is the highest step of Viṣṇu.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla, according to their respective divisions,
are the causes for the existence of the forms [of the world] and for maintenance, dissolution, and manifestation.
The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and Time itself—behold his activity, which is like that of a playing child. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2.18)
That which is the unmanifest cause is called Pradhāna by the best of seers;
it is the subtle Prakṛti, eternal, and composed of both being and non-being.
It is imperishable, having no other support, immeasurable, undecaying, and eternal;
it is devoid of sound and touch, and is not composed of form and the other [sensory qualities].
That womb of the universe, consisting of the three qualities, is without beginning, its origin and end;
by it all was pervaded at the outset, following the dissolution.
O learned one, those who know the declarations of the Vedas, being self-restrained and expounders of Brahman,
recite this very same meaning which establishes the Pradhāna.
There was neither day nor night, neither sky nor earth; there was no darkness, nor was there light, nor anything else.
At that time, there existed the one primordial Brahman, the Puruṣa, which is unperceivable by the intellect through the senses such as hearing.
O Brahmin, those others—Pradhāna and Puruṣa—are indeed distinct from the essential nature (svarūpa) of Viṣṇu;
O twice-born one, that other form of his, which is held apart by another [aspect] and then joined together, is designated as Time (kāla).
And because the manifest remains within primordial nature (prakṛti) during the past dissolution,
this dissolution is therefore called "primal" (prākṛta).
O twice-born one, the Blessed Time is beginningless and its end is not known;
therefore, these processes of creation, maintenance, destruction, and dissolution proceed from it without interruption.
Then, O Maitreya, while that equilibrium of the qualities remains established separately within the Spirit, the nature of Time belonging to Viṣṇu proceeds to evolve.
O Maitreya, that which exists as the very form of time belongs to Viṣṇu.
Then that supreme Brahman is the Supreme Self, consisting of the universe,
all-pervading, the Lord of all beings, the Self of all, the Supreme Lord.
When the time for creation had arrived, Hari, by his own will, entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa— the mutable and the immutable— and caused them to vibrate.
Just as a fragrance causes agitation of the mind by its mere presence, even though it provides no assistance to it, so too is that Supreme Lord.
O Brahmin, that very Puruṣottama is both the agitator and the object of agitation;
he exists even in the state of Pradhāna through contraction and expansion.
And likewise, Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, exists both in the form of the expansion and its subtle essence, as well as in the forms of Brahmā and others, and in his manifest nature.

Therefore, O sage, O best of the twice-born, from that equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), when presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), there arises at the time of creation the manifestation of the qualities.
The principle of Pradhāna manifested the Mahat, which completely enveloped it;
the Mahat is threefold— sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa—
and it was covered by the principle of Pradhāna, like a seed by its husk.
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is Tāmasa—
this threefold Ahaṃkāra was born from the principle of Mahat.
O great sage, because it possesses the three qualities (guṇas), he is the cause of the elements and the senses;
just as the Great Principle (mahat) is enveloped by Pradhāna, so too is he enveloped by the Great Principle.
Then the primary element (bhūtādi), undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of sound;
from that subtle element of sound, it created space, which is characterized by sound.
Space, which consists of sound alone, enveloped that [subtle element] consisting of the primary elements;
then space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch.
The wind became powerful; its quality is considered to be touch.
Space, which consists of sound alone, then enveloped the subtle element of touch.
Then the wind, undergoing transformation, emitted the subtle element of form;
light was produced from the wind, and that is said to have the quality of form.
Then the wind, having transformed, enveloped the subtle element of form;
and light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste.
From that, waters arise which are the supports of taste;
those waters consist of the subtle element of taste alone, and they envelop the subtle element of form alone.
The waters, undergoing transformation, produced mere fragrance;
from that, the aggregate (saṃghāta) is born, and fragrance is considered its quality.
Because they consist of only that [respective element] in each case, they are known as "merely-that" (tanmātra). The tanmātras are non-specific (aviśeṣa); therefore, they are called non-specific.
They are neither peaceful nor terrible, nor are they deluded; they are without distinction.
This creation of the elements and the subtle essences proceeds from the tamasic ego.
They say the sense organs are taijasa, while the ten deities are vaikārika;
here, the eleventh, the mind, is also recorded as being a vaikārika deity.
O twice-born one, the skin, the eyes, the nose, the tongue, and the ear as the fifth— these, indeed, are endowed with the intellect for the purpose of perceiving sound and the other sense objects.
The anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech as the fifth, O Maitreya— these are [the organs],
and their functions are said to be excretion, procreation, manual labor, locomotion, and speech.
O Brahmin, ether, air, fire, water, and earth are joined with their respective qualities, beginning with sound, each succeeding element possessing one more than the preceding.
Therefore, they are remembered as having these specific qualities: being peaceful, terrible, or deluded.
Possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, they were unable to create living beings without a collective union, as they had not come together in their entirety.
Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent,
they form a single composite whole, attaining complete unity.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest,
those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg.

O one of great intelligence, that [egg], having grown gradually like a bubble on the water, was formed from the elements; it rested upon the waters and was the unsurpassed natural abode of Viṣṇu in his form as Brahmā.
There, that Lord of the universe, Viṣṇu, who is both unmanifest in his essential nature and manifest in his form, abides by himself in the form of Brahmā.
Mount Meru became his amnion and the mountains his chorion;
the oceans were the fetal waters of that Great-Souled One.
O Brahmin, within that egg there came into being the collection of worlds, including the mountains, continents, and oceans, along with the luminaries, as well as gods, asuras, and humans.
Then the egg is surrounded on the outside by water, fire, air, and ether, each ten times greater than the preceding; and the *bhūtādi* is likewise surrounded by the *mahat*.
O Brahmin, the Great Principle (Mahat), together with all those [subsequent principles], is enveloped by the Unmanifest;
and by these seven primordial coverings, the cosmic egg is enclosed,
just as the seed within a coconut fruit is surrounded by its outer husks.
There, Hari himself, the Lord of the Universe, partaking of the quality of passion (rajas),
becomes Brahmā and proceeds with the creation of this world.
And having created [the world],
the Lord Viṣṇu, the sustainer of beings whose prowess is immeasurable, protects it throughout the ages until the end of the kalpa-cycle.
And at the end of the kalpa, Janārdana, assuming the form of Rudra and overflowing with fury,
becomes exceedingly terrifying, Maitreya, and devours all living beings.
Having consumed all beings when the world has been turned into a single ocean,
that Supreme Lord reclines upon his serpent-couch.
And having awakened, he again effects creation, assuming the form of Brahmā.
Because he performs the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction, the one Lord Janārdana alone assumes the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The Creator creates himself; Viṣṇu protects that which is to be protected;
and at the end, the Lord himself withdraws it as the Destroyer.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as all the senses and the internal organ— this world is indeed what is called the Puruṣa.
Since he alone is the imperishable Lord of all beings and the universal form,
therefore the creation and other processes, which abide within all beings, are his very own and serve as his benefactors.
He alone is the object of creation and He is the creator; He alone protects, devours, and is protected.
With all forms beginning with the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu is the most excellent, the giver of boons, and the one worthy of being sought.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
[Tell me] of that which is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, pure, and of stainless nature;
How is Brahman’s status as the creator of the initial creation and so forth accepted?
Parāśara said:
Since the powers of all entities fall within the domain of inconceivable knowledge,
therefore those powers of being, such as creation and the rest, belong to Brahman.
O best of those who radiate heat, they exist just as heat exists in fire.
Understand how the Blessed One,
known as Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, proceeds at the time of creation.
O wise one, he who is eternal is nevertheless called "born" only by way of figurative usage.
By its own measure, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years;
that is called a *parā*, and half of that is designated as a *parārdha*.
O sinless one, understand from that which I have told you regarding the nature of time and Viṣṇu, the demonstration of its measurement.
And likewise, O best of beings, [you know] all other creatures, both those that move and those that are stationary, including the earth, the mountains, the oceans, and so forth.
O best of sages, fifteen *nimeṣas* are said to be one *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* make one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute the duration of a *muhūrta*.
A human day and night is said to consist of that same number of muhūrtas;
a month, composed of two fortnights, consists of that same number of days and nights.
By those six [months] a year is formed; there are two solstices, the southern and the northern.
The southern solstice is the night of the gods, and the northern is their day.
Understand from me the division of the four ages—known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth—which consists of twelve thousand divine years. ViP_1,3.11 //
Those who know the past have stated that in the Yugas beginning with Kṛta, the [lifespans] are respectively four, three, two, and one thousand divine years.
The preceding twilight is said to consist of hundreds of those same units of time;
the period following the Yuga, known as the twilight-part (saṃdhyāṃśaka), is equal to that.
O best of sages, that period of time which lies between the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the twilight-period (saṃdhyāṃśa) is to be known as the "yuga," designated by the names Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga);
a thousand such periods, O Sage, is said to be one day of Brahmā.
O Brahman, during the day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus;
hear now their duration as determined by time.
The seven ṛṣis, the gods, Śakra, Manu, and his sons, the kings,
are indeed created at one and the same time and withdrawn in the same manner as before.
O best of beings, a period consisting of seventy-one yugas, plus a little more, is reckoned as a Manvantara, the time of a Manu and of the gods and others.
By divine reckoning, it is recorded as eight hundred thousand,
with an additional fifty-two thousand more.
O twice-born one, thirty full crores have been calculated by number, as well as sixty-seven other hundred-thousands (niyutas), O great sage. (ViP 1.3.20)
Likewise, [the number] is joined with one hundred and forty-two.
A divine day consists of five thousand [human] months and ten days and eight nights.
There are four yāmas, two muhūrtas, and likewise eight kalās.
A *kāṣṭhā* consists of seventeen and two *nimeṣas*; immediately after that [is the *kalā*].
It is held to be one-seventh of a single blink of the divine eye.
Furthermore, human years amount to one million and eighteen thousand.
One thousand years, increased by twenty-eight, and four hundred [years] more.
In twenty-four days and nights, six months are likewise completed.
There are twelve channels (nāḍīs), and immediately after that, an equal number of digits (kalās).
Twenty-five *kāṣṭhās* make one *nimeṣa*, and ten *nimeṣas* make one *sāyika*.
O twice-born one, twenty thousand years, plus an additional period,
is the reckoning of a manvantara in human years.
Indeed, this period of fourteen [yugas] is recorded as a day of Brahmā;
at its conclusion occurs the dissolution known as the "occasional" (naimittika) dissolution of Brahmā.
For at that time, the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ, is consumed by fire;
and the inhabitants of Maharloka, afflicted by the heat, proceed to Jana-loka.
When the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa,
lies upon the bed of the serpent, nourished by having swallowed the three worlds.
O God, while being meditated upon by the yogis dwelling in Janaloka, the lotus-born Lord,
having passed that night of the same duration, creates once again at its conclusion.
Such is a day of Brahmā, and such is his hundred years;
for the lifespan of that great-souled one is indeed a hundred of those years.
O sinless one, one *parārdha* of Brahmā’s lifespan has already passed;
at its conclusion occurred the great kalpa renowned as Pādma.
O twice-born one, this first kalpa of the current second Parārdha is proclaimed as the Vārāha.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"How did that Lord, known as Nārāyaṇa, become Brahmā at the beginning of the Kalpa?"
He created all living beings; tell that, O great sage.
Parāśara said: Listen to me as I describe how the Lord Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, the divine Lord of the Prajāpatis, created the progeny. ViP 1.4.2.
At the conclusion of the past kalpa, the Lord Brahmā, having risen from his night's sleep and overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), beheld the world as empty.
Nārāyaṇa is supreme and inconceivable; he is the Lord even of those who are supreme.
The Blessed One, whose nature is Brahman, is without beginning and the source of all things.

And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, the god whose nature is Brahman, the source and the dissolution of the world: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.4.5: "He who, having first created Brahmā from his lotus-navel, then assigned to him the Vedas; he who, at the end of time, withdraws all beings back into himself—he is the one to be known as Nārāyaṇa."
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his first place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Having perceived that the earth was submerged within the waters of the single ocean of the world,
the Lord Prajāpati, desiring to raise it up, resorted to inference.
Just as in former kalpas he assumed other bodies such as those of the fish and the tortoise, so too did he take on the form of a boar.
The Lord of Creatures, the Supreme Self, the Soul of All, whose nature is firm, remained established for the maintenance of the entire world in a form consisting of the Vedas and sacrifices.
Praised by the Siddhas, Sanaka and others, who had gone to Janaloka,
the Supporter of the Earth, whose own self is his support, then entered the water.
Then, beholding him who had arrived at the surface of the netherworld (pātāla), the goddess Earth,
bowing down and humbled by devotion, offered praise.
The Earth said:
"Homage to you, the soul of all beings, O wielder of the conch and the mace!
Lift me up from this today; for I arose from you in the past."
I was raised up by you in the past; I am composed of you, O Janārdana, as are all other beings without exception, beginning with the ether.

Salutations to you, O Supreme Self, O Soul, O Universal Person; let there be salutation to you. Salutations to you who have become both the unmanifest and the manifest, and who have become Time itself.
O Lord, you are the creator of all beings, their protector, and their destroyer;
at the beginning of creation and other cosmic cycles, you assume the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
Having consumed the entire world and it been turned into a single ocean,
you alone remain, O Govinda, being meditated upon by the wise.
No one knows that supreme form of yours;
it is only the forms you assume in your incarnations that the gods worship.
Having propitiated you, the Supreme Brahman, those seeking liberation have attained release;
without propitiating Vāsudeva, who will obtain liberation?
Whatever is to be grasped by the mind, whatever is to be grasped by the eyes and other senses,
and whatever is to be discerned by the intellect— all that form belongs entirely to you.
"I am composed of you, I have you as my support, I was created by you, and I have taken refuge in you;
for this reason, indeed, the world calls me Mādhavī."

Victory to you, who consist of all knowledge! Victory to you, the imperishable one composed of the gross! Victory to you, O Infinite One! Victory to you, the Unmanifest! Victory to you, O Lord, who consist of the manifest!
O Supreme and Lower Self, O Soul of the Universe, victory to you, O sinless Lord of Sacrifice!
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the *oṃ* syllable, and you are the sacred fires;
you are the Vedas, you are their auxiliary limbs, and you are the Person of the Sacrifice, O Hari.
The planets beginning with the Sun, all the stars and constellations,
O Supreme Person— the manifest and the unmanifest, the invisible and the visible.
In the very same way, through illusion, everything appears from you just as it does from me.
O Supreme Lord, whatever has been spoken by me here and whatever has not been spoken—all that is yours; salutations to you, again and again, salutations, salutations!
Parāśara said:
Thus being praised by the Earth,
the glorious upholder of the earth roared with a deep, rumbling sound like the resonance of a Sāman chant.
Then, having lifted up the earth with his tusk, the Great Boar, whose eyes were like blooming lotuses,
rose from the subterranean realm like a great mountain of sapphire blue, resembling the petals of a blue lotus.
As he rose up, the water of that flood, struck by the wind from his mouth,
rendered even the stainless sages such as Sanandana— who were already residing in Janaloka— once again a locus of supreme purity.
The waters flow downward into the depths of the earth, producing a continuous roar as they are churned by the tips of his hooves;
and the Siddhas who dwell perpetually among men move about on all sides, distressed by the wind of his breath.
D5 inserts: Even the body of Nārāyaṇa enters [into it]... // ViP_1,4.28*24 //
As that Great Boar, whose flanks were wet with water, rose up having lifted the earth and shook his body composed of the Vedas, the sages dwelling within the pores of his hair offered their praise.
Those yogis who dwell among the people of the world, led by Sanandana, their minds overcome with joy, praised Him—
the sustainer of the earth, whose eyes were firm yet haughty— with their necks bowed low in salutation.
O Supreme Lord of lords, Keśava, Master, wielder of the mace, conch, sword, and discus;
You alone are the Lord who is the cause of the creation, destruction, and maintenance [of the world], and there is no other supreme state than You.
The Vedas are in your feet, O Lord whose tusks are the sacrificial posts; the sacrifices and the piled altars are in your teeth;
you have the fire as your tongue, the *darbha* grasses as your body hair, and you alone, O Lord, are the Person of Sacrifice (*Yajñapuruṣa*).
O Great-Souled One, night and day are Your eyes; the supreme Brahman, the abode of all, is Your head;
all the hymns are the mass of Your mane; and all the sacrificial oblations, O God, are Your sense of smell.
O Lord, whose mouth is the *sruk* ladle, whose deep sound is the resonance of the *Sāman*, whose body is the *Prāgvaṃśa* hall, and who is the union of all sacrificial sessions;
O God, eternal Self, you are the hearing of the merit of public works and sacrifices—be gracious, O Blessed One!
O Imperishable One, whose form is the universe, you alone are the infinite beginning that stands pervading all stages;
we know you as the Supreme Lord of the universe. Be gracious, for you are the Protector of all that moves and is stationary.
O Lord, this entire circle of the earth is perceived as resting upon the tips of your fangs,
like a lotus leaf with clinging mud when you have plunged into a lotus grove.

O Lord of incomparable power, that space between heaven and earth is pervaded by your very form; O All-pervading One, whose radiant splendor is capable of encompassing the universe, may you exist for the welfare of the entire world.
But in the ultimate sense, you alone are one; there is no other, O Lord of the world.
This entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by this majesty of yours.
This which is seen as a material form is you, whose self is knowledge;
those who are not yogis perceive it as the form of the world through deluded cognition.
Those of dull intellect, perceiving this entire universe— which is in its true nature pure consciousness— as being composed of material objects, wander in the deluge of ignorance.
But those who possess knowledge and have pure minds perceive the entire world as consisting of knowledge— your very form, O Supreme Lord.
Be gracious, O Soul of All, for the welfare of the worlds;
lift up this earth, O immeasurable Self, and grant us peace, O lotus-eyed one!
"O Blessed One, Govinda, you are preeminent in the quality of goodness (sattva); O Lord, lift up this earth!
O Lotus-eyed One, grant us prosperity."
May your engagement in creation be for the benefit of the worlds;
let this be so. Homage be to you! Grant us prosperity, O lotus-eyed one.
Parāśara said:
While being thus praised, the Supreme Self, the upholder of the earth,
quickly lifted the earth and placed it upon the great ocean.
Standing above that flood of water like a great ship,
the earth does not undergo submersion because of the vast extent of its body.
Then, having leveled the earth, the Lord— the beginningless source of all— constructed mountains upon the ground according to their respective divisions.
By his unfailing power, he whose desires are never in vain created all the mountains upon the surface of the earth, which had been consumed by fire at the previous dissolution.
Then, having divided the earth into its seven continents exactly as they are,
he fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, just as before.
Then that Lord Hari, assuming the form of Brahmā and enveloped by the quality of passion (rajas),
became four-faced and performed the work of creation.
He is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creation of those things to be created,
since the creative powers truly constitute the primary cause.
O best of those who shine, nothing other than the mere sign (nimitta) is required; a thing is brought to its state of being a real entity by its own power.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"In what manner did that Lord create the gods, the ṛṣis, the ancestors, and the dānavas?"
Humans, animals, trees, and so forth, as well as those dwelling upon the earth, in the sky, and in the waters.
O twice-born one, explain to me in detail that which Brahmā created at the beginning of creation— whatever qualities, whatever nature, and whatever form the world possessed.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen with a well-composed mind as I describe how that all-pervading Lord created the gods and all other beings.
As he was contemplating creation as it had been at the beginning of previous kalpas,
a creation consisting of darkness appeared to him, arising without the intervention of conscious thought.
Darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhatāmisra)—
this fivefold ignorance (avidyā) manifested from the Great-Souled One.
The creation existing in five states consists of those who meditate yet lack awakening;
they are without light within or without, their nature is concealed, and they are characterized as immobile beings.
Since the primary mountains were mentioned first, this is therefore called the primary creation (mukhya-sarga).
Seeing that creation to be unsuccessful, he again conceived another.
As he was contemplating creation, the Tiryaksrotas (the downward-flowing stream) emerged;
because it proceeded obliquely, it is therefore known as Tiryaksrotas.
Those such as the beasts are well known to be dominated by darkness (tamas),
devoid of knowledge, treading upon wrong paths, and regarding their ignorance as knowledge.
Possessed of egoism and self-conceit, consisting of twenty-eight types,
they are all internally luminous and yet mutually veiled.
Considering even that to be ineffective, another arose from him as he meditated;
this third was the "Upstream-flowing" (ūrdhvasrotas), who moved upward with a predominance of sattva.
Abounding in happiness and joy, they are unobstructed both internally and externally;
being luminous within and without, they are known as those whose stream flows upward.
The third, however, is known as the divine creation (deva-sarga), which consists of contentment;
when that creation was completed, there arose such delight for Brahmā.
Then, having realized that those born from the primary creation and the others were unsuccessful, he then meditated upon another, supreme creation consisting of successful beings.
As he was thus meditating with true intent, there then emerged from that unmanifest state the "downward-streaming" (arvāksrotas) being who accomplishes [the world].
Because they turned back from that point, they are called *arvāk-srotasaḥ* (those with downward currents);
they abound in light, yet are dominated by darkness and characterized by an excess of passion (*rajas*).
Therefore, those men who repeatedly perform [actions] are full of suffering;
they are manifest both outwardly and inwardly, yet they are the ones who achieve success.
The fifth [section], the Anugraha-sarga, is established as fourfold.
And likewise by the opposite of these, by incapacity, by accomplishment, and by contentment.
Furthermore, all indeed know that which has ceased as well as that which is present.
That is called the sixth creation, consisting of the primary elements and the beings derived from them.
Those who possess wives are always intent on sharing their possessions during the creation of progeny.
They are to be known as wrathful and ill-behaved, beginning with Bhūta.
Thus, O best of sages, these six creations have been described here;
among them, the first is to be known as the creation of Mahat, which is indeed that of Brahmā.
The second creation is that of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which is known as the elemental creation (bhūtasarga);
the third is the creation of the sense organs (vaikārika), which is known as the sensory creation (aindriyaka).
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen preceded by intelligence;
the fourth, however, is the principal creation (mukhya-sarga), for the immovable beings are known as the principal ones.
That which is declared as the fifth is called the animal creation;
thereafter, the sixth is known as the divine creation of those whose stream flows upward.
Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which is the human race.
The eighth is the Anugraha creation, which is both characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and darkness (tāmasa).
These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations, while three are remembered as the primary (prākṛta) ones.
The Prākṛta, the Vaikṛta, and the Kaumāra is recorded as the ninth;
these indeed are declared to be the nine creations of Prajāpati.
The primary and secondary elements are indeed the root causes of the world for the Lord of the World as he creates it; what else do you wish to hear?
Maitreya said: O Sage, you have described the creation of the gods and others in brief;
O best of the foremost sages, I wish to hear it from you in detail.
Parāśara said: Impelled by their previous virtuous and non-virtuous actions,
and not yet liberated from that manifestation, they are withdrawn even during the dissolution of the world.
O Brahmā, these fourfold classes of beings, beginning with the gods and ending with the immobile,
were born as mental offspring from Brahmā while he was performing the act of creation.
Then, desiring to create the fourfold [beings]— gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans— he joined his own self to these waters.
From Prajāpati, whose self was disciplined, the quality of darkness (tamas) became predominant;
first, from his hindquarters, the Asuras were born as he desired to create.
Then he cast off that body which consisted of the quality of darkness (tamas);
once abandoned by him, O Maitreya, it became the night.
Desiring to create while residing in another body, he then experienced joy;
from his mouth, O twice-born one, the gods were born, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva).
He also abandoned that body, and the day became filled with *sattva*;
for the Asuras are strong at night, while the gods are strong by day.
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of *sattva*;
as he regarded it as his father, his ancestors were born from him.
Having created the ancestors, that Lord then emitted her as well;
once emitted, she became the twilight (saṃdhyā), situated between day and night.
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas;
from that, O best of the twice-born, human beings were born, characterized by the predominance of rajas alone.
The Lord of Creatures also quickly abandoned that body;
it immediately became the moonlight, which is designated as the morning twilight.
O Maitreya, at the arrival of the moonlight humans are strong, and likewise the ancestors; therefore, these two indeed become powerful during the time of twilight.
Moonlight, night, day, and twilight— these four, O Lord,
are indeed the bodies of Brahmā, which rest upon the three guṇas.
Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas;
from that, hunger arose in Brahmā, and from that, anger was born.
Then the Lord, the Master, created beings emaciated by hunger in the darkness;
they were born deformed and bearded, and they rushed toward that Master.
"Do not do so, sir; let him be protected. Those who said this were called *rākṣasas*.
Others said, "We shall devour him" (*khādāma*), and they were the *yakṣas* because of their act of eating (*jakṣaṇāt*).
Then, seeing those [strands] were unpleasant, the hairs of the Creator fell away;
yet, once fallen from the head, they grew back again upon that same head.

Because they slithered (sarpaṇāt), they became serpents (sarpāḥ); because they were deficient (hīnatvāt), they are known as *ahayaḥ*. Then the Creator of the World, becoming enraged, produced from his anger fierce beings of tawny complexion who subsisted on flesh.
O twice-born one, from the very limb of him as he was meditating, the Gandharvas were produced at that moment;
they were born drinking his speech, and for that reason they are called Gandharvas.
Having created these, the Lord Brahmā, impelled by His power,
then created other birds from his own will.
From his chest Prajāpati created the sheep,
from his mouth he created goats, and from his belly and his two sides he created cows.
And from his two feet [he created] horses along with elephants, donkeys, gayals, deer,
camels, mules, antelopes, and other species.
O best of the twice-born, at the beginning of the Kalpa, at the dawn of the Tretā Yuga, Brahmā produced herbs with fruits and roots from his body hairs;
having duly created the animals and the herbs, he then employed them in the sacrifice.
The cow, the goat, the man, the sheep, the horse, the mule, and the donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn from me those that are wild.
Beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth;
aquatic creatures are the sixth class of animals, while reptiles are the seventh.
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī, the Ṛg-verses, the Trivṛt-sāman, the Rathantara, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his southern mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteenfold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and likewise the Uktha.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman hymns, the Jagatī meter, the seventeen-fold Stoma, the Vairūpa chant, and the Atirātra sacrifice.
Then, from his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmaṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Vairāja.
Having created the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans, Prajāpati produced from his limbs various beings, both high and low.
Then, at the beginning of that kalpa, the Grandfather (Brahmā) again created Yakṣas,
Piśācas, Gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases.
He is the nārakīs, kiṃnaras, and rākṣasas; birds, cattle, wild animals, and serpents; that which is imperishable and that which is perishable—indeed, all this that is stationary and moving.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the original creator and the all-pervading one, emitted that [universe]. Whatever actions those beings had performed in a previous creation,
those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are created anew.

Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—impregnated by these, beings enter [into new births]; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which corresponds to their own nature.
That Lord himself, the Creator, thus emitted the diversity and the specific functions of the senses, their objects, the elements, and the bodies.
In the beginning, he fashioned from the very words of the Veda the names and forms of all beings, as well as the expansion of their activities, for the gods and others.
He established the names of all the sages according to what was heard in the Vedas, assigning them each titles appropriate to their respective duties.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle,
so too do those very same things reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas.
Endowed with the power of the desire to create and impelled by the power of that which is to be created, he repeatedly brings about such a creation at the beginning of every kalpa.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
You have described that which is the downward-flowing stream, namely the human race.
O Brahman, tell me in detail how Brahmā created him.
O great sage, please tell us how he created the social classes (varṇas) and what their qualities were,
as well as what the traditional duties of the Brahmins and the others are said to be.
Parāśara said:
O best of the twice-born, when Brahmā, intent on truth, first desired to create the world, beings abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva) were born from his mouth.
From his chest, others arose from Brahmā who were intensified by *rajas*;
likewise, from his thighs, there were those intensified by both *rajas* and *tamas*.
O best of the twice-born, Brahmā created other beings from his feet;
all of them were dominated by tamas, and from them this system of four varnas arose.
O best of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras emerged from his feet,
thighs, chest, and mouth respectively.
O highly fortunate one, Brahmā indeed created all this— the fourfold varṇa system— for the accomplishment of sacrifice, as the supreme means for performing sacrifice.
O knower of dharma, the gods, nourished by sacrifices, nourish living beings through the release of rain; thus sacrifices are the cause of all prosperity.
They are brought forth by those men who are always devoted to their own duties,
who are endowed with pure conduct, who are virtuous, and who walk upon the path of the righteous.
O Sage, O twice-born one, through human birth men attain both heaven and liberation; or rather, they go to whatever state they desire.
O best of sages, those subjects created by Brahmā were established in the system of the four castes,
possessing perfect faith and being devoted to right conduct.
Delighting in their dwellings according to their desire, free from all afflictions,
pure in their inner selves, they were purified and stainless in all their observances.
And when their minds are purified and Hari is established within them,
they perceive pure knowledge called Viṣṇu, by which that supreme state is attained.
Then, that portion of Hari which consists of Time (Kāla) is said to cast off terrible sin, even when it is very slight and possesses extremely little substance.
O Maitreya, among those creatures, the seed of unrighteousness arose— born of darkness and greed— which consists of passion and other such qualities that lead to failure.
Consequently, that innate perfection (sahajā siddhi) does not arise excessively for them;
rather, there are the other eight perfections, such as the exhilaration of rasa (rasollāsa) and so forth.
When those [virtues] have perished without remainder and sin is increasing,
the people then become afflicted by the suffering of being overwhelmed by the pairs of opposites (dvandva).
Then they constructed fortresses— those situated in trees, on mountains, and in water—
as well as artificial fortifications such as cities, villages, and hamlets.
And they constructed houses in those cities and other places according to the rules,
O high-minded one, for the sake of alleviating the afflictions of cold, heat, and the like.
Having provided this remedy for the cold and other afflictions,
those subjects then established the means of livelihood and manual labor born of action.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet, sesame, the noble *priyaṅgu*, *koradūṣa*, and *satīnaka* [beans]. (ViP 1.6.21)
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, niṣpāvas, along with kulatthas,
āḍhakīs, caṇakas, and śaṇas— these are recorded as the seventeen [types of pulses].
Thus, O Sage, these are the species of cultivated plants;
these fourteen plants are both fit for sacrifice and belong to the cultivated and wild varieties.
Rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, and *priyaṅgu* as the seventh—these are the grains; the eighth, however, is the *kulattha* pulse.
Furthermore, O Sage, śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, gavedhuka,
as well as veṇuyava and likewise markaṭaka are prescribed [as food].
These fourteen medicinal herbs are indeed known as both cultivated and wild;
they exist for the accomplishment of sacrifice, and sacrifice is likewise their supreme cause.
These, together with sacrifice, are the supreme cause of all creatures;
therefore, the wise who know the higher and the lower perform sacrifices.
O best of sages, the daily performance of sacrifices is beneficial for men; it brings about the pacification of the sins being committed.
But those in whose minds, O Great-minded One, that drop of evil produced by Time increased, they set their minds not upon sacrifices.
Thus, they censured all the declarations of the Vedas, the Vedas themselves, and whatever sacrificial rites and so forth there were; they acted as obstructors of sacrifice.
They became destroyers of the path of worldly activity,
revilers of the Vedas, evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and crooked in their intentions.
Once the means of subsistence were fully established, Prajāpati, having created living beings,
fixed the boundaries according to their respective places and qualities.
O best of the upholders of dharma, [tell me] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life,
as well as the worlds attained by those of all classes who correctly observe their duties.
The station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who perform their duties;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not retreat in battles.
The realm of the Maruts is for Vaiśyas whose souls are devoted to their own duties;
the realm of the Gandharvas is for those of the Śūdra caste who follow the path of service.
It is recorded that there are eighty-eight thousand sages who have drawn up their vital energy; the very same abode that belongs to them belongs also to those who dwell with their preceptor.
That which is remembered as the abode of the Seven Sages is indeed for forest-dwellers;
that of Prajāpati is for householders, and that of Brahmā is remembered for renunciants.
The immortal abode of the yogins is that which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
For those yogins who are single-mindedly devoted and constantly meditate upon Brahman,
that supreme abode belongs to them which the wise indeed behold.
The planets, such as the sun and the moon, return again and again;
yet those who meditate upon the twelve-syllable mantra do not return even to this day.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the terrible Asipatravana, Kālasūtra, and Avīci.
This place is declared to be for those who revile the Veda, those who obstruct sacrifices, and those who abandon their own dharma.
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Then, as he was meditating, mental offspring were born to him.
Together with those effects and instruments produced from that body,
the individual knowers (kṣetrajñas) emerged from the limbs of that wise one.
All those whom I previously mentioned—
the gods and others down to the stationary beings— were gathered together, remaining within the sphere of the three qualities (guṇas).
In this manner, all beings were created, both the moving and the stationary.
When all those offspring of that wise one did not multiply,
he then created other mental sons who were similar to himself.
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras,
as well as Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha— these were his mind-born sons.
"These are the nine Brahmās," such is the certainty established in the Purāṇa.
Khyāti, Bhūti, Sambhūti, Kṣamā, and likewise Prīti. (B2, D3, 4, T, G2, 3, M0, ed. Veṅk. insert hereafter.
Likewise humility, as well as vigor, and similarly freedom from envy.
And having then created their progeny, he bestowed it upon those great-souled ones.
Having said, "Become wives," he gave them to those very [sages].
And those such as Sanandana and others who were previously created by the Creator did not become attached to the worlds, for they were indifferent toward progeny.
All of them had acquired spiritual knowledge, were free from passion, and devoid of envy; yet,
while they remained thus indifferent toward the creation of the world,
a great wrath arose within the high-souled Brahmā, capable of consuming the three worlds.
O Sage, at that time, the entire triple world, blazing with garlands of flames arising from his wrath, became [the form] of Brahmā.
Then, from his forehead, which was furrowed with a frown and inflamed by anger,
Rudra emerged, possessing a brilliance equal to the midday sun;
he had a body that was half-female and half-male, fierce and of immense stature.
Having said, "Divide yourself," Brahmā then vanished from that place.
Thus addressed, he divided himself into two parts— femininity and masculinity—
and he further split that masculinity into ten parts and one part.
That Lord, the God, divided womanhood in many ways through forms that were gentle or harsh, peaceful or unpeaceful, and dark or fair.
Then, O twice-born one, the Lord first made himself into the Svāyambhuva Manu, born from Brahmā, for the purpose of procreation.
And the all-pervading god Svāyambhuva Manu took that woman Śatarūpā, whose sins had been shaken off by ascetic penance, as his wife.

And from that Puruṣa, O knower of dharma, the goddess Śatarūpā gave birth to Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, as well as two daughters named Prasūti and Ākūti, who were endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility.
In ancient times, the Lord of Creatures gave Prasūti to Dakṣa and Ākūti to Ruci; he accepted them as wives, and from that couple was born their son Yajña,
along with a daughter, O fortunate one— thus a pair of twins was born from the husband and wife.
From the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the sacrifice, twelve sons were born;
they are known as the Yāma gods among the deities in the period of Svāyambhuva Manu.
And at her birth, O Dakṣa, he likewise begot twenty-four daughters; hear from me their names correctly.
Faith, Fortune, Fortitude, Contentment, Nourishment, Intelligence, Action, as well as Wisdom, Modesty, Form, Peace, Success, and Fame as the thirteenth. (ViP 1.7.20)
The lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives;
from among them, eleven younger, beautiful-eyed sisters remained.
Khyāti, Satī, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, as well as Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and Svadhā.
Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and likewise the sage Aṅgiras;
Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu, that best of ṛṣis.
O best of sages, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Vahni, and the Pitṛs respectively took Khyāti and the other daughters as wives.
Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; Dhṛti gave birth to Darpam (Pride) from Niyama;
Tuṣṭi gave birth to Saṃtoṣa; and Puṣṭi gave birth to Lobha (Greed).
Medhā gave birth to Śruta, Kriyā, Daṇḍa, Naya, Vinaya,
Bodha, Buddhi, Lajjā, Vinaya, Vapus, Ātmaja,
Vyavasāya, and indeed Kṣema; while Śānti gave birth to these.
Happiness, success, glory, and fame—these are the sons of Dharma;
from Kāma she gave birth to Rati, who bore him a son, Harṣa, the grandson of Dharma.
Violence was the wife of Adharma; from those two were born Untruth and the daughter Nikṛti, as well as Fear and Hell.
Māyā and Vedanā indeed formed a pair;
from those two, Māyā then gave birth to Mṛtyu, the destroyer of beings.
Then from Raurava, Vedanā gave birth to her own son, Duḥkha;
and from Mṛtyu were born Vyādhi, Jarā, Śoka, Tṛṣṇā, and Krodha.
For all these are remembered as having suffering as their highest end and are characterized by unrighteousness;
they have neither wives nor sons, for they are all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
O son of the best of sages, these forms of Viṣṇu are indeed fierce;
they truly become the cause of the constant dissolution of this world.
Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Bhṛgu, and the other lords of progeny,
O highly fortunate one, are the constant causes of creation in this world.
The Manus, the sons of Manu, and those kings who possess valor—
being heroes devoted to the path of the righteous— they are the perpetual upholders of the world's stability.
Maitreya said: O Brahman, please tell me the true nature of that which is described as eternal persistence, eternal creation, and likewise eternal non-existence regarding those things.
Parāśara said: The Lord Madhusūdana, the all-pervading one whose nature is inconceivable, effects creation, maintenance, and destruction through those various forms, unimpededly.
O twice-born one, this dissolution of all beings is fourfold: occasional, elemental, ultimate, and constant.
Among these, the occasional dissolution is the Brāhma, wherein the Lord of the universe lies asleep;
and during the elemental dissolution, the cosmic egg itself goes to dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti).
Through knowledge of the Supreme Self, the yogi is said to have attained the absolute [state],
wherein the constant destruction of all beings that occurs day and night is forever ceased.
That which is the manifestation of primordial nature (prakṛti) is known as the natural creation (prākṛta-sṛṣṭi);
likewise, that which occurs after the intermediate dissolution is called the daily creation (dainandinī).
O best of sages, that place where beings are born every day is called the "eternal creation" (nityasarga) by those expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas.
Thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the creator of beings, abiding within all bodies, performs their creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Maitreya, the powers of creation, maintenance, and destruction belonging to Viṣṇu perpetually revolve day and night within all embodied beings.
For this great triad of powers, O Brahmin, consists of the three qualities (guṇas);
he who transcends it indeed goes to the Supreme and does not return again.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O great sage, the Tāmasa creation of Brahmā has been described to you.
I shall proclaim the creation of Rudra; listen to me as I speak it.
Then, at the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord meditated upon a son equal to himself,
a youth named Nīlalohita appeared on his lap.
O best of the twice-born, as he was weeping with a melodious voice and running about, Brahmā spoke to him as he cried: "Why do you weep?"
Then Prajāpati replied to him, "Give me a name," and said, "O God, you shall be named Rudra; do not weep, maintain your composure.
Though addressed in this way, he wept seven times more.
Then that Lord, the All-pervading One, gave him seven other names,
as well as the stations for these eight, their wives, and their sons.
O twice-born one, the Grandfather then spoke to Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, as well as Paśupati, Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva.
Then he gave them these names and established their respective abodes:
the Sun, Water, Earth, Wind, Fire, Space, the Initiated Brāhmaṇa, and Soma; these are his forms in sequence.
Likewise Suvarcalā, Uṣā, Vikeśī, and another Śivā; and Svāhā, Diś, Dīkṣā, and Rohiṇī, in their respective order.
O best of men, O illustrious one, the wives of Sūrya and the others are recorded along with their names, beginning with Rudra; now hear from me about their offspring.
By their offspring and descendants, this entire world has been filled.
Śanaiścara, Śukra, Lohitāṅga, Manojava,
Skanda, Svarga, Santāna, and Budha were their sons in due order.
Rudra, being of such a nature, obtained Satī as his wife;
however, due to Dakṣa’s wrath, that Satī abandoned her own body.
He married the daughter of Dakṣa himself, the Prajāpati. (D3,5,G3,M0, ed. Veṅk. ins.)
O best of the twice-born, she became the daughter of Himavat through Menā;
and the blessed Lord Bhava again married Umā, who was devoted to no other.
Khyāti gave birth to the two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ from Bhṛgu,
as well as Śrī, who is the consort of Nārāyaṇa, the god of gods.
Maitreya said:
It is heard that Śrī was born from the ocean of milk during the churning for the nectar of immortality;
how is it that you say she was born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti?
Parāśara said:
This Śrī, the mother of the world, is eternal and inseparable from Viṣṇu;
O best of the twice-born, as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too is she.
Viṣṇu is wealth and this is speech; Hari is policy and this is conduct;
Viṣṇu is awakening and this is intellect; He is dharma and this is virtuous action.
Viṣṇu is the creator and this creation is Śrī; the earth is Bhūmi and Hari is the mountain;
the Lord is contentment and Lakṣmī is eternal satisfaction, O Maitreya.
Desire is Śrī, the Blessed One is Kāma, he is the sacrifice, and she is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
that goddess is the oblation of clarified butter, and Janārdana is the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
O Sage, Lakṣmī is the wife’s chamber (patnīśālā), and Madhusūdana is the fore-chamber (prāgvaṃśa);
Cit (Consciousness) is Lakṣmī, Hari is the sacrificial post (yūpa), Śrī is the fuel (idhmā), and the Blessed One is the kuśa grass.
The Lord is the essence of the Sāman chants; the Udgītha is Kamalālayā;
Svāhā is Lakṣmī; and Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, is the sacrificial fire.
O best of the twice-born, Maitreya, the Lord Śaṅkara is Śauri, Gaurī is Lakṣmī, Keśava is the Sun, and his radiance is Kamalālayā.
Viṣṇu is the host of ancestors; Padmā is the eternal Svadhā who bestows nourishment;
Dyauḥ is Śrī; and Viṣṇu, the soul of all, is the exceedingly vast space.
Śaśāṅka, Śrīdhara, Kānti, and Śrī are his inseparable attendants; Hari is Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, the activity of the world, and the all-pervading wind.
O twice-born one of great intelligence, Govinda is the ocean; Śrī is his shore;
Indrāṇī is the very form of Lakṣmī; and Madhusūdana is the Lord of the Gods.
Yama was the wielder of the discus in person, and Dhūmorṇā was Kamalālayā;
Ṛddhi was Śrī, and the god Dhaneśvara himself was Śrīdhara.
Gaurī is Lakṣmī, the highly fortunate one; Keśava is Varuṇa himself;
Śrī is Devasenā, O best of Brahmins, and Hari is the commander of Devasenā.
O best of the twice-born, Avaṣṭambha was Gadāpāṇi, Śakti was Lakṣmī,
Kāṣṭhā was Lakṣmī, Nimeṣa was he, Muhūrta was she, and Kalā was she.
The moonlight is Lakṣmī, and that lamp is Hari, the Lord of all;
Śrī, the mother of the world, has become the creeper, while Viṣṇu is established as the tree.
The night is Śrī, and the day is the god who bears the discus and mace;
Viṣṇu is the bridegroom who grants boons, and the lotus-pond-dweller is the bride.
The Blessed Lord is the embodiment of the Nanda [mountain], while Śrī is established in the form of the river;
the lotus-eyed Puṇḍarīkākṣa is the banner, and Kamalālayā is the pennant.
Thirst is Lakṣmī, and greed is the supreme Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the worlds;
O knower of dharma, passion and desire are Lakṣmī, and Govinda himself is greed.
What is the use of saying much more here? This is stated in brief.
Among gods, animals, and humans, O Maitreya, the Lord Hari exists in whatever bears a male name, and Lakṣmī exists in whatever bears a female name; there is nothing beyond these two.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Listen further to this, Maitreya, concerning that which I have been asked by you here.
I too have heard this account concerning Śrī from Marīci.
Durvāsas, an emanation of Śaṅkara, was wandering this earth;
that seer beheld a divine garland in the hand of a Vidyādharī.
O Brahmin, because its entirety was perfumed by the fragrance of *saṃtānaka* trees, that forest became exceedingly pleasant for those who roam the woods.
Then that brahmin, observing the vow of a madman, seeing that beautiful garland,
asked for it from the lovely-limbed wife of the Vidyādhara.
Requested by him, that slender-limbed and large-eyed Vidyādhara woman respectfully prostrated before him and gave him a garland.
Taking that garland and placing it upon his own head, O Maitreya, that brahmin, assuming the appearance of a madman, wandered over the earth.
He beheld the god who is the sovereign of the three worlds, the husband of Śacī, approaching together with the deities, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, though appearing like one intoxicated.
Taking that garland from his own head, which was frequented by intoxicated bees,
the sage cast it toward the king of the immortals like one who has lost his senses.
Having taken the garland, the king of the gods placed it upon the head of Airāvata;
it shone like the Gaṅgā upon the peak of Kailāsa.
With his eyes blinded by intoxication, that elephant, drawn by the scent,
sniffed the garland with his trunk and threw it onto the surface of the earth.
Then the blessed Durvāsas, the best of sages, became enraged;
O Maitreya, being angry, he spoke thus to the king of the gods.
Durvāsas said:
O Vāsava, your soul is corrupted by the intoxication of power; you are exceedingly arrogant, since you do not welcome this garland given by me, which is the very abode of prosperity.
"You did not say 'I am pleased' preceded by a prostration,
nor was it accepted with a head bowed and cheeks blooming with joy."
"O fool, because you do not hold in high regard this garland given by me, the splendor of the three worlds shall therefore meet its destruction."
"O Śakra, you surely consider me to be equal to other brahmins;
therefore, you, being proud, have shown us this contempt."
"Since the garland given by me has been cast upon the ground by you,
therefore the three worlds shall be deprived of their prosperity."
When he has become enraged, all that moves and is stationary comes to fear;
yet you, O King of the Gods, out of excessive pride, treat me with contempt.
Parāśara said:
Having descended from the shoulder of his elephant with great haste,
Mahendra sought to propitiate the stainless sage Durvāsas.
Being thus propitiated with prostrations,
Durvāsas, the best of sages, then replied to the thousand-eyed Indra.
Durvāsas said:
"I am not compassionate of heart, nor does forbearance dwell within me;
those others are sages, O Śakra, but know me to be Durvāsas."
"You have been made to feel vain pride in vain by Gautama and others;
know me to be Durvāsas, whose entire essence consists of impatience."
"Because you have become so arrogant while Vasiṣṭha and others, whose essence is compassion, were loudly chanting hymns of praise, that you now treat even me with such contempt."
Having beheld my face— with its mass of flaming matted hair and frowning, crooked brows— who in the three worlds has not succumbed to fear?
O Śatakratu, why say more? I shall not forgive this further mockery of yours, though it is couched in conciliation.
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, the sage departed; and the king of the gods, having mounted Airāvata, likewise returned to Amarāvatī.
From that time forward, O Maitreya, the three worlds, including Śakra, became bereft of splendor, fallen into ruin, and their medicinal herbs and creepers were utterly exhausted.
Sacrifices were no longer performed, ascetics did not practice austerities,
and at that time, people set their minds upon the duties of charity and other such virtues no more.
O best of the twice-born, all people became devoid of strength; their senses were afflicted by greed and other passions, so that they felt desire even for the most trivial things.
Where there is courage, there is prosperity; and courage follows from success.
For those devoid of prosperity, whence can there be courage? And without that, whence can there be virtues?
Without virtues, men lack strength and valor;
one who is devoid of strength and valor is disregarded by everyone.
A man who has been surpassed becomes notorious for his ruined intellect.
Thus, in the three worlds that were utterly devoid of splendor and bereft of living beings,
the Daityas and Dānavas made preparations for war against the gods.
Then the Daityas, overcome by greed, shorn of splendor, and devoid of courage,
waged war against the gods who were likewise bereft of fortune and lacking in strength.
The thirty gods, led by Indra, having been defeated by the Daityas, went for refuge to the illustrious Grandfather (Brahmā), preceded by Agni.
When this had been related by the gods exactly as it was, Brahmā then said to the deities:
"Go for refuge to the Lord of the high and the low, the subduer of the Asuras."
He is the causeless cause of arising, persistence, and destruction;
he is the Lord, the Master of Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, the infinite and unconquered.
May that Viṣṇu, the cause of the unmanifest Pradhāna and the unproduced Puruṣa who have become the effect, and the remover of the distress of those who bow to him, bestow welfare upon you all.
Parāśara said: Having thus addressed all the gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk accompanied by them.
Having gone there, the Grandfather, joined by all the gods of the thirty-three,
praised Hari, the Lord of the high and the low, with pleasing words.
Brahmā said:
I bow to the All, the Lord of all, the infinite, unborn, and imperishable;
the support of the earth that is the abode of the worlds, unmanifest and indivisible.
Nārāyaṇa is the most minute of all that is minute,
and the most venerable of all that is venerable, including the earth and the other elements.
In whom all exists, from whom all has arisen with me as its precursor;
he who is the god of all beings, and who is higher than even the highest.
He who is beyond the supreme Puruṣa, who bears the nature of the Supreme Self,
and who is meditated upon by yogis seeking liberation for the sake of release— [that is he].
May that primordial Person, who is pure and superior to all that is pure, be gracious— he in whom the primal qualities such as *sattva* and the rest do not exist.
May that Hari be gracious to us— he whose power, though pure, is not within the scope of time, measured by units such as *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *nimeṣa*.
May that Viṣṇu, who is the Supreme Lord, though pure, yet spoken of by way of metaphorical designation, and who is the Self of all embodied beings, be gracious unto us.
May that Hari be gracious to us— he who is both cause and effect, the cause of the cause, and the effect of the effect.
I bow down to him who is himself the effect of that which is the effect of the effect of the effect, and who is the cause of the cause of the cause of that very effect.
I bow down to that Lord of the Gods, who is the cause of even the cause, the cause of the cause of that [cause], and the ultimate source of all those causes.
I bow down to that supreme state, which is the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, the creator and the created, and whose nature is both the effect and the agent.
That which is like pure awakening, eternal, unborn, imperishable, undecaying,
unmanifest, and changeless— that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
I perpetually bow to that stainless, supreme state of Viṣṇu, which is neither gross nor subtle, and which is not within the range of any qualifying attribute.
I bow to that imperishable one, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, in a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth fraction of whom this power of the universe resides.
Neither the gods, nor the sages, nor I, nor even Śaṅkara know that supreme station of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
That which yogis, ever-striving for the destruction of merit and demerit,
perceive within the *praṇava* as the object of contemplation— that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
That supreme state of Viṣṇu belongs to that God who was never before born, and whose powers consist of the natures of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Lord of all, O Self of all beings, O All, O Acyuta who is the refuge of all!
Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, and come within the range of our vision, for the sake of your devotees.
Parāśara said:
Having heard what was thus spoken by Brahmā, the thirty gods then bowed and said, "Be gracious! Let us come within the range of your sight."
O Acyuta, who pervades all, we bow to you, the abode of the universe, that supreme state which even this Lord Brahmā does not know.
At the conclusion of those words of the gods and of Brahmā,
all the celestial sages, led by Bṛhaspati, spoke as follows.

We bow to that one who is the primordial sacrifice, the man to be praised, and the first-born of even the ancients; we bow to the creator of the creator of the world, who is without any distinguishing attributes.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, imperishable one who bears the form of sacrifice, be gracious;
grant your vision to all of us who have bowed before you.
This is Brahmā, and likewise this three-eyed one is with the Rudras;
Pūṣan is here together with all the Ādityas, and this is Pāvaka along with the Agnis.
The Aśvins, these Vasus, and all these hosts of Maruts, as well as the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and this lordly Indra; ViP_1,9.63 //
"O Lord, defeated by the army of the Daityas, all the hosts of deities, intent on prostration, have come to you for refuge."
Parāśara said:
Thus being praised, O Maitreya, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord who bears the conch and the discus, appeared before their very eyes.
Then, seeing him bearing the conch, discus, and mace, possessing an unprecedented form and stature, a powerful mass of splendors, those gods—
Having first bowed down with their eyes fixed and motionless due to agitation,
those led by the Grandfather (Brahmā) praised the lotus-eyed Lord.
The gods said:
Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of the Universe! You are Brahmā; you are the wielder of the Pināka bow;
you are Indra, Agni, Pavana, Varuṇa, Savitṛ, and Yama.
The Vasus, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of the Viśvedevas—you are they all.
O Lord, this host of deities who has come into your presence is none other than you yourself,
for you are the creator of the world and are omnipresent.

You are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and you are Prajāpati; O Soul of All, you are the knower and that which is to be known, and the entire universe is composed of you.
"O Viṣṇu, we have come to you for refuge, afflicted and defeated by the Daityas; be gracious, O Soul of All, and invigorate us with your splendor."
So long does there exist affliction, as well as longing, delusion, and unhappiness,
as one does not come for refuge to you, the destroyer of all sins.
O you of serene soul, grant your grace to us who have sought refuge in you;
O Lord of all splendors, nourish us with your own power.
Parāśara said:
Thus being praised by the immortals who bowed before him, the blessed Lord Hari,
the creator of the universe, looked upon them with a gracious gaze and spoke these words.
The Blessed One said:
"O gods, I shall provide an augmentation of your splendor.
O deities, listen to what I say; let this be done by you."

"Having brought all the medicinal herbs together with the Daityas to the Ocean of Milk, and having made Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope, let the nectar be churned, O gods, while I stand as your helper. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9.76)
And you Daityas, having first employed conciliation, shall be addressed thus regarding the act of assistance: "You shall be sharers in the common fruit."
And when that ocean is being churned, whatever nectar (amṛta) arises there,
by drinking it you shall become strong and immortal.
