And so I shall act for you in such a way that the gods, the enemies of the thirty [gods], shall not obtain the nectar, but shall experience only affliction.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, all the deities then entered into an alliance with the Asuras and exerted themselves for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Having gathered various medicinal herbs, the gods, Daityas,
and Dānavas cast them into the waters of the Ocean of Milk, which possessed the pure luster of an autumnal cloud.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
O Maitreya, they then began to churn for the nectar of immortality with great speed.
All the gods were stationed together where the tail was;
O Daityas, Kṛṣṇa placed them in the front part of Vāsuki’s body.
O you of immeasurable luster, all those Asuras, their radiance destroyed by the fire of his hood's breath, became devoid of splendor.
By that very wind from his breath,
which dispelled the clouds and rained down upon the region of his tail, the gods were then restored.
O great sage, in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord Hari himself, in the form of a tortoise,
became the support for Mount Mandara as it was being whirled around.
In another form, the wielder of the discus and mace dragged the king of the Nāgas from among the gods, and in yet another form, he did so from among the Daityas.
O Maitreya, Keśava ascended the mountain in a massive form such that he could not be seen by the gods or the asuras.
The Lord Hari invigorated the king of serpents with his splendor,
and the omnipresent one strengthened the gods with another splendor.
Then, as that ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and the dānavas,
Surabhi, the source of sacrificial offerings and honored by the gods, first emerged.
Then, O great sage, the gods and the Dānavas attained joy;
yet their minds became distracted, and they stood with fixed gazes.
Then, as the Siddhas in heaven were wondering what this could be,
the goddess Vāruṇī appeared, her eyes rolling with intoxication.
Then, from that churned Ocean of Milk which was nourishing the world,
there arose the Pārijāta tree, a delight to the wives of the gods, by its fragrance.
Then, O Maitreya, a most wonderful host of Apsarases, endowed with the quality of magnificent beauty, emerged from the Ocean of Milk.
Then the moon arose, and Maheśvara took it;
and the serpents took the poison produced from the Ocean of Milk.
Then the god Dhanvantari himself arose, wearing white garments and carrying a water-pot filled with nectar.
Then, O Maitreya, all those Daityas and Dānavas, together with the sages, immediately became joyful and composed in mind.
Then the goddess Śrī, radiant with splendor, emerged from those waters, standing upon a blossoming lotus and holding a lotus in her hand.
Filled with joy, the great seers praised her with the Śrīsūkta.
O Brahmin, the Gandharvas, headed by Viśvāvasu, sang before her, while the hosts of Apsarases, led by Ghṛtācī, danced.
The rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, approached for the purpose of bathing her; the elephants of the quarters, having taken pure water held in golden vessels,
bathed the Goddess, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds.
The Ocean of Milk, assuming a physical form, gave her a garland of unfading lotuses,
and Viśvakarman fashioned ornaments for her body.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, bathed and adorned with ornaments,
she went to the chest of Hari while all the gods looked on.
Then, O Maitreya, the gods beheld Lakṣmī stationed upon the chest of Hari and suddenly attained supreme bliss.
O highly fortunate one, the Daityas, led by Vipracitti, turned their backs on Viṣṇu and fell into the utmost distress,
abandoned by Lakṣmī.
Then those Daityas of great prowess seized the water-pot held in the hand of Dhanvantari, wherein that nectar for the twice-born resided.
Having deluded them with his illusory power (māyā), the all-pervading Viṣṇu assumed a female form;
taking that [nectar] from the Dānavas, he bestowed it upon the gods.
Then the hosts of gods, led by Śakra, drank that nectar;
meanwhile, the Daityas, with weapons and swords raised, rushed toward them.
Then, while the nectar was being drunk by the powerful gods, the army of the Daityas,
being slaughtered, fled in all directions and indeed entered the netherworld (pātāla).
Then the gods, filled with joy, prostrated before the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
and governed that triple heaven as they had done before.
When that god of gods had departed, [he went to] Hari, the Lord of Vāsudeva.
They praised Hari, the lotus-eyed one, who had become invisible.
Then, O best of sages, the sun, its radiance restored, proceeded along its own path, and the luminaries likewise moved according to their respective courses.
The blessed Lord Vibhāvasu blazed forth with intense and beautiful radiance,
and at that time, the minds of all beings were turned toward dharma.
O best of the twice-born, the three worlds became endowed with splendor once more,
and Śakra, the foremost of the thirty gods, was restored to his glory.
Having returned to the third heaven and seated upon his throne, Śakra,
established in the sovereignty of the gods, then praised the goddess who holds a lotus in her hand.
O Hari, let this [earth] not again be subject to the fall of Durvāsas’s curse.
And with the intention that it was true, he praised Śrī from his very core.
Indra said:
I pay homage to the mother of all the worlds,
the lotus-born Śrī, whose eyes are like blooming lotuses, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
B2, D3, 5, T1, 2, G3, M0, ed. Veṅk. insert:
[She who] has her abode in the lotus, holds a lotus in her hand, and has eyes resembling lotus petals.
I salute the goddess Padmāsyā, the beloved of Padmanābha.
You are accomplishment; you are *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and the nectar of immortality (*sudhā*); you are the purifier of the worlds.
You are the twilight, the night, radiance, prosperity, intelligence, faith, and Sarasvatī.
O beautiful goddess, you are the science of sacrifice, the great science, the secret science, and the science of the self; you are the bestower of the fruit of liberation.
Logic, the three Vedas, commerce, and the science of government—you alone are these.
O Goddess, this world is filled by you with both gentle and fierce forms.
O Goddess, who else but you could occupy this body of the God of gods, which consists of all sacrifices, is conceivable only by yogis, and belongs to the wielder of the mace?
O Goddess, the entire triple world was abandoned by you and had become almost ruined; it has now been restored to prosperity by you.
O highly fortunate lady, for men, wives, sons, home, friends, grain, wealth, and so forth, all these become eternal through the sight of you.
O Goddess, physical health, sovereignty, the destruction of the enemy faction, and happiness are not difficult to obtain for those men who have been beheld by your glance.
You are the mother of all beings, and Hari, the god of gods, is the father;
by you and by Viṣṇu, O Mother, this entire world of moving and unmoving things is pervaded.
O purifier of all, do not abandon our treasury, nor our cow-pen, nor our home, nor our belongings, nor our bodies, nor our wives.
O you who dwell upon the chest of my god Viṣṇu, do not abandon your sons, nor your circle of friends, nor your cattle, nor your ornaments.
O stainless one, those men who have been abandoned by you are instantly forsaken by goodness, truth, purity, as well as by virtues such as moral conduct.
Beheld by you, even men devoid of merit are immediately endowed with all virtues such as moral conduct, as well as noble lineage and sovereignty.
He is praiseworthy, he is virtuous, he is blessed, he is of noble birth, he is wise,
he is a hero, and he is valiant— he who, O Goddess, has been beheld by you.
All virtues, such as moral conduct and the rest, immediately fall into disarray for one from whom you,
O beloved of Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world, have turned your face away.
Even the tongue of the Creator is not able to describe your virtues;
be gracious, O lotus-eyed goddess, and never forsake us.
Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, having been thus properly praised, Śrī, dwelling within all beings, spoke joyfully to Śatakratu in the hearing of all the gods.
Śrī said: "O Lord of gods, O Hari, I am well-pleased with this hymn of yours.
Choose whatever boon you desire; I have come here as the giver of boons to you."
Indra said:
"O Goddess, if you are a giver of boons and if I am worthy of a boon, then the three worlds must not be abandoned by you; let this be my supreme boon."
O one born from the ocean, he who shall praise you with this hymn must not be abandoned by you; let this be my second boon.
Śrī said: "O Vāsava, best of the thirty gods, I shall not abandon the three worlds;
this boon has been granted by me to you, as I am pleased with your hymn of praise and your worship."
And whatever man shall praise me with this hymn both in the evening and in the morning, I shall not turn my face away from him.
Parāśara said: Thus, O Maitreya, in former times the highly fortunate goddess Śrī, gratified by his hymn of praise and worship, granted these two boons to the king of the gods.
Śrī was first born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti;
she was born again from the ocean during the churning for nectar through the efforts of the gods and the Dānavas.
Thus, whenever Janārdana, the Lord of the world and God of gods,
takes an incarnation, Śrī then becomes his companion.
Furthermore, when Hari was the Sun, Padmā was born;
and when he was Rāma Bhārgava, this earth became [Padmā].
In his incarnation as Rāghava she became Sītā, and in his birth as Kṛṣṇa she was Rukmiṇī; in all other incarnations of Viṣṇu, she is his companion.
In the state of divinity she possesses a divine body, and in the state of humanity she is human;
indeed, she assumes for herself a form that is truly commensurate with the body of Viṣṇu.
The man who hears this account of Lakṣmī’s birth, or who recites it,
shall not suffer a loss of fortune in his home for as long as three generations.
O Sage, in those houses where this praise of Śrī is recited,
misfortune— the source of strife— never dwells at any time.
This has been told to you, O Brahmin, which you asked of me:
how Śrī was formerly born from the Ocean of Milk, being the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Thus, this hymn to Lakṣmī, which is the cause for attaining all prosperity and has indeed issued from the mouth of Indra,
is recited daily here by those men in whom misfortune never dwells at any time.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
O great sage, you have related to me everything about which I questioned you.
"Tell me again of this creation, beginning from the lineage of Bhṛgu."
Parāśara said: Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, was born to Bhṛgu by Khyāti;
likewise, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were born as two sons to Bhṛgu by Khyāti.
Āyati and Niyati were the two daughters of the high-souled Meru;
they became the wives of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and from them both sons were born.
Prāṇa, Mṛkaṇḍu, and Mārkaṇḍeya [were born]; from Mṛkaṇḍu was born Vedaśiras. Now hear also of the son of Prāṇa.
Prāṇa’s son was Dyutimat, and from him Rājavat was born;
O fortunate one, from him the lineage of Bhārgava attained great expansion.
Marīci’s wife was Saṃbhūti; she gave birth to Paurṇamāsa.
Virajas and Parvata were the two sons of that high-souled one.
O twice-born one, I shall then recount his sons in the proclamation of the lineage.
Smṛti was the wife of Aṅgiras, and she likewise gave birth to daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumatī.
In the same way, Anasūyā bore to Atri three stainless sons:
Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya.
Dattoli was born as the son of Pulastya by his wife Prīti;
in a previous birth during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, he is remembered as Agastya.
Kardama, Ārvarīvat, and Sahiṣṇu were the three sons born to Kṣamā,
the wife of the patriarch Pulaha.
And Sannati, the wife of Kratu, gave birth to the Vālakhilyas—
sixty thousand sages with vital seed drawn up,
each the size of a thumb's joint, and possessing the blazing splendor of the sun.
And in Ūrjā, seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha.
Raja, Gotra, Ūrdhvabāhu, Savana, Anagha, Sutapas, and Śukra— these were all the stainless Saptarṣis.
O twice-born one, from that Agni— who was the presiding deity and the first-born son of Brahmā— Svāhā obtained three sons of noble vigor.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Śuci, and also Jalāśin;
In their lineage, forty-five other fires are said to have arisen, as well as the father and his three sons.
Thus, forty-nine fires have been proclaimed.
The Pitṛs created by Brahmā, whom I have described to you,
are those who eat from fire (Agniṣvāttas), those who sit on the sacrificial grass (Barhiṣadas), and those who are without fire as well as those who possess fire.
From them, Svadhā gave birth to Sūtā and likewise to Menā and Dhāriṇī;
both of them, O twice-born one, were exponents of the Veda and practitioners of yoga.
Endowed with supreme knowledge and all qualities combined, [he was]—// ViP_1,10.20 //
Thus has been described this lineage of offspring of the daughters of Dakṣa;
one who, full of faith, remembers this, shall never be childless.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
"Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Manu Svāyambhuva."
Two sons of great heroism, knowers of dharma, have been described to you.
O Brahmin, of those two, Uttānapāda had a son named Uttama by his beloved wife Suruci; he was exceedingly dear to his father.
O twice-born one, that king had a queen named Sunīti;
he was not very fond of her, yet she gave birth to a son named Dhruva.
Seeing his elder brother Uttama seated on the lap of their father as he sat upon the royal throne, Dhruva formed the desire to ascend it himself.
The king did not welcome Suruci’s son with joy when he approached affectionately, eager to climb onto his father’s lap, even as it was before his very eyes.
Seeing her co-wife’s son eager to climb onto his lap, and her own son already seated there, Suruci spoke these words: ||| ViP_1,11.6 |||
"O child, why do you act in vain? This is a great desire of yours;
born from the womb of another woman and not having been conceived in my own womb, you, lacking discernment, yearn for that which is most supreme and unattainable."
It is true that you too are his son, but you were not held by me.
"This royal throne, the banner of refuge for all sovereigns, is worthy of my son alone; why do you weary yourself? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11.9)
Why is this lofty aspiration of yours in vain, like that of my son?
Do you not perceive your own birth in Sunīti?
Parāśara said:
Having heard those words spoken by his mother, the boy, abandoning his father,
went in anger to the residence of his own mother, O twice-born one.
Seeing her son thus enraged with his lower lip slightly quivering, Sunīti placed him on her lap and spoke these words, O Maitreya: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11.12.
Sunīti said:
"My child, what is the cause of your anger? Who does not greet you with joy?
Who disregards your father? Tell me who has offended you."
Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus, he related everything to his mother exactly as Suruci,
who was exceedingly arrogant, had spoken in the presence of the king.
When her son had spoken thus,
Sunīti, dejected and with eyes weakened by sighing, spoke these words.
Sunīti said: "Suruci has spoken the truth; you are indeed of little fortune, my son.
For those who possess merit, my child, are not addressed in such a manner by their rivals."
"O dear one, you should not feel distressed; for what was done by you in the past, who is able to take it away? And as for that which was not done by you, who could give it? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11.17)
Therefore, you should not feel any sorrow here arising from his words.
"The royal throne, as well as the parasol, the excellent horses, and the noble elephants—
knowing that these belong only to him who possesses merit, be at peace, my son."
Through merits performed in other births, the king was called Suruci because of his beautiful wife; another wife, such as I am, was said to be devoid of merit.
Her son was likewise supreme, endowed with an accumulation of merit;
my son, however, was born as Dhruva, possessing very little merit.
Nevertheless, my dear son, you ought not to cause yourself distress;
for a wise man is satisfied with whatever he himself possesses.
If indeed this excessive suffering has come upon you because of Suruci’s words,
then, O bestower of all fruits, exert yourself in the accumulation of merit.
Be virtuous, righteous in soul, friendly, and devoted to the welfare of living beings;
for just as water flows downward by its own inclination, so do prosperity and blessings come to such a person.
Dhruva said:
Mother, these words which you have spoken for my sake are for the purpose of calming me;
yet they do not remain within my heart, which has been pierced by harsh speech.
Therefore, I shall strive in such a way that I may attain the most supreme of all supreme stations,
honored by all the worlds without exception.
Suruci was the beloved wife of that king, and I was not born from her womb;
behold my power, O Mother, even though I have been held within your own belly.
"He who was carried by her in her womb is my most excellent brother;
let him obtain the royal throne granted by his father—so be it."
"O Mother, I do not desire any station bestowed by another; I seek through my own karma that station which even my father did not attain."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus to his mother, Dhruva departed from his mother’s house;
and having gone out from the city, he then proceeded to the grove outside it.
There Dhruva saw seven sages who had arrived previously,
seated upon mats covered with black antelope skins.
Having prostrated before them all, that prince, bowing low with humility, addressed them properly after first offering his salutations.
Dhruva said:
"O best of beings, know me to be the son of Uttānapāda, born of Sunīti; out of world-weariness, I have come into your presence."
The sages said:
"O prince, you are but a child, having reached the age of four or five; even now, no cause for world-weariness exists within you."
"Nothing need be thought of by you; your father, the king, is still living. Nor do we see any separation from loved ones or such misfortunes for you, my child."
No illness is observed in your body by us;
tell us, if it exists, what is the cause of your world-weariness?
Parāśara said: Then he related what Suruci had said;
having heard that, those sages spoke among themselves.
Oh, what supreme kṣatriya splendor! Even though he was but a child, when addressed by his stepmother, that intolerance did not depart from his heart.
"O scion of the Kṣatriyas, if it pleases you, tell us what it is that you have now resolved to do out of world-weariness."
And whatever task must be performed for you by us, O one of immeasurable luster, let it be told; we perceive that you have something you wish to say.
Dhruva said:
"O best of the twice-born, I do not desire wealth nor do I desire sovereignty;
I seek only that one place which has never been enjoyed by anyone before."
O best of sages, let this be properly performed for me; let it be told how that supreme station, which is higher than all other stations, may be attained.
Śarabhaṅga said:
"O Prince, that supreme station is certainly not attained by men who have failed to worship Govinda; therefore, worship Acyuta."
Śatru said:
"He with whom Janārdana, the Supreme Person among all supreme beings, is pleased, attains the imperishable state; this which I have spoken is the truth."
Śaṅkara said:
"Worship Govinda, within whom all this exists— the Imperishable One of unchanging nature— if you desire that supreme state."

§ Pulastya said: Having propitiated Hari—who is the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and that which is the highest Brahman—one attains even liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to achieve. (ViP 1.11.45)
Kratu said: When Janārdana— the Lord of Sacrifice in the sacrifice, the Supreme Person in yoga— is pleased, what is there that remains unattainable?
Pulaha said:
O observer of noble vows, propitiate that Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe and the Lord of sacrifice, by worshipping whom Indra attained his supreme station as Indra.
Vasiṣṭha said: When Viṣṇu has been propitiated, you shall obtain by means of your mind whatever you desire,
even a station within the three worlds— how much more so, O child, the most excellent of the excellent?
G2,3 insert:
"The worship of Kṛṣṇa alone bestows all fruits upon a person."
All of them spoke in this very manner, and he [the Lord] adopted that means for the sake of the virtuous.
Dhruva said:
"The deity to be propitiated has been described by you to me who am bowed before you;
please tell me that which is to be chanted by me for his gratification."
And how I should perform the propitiation of that Great-Souled One—
may the great seers, with faces brightened by grace, tell that to me.
The sages said:
"O prince, you ought to hear from us duly how the worship of Viṣṇu is to be performed by men who are intent upon his propitiation."
First, a person should cause the mind to abandon all external objects;
thereafter, one should make it steady within that very abode of the world.
O delighter of the kings, learn from us this which is to be recited with a one-pointed mind, absorbed in that, and with the self held firm. ViP_1,11.53.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure knowledge, who possesses the forms of Hiraṇyagarbha, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and the Manifested.
The blessed Svāyambhuva Manu, your grandfather, formerly recited this prayer; Janārdana was pleased with him.
Just as he granted that supernatural power, difficult to obtain even in the three worlds,
so too should you satisfy Govinda by constantly reciting this.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having heard this in its entirety, O Maitreya, the son of the king—
Having prostrated before those sages, he departed from that forest.
O twice-born one, considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose,
he then went from there to the highly meritorious bank of the Yamunā known as Madhu.
Furthermore, because it was presided over by the Daitya named Madhu,
it became renowned on this earth by the name Madhuvana.
And having slain the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu,
Śatrughna indeed founded the city named Mathurā.
In that sacred bathing place (tīrtha), which removes all sins and where the presence of the god of gods, Hari-medhas, resides, he performed his ascetic penance.
Just as it had been instructed by the sages headed by Marīci, so it came to pass;
he perceived Viṣṇu, the Lord of all gods, residing within his own self.
O Brahmin, as he meditated with a mind focused on nothing else, Lord Hari, who dwells within all beings and pervades all states of being, appeared before him.
O Maitreya, while that yogi’s mind was thus established in Viṣṇu,
the earth, the supporter of all beings, was unable to bear his weight.
When he stood upon his left foot, half of the earth bowed down;
and when he stood upon his right, the other half of the earth bowed down.
O Brahmin, when he stood pressing the earth with his big toe,
then that earth, along with its mountains, trembled.
The rivers, streams, and oceans underwent extreme agitation;
because of that agitation, O great sage, the immortals fell into a state of supreme distress.
Then, O Maitreya, the gods known as the Yāmas, being extremely distressed,
consulted with Indra and proceeded to break their meditative concentration.
O great sage, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, assuming various forms, became intensely distressed and began to strive to break Mahendra’s meditative absorption.
His mother, named Sunīti, stood before him with tears in her eyes; then, composed of illusion, she spoke these piteous words: "O son! *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 1.12.14.
"O son, turn back from this act which is as terrible as the destruction of the body;
you were obtained by me through many long-cherished desires."
O child, you ought not to abandon me alone, wretched and helpless, merely because of the words of a co-wife; for when I have nowhere else to go, you are my refuge.
Where are you, a boy of five years, and where is this harsh asceticism?
Let your mind be turned away from this painful persistence that is devoid of fruit.
The time for your playthings has passed, as has the time for study;
thereafter comes the time for all enjoyments, and at the end of that, austerity is prescribed.
O dear son, that which was the time for your play as a child— why are you now thus devoted to asceticism, intent on your own destruction?
Devotion to me is the supreme dharma; follow the sequence of actions appropriate to your stage of life. Do not yield to delusion; turn away from this unrighteousness.
"O child, if you do not undertake this asceticism today,
then I too shall surely give up my life while you look on."
Parāśara said:
Though he was looking at her as she lamented thus with eyes clouded by tears,
his mind being concentrated on Viṣṇu, he did not truly see her.
"Child, child! These most terrible Rākṣasas, with weapons raised, are approaching in this fearsome forest; depart from here."
Having spoken thus, she departed; then the Rākṣasas appeared, with faces wreathed in garlands of flames, raising their fierce weapons.
Then, brandishing their flaming weapons, those night-stalkers released extremely fierce roars before the prince.
And hundreds of jackals howled from all sides with mouths full of flaming morsels, to terrify that boy who was absorbed in yoga.
"Let him be slain, let him be slain! Let him be cut to pieces, let him be cut to pieces!
Let him be devoured, let him be devoured!"—thus those night-stalkers cried out.
Then those night-stalkers, with the faces of lions, camels, and sea-monsters, let out various kinds of roars to terrify the prince.
For him whose mind was fixed on Govinda, those Rākṣasas became mere sounds, those Śivās became mere echoes, and those weapons did not even come within the range of his senses.
With a mind constantly one-pointed, the son of the lord of the earth saw nothing else whatsoever, but Viṣṇu alone as his own refuge.
Then, when all the illusions had dissolved, the gods again fell into a state of supreme agitation, fearing his defeat.
Having come together and being tormented by that asceticism, they sought refuge with Hari, the source of the universe, who is without beginning or end and the protector of those who seek shelter.
The gods said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Supreme Lord, Puruṣottama!
We, scorched by the austerity of Dhruva, have come to you for refuge.
O Lord, just as the moon is filled day by day by its remaining digits,
so does he attain prosperity day and night through his ascetic penance.
"O Janārdana, we have come to you for refuge, terrified by the penance of Uttānapāda; therefore, cause that penance to cease."
We do not know whether he desires the state of Śakra, or the state of Sūrya, or whether he has a longing for the positions of Kubera, Varuṇa, or Soma.
Therefore, O Lord, be gracious to us; extract this thorn from our hearts and cause the son of Uttānapāda to desist from his ascetic penance.
The Blessed One said:
"O gods, he does not seek the status of Indra, nor that of the Sun, nor even the lordship over the waters or wealth; whatever desire he prays for, I shall fulfill it all."
"O gods, go to your own abodes as you desire, free from anxiety;
I shall turn back this boy whose mind is intent on asceticism."
Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, the deities, led by Śatakratu, then bowed down and departed for their own abodes.
The Blessed One, the Self of All, being gratified by his absorption in that [devotion], assumed a four-armed form as Hari and, having gone to Dhruva, spoke this: *Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.12.41*
The Blessed One said:
"O son of Uttānapāda, may it be well with you! Pleased by your asceticism, I have arrived as a granter of boons; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
"Since you have fixed your mind upon me, independent of external objects, I am pleased with that; therefore, choose a supreme boon."
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words spoken by the God of gods, the boy opened his eyes and beheld Hari, whom he had previously seen through meditation, standing before him.
Beholding Acyuta, who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the excellent sword,
and who is adorned with a crown, he touched the earth with his head.
With his limbs bristling with horripilation, Dhruva was suddenly seized by supreme awe,
and he set his mind upon praising the God of gods.
"What shall I say in his praise? By whom has he been described so that I might offer him hymns?"—with such a troubled mind, he went for refuge to that very God.
Dhruva said:
"O Blessed One, if you have attained supreme satisfaction with my asceticism, then I wish to offer praise; grant this boon to me."
O Lord, how shall I, a mere child, be able to praise you, whose true nature is not known even by Brahmā and others who are masters of the Vedas?
O Supreme Lord, this mind of mine is indeed inclined toward devotion to you;
as it has set out to praise your feet, grant me wisdom therein.
Parāśara said: O best of the twice-born, Govinda, the Lord of the World, touched with the edge of his conch-shell that son of Uttānapāda, who stood with palms joined in reverence.
Then, at that moment, the prince, his face radiant with joy,
bowed down and offered praise to the imperishable Sustainer of all beings.
Dhruva said: I bow to Him whose form is earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and the source of the elements—
the primordial nature.
Pure, subtle, and all-pervading, the Person (Puruṣa) is beyond primordial matter (pradhāna);
salutations to that Puruṣa, whose form consists of the qualities (guṇas).
He is the eternal one who transcends all the elements beginning with earth, as well as smell and the other qualities,
and who is beyond the intellect and the rest, the primal matter (pradhāna), and the individual soul (puruṣa).
I take refuge in that pure form of yours, O Supreme Lord, which has become Brahman, the self, and the lord of the entire world.
Salutations to You, O Soul of All, who possess a form designated as Brahman because of its vastness and its capacity to nourish, which is inconceivable by yogis and free from transformation.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
pervading all, he transcended the earth by a distance of ten fingers' breadth.
Whatever has been and whatever is yet to be, O Supreme Person, that you are;
from you comes the Virāj, the Svarāj, and the Samrāj, and from you also the Adhipūruṣa.
He extended beyond this earth—below, across, and above;
from you this entire universe was born, and from you shall come the past and the future.
This entire world of all beings exists within you, assuming your form;
from you comes the sacrifice in which everything is offered, as well as the speckled butter and the two-fold sacrificial animal.
From you the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born; from you the meters arose;
from you the Yajus-formulas were produced, and from you the horses with one set of teeth.
From you the cows were produced; from you came goats, sheep, and wild animals.
From your mouth the Brāhmaṇas arose, and from your arms the Kṣatriya was born.
The Vaiśyas arose from your thighs, and the Śūdras emerged from your feet;
the sun [arose] from your eyes, the wind from your breath, and the moon from your mind.
From your internal cavity was born the vital breath (prāṇa), and from your mouth fire was born;
from your navel arose the atmosphere and the sky from your head;
the quarters of space from your ears and the earth from your feet—from you all this has come into being.
Just as a vast banyan tree is contained within a tiny seed,
so too is the entire universe situated within you, who have become the seed of all things, through self-restraint.
Just as a lofty Nyagrodha tree arises from a seed and attains great expansion,
so too does the world proceed from you in its creation.

For just as no other substance is seen apart from the bark and leaves of the plantain tree, O Lord, so no other reality is seen apart from you; O Sovereign, you alone are perceived as that in which the universe subsists.
Bliss, existence, and consciousness are unified in You, who are the foundation of all;
yet joy and suffering, which are mixed, do not exist in You, who are devoid of the material qualities (guṇas).

Salutations to you who have become distinct and who have become one; salutations to you who have become the elements and who are the self of the elements; salutations to you, the soul of the elements, who have become the abundant elements.
As the manifest, the unmanifest, Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Virāṭ, Saṃrāṭ, and likewise Svarāṭ,
you, the imperishable one, are meditated upon within the internal organ by men.
You are all things in everything; you are the All, assuming every form.
Everything originates from you, and therefore you are the All. Homage be to you, the Soul of All!
Since you are the self of all, O Lord of all, and abide within all beings, what then shall I tell you? You know everything that dwells within the heart.
O Soul of all, Lord of all beings, source of all creatures,
you are the essence of every being and you know the heart's desire of every living soul.
O Lord, that desire of mine has been made fruitful by you;
and my ascetic penance has borne fruit, since you, O Master of the World, have been seen by me.
The Blessed One said:
"O Dhruva, that you have seen me is the fruit obtained from your ascetic penance;
for the sight of me, O prince, never goes in vain."
Therefore, choose a boon according to your own desire;
for when I have come within the range of one's vision, everything is accomplished for men.
Dhruva said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, you reside in the heart of everyone.
O Master, what is unknown to you regarding that which is desired by my mind?"
Nevertheless, O Lord of Gods, I shall tell you that which is being prayed for by me with a most ill-behaved heart— something exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Or rather, what is difficult to obtain when you, the creator of the entire world, are pleased?
Even Maghavan enjoys the three worlds as the fruit of your grace.
"This royal throne is not worthy of me, who was never born from a womb," so my stepmother spoke loudly to me out of pride. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.12.81)
O Lord, I therefore pray for that imperishable station, the most excellent of all, which is the support of the entire world, through your grace.
The Blessed One said:
"O child, you shall indeed attain this station which has been prayed for by you; I was previously gratified by you in another birth."
Formerly, you were a brahmin, always single-mindedly devoted to me,
serving your mother and father, and observing your own duties.
As time passed, a prince became your friend;
in his youth, he was rich in all enjoyments and possessed a handsome, radiant form.
Through association with him, having beheld that exceedingly rare supernatural power of his, you formed the desire: "May I become a prince."
Thus, you have obtained that state of being a prince as you desired;
O Dhruva, you were born in the house of Uttānapāda, which is so difficult to attain.
That excellent station which belongs to the family of Svāyambhuva is not for others.
This is another [reason] why I am pleased with you, O child:
by propitiating me, a man attains liberation without delay.
O child, with your mind fixed upon me, what need have you for such states as heaven?
By my grace, O Dhruva, you shall undoubtedly become the abode of all stars and planets in a station superior to the three worlds.
From the Sun, from the Moon, from Mars, from Mercury, from Jupiter,
from Venus and Saturn, and likewise from all the constellations, O Dhruva.
O Dhruva, a station above all the seven ṛṣis and those gods who dwell in celestial chariots has been granted to you by me.
Some gods shall remain for the duration of four yugas, and some for the duration of a manvantara;
indeed, I have granted you a stay lasting for an entire kalpa.
Your mother Sunīti as well, having become exceedingly pure through her proximity to you,
shall dwell for that same length of time in a celestial chariot as a star.
And those men who, being well-composed, shall recite your praises in the morning and in the evening, for them there will be great merit.
Hari delayed [him].
Dhruva, too, having paid homage to him, went to the house of his own father.
Having heard that his son was returning as if he had departed for the next world, he [acted].
I have faith in King Candra; he is my son, the offspring of Candra.
Having heard the truth spoken by the divine sage, he became joyful.
Even for the messenger, through the favor of the one who conveys the news, there shall be great wealth from those who have fled in defeat.
With the sounding of conchs and trumpets, and with the abundant chanting of the Veda.
He quickly went forth from the city in the past, mounted upon an excellent horse-chariot.
Seeing him approaching swiftly toward the vicinity of the wind-god from his chariot, he [leapt down].
Having descended, the kings embraced him with their arms.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he was greeted with joy by all his kinsmen.
Having been saluted by him, they all entered together with Ṛcīka.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord vanished right there.
Parāśara said: Having thus previously obtained a boon from Janārdana, the Lord of the World and God of gods, that high-minded one now occupies his eternal station.
And likewise, from personally serving one's mother and father, [one obtains] the merit pertaining to dharma.
Through the greatness of the twelve-syllable mantra and by the power of his ascetic penance.
Having observed his pride, his supernatural power, and his greatness, Uśanas, the preceptor of the gods and asuras, sang this verse on that occasion: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.12.97.
"Oh, the power of this asceticism! Oh, the fruit of this asceticism!
For the Seven Sages stand with Dhruva placed before them."
And this mother of Dhruva is named Sunīti, who is the personification of truth;
and who on earth is capable of describing her greatness?
Having attained the supreme state that is the refuge of the three worlds, she remains steadfast; having reached that highest station, she dwells permanently within the cavity of her womb.
And whoever should constantly recite this account of Dhruva’s ascent to heaven,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Svarga.
He does not suffer the loss of his station, whether in heaven or on earth;
endowed with every auspicious thing, he lives for a long time.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: From Dhruva were born Śiṣṭi and Bhavya; from Bhavya, Śambhu was born.
Succhāyā bore five sinless sons to Śiṣṭi.
Bṛhatī bore to Ripu a son named Ripuñjaya, and to Vipra she bore Vṛkala, who possessed the splendor of a wolf; furthermore, she bore to Ripu Cākṣuṣa, who was endowed with all-encompassing energy.
Cākṣuṣa begot Manu upon Puṣkariṇī, the daughter of the high-souled Vīraṇa and the wife of Prajāpati Varuṇa.
O best of those who practice austerities, ten sons of great prowess were born to Manor, the daughter of Naḍvalā, by Vairāja Prajāpati.
Kuru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavān, Śuci,
Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and Sudyumna— these nine were born of great power from Naḍvalā, with Abhimanyu as the tenth.
Āgneyī, the daughter of Agni, bore to Kuru six sons of great splendor:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Khyāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Śibi.
From the body of Sunītha, one son, Vena, was indeed born;
for the sake of progeny, the seers churned his right hand.
O great sage, when Vena’s hand was churned,
there arose a protector of the earth named Vainya, who is celebrated as Pṛthu.
By whom the earth was formerly milked for the sake of the welfare of all creatures.
Maitreya said:
For what purpose was Vena’s hand churned by the supreme sages,
from which that Pṛthu of great heroism was born, O best of sages?
Parāśara said:
The maiden named Sunīthā, who was the first-born of Mṛtyu, was given as a wife to Aṅga; from her Vena was born.
O Maitreya, due to that defect of his maternal grandfather, the son of Mṛtyu’s daughter was born with a wicked disposition by his very nature.
When that Vena was consecrated in the kingdom by the supreme ṛṣis, he,
the lord of the earth, then issued a proclamation throughout the world.
"One should not sacrifice, one should not offer oblations, and one should not give anything whatsoever.
For who else is the enjoyer of the sacrifice? Indeed, I am the Lord and Master of the sacrifice."
Then, O Maitreya, having first honored that lord of the earth, the sages approached him and spoke with perfect composure and gentleness.
The sages said:
"O King, O Lord, listen to what we say for you,
which is for the benefit of your kingdom and body, and for the supreme welfare of your subjects."
"O Lord of Gods, we shall worship Hari, the Lord of all sacrifices, with a long-duration sacrifice; may prosperity be yours, and therein you shall have a share."
O King, when Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, has been fully propitiated by us through this sacrifice,
he will grant you all your desires.
O King, in whose kingdom Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, is worshipped with sacrifices,
He grants those rulers the attainment of all their desires.
Śeṣa said: Who else is superior to me, and who else is worthy of my worship?
Who is this one known as Hari, who is considered the Lord of Sacrifice? (ViP 1.13.20)
Brahmā, Janārdana, Śambhu, Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Ravi, Hutabhuj, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Pūṣan, Bhūmi, and Niśākara; 1.13.21.
These and other gods who bestow both curses and favors reside within the body of the king; thus, the king is composed of all the gods.
Having understood this, O twice-born ones, act exactly as I have commanded: nothing should be given, nothing should be offered in sacrifice, and no worship should be performed.
O twice-born ones, just as service to the husband is considered the supreme duty for women,
so too is the observance of my command your duty.
The sages said:
"Grant us permission, O Great King; let not dharma go to destruction.
This entire world is the transformation of sacrificial oblations. (ViP 1.13.25)
And when Dharma has gone to its destruction, the entire world perishes.
Parāśara said:
Although he was thus entreated by the supreme sages, that sinful Vena did not grant permission, even though he was addressed again and again.
Then all those sages, filled with anger and indignation, said to one another, "Let the sinner be slain! Let him be slain! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.13.27).
He who, being of base conduct, reviles Viṣṇu, the Lord of sacrifice, who is without beginning or end, is not fit to be the lord of the earth.
Having spoken thus, the hosts of sages struck the king with those *kuśa* grasses purified by mantras—
[the king] who had already been slain previously by the Lord’s censure and other means.
Then, O twice-born one, the sages saw dust rising on all sides;
they asked the people who had approached them, "What is this? at that time.
And it was reported by the people that, in a kingless realm, those who had become thieves and the rest of the world, driven by affliction, began seizing the property of others.
O best of sages, a vast cloud of dust was seen arising from those thieves who were rushing with great speed to plunder the wealth of others.
Then, having deliberated together, all those sages diligently churned the thigh of that childless king for the sake of a son.
And as he was being churned, a man indeed rose up from his thigh—
one who resembled a burnt pillar, with a hunchbacked face and extremely short in stature.
"What shall I do? he asked all those brahmins in great haste;
they told him, "Sit down," and because of that, he became a Niṣāda.
From them were born the Niṣādas, O tiger among sages, who dwell on the Vindhya mountains and are characterized by their evil deeds.
Through that opening, the sin of that king emerged;
from it were born those Niṣādas, who destroyed the impurity of Vena.
Then those best of the twice-born churned his right hand.
And as he was being churned there, the powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena,
appeared, blazing with his own body like a fire burning in person.
Then, from the sky, the first bow named Ājagava fell from the firmament,
and divine arrows and armor also descended.
But when he was born, all living beings were filled with joy in every way.
And by the birth of a virtuous son, even Vena went to the third heaven;
he was rescued from the hell named Put, by that great-souled one.
Then the oceans and the rivers, bringing jewels from every quarter and all their waters for the purpose of the consecration, presented themselves before him.
And the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā), together with the gods and the descendants of Aṅgiras,
as well as all beings, both stationary and moving,
having assembled, then consecrated the son of Vena as the lord of men.
Seeing the discus in his right hand, the Grandfather (Brahmā),
considering Pṛthu to be an incarnation of Viṣṇu, attained supreme satisfaction.
The mark of Viṣṇu, the discus, appears on the hand of all universal emperors,
whose power remains unimpeded even by the gods.
The powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, was consecrated according to the prescribed rites by those learned in dharma with great royal sovereignty and immense splendor.
The subjects were not won over by his father, but they were won over by him;
because of that affection for him, the name "Rāja" (King) arose for him.
As he set out toward the ocean, the waters stood still for him;
the mountains yielded the way, and his banner suffered no breakage.
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed; food was accomplished by mere thought;
cows milked all desires; and in every leaf-cup there was honey.
Indeed, as soon as he was born at that auspicious paternal sacrifice,
the high-minded Sūta was produced during the Sautya rite on the day of the Soma-pressing.
He became Pṛthu himself; from him, Pṛthu was born.
At that very great sacrifice, the wise Māgadha was born;
then those two, the Sūta and the Māgadha, were both proclaimed by the best of sages.
Let this powerful King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, be praised; for this deed is worthy of him, and he is indeed a fit object for praise.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the two of them said to all the brahmins:
"The ritual for this lord of the earth, who has been born today, must now be performed."
His virtues are not known, nor is his fame celebrated;
tell us, upon what basis should a hymn of praise for him be composed by us?
The sages said:
"Let this king be praised for those qualities which this mighty universal monarch will possess and for the deeds that he, the powerful one, shall perform."
Parāśara said:
Then that king, having heard that, attained supreme satisfaction;
for one attains praise through excellent qualities, and these qualities of mine are worthy of praise.
Therefore, whatever description of my virtues you two shall perform here in this hymn,
that very thing I too shall perform with a concentrated mind.
The king formed this resolve: "Whatever these two may say here that ought to be avoided, I shall avoid that. (ViP 1.13.59)
Then the two, the Sūta and the Māgadha, possessing beautiful voices, properly performed a hymn of praise for the wise Pṛthu, the son of Vena, by means of his future deeds.
This lord of men is truthful in speech, generous by nature, faithful to his promises,
modest, friendly, patient, valiant, and a punisher of the wicked.
He was a knower of dharma, grateful, compassionate, and pleasant of speech;
he honored those worthy of honor, was a performer of sacrifices, devoted to the Veda, and affectionate toward the virtuous.
The king should be impartial toward both enemy and friend when established in legal proceedings.
Having thus heard the qualities described by the charioteer and by the Magadhan king,
he took them to heart and performed corresponding actions accordingly.
Thereafter, that protector of the earth, while ruling this world,
performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Afflicted by hunger at that time when there was no king and plants had perished, the subjects approached that lord of the earth;
being questioned by him, they told him the reason for their coming.
[He saw] Pṛthu, who possessed the qualities of Prajāpati, a hero of true prowess.
The subjects said:
"O best of kings, O lord of subjects, in a kingless state all medicinal herbs on earth were devoured; consequently, all living beings went to their destruction."
"You have been appointed by the Creator as our provider of livelihood and protector of the subjects;
grant to us, your subjects who are overwhelmed by hunger, the medicinal herbs that sustain life."
Parāśara said:
Then the king, enraged, took up his divine bow Ājagava and celestial arrows, and pursued the Earth.
Then the Earth, having quickly become a cow, vanished;
out of terror, that Great One fled to the worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā.
Wherever that goddess, the supporter of beings, went at that time,
there she beheld the son of Vena with his weapons raised.
Then the Earth, trembling and intent on protecting herself from his arrow, spoke to Pṛthu of vast prowess.
The Earth said:
"O lord of men, do you not see the great sin in the killing of a woman,
such that you make such an effort, O King, to slay me?"
Pṛthu said:
When the death of a single evildoer brings security to many, his killing bestows merit.
The Earth said:
"If you will kill me for the sake of benefiting living beings,
O best of kings, what support will there be for those beings?"
Pṛthu said:
"O Earth, having slain you with my arrows for being averse to my command,
I shall sustain these subjects by the power of my own yoga."
Parāśara said:
Then, having bowed down to him, the Earth, her limbs trembling and overcome with great trepidation, spoke again to the king.
The Earth said:
"All undertakings, when commenced with the proper means, achieve success;
therefore, I shall tell you the means—employ it if you so desire. (ViP 1.13.78)
"O Lord of Men, all those great medicinal herbs that I have consumed,
if you so desire, I shall give them back to you, transformed into milk."
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, for the sake of the welfare of all creatures, grant me that calf so that I, who am fond of my young, may yield milk.
"And make it level everywhere, O Hero, so that the milk—
which is the seed of excellent medicinal herbs— may nourish everything on all sides."
Parāśara said:
Then the son of Vena cleared away mountains by the hundreds of thousands with the tip of his bow; by that means, the mountains were increased [in size].
Indeed, during that previous creation, when the surface of the earth was uneven,
there was no division of cities or villages at that time.
O Maitreya, neither crops, nor cattle-rearing, nor agriculture, nor trade existed; it was from the time of Vainya that the origin of all these came to be.
Wherever that lord of men found the ground level, there he caused his subjects to settle.
At that time, when the medicinal herbs had indeed perished, food for the people consisted of fruits and roots,
which were obtained only with great hardship.
Having appointed the lord Svāyambhuva Manu as his calf, Pṛthu,
the ruler of the earth, milked the earth from his own hand out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures, [obtaining] every kind of grain.
By that food, O dear one, living beings subsist even today constantly.
Because that Pṛthu became the father of the earth by granting her life,
she therefore obtained the name "Pṛthivī," the bearer of all things.
And then [he was honored] by the gods, sages, Daityas, Rākṣasas, mountains,
Gandharvas, Uragas, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, and likewise by the trees.
O Sage, having taken up various vessels, he milked that very same milk;
and according to the differences in the calves and the milkers, those [vessels] became their respective sources.
This very earth, produced from the sole of Viṣṇu’s foot, is the supporter, the ordainer, the sustainer, and the nourisher of the entire world.
Such was the power of that mighty son of Vena, Pṛthu;
he was born as a lord of the earth in ancient times and became a king because he delighted the people.
Whatever man shall proclaim this birth of Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
no evil deed of his shall ever bear fruit.
This supreme account of Pṛthu’s birth and power brings about the constant pacification of bad dreams for those men who hear it.
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
§ Parāśara said: Two sons of great heroism were born to Pṛthu, known as Antardhi and Vādin.
Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to Havirdhāna from within her own body.
From Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā Āgneyī gave birth to six sons:
Prācīnabarhis, Śukra, Gaya, Kṛṣṇa, Vṛka, and Ajina.
The venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great Prajāpati;
he was the great king Havirdhāni, by whom all creatures were nourished.
O Sage, because his *kuśa* grass blades were pointed toward the east on the earth,
he became renowned as Prācīnabarhis, the one of great strength celebrated throughout the world.
Having taken the daughter of the Ocean as his wife,
the lord of the earth [resided] at the conclusion of great ascetic penance with Savarṇā, the daughter of the lord of the earth.
Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis of the same lineage;
all were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing their religious duties without deviation, they performed great austerities for ten thousand years while lying within the waters of the ocean.
Maitreya said:
O great sage, you ought to explain this matter for which those high-souled Pracetasas performed penance in the waters of the ocean.

Parāśara said: The Pracetasas were addressed by their father, who was of immeasurable soul and had been appointed as a Prajāpati, with words preceded by great respect for the sake of creating progeny.
Prācīnabarhis said:
"O sons, I have been commanded by Brahmā, the god of gods: 'Your subjects must be increased by you. And I replied to him, 'So be it.'"
Therefore, for my pleasure, O sons, perform the increase of progeny without weariness; the command of Prajāpati is worthy of honor and must be duly observed.
Parāśara said:
Then, O Sage, having heard those words of their father, those sons of the king replied, "So be it," and questioned their father further.
The Pracetases said:
"O father, you ought to explain to us in its entirety that action by which we may become capable of increasing our progeny."
The father said:
"By propitiating Viṣṇu, the granter of boons, a mortal undoubtedly attains his desired object; it cannot be otherwise. What else shall I tell you?"
Therefore, for the sake of the increase of progeny, worship Hari, the lord of all beings,
Govinda, if you desire success.
By one who always desires righteousness, wealth, pleasure, and liberation,
the Blessed One— the beginningless Supreme Person— should be propitiated.
When that Acyuta is propitiated, by whom Prajāpati performed creation in the beginning,
through his worship, there shall be prosperity for your progeny.
Parāśara said:
Having been thus addressed by their father, those ten Pracetas sons plunged into the waters of the ocean and performed austerities with concentrated minds.
For ten thousand years, O best of sages, they fixed their minds upon Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, the ultimate refuge of all the worlds.
Remaining right there with one-pointed minds, they praised Lord Hari,
who, when lauded, bestows upon his worshiper the desired objects of their longing.
Maitreya said: O best of sages, you ought to relate to me that most meritorious hymn which the Pracetasas, while stationed upon the waters of the ocean, offered to Viṣṇu.
Parāśara said:
Listen, Maitreya, to how the Pracetasas, who had become absorbed in Him and were lying within the waters of the ocean, praised Govinda as they did in former times.
The Pracetases said:
We bow to that supreme Lord of the entire world, who is without beginning or end, and in whom the eternal foundation of all speech is established. *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 1.14.23.
Having bowed to [the Lord] as the seed of the world, by way of the division of his beautiful forms; 1,14.23*39:1.
Viṣṇu was pleased by the prostration of the Pracetasas, who were pure in form.
He is the primordial light, incomparable, subtle, infinite, and boundless;
he is the source of all that is stationary and all that moves.
Salutation to that Supreme Lord whose first form is day, from whom comes night, and who is the twilight; salutation to him whose nature is Time.
He who consists of nectar is consumed daily by the gods and the ancestors;
he who is the life-force of all—to that one in the form of Soma, obeisance!
Salutation to that one whose nature is the Sun, who destroys darkness, who illuminates the sky with his own rays, and who is the source of heat and cold water.

Salutation to that one whose nature is earth, who possesses solidity, who supports this entire world without exception, who is the locus of sound and the other sense objects, and who is all-pervading.
We bow to that which is the source of the world, the seed of all embodied beings, and which takes the form of water belonging to the Lord Hari-medhas.
Salutation to that Viṣṇu, whose nature is fire, who is the mouth of all the gods, as well as the consumer of sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya) for the ancestors.
Salutation to that Lord whose nature is wind, who has space as his source, and who, abiding in the body in five ways, performs activity incessantly.
Salutation to Him whose nature is space, who provides room for all beings without exception, who possesses infinite forms, and who is pure.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the creator, who is the eternal and supreme abode of the entire collection of sense organs, and whose form consists of sound and the other objects of perception.
We bow to that Hari-meghasa, the root of all knowledge, who is both perishable and imperishable, and whose nature as the senses perpetually perceives sense objects.
Salutation to that Universal Self, the inner organ, who receives from the senses the objects perceived and presents them to the soul.
Salutation to Him whose nature is primordial matter (prakṛti), in whom the entire universe resides, from whom it has likewise arisen, and who is its place of dissolution— He who is infinite.
We bow to that Puruṣottama, the divine one whose nature is the Self, who, though devoid of qualities, appears through delusion as if possessed of qualities, yet remains pure.
We bow to that supreme Brahman, the highest state of Viṣṇu, which is changeless, unborn, pure, devoid of qualities, and stainless.
Neither long nor short, neither gross nor subtle, without tip, without blood, without oily luster, without body, unattached, and without wind.
That which is without space, without touch, without smell, and without taste;
which is without eyes, ears, motion, speech, hands, or mind.
It is without name or lineage, without pleasure, without splendor, and without cause;
it is fearless, free from delusion, sleepless, and ageless and deathless.
That which is free from dust, soundless, immortal, unfathomable, and unenclosed;
that in which there is no before or after—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
We bow to that supreme state of Viṣṇu, which possesses the quality of sovereignty, which is the refuge of all beings, and which is beyond the range of speech and sight.
Parāśara said: Thus, praising Viṣṇu with their minds absorbed in Him,
the Pracetasas performed austerities in the great ocean for ten thousand years.
Then the blessed Lord Hari,
appearing within the water with a complexion like that of a blooming blue lotus petal, granted them his vision.
Beholding him mounted upon the king of birds,
the sons of Pracetas prostrated themselves before him with their heads bowed down by the weight of devotion.
Then the Blessed One said to them: "Choose the boon you desire;
with a face brightened by grace, I have appeared before you as a granter of boons."
Then, having prostrated before that granter of boons, the Pracetasas spoke to him concerning the cause for the increase of progeny as commanded by their father.
And that god, having granted him the boon as desired, quickly vanished; and they emerged from the water.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
While the Pracetasas were performing austerities upon the earth, trees grew [there].
When they were left unprotected, they were overwhelmed by calamities, and then there occurred a destruction of the people.
The wind was unable to blow, for the sky became covered with trees;
for ten thousand years, living beings were unable to move.
Seeing them, all the Pracetasas emerged from the water; filled with rage and their anger aroused, they emitted wind and fire from their mouths.
Then, having uprooted those trees, the wind dried them up;
thereafter, a terrible fire consumed them, and thus occurred the destruction of the forest.
Then, seeing that the trees were exhausted and only a few branches remained, King Soma approached those Prajāpatis and said to them: ||| ViP_1,15.5 |||
"Restrain your anger, O kings, and listen to my words:
I shall bring about peace for you with these trees."
This maiden, the daughter of Vṛkṣa, is a jewel of excellent complexion;
knowing her future destiny, I previously caused her to be reared by cows.
She was created by name as Māriṣā among trees;
let this highly fortunate woman be your wife, for she will certainly increase your lineage.
"By half of your splendor and by half of my own splendor,
a wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa shall be born from her."
Endowed with a portion of myself and with the fire consisting of your own splendor,
he shall further increase the creatures, being himself like fire.
Formerly, there was a sage named Kaṇḍu, the best among the knowers of the Vedas;
on the beautiful bank of the Gomatī, he performed supreme austerity.
To disturb him, the lord of the gods dispatched a choice Apsaras named Pramlocā;
she, of radiant smiles, sought to disturb that seer.
Agitated by her, his mind attached to sensual pleasures, he remained for more than a hundred years in the valley of Mount Mandara.
She said to him, "O illustrious one, I wish to go to heaven;
O Brahmin, being well-disposed toward me with favor, you should grant me permission."
Thus addressed by her, that sage, his mind attached to her, said:
"O blessed lady, please stay for a few days."
Having been addressed thus by him, that slender woman again enjoyed the objects of the senses together with that great-souled one for more than a hundred years.
"Grant me leave, O Blessed One; I am going to the abode of the thirty gods.
When she had spoken thus, the sage replied, "Stay! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.15.17).
When another hundred years had passed, that lady of auspicious countenance said,
"I shall go to heaven," O Brahmin, with a face beautiful with a loving smile.
Having been addressed thus by her, the sage embraced the large-eyed lady and said: "O fair-browed one, wait for a moment; you shall depart after a long time."
Fearing that curse, the woman of beautiful hips remained with that ṛṣi for a little less than two hundred years.
Though repeatedly urged by that slender lady to go to the abode of the king of the gods, the illustrious one replied, "Stay."
She went forth with sound, fear, love, and true devotion toward her former lord.
Even when attached to another, she does not abandon him; she should be known as *dakṣiṇā* by the wise.
Terrified by the fear of a curse, yet yielding to courtesy because she was his sacrificial fee, she—
knowing the pain of a broken request— did not abandon the sage when thus addressed.
And as that supreme ṛṣi took delight with her day and night, his love became ever new, for his mind was possessed by the god of love.
Once, however, the sage emerged from his hut in a hurry;
as he was departing, that auspicious woman asked him, "Where are you going?"
Thus addressed by her, he said: "O auspicious lady, the day has turned;
I shall perform the twilight worship, for otherwise there would be a lapse in my ritual duties."
Then, smiling with joy, she said to that great sage:
"O knower of all dharmas, why has the day changed for you today?"
O Brahmin, tell me: whom does this fact—that many years have passed for you in a single day—not cause wonder? (ViP 1.15.27)
The sage said:
"O blessed lady, you came to this auspicious riverbank at dawn;
O slender-limbed one, you were seen by me and entered my hermitage."
After verse 28, M₃ inserts:
"In every single moment, this supreme sūtra has indeed been offered by me."
The twilight has arrived and the day has come to its end;
for what purpose is this laughter? Let my true intention be told to me.
Pramlocā said:
"O Brahmin, it is true that you arrived at dawn; this is not false.
However, hundreds of years have passed for you since that time."
Soma said:
Then, filled with trepidation, the brahmin asked that large-eyed woman,
"Tell me, O timid one, how much time has passed while I have been sporting with you?"
Pramloca said: "Nine hundred and seven years have passed for you,
as well as six months and another three days."
The sage said:
"O timid one, you speak this truth, or perhaps it is a jest, O auspicious lady;
I believe that I have spent a single day here together with you."
Pramloca said: "O Brahmin, how could I speak an untruth here in your presence,
especially since I have been questioned today by you who follow the path?"
Soma said:
O sons of the king, having heard those words of hers, that sage reproached himself with himself, saying, "Fie on me! Fie on me! in this manner.
The sage said:
"My austerities have perished; the wealth of those who know Brahman has been destroyed;
my discernment has been stolen by someone who created this woman for the sake of delusion."
"Brahman, which transcends the six waves, is to be known by me through self-conquest; fie on that great-grasping desire by whom this mind of mine has been carried away! (ViP 1.15.37)
Hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death— these are the six waves.
All my vows, which were the means for attaining the knowledge of the Vedas,
have been carried away by attachment, which leads along the path to the village of hell.

"Go, O sinful woman, as you please; that which was to be done has been accomplished by you, who sought to agitate me—the king of the gods—through your amorous gestures."
"I shall not reduce you to ashes with the fierce fire of my wrath;
for I have dwelt with you, and friendship among the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together."
Or rather, what fault is there in you, or why should I be angry with you?
The fault lies entirely with me, since I have failed to conquer my senses.
"By you— who, desiring to please Śakra, have caused the ruin of my asceticism— fie upon you, a most loathsome casket of great delusion!"
Soma said:
While that brahmin-sage was speaking thus to the slender-waisted woman,
she began to tremble violently, with drops of perspiration trickling down her body.
To her, who was trembling incessantly with her vine-like limbs exhausted, that best of sages spoke angrily: "Go! Go! (ViP 1.15.45).
Rebuked by him, she departed from that hermitage and,
traveling through the sky, wiped away her sweat with the tender leaves of trees.
The young woman went from tree to tree, rubbing her limbs— dripping with perspiration— with their tips of reddish shoots.
The embryo that had been placed within her body by the sage then emerged from her limbs in the form of perspiration accompanied by horripilation.
The trees received that embryo, and the Wind-god made it into one;
nourished by me with rays of light, it then grew gradually.
A woman of beautiful countenance named Māriṣā, born from the interior of the treetops, shall give herself to you; let this anger be appeased.
Thus she was the offspring of Kaṇḍu, yet she emerged from the trees;
likewise, she was my own offspring through Vāyu, and she was the daughter of Pramlocā.
And when his ascetic penance was exhausted, O best of beings, that Blessed One Kaṇḍu went to the mountain lord named Puruṣottama, the abode of Viṣṇu.

There, O sons of the king, that great yogi, standing with his arms raised and his mind one-pointed, performed the worship of Hari while reciting the *japa* consisting of the *Brahmapāra* with a concentrated mind.
The Pracetases said:
O Sage, we wish to hear the supreme hymn to the Far-Reaching One (Brahmapāra),
by which the god Keśava was propitiated while being chanted by Kaṇḍu.
Soma said:
Viṣṇu is the further shore, the supreme, whose own shore is shoreless; he is beyond the beyond, whose form is the ultimate reality.
He is the shore of Brahman, the embodiment of the further shore, the highest even of the high, and the shore of the shore itself.
Having proclaimed [the Lord] with three verses, the prayer follows as the fourth.
Thus, Hari was soon gratified by Kaṇḍu with this hymn to Brahmapāra.
He is the cause by way of causality; beyond that, he is the cause of even that, the cause of the supreme cause.
And thus, within all effects, he exists in every respect through his various forms as both action and agent; herein, everything is contained.
He is the Lord Brahmā, he is that which has become all beings, he is Brahmā, the infallible lord of creatures;
he is Viṣṇu, the imperishable, eternal, unborn, unattached to decay and all other such changes.
Just as this Supreme Person is the imperishable syllable, unborn and eternal,
so may my defects, such as passion and the rest, come to complete pacification.
Soma said:
By reciting this supreme hymn known as the *Brahmapara*,
and by propitiating Keśava, he attained the highest perfection.
Whoever constantly recites or even hears this hymn—B2, T3, ed. Veṅk. insert: // ViP_1,15.59*44:1 // —[attains the fruit].
Freed from all the defects of desire, he attains what he wishes for.
Whoever recites or even hears this hymn constantly— T3 (sic) ins: yaḥ imaṃ stavaṃ paṭhate śṛṇuyād api nityaśaḥ // ViP_1,15.59*45:1 //
He certainly becomes liberated from all the defects of desire.
And this Māriṣā was formerly she whom I am telling you about;
due to the importance of the matter, speaking of her will be fruitful for you.
O best of men, previously childless, this highly fortunate queen of the king propitiated Viṣṇu with devotion after her husband had died.
Viṣṇu, being propitiated by her, appeared before her in person and said, "Choose a boon. She then spoke of the auspicious desire of her own heart.
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, due to my childhood widowhood, I am one whose birth is thus in vain; I have arisen with such meager fortune and am fruitless."
"By your grace, may I have praiseworthy husbands in birth after birth; likewise, may I have a son equal to Prajāpati."
[The qualities are] lineage, character, age, truthfulness, courtesy, and promptness in action. (ViP 1.15.64)
Reliability, strength, service to the elders, and gratitude.
"Endowed with perfect beauty, pleasing to the sight of all,
and not born from a womb, may I be so born through your grace, O Adhokṣaja."
Soma said:
Thus addressed by her, the Lord of Gods, Hṛṣīkeśa,
the Supreme Lord and giver of boons, raised her up as she was bowing low in prostration and spoke to her.
The god said:
"In a single birth alone, there shall be ten husbands for you, men of great heroism whose noble deeds will be renowned."
And you shall obtain, O beautiful one, a son of great soul, endowed with exceeding heroism and prowess, and possessed of the qualities of a Prajāpati.
He shall be the founder of lineages in this world,
and his progeny shall fill the entirety of the three worlds.
And you too, O virtuous lady, shall by my grace be born not from a womb, endowed with beauty, nobility, and excellent qualities,
and a source of delight to the minds of men.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished before that large-eyed woman;
and she has been born as this Māriṣā, your wife, O sons of kings.
Parāśara said: Then,
at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas withdrew their anger from the trees and accepted Māriṣā as their wife according to the dharma of matrimony.
From the ten Pracetas, however, the illustrious Prajāpati Dakṣa was born of Māriṣā— he who had previously been born from Brahmā.
But that highly fortunate Dakṣa, O great-minded one,
begot sons for the sake of creation, for the purpose of his own progeny.
Commanding both the immobile and the mobile, as well as bipeds and quadrupeds, he remained intent upon the purpose of creation, acting according to the instruction of Brahmā.
Having first created by means of his mind, the skillful Dakṣa then produced fifty daughters;
he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven, who were appointed to the measurement of time, to Indu.
From them were born the gods, as well as the Daityas, Nāgas, cattle, birds,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Dānavas, and others.

From that time forth, O Maitreya, living beings were born from sexual union; whereas previously, the offspring of those ancient beings— who were kindled by the excellence of their austerities and were practitioners of extreme penance— were produced through mere intention, sight, or touch.
Maitreya said:
I have heard that Dakṣa was born previously from the right thumb;
O great sage, how was he born again as the son of Pracetas?
O Brahmin, this very great doubt dwells within my heart:
that the daughter’s son of Soma has, in turn, become his father-in-law.
Parāśara said:
O best of beings, the origin and the cessation [of things] among all creatures is eternal;
regarding this, the sages and others who possess divine vision are not deluded.
O best of sages, these beings, beginning with Dakṣa, come into existence age after age, and they are likewise dissolved again; the wise man is not deluded by this.
O best of the twice-born, neither the state of being youngest nor that of being eldest existed among them previously;
austerity alone was weightier, and spiritual power was the sole cause [of their status].
Maitreya said: O Brahmin, proclaim to me here in detail the origin of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas.
Parāśara said:
O high-minded one, hear how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-born One to "create progeny," brought forth all beings.
At that time, Dakṣa first created all beings by means of his mind alone:
the gods, the sages, along with the Gandharvas, as well as the Asuras and the Pannagas.
When those creatures being created by him did not multiply,
the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) then reflected at length upon the purpose of creation.
Desiring to create various offspring through the very law of sexual union,
he married Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa,
who was endowed with great ascetic merit and was a mighty sustainer of the world.
Then, for the sake of creation, the powerful Prajāpati begot five thousand sons upon Vairiṇī and Asiknī.
O Brahmin, seeing them desiring to multiply their offspring, the celestial sage Nārada, whose speech is pleasant, approached them and spoke as follows.
Nārada said:
O Haryaśvas of great prowess, you shall create progeny;
such effort is observed on your part—listen to this.
"Alas, you are indeed foolish; you do not know the interior, the heights, and the depths of this earth. How then will you create progeny?"
When your movement is unimpeded upwards, across, and downwards,
then why, O fools, do you all not see the end of the earth?
Parāśara said:
Having heard those words, they departed in all directions;
even today they do not return, like rivers into the oceans.
Then, when the Haryaśvas had perished, the lord Dakṣa,
the son of Pracetas, again begot a thousand sons upon Vairiṇī.
O Brahmin, those Śabalāśvas, desiring to increase their progeny once again, were urged by Nārada with the very words previously mentioned.
They all said to one another, "The great sage has spoken correctly;
the path of our brothers must indeed be followed, there is no doubt about this."
And having ascertained the extent of the earth, we shall thereafter create living beings.
They too set out along that very same path in every direction,
and even today they do not return, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
From that time forward, O twice-born one, a brother who sets out in search of another brother perishes; therefore, a wise man should not do so.
Having realized that his sons were lost, the illustrious Prajāpati Dakṣa became enraged and cursed Nārada.
Then, when the Haryaśvas had perished, the twice-born Dakṣa, filled with rage, uttered a curse.
"Nārada, he shall go to destruction and dwell within the womb."
Then, on that most excellent day, he gave him his beloved daughter, the offspring of Dakṣa.
Therefore, by the power of that curse, Nārada was born again from the sages.
Then, O Maitreya, that wise Prajāpati Dakṣa, desiring creation, begot sixty daughters by Vairiṇī; so we have heard.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were born to Bahuputra, two likewise to Aṅgiras, and two to the learned Kṛśāśva; hear their names from me.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Jāmi, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī,
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā—
these ten were the wives of Dharma; hear from me now of their offspring.
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas; from Marutvatī came the Marutvats, and the Vasus are said to have been born from Vasu.
The Bhānus were born there from Bhānu; the Muhūrtas were born from Muhūrtā;
Ghoṣa was born from Lambā; and Nāgavīthī was born from Jāmī.
The entire realm of the earth was born from Arundhatī;
and from Saṃkalpā was born the Universal Soul (Sarvātman), as well as Saṃkalpa himself.
But as for those gods who possess manifold wealth and vital power, led by Jyotis,
who are known as the eight Vasus— I shall describe them in detail.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are remembered by name as the Vasus.
Āpa’s sons were Vaitaṇḍa, Śrama, Śrānta, and likewise Adhuni;
and the lordly Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds, was the son of Dhruva.
The venerable Varca was born from Soma as one endowed with splendor.
Dhara’s sons were Draviṇa, Hutahavyavaha,
Śiśira, Prāṇa, and Ravaṇa, born of Manoharā.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Purojava;
Avijñātagati was also his son—thus Anila had two sons.
The son of Agni, Kumāra, was born in a clump of reeds;
Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya were his younger brothers.
The offspring of the Kṛttikās is known as Kārttikeya.
They know Pratyūṣa’s son to be the sage named Devala;
Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise.
The sister of Bṛhaspati was an excellent woman who observed celibacy;
perfected in yoga, she wanders through the entire world unattached.
She was indeed the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus.
From her was born the illustrious Prajāpati Viśvakarman,
the creator of thousands of arts and the architect of the gods.
He was the creator of all ornaments and the best among artisans;
he indeed fashioned the celestial chariots for all the deities,
and men subsist upon the craftsmanship of that high-souled one.
