He had four sons; hear their names from me.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the wise Rudra;
and from Tvaṣṭṛ was born his son Viśvarūpa, who possessed great ascetic power.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Aparājita,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kapālī— O great sage,
these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
Thus, a hundred Rudras of immeasurable splendor have been enumerated.
Now hear from me the names of those who were the wives of Kāśyapa. (D3,4,T,G2,3,M0,3,4,ed. Veṅk. ins.)
O knower of dharma, Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, her sister Vinatā, Surabhi, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, and Muni— listen now to me regarding their offspring. *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 1.15.125.
In a previous Manvantara, there were twelve excellent and supreme gods known as the Tuṣitas; during the Vaivasvata interval, they spoke thus to one another:
When the highly illustrious Cākṣuṣa Manu had arrived,
they all came together and assembled with one another.
"Come quickly, O gods, and indeed enter into Aditi;
let us be born during a Manvantara, for that would be for our welfare."
O Lord, he was indeed Svāmin, as well as Pitṛ and Mitra-Varuṇa.
Having spoken thus, they were all born during the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, and Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa.
There, Viṣṇu and Śakra were indeed born once again,
as were Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aṃśa, and Bhaga of exceeding splendor— these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
Those gods who were formerly the Tuṣitas during the interval of Cākṣuṣa are indeed remembered as the twelve Ādityas during the interval of Vaivasvata.
Now, those twenty-seven wives of Soma who were proclaimed as being of virtuous vows—
After verse 133ab, Ś, Ñ₁, D₁.₂.₇, D₅, and the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition insert:

"All the Nakṣatrayoginīs are likewise remembered as having those [same] names. D₅ further inserts after 133: "All the Nakṣatrayoginīs are likewise remembered as having those [same] names. (ViP 1.15.133ab*51)
T3 inserts after 133ab:
"Among those [wives] who were rendered childless by the curse of Dakṣa, she was requested for the purpose of becoming a Yakṣa-dwelling."
From them were born offspring who were radiant and possessed immeasurable splendor.
The children of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi were sixteen in this world.
It is recorded that four types of lightning belong to the learned Bahuputra.
The Ṛgvedic verses born of Aṅgiras were the most excellent, honored by the Brahman-sages.
The sons of the divine sage Kṛśāśva were the Devapraharaṇas.
At the end of a thousand yugas, O dear one, all these thirty-three classes of gods born of the Vedas are indeed born again;
for them also, the constant cycle of cessation and origination is proclaimed here.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun occur here, O Maitreya,
so do those classes of gods come into being age after age.
We have heard that Diti gave birth to two sons from Kaśyapa:
Hiraṇyakaśipu and the invincible Hiraṇyākṣa.
And Siṃhikā became the daughter who was the wife of Vipracitti.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of renowned prowess:
Anuhlāda, Hlāda, the righteous Prahlāda, and Saṃhlāda;
they were of great heroism and increased the lineage of the Daityas.
Among them, the illustrious Prahlāda, who possessed self-mastery and looked upon all things with equanimity, bore supreme devotion toward Janārdana.
As for Prahlāda, [he was thus] for the sake of the state of exclusive devotion to Nṛsiṃha for embodied beings.
It aroused a longing to hear [it] and indicated its power.
O twice-born one, the fire kindled by the lord of the Daityas, though it enveloped all his limbs,
did not previously burn him while Vāsudeva remained within his heart.
While that wise one remained within the waters at the edge of the great ocean, the entire earth shook as he moved about, bound by his cord.
The body of him whose mind was never diverted from Acyuta remained unbroken by the various weapons hurled by the lord of the Daityas, for it was as hard as a mountain.
The lords of serpents, though possessed of great splendor and urged on by the Daityas, with their mouths blazing like poisonous fire, were not able to bring about his end.
Even though his body was crushed by mountains, he who remembered Puruṣottama did not relinquish his life-breaths, being armored by the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
The earth, having approached that high-minded one as he fell from on high—
having been hurled by the lord of the Daityas who dwells in heaven— sustained him.
The wind sent by the lord of the Daityas, which was intended to dry up his body,
immediately met its destruction as soon as Madhusūdana was established in his heart.
The elephants of the quarters, transformed by the Lord of the Daityas, encountered the breaking of their tusks and the loss of their pride upon his chest.
And the *kṛtyā* that had been produced by the priests of the Daitya king formerly did not lead to the end of him whose mind was attached to Govinda.
And the thousand illusions of Śambara, the master of magic,
were rendered futile by Kṛṣṇa’s discus when they were employed against him.
And that wise one, free from malice, digested without any adverse effect the Hālāhala poison presented by the cook of the lord of the Daityas.
He whose mind is equanimous toward all beings in this world, who possesses the supreme quality of friendliness and regards others just as he does himself; ViP_1,15.155.
He was a righteous soul, a supreme mine of virtues such as truthfulness and purity,
who always served as the standard of comparison for all virtuous men.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
O great sage, you have related to me the lineage of the descendants of Manu.
And the eternal Viṣṇu alone is the cause of this world.
As for what the Blessed One said regarding Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas:
"Neither fire consumed him nor did he lose his life when struck by missiles."
The earth shook where he stood upon the waters of the ocean;
though bound by fetters, it trembled, struck by his outstretched limbs.
Even though his body was crushed by mountains in the past, he did not die;
you yourself have described the extreme majesty of that wise one.
O Sage, I wish to hear of the incomparable power of that devoted Viṣṇu of immeasurable luster, whose life-story this is.
O Sage, for what reason was he wounded with weapons by the sons of Diti,
and for what purpose was he cast into the waters of the ocean, he who was so devoted to righteousness?
Why was he overwhelmed by mountains? Why was he bitten by great serpents? Was he hurled from a mountain peak, or cast into a mass of fire?
And why was that land of the tusks of the world-elephants designated as such?
And why was the withering wind employed against it by the great Asuras?
And did those preceptors of the Daityas employ a *kṛtyā*, O sage?
And what did Śambara do when he deployed a thousand illusions?
Why was the terrible *hālāhala* poison given for his destruction by the slayers of the Daityas to that high-souled and wise one, since it was digested by him?
O highly fortunate one, I desire to hear all this account of the high-souled Prahlāda, which indicates his great majesty.
Indeed, there was no cause for wonder in that he was not slain by the Daityas;
for who would be capable of striking down one whose mind is fixed on no other than Viṣṇu?
While he was thus constantly devoted to dharma and intent upon the worship of Keśava,
it was exceedingly difficult for the Daityas born of his own lineage to harbor hatred toward him.
O illustrious one, whose nature is dharma, devoted to Viṣṇu, and free from envy,
you ought to tell me why the Daityas have struck you.
Great-souled beings strike even at such an adversary;
how much more so against a virtuous person endowed with good qualities who is born of their own side?
Therefore, O best of sages, let all this be told in detail;
I wish to hear the life-story of the lord of the Daityas in its entirety.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen attentively to the life-story of that wise one.
Of the high-souled Prahlāda, whose conduct was ever noble.
In ancient times, Hiraṇyakaśipu, the son of Diti, who possessed great heroism and was arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, brought the three worlds under his control.
That Daitya assumed the status of Indra, and he himself became the Sun;
the great Asura likewise became Vāyu, Agni, the Lord of Waters, and Soma.
He became the lord of riches; he himself was Yama;
and that asura personally consumed all the sacrificial portions without exception.
O best of sages, out of fear of him, all the gods abandoned heaven and wandered upon the earth,
assuming human bodies.
Having conquered the entire triple world and being intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty over the three realms,
he enjoyed his beloved sense-objects while being celebrated in song by the Gandharvas.
Then all the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas waited upon the high-souled Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was devoted to drinking.
Others played musical instruments and sang, while still others uttered cries of victory;
thus the Siddhas, filled with joy, performed before the lord of the Daityas.
There, in that most enchanting palace made of crystal, where Apsarases were dancing, the Asura drank his beverage with great joy.
His son, a highly fortunate youth named Prahlāda,
went to his teacher’s house and studied the lessons prescribed for children.
Once, however, that righteous-souled one went with his preceptor into the presence of his father, the lord of the Daityas, who was then addicted to drink.
Raising up his son Prahlāda, who was of immeasurable splendor and prostrate at his feet in salutation, his father Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke to him.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Recite, my dear child, that essential well-spoken verse which you have learned through such long time by being ever-diligent."
Prahlāda said:
"Listen, dear father; at your command I shall speak that which is the very essence, which dwells within my mind, with your attention fully composed."
I bow to Him who is without beginning, middle, or end; who is unborn, without increase, decay, or fall; whose internal continuum is eternal; and who is the cause of all causes.
Parāśara said: Having heard this, the lord of the Daityas, his eyes bloodshot with anger and his sprout-like lips quivering, looked at his preceptor and spoke.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O wretched Brahmin, why have you, disregarding me, caused this foolish boy to be instructed in this worthless praise of my enemies, O evil-minded one?"
The Guru said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, you ought not to fall under the sway of anger;
this son of yours does not speak [thus] because of my instruction."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"By whom have you been instructed thus, my child Prahlāda? Tell me;
your teacher here says that he did not instruct you."
Prahlāda said: O dear one, apart from that Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, who dwells in the heart of the entire world as its teacher, who could be taught by whom?
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Who is this Viṣṇu, O evil-minded one, whom you speak of again and again so forcefully here in the presence of me, the Lord of the worlds?"
Prahlāda said: He whose supreme state is beyond the range of sound, who is the object of meditation for yogis,
from whom [the world arises], and who is himself the universe— he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O ignorant one, while I am present, who else is there known as the Supreme Lord?
You wish to die, yet you speak thus again and again."
Prahlāda said:
O dear father, that Viṣṇu is not only the creator of my subjects, but also of yours;
he is the sustainer, the ordainer, and the Supreme Lord. Be gracious; for what reason do you display anger?
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Who has entered the heart of this evil-minded man, this perpetrator of great sins,
by whom his mind is so possessed that he utters such wicked words?"
Prahlāda said:
O father, that Viṣṇu does not merely abide pervading my heart; rather, having pervaded all the worlds, he, the omnipresent one, joins me, you, and all others to every activity.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Let this wicked one be expelled and let him be punished in the house of his preceptor; by whom was this evil-minded one employed in the false praise of our enemies?"
Parāśara said:
Having been told this, he was then led back to the preceptor’s house by the Daityas;
intent on serving his teacher, he acquired knowledge incessantly.
When a very long time had passed, Prahlāda, the lord of the Asuras, summoned him and said: "My son, let some verse be sung."
Prahlāda said:
May that Viṣṇu, from whom both Pradhāna and Puruṣa arise, and from whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings proceeds— the cause of all this— be gracious unto us.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Let this evil-souled one be slain; there is no purpose in him remaining alive, for he has become a charcoal of his own lineage by causing the destruction of his kin."
Parāśara said: Thus commanded by him, hundreds of thousands of Daityas, seizing their great weapons, rose up for his destruction.
Prahlāda said: "O Daityas, by that truth that Viṣṇu resides within your weapons, within you, and within me, let your weapons not strike me."
Parāśara said:
Then, although struck by those hundreds of Daityas with floods of weapons,
he did not experience even the slightest pain and became as if newly born again.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O evil-minded one, desist from this faction of your enemies;
I grant you safety, so do not be so utterly deluded in mind. (ViP 1.17.35)
Prahlāda said:
O remover of all fears, while You, the Infinite One, abide within my mind, where can fear remain?
For when You are remembered, O Father, all fears such as birth, old age, and death depart.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O serpents, bring this man of evil conduct and exceedingly wicked mind to his destruction immediately with your mouths filled with the flames of poison!"
Parāśara said: Having been addressed thus by him, those serpents— Kuhaka, Takṣaka, and the others,
who were exceedingly fierce with their potent venom— began to bite him in all his limbs.
But he, his mind deeply attached to Kṛṣṇa, though being bitten by great serpents,
did not perceive his own body, remaining established in the joy of that remembrance.
The serpents said:
"Our fangs are shattered, the jewels on our hoods are bursting, there is heat in our hearts and trembling;
not even the slightest part of his skin is pierced here. O Lord of Daityas, command another course of action."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O elephants of the quarters, you whose tusks are mingled with the points of his trident, slay this one who has betrayed our enemy's faction!
For those born from that [enemy] lead to his own destruction, just as the blazing fire born from wood destroys the wood itself."
Parāśara said:
Then that boy was thrown to the surface of the earth by the elephants of the quarters, who resembled mountain peaks,
and was even tormented by their tusks.
As he was remembering Govinda, thousands of the elephant's tusks shattered upon reaching his chest; then he spoke to his father.
Prahlāda said:
"That these tusks of the elephants, as hard as the tip of a thunderbolt, have been shattered is not due to my own strength;
rather, it is the power of recollecting Janārdana, which destroys great calamities and sins."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O Asuras, let the fire be kindled; O elephants of the quarters, withdraw!
O Vāyu, fan the fire; let this evildoer be consumed!"
Parāśara said: Then, having kindled a fire, the Dānavas, urged by their lord, burned the son of the Asura king, who was covered by a great heap of wood.
Prahlāda said:
"O father, although this fire is fanned by the wind, it does not burn me;
here I see all the quarters of the sky as cool, covered with carpets of lotuses."

I always, indeed, forever praise this Sthāṇu, who is the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving—Viṣṇu, the victorious, the powerful, the worthy of praise, the one who makes [all] sufficient, the unconquerable. M2.3 ins: I always, indeed, forever praise this Sthāṇu, who is the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving—Viṣṇu, the victorious, the powerful, the worthy of praise, the one who makes [all] sufficient, the unconquerable. // ViP 1.17.47*54 //
Parāśara said:
Then the sons of Bhārgava, the high-souled and eloquent priests, praised the lord of the Daityas with conciliatory words and spoke to him.
The family priests said: "O King, let your anger be restrained toward this child, your own son;
for your wrath would be more fruitful when directed against the hosts of gods."
Then, as told by his own family priests, Hiraṇyakaśipu was addressed [as follows].
O King, we shall discipline this boy in such a manner that he will become trained for the destruction of his enemies.
Since childhood is the abode of all faults and the very foundation of the Daitya kings,
you ought not to direct excessive anger toward this boy.
"If he does not abandon the side of Hari at our word,
then we shall create an unstoppable magical spell (kṛtyā) for his destruction."
Parāśara said:
Thus entreated by those priests and the Daityas,
the king of the Daityas caused his son to emerge from the mass of fire.
Then, while living in his teacher’s house, that boy repeatedly taught the young sons of the Dānavas during the intervals between his own lessons from the guru.
Prahlāda said:
"Listen, O sons of Diti, offspring of the Daityas, to my ultimate truth;
this must not be thought otherwise, nor is there any cause here such as greed."
After birth, every living being attains childhood and then youth;
thereafter, old age follows day by day without obstruction.
And from that, O sons of the lord of the Daityas, a living being goes to death;
this is seen directly by us as well as by you.
Furthermore, for one who has died, rebirth occurs; this is not otherwise.
This is the traditional teaching (āgama), and likewise, there is no arising without a material cause (upādāna).
From dwelling in the womb until the production of rebirth, let it be understood that all these states are nothing but suffering.
Due to his childish intellect, he considers the allaying of hunger and thirst, as well as the allaying of cold and so forth, to be happiness; yet that, too, is indeed nothing but suffering.
For those whose limbs are utterly exhausted, who seek pleasure through physical exertion,
and who possess deluded cognition, even a blow feels like a source of pleasure.
Where is this body— a vast accumulation of phlegm and all other such impurities— and where are qualities such as physical beauty, fragrance, and charm?
If a fool feels attachment toward this body— a mere collection of flesh, blood, pus, feces, urine, sinews, marrow, and bones— he will find himself even in hell.
Fire produces pleasure through cold, water through thirst, and food through hunger; conversely, these same things produce the opposite effect when they are contrary [to what is needed].
O sons of Daitya, to whatever extent he makes an acquisition,
to that same extent it inflicts suffering upon his mind.
As many beloved connections as a living being forms with the mind,
so many spikes of sorrow are driven deep into his heart.
Whatever is in the house remains in the mind wherever one dwells;
how can there be destruction, burning, or removal of that which persists right there?
In this birth there is great suffering, as is that of one who is dying;
likewise, there is fierce agony in the hells of Yama and during the transitions into the womb.
If even a slight trace of happiness is inferred by you to exist within the womb,
then let it be explained how this entire world is thus composed of nothing but suffering.
Therefore, in this ocean of worldly existence, which is the abode of extreme miseries,
it is truly said to you that Viṣṇu alone is the supreme refuge.
"Do not think that we are fools; the embodied soul is eternal within bodies.
Old age, youth, birth, and so forth are attributes of the body, not of the self."
"As long as I am a child, I shall strive for my welfare according to my desire;
when I am young, I will do so; and once old age has arrived, I shall accomplish what is beneficial for myself."
"I am old; all my duties are beyond my reach.
What shall I, a dull-witted man, do that has not been accomplished by one who was capable?"
In this way, a man whose mind is seized by evil intentions always moves away from what is beneficial; one who is thirsty never turns toward it.
Attached to playthings in childhood, intent upon sense-objects in youth,
they do not realize that old age has arrived due to ignorance and incapacity.
Therefore, while still a child, one whose self is discerning should always strive for the highest good,
remaining unattached to the states of the body such as childhood, youth, and old age.
This which has been told to you by me— if you know it to be no falsehood—
then for our pleasure, let Viṣṇu, the giver of liberation from bondage, be remembered.
What effort is required for his remembrance? When remembered, he bestows auspiciousness;
and for those who remember him day and night, there occurs the destruction of their sins.
May your minds, day and night, be fixed upon Him who dwells within all beings with a spirit of loving-kindness;
in this way, you shall abandon all afflictions.
Since this entire world is afflicted by the threefold suffering,
what wise person would harbor hatred toward beings who are themselves objects of pity?
Furthermore, even if all beings are auspicious while I am of inferior power, one should nevertheless feel joy; for loss is the fruit of hatred.
If beings who have harbored enmity harbor hatred [toward one another], then, alas, they are to be pitied by the wise as being overwhelmed by extreme delusion. (ViP 1.17.82)
These conceptual constructions of those with divergent views have been described by me;
having accepted that, now hear from me the summary.
This entire world is the expansion of Viṣṇu, who is the self of all beings;
therefore, it should be viewed by the wise as non-different from the Self.
Therefore, having cast off this asuric nature, we shall all exert ourselves just as you have done,
so that we may attain final liberation.
Neither by fire, nor by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by the wind; neither by Parjanya nor Varuṇa, nor by the Siddhas, nor by the Rākṣasas.
Neither by Yakṣas, nor by lords of Daityas, nor by Uragas, nor by Kiṃnaras;
neither by humans, nor by animals, nor by faults arising from oneself.
Likewise, [he may suffer] decline due to fever, eye disease, dysentery, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and the like;
or through hatred, envy, malice, and so forth; or through passion, greed, and the like.
It cannot be led by anyone else; it is eternal and utterly pure.
A man attains that [state] by fixing his heart upon the stainless Keśava.
"Do not find satisfaction in wandering through this essence-less saṃsāra; I tell you this emphatically.
O Daityas, attain equanimity toward all things, for equanimity is the means of propitiating Acyuta."
When he is pleased, what is there in this world that cannot be obtained? Dharma, artha, and kāma are of little consequence;
by taking refuge in the infinite tree of Brahman, you will undoubtedly attain a great fruit.
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having observed these actions of that lord of the Daityas, the Dānavas, out of fear, [acted accordingly].
They reported this, and he, having summoned the cooks, spoke to them with haste.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O cooks, this son of mine is evil-minded toward others as well;
let this wicked teacher of the wrong path be killed without delay."
"Let the hālāhala poison be given to him among all the foods;
let that wicked man be executed without being recognized, and let there be no deliberation."
Parāśara said:
Then they did exactly as they were commanded by his father; they administered poison to the high-souled Prahlāda, that great being.
O Maitreya, having consecrated the terrible hālāhala poison with the infinite recitation [of mantras], he then consumed it along with his food.
Having consumed that poison without any change in his condition, Prahlāda, with a composed mind,
digested that most dreadful venom which was powerless against his infinite renown.
Then the cooks, terrified with fear upon seeing the great poison had been digested, approached the lord of the Daityas, prostrated themselves, and spoke as follows: ||| ViP_1,18.7 |||
The Sūdas said: "O King of the Daityas, most terrifying poison was administered by us;
yet it was digested along with the food by your son Prahlāda."
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Hurry, hurry at once, O priests of the Daityas!
Produce a magical spell (kṛtyā) for his destruction without delay!"
Parāśara said: Then the priests of Prahlāda, having approached him,
spoke with conciliation and humility to the disciplined Prahlāda.
The family priests said:
"O long-lived one, you are born in the lineage of Brahmā, renowned throughout the three worlds;
you are the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the king of the Daityas."
What need have you for the gods, what need for Ananta, or what need for anyone else? You shall remain the refuge of all the worlds, even as your father was.
Therefore, abandon her who is allied with your enemies;
your father, the supreme preceptor of all gurus, must be informed.
Prahlāda said:
"It is even so, O highly fortunate ones; this great lineage is praiseworthy.
Within this entire triple world of Marīci, one may not speak otherwise."
And my father is one whose deeds are most excellent in the entire world;
I understand this also to be true, and not false in this regard.
Of all gurus, the father is the supreme guru;
for even the slightest error regarding what he has said does not exist.
"The father is the guru; of this there is no doubt, and he must be honored with great effort.
Even in that regard, 'I shall not offend him'—this is the resolve established in my mind."
As for this which you have stated, "What is the use of Ananta?", who says such a thing? It may be as you suggest, but these words are not meaningful.
Having spoken thus, he became silent, constrained by their respect;
and laughing again, he said: "What is the use of saying 'well done' to Ananta?"
"Excellent, O Ananta! Excellent, O my teachers!
Listen to what Ananta has to say, if you will not be weary."
The goals of human existence (puruṣārtha) are declared to be fourfold, namely dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; since these four exist, why then is this [other pursuit] in vain?
Dharma was attained by Dakṣa together with Marīci and others in infinite numbers; likewise, Artha was attained by some, and Kāma by others.
Having become knowers of those respective principles through knowledge, meditation, and absorption,
other persons, their bonds destroyed, attained liberation.
The propitiation of Hari is the sole root from which may be obtained prosperity, sovereignty, majesty, knowledge, lineage, ritual action, and liberation.
"Since the fruits known as dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation [are obtained] from him, O twice-born ones—what, then, is the use of even such an infinite being? Thus it was said."
What is the use of much speaking here, O venerable ones, my teachers?
Speak what is right or what is wrong; our own discernment is but slight.
What is the use of saying more here? He alone is the Lord of the universe. (ViP 1.18.26*)
He is the creator, the transformer, and the destroyer, abiding within the heart.
He is the enjoyer and likewise the object of enjoyment; he alone is the Lord of the universe.
"You must forgive this which was spoken by me out of childishness."
The family priests said:
"O child, though you were being consumed by us with fire, you were protected [by us] so that you would not speak further; thus you were not recognized as one lacking intelligence."
If you do not abandon this deluded obsession because of our words, then,
O evil-minded one, we shall create a magical spirit (*kṛtyā*) for your destruction.
Prahlāda said:
What living being is protected by whom? What living being is slain by whom?
It is the Self alone that slays and protects the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile.
Everything is born of action; action alone is the means for attaining one's destiny.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform virtuous deeds.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those enraged priests of the Daitya king produced a magical creation (kṛtyā) whose face blazed with a garland of flames.
Approaching with great ferocity, she who mangled the earth with her footsteps,
being highly enraged, then struck him in the chest with her trident.
Having reached the heart of that boy, the blazing spear shattered upon the ground and there too it split into a hundred pieces.
Wherever the Lord Hari, the imperishable Sovereign, dwells within the heart, there even the thunderbolt is shattered; what then to say of a mere spear?
Although he was sinless, she was cast down there by the sinful sacrificers of the Daityas;
she swiftly slew those very men and then herself met her destruction.
Seeing them being consumed by that magical spell, the high-minded one approached them, crying out, "Save us, O Kṛṣṇa! Save us, O Ananta!"
Prahlāda said:
O all-pervading one, whose form is the world, creator of the world, Janārdana!
Protect these brahmins from this unbearable fire of mantras.
Just as Viṣṇu alone is the all-pervading teacher of the world among all beings, so may all these domestic priests live.
Just as I regard Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent and never-failing, so do I think even of those on the side of my enemies: "May these twice-born ones live."
By those who came to kill me, by those who gave poison, by those who kindled the fire, by those world-elephants by whom I was crushed, and by those serpents by whom I was bitten; ||| ViP_1,18.39 |||
I am impartial toward them and toward my own circle of friends; I have committed no sin anywhere.
By that truth, may the sacrificers for the Asuras live today!
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by him, all those twice-born ones, touched by him, rose up free from affliction and spoke to him with humility.
The family priests said:
"O child, may you be long-lived, unassailable, endowed with strength and heroism, and preeminent, possessed of sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty."
Parāśara said:
O great sage, having spoken thus to him and then departed, the priests related everything exactly as it had occurred to the king of the Daityas.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having heard that the magical spell had been rendered futile, Hiraṇyakaśipu—
Having summoned his son, he asked him the cause of this power.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Prahlāda, you possess great power; what is this behavior of yours?
Is it produced by mantras and the like, or is it innate to you?"
Parāśara said:
Thus questioned by his father, the Asura youth Prahlāda prostrated at his father’s feet and spoke these words.
"O dear one, this power of mine is neither produced by mantras and the like, nor is it innate;
rather, it is common to whomever Acyuta resides in the heart."
O dear one, for him who does not contemplate the misdeeds of others as he would his own,
the arrival of sin does not exist due to the absence of its cause.
He who inflicts suffering upon others by deed, thought, or word,
that seed bears for him a profuse and inauspicious fruit in his next birth.
Therefore, I desire no evil, nor do I commit it, nor do I speak it;
for I meditate upon Keśava as abiding in all beings and within myself as well.
How could physical, mental, divine, or elemental suffering ever arise for me, whose mind is everywhere auspicious?
Thus, having realized that Hari consists of all beings, the wise should practice unwavering devotion toward all living creatures.
Parāśara said:
Having heard this, that lord of the Daityas, standing upon the roof-peak of his palace,
his face darkened by rage, spoke to the servants of the Daityas.
"Let this evil-souled one be hurled from this palace a hundred yojanas high;
let him fall upon the mountain peak with his mass of limbs shattered by rocks."
Then all those servants of the Daityas threw that boy down;
yet even when thrown, he fell facing downwards, bearing Hari within his heart.
As he was falling, the Earth, the sustainer of the world, approached Keśava, the sustainer of the world,
and supported him with devotion.
Then, seeing him composed with his skeletal joints unbroken,
Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke to Śambara, the best among magicians.
"We are not able to kill this boy of wicked conduct;
you, however, know the art of illusion (māyā), therefore destroy him by means of illusion."
Śambara said:
"O Lord of Daityas, here I destroy [you]; behold my power of illusion!
Behold here a thousand illusions, and likewise hundreds of millions."
Parāśara said:
Then the evil-minded Asura Śambara, desiring his destruction, unleashed illusions against Prahlāda, who perceives the same everywhere.
Having composed his mind and being free from envy even toward Śambara,
that Prahlāda, O Maitreya, also called to mind Madhusūdana.
Then, for his protection, the supreme discus Sudarśana, garlanded with flames, arrived as it had been commanded by the Blessed One.
By him, moving with great speed, that thousandfold illusion of Śambara was destroyed one by one as he protected the body of the boy.
Then the lord of the Daityas spoke thus to the wind that causes desiccation:
"By my command, let this evil-souled one be swiftly led to his destruction."
Having said "So be it," that wind also swiftly entered him—
cool yet exceedingly harsh, unbearable for the drying up of his body.
Perceiving himself thus possessed by him, the young Daitya held that Great Soul,
the Supporter of the Earth, within his heart.
Then Janārdana, filled with wrath, drank up that excessively drying wind situated within his heart; thus that wind went to its destruction.
When all illusions had perished and the wind had subsided,
that highly intelligent one also went to the abode of his preceptor.
Then, day after day, the preceptor taught that boy the political science composed by Uśanas, which yields the fruit of sovereignty for kings.
When the teacher perceived that he had been disciplined and had mastered the science of ethics,
he then informed his father that he had been instructed.
The Teacher said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, your son Prahlāda has been made a master of the treatises on political ethics;
he knows in truth that which was uttered by Bhārgava."

Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O Prahlāda, how should a king behave toward his friends, toward the ranks of his enemies, and how should he conduct himself toward those who are neutral during the three periods of time?"
How [did he act] toward his ministers and counselors, both those from outside and those from within, toward his spies and the body of citizens, and toward those who were suspected as well as others?
O Prahlāda, let the rules for what ought and ought not to be done, the means of subduing forts and forest tribes, and likewise the clearing away of thorns, be properly explained.
Just as you have studied all this and more, let it be told to me; I wish to know what is in your mind.
Parāśara said: Then Prahlāda, adorned with humility, having prostrated at his father’s feet,
stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke to the lord of the Daityas.
Prahlāda said:
"Everything has been taught to me by my teacher; there is no doubt about this.
And it has been grasped by me, yet this doctrine is not considered true by me."
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment—
these are indeed declared to be the means for winning over friends and others.
"I do not see those very things—friends and the rest, my dear—so do not be angry.
O mighty-armed one, in the absence of that which is to be accomplished (the goal), what is the use of the means?"
O dear one, since Govinda is the self of all beings, the lord of the world, and identical with the world—
the Supreme Self— whence can there be any talk of friend or foe?
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu resides in you, in me, and elsewhere as well;
since he is everywhere, how can there be a distinction such as "this one is my friend" or "that one is my enemy"?
Therefore, enough with these excessively detailed discourses on evil undertakings, which are rooted in ignorance; O dear one, you should instead apply yourself to what is auspicious.
O dear one, O Lord of Asuras, the notion of knowledge regarding ignorance arises from lack of understanding; does a child not mistake a firefly for a flame?
That action which does not lead to bondage is knowledge, while that which leads to liberation is also knowledge; other action leads to weariness, and other knowledge is merely skill in the arts.
Having understood this, O illustrious one, listen to what I say after prostrating myself: that which is the supreme goal, though it appears to be without substance.
No one reflects upon who shall possess the kingdom or who shall desire wealth;
nevertheless, both of these are inevitably obtained by men.
O highly fortunate one, all beings indeed exert effort toward greatness;
nevertheless, for men, it is their fortunes, not their efforts, that are the cause of prosperity.
O Lord, even for those who are dull-witted, lacking discrimination, and unheroic—
even for those devoid of statesmanship— kingdoms exist as things to be enjoyed through sheer fortune.
Therefore, one who desires great prosperity should strive for meritorious deeds;
and by one who desires even Nirvana, equanimity must be pursued.
Gods, humans, animals, birds, trees, and reptiles—
this entire form of the infinite Viṣṇu stands as if it were divided.
One who understands this should regard the entire world, both stationary and moving,
as being like the Self, because this Viṣṇu assumes the form of the universe.
When he is thus known, that Blessed One, the beginningless Supreme Lord, the Infallible, becomes gracious; when he is gracious, there is the destruction of the afflictions.
Parāśara said:
Having heard this, Hiraṇyakaśipu rose up from his excellent throne in a rage and struck his son on the chest with his foot.
And he spoke with fury, as if blazing with indignation,
wringing his hands together like one desiring to destroy the world.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Vipracitti, O Rāhu, O Bala! Having bound him firmly with serpent-nooses in this great ocean, let him be cast in; do not delay!"
Otherwise, all the worlds, as well as the Daityas and Dānavas,
will follow the opinion of this foolish and evil-minded man.
Although we have repeatedly restrained this wicked one, he nevertheless offers praise to our enemy; for the very killing of the evil is a service.
Parāśara said:
Then those Daityas, acting with haste and honoring their master’s command, bound him with serpent-nooses and cast him into the ocean.
Then, as Prahlāda moved, the great ocean shook;
it overflowed its shores and reached a state of extreme agitation on all sides.
O great sage, having seen the entire world of Bhūr being flooded by the great waters, Hiraṇyakaśipu said this to the Daityas: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19.57.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O sons of Diti, let this evil-minded one be piled up right here in the abode of Varuṇa with all the mountains, on every side and without any gaps."
Fire does not burn him, nor is he cut by weapons,
nor is he brought to destruction by serpents, by wind, by poison, or by magical spells.
"He has not been brought down by illusions, nor by falling from a height, nor by the elephants of the quarters;
this boy is of an exceedingly wicked mind, and there is no purpose in his remaining alive."
Therefore, let this ocean, overwhelmed here by these mountains, remain for the end of a thousand years; the evil-minded one shall lose his life.
Then the Daityas and Dānavas, having overwhelmed him with mountains in the great ocean,
constructed a sacrificial altar extending for thousands of yojanas.
That high-minded one, situated within the ocean amidst the mountains,
praised Acyuta with one-pointed mind at the time of his daily ritual.
Prahlāda said:
Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one; homage to you, O Supreme Person;
homage to you, the self of all worlds; homage to you, the wielder of the sharp discus.
Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to Him who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins;
homage again and again to Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, for the welfare of the world.
Obeisance to you, the threefold form, who as Brahmā creates the universe, and again protects it during its maintenance; and who, in the form of Rudra, [dissolves it] at the end of the aeon.
Gods, yakṣas, asuras, siddhas, nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras,
piśācas, rākṣasas, humans, and likewise animals.
Birds, as well as stationary beings, ants, and reptiles;
earth, water, fire, ether, wind, sound, touch, and likewise taste.
Form, smell, mind, intellect, the self, time, and likewise the qualities—
O Acyuta, you are all these and their ultimate reality as well.
You are truly knowledge and ignorance, truth and falsehood, poison and nectar;
you are the action enjoined by the Vedas, both that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to its cessation.
O Viṣṇu, you alone are the enjoyer of all karma, as well as the instruments of karma, and whatever fruit results from all karma.
O Lord, your pervasion alone— indicative of the quality of sovereignty— extends through me, through others, as well as through all beings and all worlds.
Yogis meditate upon you, and sacrificers worship you;
you alone are the consumer of the oblations to gods and ancestors, assuming the forms of both the deities and the manes.
O Acyuta, Your form is great, wherein the universe resides and from which this subtle world proceeds, O Lord;
the subtle forms are the various elements, and within them is that which is called the inner self, exceedingly subtle.
And because that ultimate form of yours, which is beyond the scope of qualifiers such as "subtle" and so forth,
is some inconceivable form of yours— homage to you, the Supreme Person!
O Soul of all, O Lord of gods, salutations to that eternal, inferior power of yours which resides in all beings and rests upon the qualities (guṇas).
I bow to that supreme Sovereign Goddess, who transcends the range of words and the mind, who is without distinctions, and who is to be discerned by the knowledge of the wise.
Oṃ, salutations always to that Blessed One, Vāsudeva,
for whom there is nothing separate, and who is separate from everything.
Salutations to him, salutations to him, salutations to that Great Self,
whose name and form are not [perceived], and who alone is apprehended through his mere existence.
Salutations to that Great Soul, whose forms as incarnations the gods worship while failing to perceive his supreme form.
I bow to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord and witness of all, who, dwelling within the entirety of creation, beholds both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Homage be to that Viṣṇu, for whom this world is non-different;
may he, the primordial source of the worlds, the imperishable one, be gracious toward me.
May that Hari, in whom this entire universe is woven both lengthwise and crosswise within that which is designated as the Imperishable (akṣara), and who is the support of all, be gracious to me.
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation again and again to Him, in whom is all, from whom is all, who is all, and who is everywhere.
Because the Infinite is all-pervading, He alone abides as I;
from me everything proceeds, I am everything, and everything exists within me, the Eternal.
I alone am the imperishable and eternal Supreme Self, the refuge of all selves;
I alone am known as Brahman in the beginning, and likewise at the end, the Supreme Person.
[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, thus reflecting upon Viṣṇu as non-different from his own self—
He attained supreme absorption in that and considered himself to be the infallible Acyuta.
He thus forgot his own self and was unaware of anything else;
he thought, "I alone am the imperishable, infinite Supreme Self."
Because of his application to that meditation, his sins were gradually exhausted;
then, when his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) was purified, the imperishable Viṣṇu, who consists of knowledge, took up residence within him.
O Maitreya, when the asura Prahlāda had become one with Viṣṇu through the power of yoga, those serpent-bonds that were holding him began to move and snapped in an instant.
The great ocean, with its multitude of crocodiles and its surging waves, was thrown into agitation;
and the entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
Then that high-minded one, having cast back upon himself that mass of rocks placed by the Daityas, emerged from those waters.
And having again beheld the world characterized by the sky and other elements, Prahlāda remembered himself by means of his own mind, thinking, "I am [Prahlāda]."
And once again, the wise one, with a one-pointed mind, undistracted, and with his speech, body, and mind restrained, praised the beginningless Supreme Person.
Prahlāda said:
Oṃ, salutations to you, the ultimate reality, the goal; to the gross and the subtle, the perishable and the imperishable;
to the manifest and the unmanifest, beyond all parts, the Lord of all, the stainless one.
O you who are the collyrium of qualities, the substratum of qualities, whose self is beyond qualities yet abides within them;
O you who are both with form and without form, the great-formed, the subtle-formed, the manifest, and the unmanifest!
O Acyuta, whose nature consists of both terrible and gentle forms; O you who are composed of both knowledge and ignorance;
O you whose true being is both existent and non-existent; O you who contemplate the states of both existence and non-existence.

O You who are both eternal and non-eternal, whose nature transcends the manifold world, the stainless substratum beyond all conceptual proliferation, the one and the many— homage to You, Vāsudeva, the primordial cause!

Salutation be to that Supreme Person, who is both gross and subtle, manifest and luminous; who is all beings and yet not all beings; and from whom this universe proceeds, though he is not the cause of the universe.
Parāśara said:
As he was thus offering praise with that mind,
the Blessed Lord Hari, wearing yellow garments, appeared before him.
Seeing him with agitation, the twice-born rose up and, with faltering words, repeatedly uttered this: "Homage be to Viṣṇu!"
Prahlāda said:
O Lord, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, O Keśava, show me favor; O Imperishable One, purify me once again by granting me your glance.
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with you for performing this unwavering devotion;
O Prahlāda, choose from me whatever boon you desire."
Prahlāda said:
O Lord, in whatever thousands of wombs I may enter,
may my devotion to You, O Acyuta, remain forever unswerving toward You, the Imperishable.
May that pleasure which the undiscriminating feel toward sense objects, and which never departs from them, depart from my heart as I remember you.
The Blessed Lord said:
"You indeed possess devotion toward me; it shall be even greater still.
O Prahlāda, choose from me whatever boon you desire."
Prahlāda said: "O Lord, because of my praise of you, an attachment to hatred arose in my father; may the sin committed by him toward me perish."
Weapons were hurled at my limbs, and I was cast into a mass of fire;
I was bitten by serpents, and poison was placed in my food.
Whether I was bound and cast into the ocean, or whether I was piled up with heaps of rocks, and whatever other misdeeds were committed against me by my father; ||| ViP_1,20.23 |||
O Lord, by Your grace, may my father be instantly liberated from the sin arising from his hatred toward one who is devoted to You, as well as from whatever [suffering] is born thereof.
The Blessed One said: "O Prahlāda, all this shall come to pass for you through my grace;
and I grant you another boon—choose it, O son of the Asuras."
Prahlāda said:
O Blessed One, I have achieved my purpose through this boon, in that by your grace there shall be unswerving devotion toward you. *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 1.20.26.
What need has he for dharma, artha, or kāma? Liberation stands in his very hand, he whose devotion to you is firm at the root of the entire world.
The Blessed One said:
"Since your mind is thus unwavering and endowed with devotion toward me, you shall,
by my grace, attain supreme liberation."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O Maitreya, Viṣṇu vanished while he was looking on;
and he, having returned once more, prostrated at the feet of his father.
Having smelled him on the head and embraced him tenderly, the father, his eyes moist with tears, said, "Do you live, my child? O twice-born one.
The great Asura became full of joy and free from remorse;
likewise, that knower of dharma performed service to his preceptor and father.
O Maitreya, when his father had been brought to his end by Viṣṇu in the form of Narasiṃha, he then became the lord of the Daityas.
O twice-born one, having attained that royal prosperity which purifies one's karma,
and having obtained many sons and grandsons as well as sovereign power, [he shall dwell in heaven].
When his office had expired and he was freed from both merit and sin,
he then attained supreme nirvāṇa through meditation upon the Blessed One.
Such was the power of that high-minded Daitya Prahlāda, O Maitreya,
who was a devotee of the Blessed One, about whom you have questioned me.
But whoever hears this life-story of that great-souled Prahlāda, his sins immediately go to complete destruction.
O Maitreya, by hearing and reciting the life-story of Prahlāda, a person undoubtedly dispels the sin committed during a day and a night.
O twice-born one, by reciting this on the full moon day, the new moon day, the eighth day,
or the twelfth day, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
Just as Hari protected Prahlāda from all calamities,
so does he protect whoever constantly hears his life-story.
Compassionate toward those who bow at his feet, and beautiful toward those who are hostile when prostrate.
I bow to the one who grants boons to Prahlāda, who is both terrifying as Narasiṃha and compassionate.
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The sons of Saṃhlāda were Āyuṣmat, Śibi, and Bāṣkala.
Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, begot Bali from Virocana.
O great sage, Bali had a hundred sons with Bāṇa as the eldest;
and all the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were likewise possessed of great strength.
Jharjhara, Śakuni, and likewise Bhūtasaṃtāpana;
Mahānābha, Mahābāhu, and another, Kālanābha.
And the sons of Danu were Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkara,
Ayomukha, Śaṅkuśiras, Kapila, and Śambara.
Ekacakra, the long-armed Tāraka of great strength,
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the very powerful Puloman.
These are known as the sons of Danu, along with the powerful Vipracitti.
Svarbhānu’s daughter was Prabhā, and Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan; Upadānavī, Hayaśiras, and the famous Varakanyakā were also his daughters.
Both Vaiśvānarasūti and Pulomā were likewise Kālakā;
both of those illustrious women became the wives of Mārīci.
From those two were born sixty thousand sons, the most excellent of the Dānavas,
known as the Paulomas and Kālakeyas, the offspring of Mārīca.
Then others of great prowess, who were cruel and exceedingly pitiless,
were likewise born from Siṃhikā as the sons of Vipracitti.
Tryaṃśa, the powerful Śalya, and the exceedingly mighty Nabhas;
likewise Vātāpi, Namuci, Ilvala, and Khasṛma.
And Andhaka, as well as Kālanābha,
and the great Asura Svarbhānu, who possessed immense prowess and fought with his mouth.
These indeed were the foremost of the Dānavas, the increasers of Danu’s lineage;
their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
In the lineage of the Daitya Prahlāda, the Nivātakavacas were born,
their souls purified by great ascetic penance.
Six sons of great being are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Śuci, and Gṛdhrikā.
Śukī gave birth to parrots, Ulūkī to owls,
Śyenī to hawks, Bhāsī to bhāsa birds, and Gṛdhri also to vultures.
Sugrīvī gave birth to the pure water-birds;
the horses, camels, and donkeys are proclaimed to be the offspring of Tāmrā.
Vinatā had two famous sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa;
Suparṇa was the best of those who fly, while Aruṇa was fierce and a devourer of serpents.
O Brahmin, there were a thousand great-souled serpents of immeasurable power belonging to Surasā, who possessed many heads and moved through the sky.
O Brahmin, a thousand powerful sons of Kadrū, possessed of immeasurable energy and having many heads, were born under the dominion of Suparṇa.
Among them, the principal ones were Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka,
Śaṅkha, Śveta, Mahāpadma, and both Kambala and Aśvatara.
Elāputra, as well as the nāgas Karkoṭaka and Dhanañjaya—
these and many other venomous serpents with fierce poison [were there].
Know that the Gaṇa Krodhavaśa consists of all those fanged creatures—
beasts of the land, birds, and aquatic beings— who are fierce and flesh-eaters.
Out of anger, however, he gave birth to the Piśācas of great strength. (Ś, D1.7, ed. Veṅk.)
Surabhi likewise gave birth to cows and buffaloes,
as well as trees, creepers, climbing plants, and all varieties of grasses.
Khaṣā gave birth to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, while Muni likewise gave birth to the Apsarases;
Ariṣṭā, however, gave birth to the Gandharvas of great being.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been proclaimed;
their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
This creation is recorded as having occurred during the Svārociṣa Manvantara, O Brahmin,
and during the great Vaivasvata Manvantara at the extensive sacrifice of Varuṇa.
The creation of progeny by Brahmā while performing sacrifice is here described,
wherein the seven mind-born Saptarṣis were previously produced.
O best of beings, the Grandfather himself ordained [him] as the son of the Gandharvas, the Bhogis, the gods, and the Dānavas.
Diti, whose sons had indeed been destroyed, propitiated Kaśyapa;
and Kaśyapa, the best of those who practice austerities, was duly honored by her.
He invited her to choose a boon, and she then chose this boon:
a son of immeasurable splendor, capable of slaying Indra.
And that best of sages granted a boon to his wife;
having bestowed the boon, Kaśyapa, remaining unperturbed, spoke to her.
"Your son shall slay Śakra [Indra] if the fetus remains for a hundred autumns."
O fair-complexioned lady, a pregnant woman must never eat during the twilight hours.
One should never stand nor eat at the roots of trees.
Composed, exceedingly diligent, and pure, you shall maintain it.
Having spoken thus to that goddess, the sage Kaśyapa departed;
and she, endowed with perfect purity, conceived that embryo.
Having learned that she was pregnant for the purpose of taking his own life, Maghavan,
the lord of the immortals, approached her with humility, desiring to serve her.
Seeking a lapse in her conduct, the subduer of Pāka remained there;
when the hundred years were nearly complete, the self-possessed one perceived a vulnerability.
Without having performed the purification of her feet, Diti went to bed and fell asleep;
he entered her womb.
Then Vajrapāṇi cut that Mahāgarbha into seven pieces;
as he was being split by the vajra, he wailed most piteously.
"Do not weep," Śakra said to him again and again;
yet that embryo split into seven parts, and Indra became enraged once more.
With his thunderbolt that rends enemies, he split each one of them into seven parts;
they became the gods known as the Maruts, who were exceedingly swift.
By that very act which was spoken by Maghavan, the Maruts became the forty-nine gods who were the companions of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the first book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Parāśara said:
When that Pṛthu was formerly consecrated in the kingdom by the great seers,
Then, in due order, the Grandfather of the World bestowed the kingdoms.
Brahmā appointed Soma to the sovereignty over the stars, the planets, the Brahmins, and all plants without exception, as well as over sacrifices and ascetic penances.
Among kings, he appointed Vaiśravaṇa to the kingdom; likewise, Varuṇa over the waters;
Viṣṇu as the lord of the Ādityas; and Pāvaka (Fire) over the Vasus.
He appointed Dakṣa as the lord of the Prajāpatis, Vāsava of the Maruts,
and Prahlāda as the sovereign of the Daityas and Dānavas.
D7 inserts: He gave Vāsava as the overlord of the Maruts, the sons of Diti.
He consecrated Yama, the King of Dharma, in the sovereignty over the ancestors,
and gave Airāvata as the lord of all the elephant-kings without exception.
Among winged creatures he is Garuḍa; among the gods, Vāsava;
among horses, Uccaiḥśravas; and among cattle, the bull.
After verse 6, D₃, T₂.₃, M₀, and G₃ insert; while G₃ inserts line 1 of *63 and the margin continues:
himālayaṃ sthāvarāṇāṃ munīnāṃ kapilaṃ munim // ViP_1,22.6*62 //
But Śeṣa among the serpent kings, and the lion as the lord of wild beasts.
For 7ab, D₄ and G₁.₂ substitute [the following], while G₃ inserts line 1 after verse 6 and line 2 before 7cd;
M₀ inserts line 2 only after 7ab; and M₃.₄ substitute line 1 only for 7ab: [Insert lines here]
The Lord also appointed a lion as king over all the deer.
And for the carnivorous, fanged beasts, he appointed the tiger as their lord.
He consecrated the Plakṣa tree as the king of the lords of the forest (vanaspati).
Having thus divided the castes, he established lords over them according to their preeminence.
Having thus divided the kingdoms, Brahmā, the Lord of the Progenitors, immediately thereafter established the guardians of the quarters everywhere.
In the eastern direction, he consecrated Sudhanvan as king, the guardian of the quarter and the sovereign of Vairāja Prajāpati.
Likewise, in the southern direction, he consecrated the son of the Prajāpati Kardama,
named Śaṅkhapada, as king.
In the western direction,
he consecrated the high-souled Ketumān, the son of Rajas and the infallible king.
Likewise, he consecrated Hiraṇyaroman as the invincible king over the northern quarter of Parjanya Prajāpati.
By them, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its forests—
is even today protected according to their respective regions and in accordance with righteousness.
O best of sages, all these kings and others who exist are manifestations of the power of the high-souled Viṣṇu while he is engaged in the work of world-maintenance.
O twice-born one, those who will be and those who have been— all the lords of beings—
are portions of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings, O best of the twice-born.
Those who were the lords of the gods, as well as the lords of the Daityas,
those who were the masters of the Dānavas, and those who were the masters of the flesh-eaters;
Those who are the lords of beasts, those who are the lords of birds, and those who are the sovereigns over humans, serpents, and nāgas; ||| ViP_1,22.17 |||
Those who are the lords of trees, mountains, and even the planets—
those of the past, those of the present, and those others who will exist in the future—
all of them have arisen from a portion of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings.
For indeed, O highly wise one, the capacity for protection does not belong to anyone else established in the state of maintenance except for Hari, the Lord of All.
This eternal one creates the world during its creation, protects it during its maintenance,
and destroys it during its dissolution, relying upon the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
Divided into four parts in his manifestation, Janārdana exists established in a fourfold manner; at the end, he brings about dissolution through his fourfold division.
By one portion he becomes Brahmā, possessing an unmanifest form;
by another portion, he becomes the lords of creatures together with Marīci and the others.
Time is its third part, and all beings are its other part;
thus, this quality of passion (rajas) exists in a fourfold combination.
Established in one part, Viṣṇu performs the task of protection;
in another part, he appears in the form of Manu and others, and in yet another, he takes the form of Time.
And abiding elsewhere within all beings,
the Supreme Person establishes his presence by relying upon the quality of *sattva* for the sake of the world.
Likewise, at the time of the end, the unborn Lord, assuming the form of Rudra, resorts to the function of darkness and becomes manifest with one portion.
He exists through one portion in the form of Agni, Antaka, and others;
another portion is the nature of Time (kāla), and yet another is all living beings.
O Brahmin, as that great-souled one was undergoing destruction, this fourfold conceptualization of his division is described as being applicable at all times.
Brahmā, Dakṣa and the others, Time, and likewise all living beings—
these are the manifestations of Hari, the causes of the creation of the world.
O twice-born one, Viṣṇu, Manu and the others, time, and all living beings—
these are the manifestations of Viṣṇu, who is the instrumental cause of their continued existence.
Rudra, Kāla, Antaka, and all living beings—
these are the manifestations of Janārdana for the fourfold dissolution.
O twice-born one, in the beginning, in the middle, and until the dissolution of the world, the creation is performed by the Creator,
by Marīci and the others, and likewise by living beings.
In the beginning of time, Brahmā creates; thereafter, Marīci and the others produce offspring, and living beings are born at every moment.
O twice-born one, without Time, neither Brahmā is the accomplisher of creation,
nor all the Prajāpatis, nor indeed all living beings.
In this very same way, O Maitreya, this fourfold division of the God of gods is taught to exist even during the period of stability, as it is likewise at the time of dissolution.
O twice-born one, whatever being is created by whatever means,
in the production of all that which is created, everything indeed is the body of Hari.
O Maitreya, that fierce form of Janārdana, which destroys whatever being exists anywhere, whether stationary or moving, is his form that brings about the end of all things.
In this very way, Janārdana is the creator of the world, the protector of the world, as well as the consumer of the world— the God of all.
Thus, at the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he proceeds in these three ways through the activity of the qualities (guṇas); yet his supreme state is great and devoid of qualities.
And that [nature] consists of knowledge, is all-pervading, self-cognizable, and incomparable;
it is the fourfold essential nature of the Supreme Self.
Maitreya said:
O Sage, explain to me according to the proper method the fourfold nature of that which has become Brahman, which is called the supreme state.
Parāśara said: O Maitreya, the cause has been declared as the means for all things,
as well as the desired object to be accomplished by oneself.
For the yogin desiring liberation, the practice consists of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other such means,
and the goal to be attained is the Supreme Brahman, from which one does not return again.
O Sage, that knowledge which is the support for the means of liberation for yogins is indeed the first division of that [knowledge] which has become wisdom.

O Great Sage, that consciousness which takes as its object that which is to be accomplished by the Brahman-yogin who exerts himself for the sake of liberation from the afflictions— that is the second part.
Indeed, that non-dual consciousness which arises from the inseparable union of both the means and the end— that other aspect has been described by me.
O Great Sage, the distinction between these three types of knowledge is like the true nature of the Self, which is revealed through the door of their negation.
It is devoid of activity, ineffable, mere pervasion, incomparable,
the object of self-awakening, pure existence, and without defining characteristics.
Tranquil, fearless, pure, difficult to conceive, and without support—
that which is declared as the knowledge of Viṣṇu, who consists of knowledge, is that supreme state.
In that regard, O twice-born one, those yogins who attain dissolution through the cessation of ignorance reach a state of seedlessness when sown in the field of saṃsāra.
Such is the supreme state called Viṣṇu: stainless, eternal, all-pervading, imperishable, and devoid of everything that is to be abandoned.
That is the supreme Brahman from which the yogi does not return again;
when merit and demerit have ceased, his afflictions are exhausted, and he is utterly stainless.
That Brahman has two forms, both the embodied and the unembodied;
these consist of the perishable and the imperishable, and they abide within all beings.
That Imperishable is the Supreme Brahman; this entire world is the Perishable.
Just as the moonlight spreads out from the moon situated in one place, so too is this entire universe the power (śakti) of the Supreme Brahman.
Even there, O Maitreya, a distinction in the moonlight exists due to its power, consisting of greater or lesser intensity according to whether it is near or far; so it is in this case as well.
O Brahmin, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the primary powers of Brahman;
after them, O Maitreya, come the gods, and after them, Dakṣa and the others.
From that [arose] humans, cattle, wild animals, birds, and reptiles;
and from that, those inferior and even more inferior, such as trees, shrubs, and so forth.
Thus, O best of sages, this entire world is imperishable and eternal,
yet it possesses the conceptual distinctions of manifestation and disappearance, and of birth and destruction.
Viṣṇu, who consists of all powers, is the secondary form of Brahman,
which is embodied and meditated upon by yogis at the commencement of their practice.
O Sage, for those who practice correctly with an undisturbed mind, the great yoga with an object and with seed arises when it is firmly established therein.
He is the supreme among all powers, the immediate successor to Brahmā;
O fortunate one, Hari is the embodied Brahman, consisting of the entirety of Brahman.
In that [Brahman], O Sage, this entire world is woven as warp and woof;
therefore, the world is within the world, and that [Brahman] is the entire world.
Lord Viṣṇu, consisting of both the perishable and the imperishable, sustains the entire universe—
composed of the Puruṣa and the unevolved (avyākṛta)— in the form of his ornaments and weapons.
Maitreya said:
You ought to explain to me how the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu sustains this entire world, which exists in the form of ornaments and weapons.
Parāśara said: Having paid homage to the immeasurable Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord,
I shall relate to you what was told to me by Vasiṣṭha.
The Blessed Lord Hari bears his own self, which is untainted, free from qualities, and stainless, in the form of the Kaustubha gem for this world.
D7 inserts: [He saw] the Self of this world, the Puruṣa, pure and the knower of the Kṣatra.
Bearing the mark of Śrīvatsa and resting upon Ananta,
Pradhāna and Buddhi also abide in Mādhava in the form of a mace.
The Lord bears the twofold ego— consisting of the elements and the senses—
in the form of the conch and in the form of the Śārṅga bow.
The mind, whose nature is to move and which surpasses the wind in speed,
assumes the form of a wheel while abiding in the hand of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, that fivefold garland of Vaijayantī belonging to the wielder of the mace is indeed a collection of the causes of all beings; thus it is truly called the Bhūtamālā.
Janārdana indeed sustains all the sense organs without exception, which consist of both intellect and action, as well as all the forms of the body without exception.
And that sword-jewel which Acyuta bears is utterly stainless;
it consists of knowledge, yet it is encased in the skin of ignorance.
In this manner, O Maitreya, both the Spirit (puruṣa) and primordial matter (pradhāna), as well as the intellect (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra),
the elements, the mind, all the senses, knowledge and ignorance— all of this is entirely supported by Hṛṣīkeśa.

Though devoid of material form, Hari, who possesses a form created by his creative power (māyā), assumes the nature, appearance, and configuration of weapons and ornaments for the welfare of living beings.
The lotus-eyed one sustains the primary matter (pradhāna) along with its modifications, as well as the individual soul (puruṣa) and the entire world; thus is the Supreme Lord.
Whatever is knowledge and whatever is ignorance, whatever is existent and whatever is non-existent in the imperishable— that all, O Maitreya, resides in Madhusūdana, the Lord of all beings.
Through the divisions of time such as *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *nimeṣa*, up to days, seasons, solstices,
and years, the Lord Hari— the shoreless and imperishable— is the very nature of time.
O best of sages, the Lord [created] these seven worlds: Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya.
The embodiment of the self of the worlds, the first-born even of all the ancients,
Hari himself stands as the foundation of all branches of knowledge.
The all-pervading Lord, the infinite Sovereign of all, who possesses no form yet assumes the forms of all beings, exists through many manifestations such as gods, humans, and animals.
The Ṛg-veda, Yajur-veda, Sāma-veda, and likewise the Atharva-veda;
the Itihāsas, the Upavedas, and the declarations found within the Vedāntas.
All the Vedāṅgas, the treatises proclaimed by Manu and others, all the scriptures without exception, and whatever narratives or recitations exist anywhere; ||| ViP_1,22.82 |||
Whatever poetic compositions there may be, and all songs whatsoever—
these are the body of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears sound as his form.
Whatever classes of entities exist— whether they are corporeal or incorporeal, whether here or elsewhere—
they are all indeed his body.
"I am Hari; all this is Janārdana; there is no other collection of causes and effects than that.
For one whose mind is thus disposed, the diseases of the dualities arising from worldly existence do not recur.
"Thus, O twice-born one, this first portion of this Purāṇa has been duly told to you; by hearing which, one is liberated from sins."
O Maitreya, whatever fruit a person obtains by bathing at Puṣkara for twelve years on the full moon day of Kārttika, all that he attains simply by hearing this.
O Sage, as a man hears of the origin of the gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, and others, the gods and the rest become bestowers of boons upon him.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the first book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. The first book is completed.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, O Guru, you have related to me in its entirety all that pertains to the creation of the world about which I questioned you.
O best of sages, regarding this portion concerning the creation of the world which has been narrated by you, I desire to hear it once more.
Of the two sons of Svāyambhuva, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda,
you have mentioned that Dhruva was the son of Uttānapāda.
"O twice-born one, you have not yet mentioned the progeny of Priyavrata;
I wish to hear about it, so please, being gracious, deign to speak."
Parāśara said:
Priyavrata married the daughter of Kardama;
Samrāṭ and Kukṣi were his two daughters, and there were likewise ten other sons.
They were possessed of great wisdom and great heroism, disciplined and beloved by their father;
they were the renowned sons of Priyavrata—listen to their names from me.
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vapuṣmat, Dyutimat, as well as Medhā, Medhātithi, Bhavya, Savana, and Putra.
Jyotiṣmat was the tenth among them; his son was Satyanāman, who was renowned for his strength and heroism among the sons of Priyavrata.
Medhāgni, Bāhu, and Putra—these three were devoted to yoga;
being highly fortunate and possessing the memory of their past lives, they did not set their minds upon sovereignty.
O Sage, at all times they were indeed free from possessiveness regarding all objects; performing their duties according to what was right, they were indeed seekers of no reward.
O best of sages, O Maitreya, Priyavrata divided the seven continents among those seven high-souled ones and gave them to them.
O highly fortunate one, his father gave Jambūdvīpa to Agnīdhra,
and likewise bestowed the other, Plakṣadvīpa, upon Medhātithi.
And on Śālmala, the Lord consecrated Vapuṣmat as the lord of men;
he made Jyotiṣmat the king in Kuśadvīpa.
And Priyavrata appointed Dyutimat as the king in Krauñcadvīpa,
and he also made Bhavya the lord of Śākadvīpa.
That lord also made Savana the ruler of Puṣkara;
and he who was Āgnīdhra, O best of sages, became the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa.
He had nine sons who were equal to the Prajāpatis.
Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta,
Ramya, Hiraṇvān as the sixth, Kuru, Bhadrāśva, and another, Ketumāla— these were the kings who acted with virtuous conduct.
O Brahmin, listen now to the divisions of Jambūdvīpa:
the region called Himavat was given by his father to Nābhi as his southern portion.
He gave the region of Hemakūṭa to Kiṃpuruṣa,
and he gave the third region, Naiṣadha, to Harivarṣa.
He gave Ilāvṛta to Meru, which is situated in the center;
and the father gave the region resting against the Nīla mountain to Ramya.
That which was white and to the north was given by his father to Hiraṇvat.
He gave the region north of Śṛṅgavat to Kuru,
and the region east of Meru he bestowed upon Bhadrāśva.
He gave the region of Gandhamādana to Ketumāla;
thus did that lord of men bestow these [regions] upon his sons.
O Maitreya, after consecrating those sons in these realms during those years, that lord of the earth departed for the highly meritorious Sālagrāma to practice asceticism.
O Great Sage, in those eight regions beginning with Kiṃpuruṣa,
supernatural powers are innate, consisting mostly of happiness and attained without effort.
In them there is no error, nor is there the fear of old age and death;
neither merit nor demerit exists in them, nor are there high, low, or middling states.
In those eight regions, there was never any division of the Yugas at any time. However, the region called Himavat belonged to the high-souled Nābhi;
his son was the immensely radiant Ṛṣabha, born of Merudevī.
From Ṛṣabha was born Bharata, the eldest of his hundred sons;
having ruled the kingdom according to his own dharma and likewise having performed various sacrifices.
Having consecrated his heroic son Bharata as lord of the earth,
that illustrious sovereign departed for the hermitage of Pulaha to practice asceticism.
Having resolved even there to follow the rules for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*),
that lord of the earth performed austerities according to the prescribed method and offered sacrifices in accordance with tradition.
Exhausted by his austerities, exceedingly emaciated and covered with visible veins,
he went forth upon the path of heroes, naked and with a betel nut placed in his mouth.
And therefore, this land is celebrated among the worlds as Bhāratavarṣa,
because it was given to Bharata by his father when he departed for the forest.
Sumati was the son of Bharata, most righteous;
having performed sacrifices perfectly, his father gave the kingdom to him as he desired.
O Sage, that lord of the earth, Bharata, having transferred his royal fortune to his son and being devoted to the practice of yoga, gave up his life-breaths at Sālagrāma.
And that brahmin was born into a family of the most eminent among yogins;
O Maitreya, I shall relate his life story to you again.
From that Sumati was born Indradyumna;
from him came Parameṣṭhin, and from him Pratīhāra, who belonged to that lineage.
His son was born as the one renowned as Pratihartṛ;
from him came Bhuva, from him Udgītha, and his son was the powerful Prastāva.
From him was born Pṛthu; from him, Nakta; Nakta’s son was Gaya;
Nara was the son of Gaya, and his son was Virāṭ.
From him was born a wise son of great heroism;
from him came Mahānta, and his son was Manasyu.
Tvaṣṭṛ was born from Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viraja was his son;
from that Viraja, Śatajit was born, O Sage, and from Śatajit, a hundred sons were born.
These sons, whose primary characteristic was universal light, by whom these subjects were nourished,
have adorned this land of Bhārata with its nine divisions.
This land of Bhārata was enjoyed in former times by those born of their lineage,
through seventy-one cycles known as Yugas, consisting of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
This is the Svāyambhuva creation by which this world was filled;
O Sage, he was the lord of the previous Manvantara during the Vārāha Kalpa.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
O Brahmin, you have described to me the creation of Svāyambhuva.
I desire to hear from you the entire mandala of the earth.
O Sage, as many oceans, islands, regions, mountains, forests, rivers, and cities belonging to the gods and others as there may be—
O Sage, you ought to explain correctly what the measure of all this is, what its support is, what its essential nature is, and what its configuration is.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to this as I speak it in brief;
I am not able to describe its full detail even in a hundred years.
O twice-born one, the islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and another called Śālmala,
as well as Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara is the seventh.
These continents are surrounded by seven oceans,
which are equal in size to them and consist respectively of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
Jambūdvīpa stands in the center of all these;
and in its center, Maitreya, is Mount Meru, the golden mountain.
And its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas.
It enters sixteen thousand yojanas below and extends thirty-two thousand at the summit;
its circumference at the base is sixteen thousand on all sides.
This mountain stands in the form of the pericarp of this earth-lotus.
To its south are the Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha;
to the north are the Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin—the mountain ranges that demarcate the regions.
The two middle ones measure one hundred thousand [yojanas], while the others are each ten thousand less;
they are two thousand yojanas in height and an equal extent in width.
O twice-born one, Bhārata is the first region; beyond that, Kiṃpuruṣa is recorded, and likewise Harivarṣa is another, all situated to the south of Meru.
The northern region is Ramyaka, and following that is Hiraṇmaya;
and the Uttarakurus are just as the Bhārata region is.
Each of these, O best of the twice-born, is nine thousand [yojanas] in extent;
and in their midst is Ilāvṛta, where the golden Meru rises aloft.
O fortunate one, there, on the four sides of Meru, lies Ilāvṛta, extending nine thousand [yojanas],
and there are four mountains therein.
The supporting ridges of Meru are ten thousand yojanas in height.
Together with all the lakes, these Kesara mountains are situated in the cardinal directions. (ViP 2.2.17ab*) [Ed. Veṅk. inserts: "Together with all the lakes..."
To the east is the mountain named Mandara, and to the south is Gandhamādana.
