Vipula is said to be on the western side, and Supārśva on the north.
Among them are the kadamba, jambū, pippala, and vaṭa trees;
these eleven hundred-foot-high trees serve as the banners of the mountain.
O Great Sage, that Jambū tree is the reason for the name of Jambūdvīpa; indeed,
the fruits of that tree are as large as great elephants,
and they fall, shattering on all sides, upon the back of the mountain.
From their juice, the river known as Jambūnadī flows there; it is indeed drunk by those inhabitants.
Neither perspiration nor foul odor, neither old age nor the decay of the senses arises there for those people of pure minds who drink that [water].
Having reached its banks and its waters, which are dried by pleasant breezes,
that earth becomes the gold known as Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.
To the east of Meru is Bhadrāśva, and to the west is Ketumāla;
O best of sages, between those two regions lies Ilāvṛta.
The Caitraratha forest is in the east, Gandhamādana in the south,
Vaibhrāja likewise in the west, and Nandana is recorded as being in the north.
Aruṇoda, Mahābhadra, Asitoda, and Samānasa—
these are the four lakes that are always enjoyed by the gods.
Śītāmbhas, Kumuda, Kurarī, Mālyavat,
and those headed by Vaikaṅka are the filament-mountains (kesarācala) to the east of Meru.
Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, and Rucaka,
as well as Niṣadha and others, are the Kesara mountains situated to its south.
Śikhivāsa, Savaiḍūrya, Kapila, Gandhamādana,
and likewise Jārudhi and others are the Kesara mountains in the west.
Situated on the intermediate ridges of Meru, beginning with Jaṭhara,
are Śaṅkhakūṭa, Ṛṣabha, Haṃsa, Nāga,
and others such as Kālañjana; these are the filament-mountains (kesarācala) to the north.
After verse 29, G1,2 insert:
"But the filaments have the same height, and they are eighty units in width and length."
O Maitreya, the great city of Brahmā is renowned in heaven as being fourteen thousand yojanas above Mount Meru.
And all around it, in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions,
were the renowned and preeminent cities of the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
Issuing from the foot of Viṣṇu and having flooded the orb of the moon,
the Gaṅgā indeed falls from heaven all around the city of Brahmā.
Having fallen there, it flows forth in four directions as the Sītā,
the Alakanandā, the Cakṣus, and the Bhadrā, respectively.
Moving through the air, Sītā goes from one mountain to another to the east;
then she proceeds across the eastern continent of Bhadrāśva until she reaches the ocean.
In the same way, O great sage, the Alakanandā also flows southward to Bhārata and enters the ocean after dividing into seven streams.
And the Cakṣu river, having passed beyond all the western mountains,
then goes to the western region called Ketumāla and enters the ocean.
O great sage, having passed beyond Bhadrāśva, the Northern Mountains, and the Northern Kurus, she reaches the northern ocean.
The Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains extend as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha ranges;
situated between them stands Mount Meru, shaped like the pericarp of a lotus.
The Bhāratas, the Ketumālas, the Bhadrāśvas,
and likewise the Kurus are the petals of the world-lotus, situated outside the boundary mountains.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are both boundary mountains;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha.
Both Gandhamādana and Kailāsa extend from east to west;
eighty yojanas in length, they are situated within the ocean.
Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are both boundary mountains situated on the western side of Meru,
positioned exactly as the two [preceding] ones were on the eastern side.
Triśṛṅga and Jārudhi are the two northern mountain ranges;
both extend from east to west and are situated within the ocean.
Thus, these boundary mountains beginning with Jaṭhara, which stand in pairs on the four sides of Meru, have been described to you by the best of sages.
O Sage, those Kesara mountains which are said to lie in the four directions of Meru, as well as the Śītā and other rivers, are exceedingly beautiful;
the valleys between these mountains are frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Likewise, O best of sages, there are delightful forests and cities upon those [continents], as well as excellent abodes belonging to the gods such as Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Sūrya,
frequented by choice kinnaras.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, as well as daityas and dānavas,
sport day and night in those delightful mountain valleys.
O Sage, these are indeed remembered as terrestrial heavens, the abodes of the righteous;
those who have committed evil do not go to them even in hundreds of births.
O twice-born one, in Bhadrāśva the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu resides as Hayaśiras;
in Ketumāla he is Varāha, and in Bhārata he assumes the form of a tortoise.
Govinda Janārdana exists among the Kurus in the form of a fish;
Hari, the Lord of All and the Universal One, is everywhere through his universal form.
O Maitreya, he who is the essence of all things remains as the foundational support for everything.
O Great Sage, in those eight regions beginning with Kimpuruṣa,
there is no sorrow, no exertion, no agitation, nor hunger, fear, and the like.
The subjects will be healthy, free from fear, and devoid of all suffering;
they will have a stable lifespan of ten or twelve thousand years.
The rain-god does not pour down upon them, for those places indeed possess waters from the earth;
nor do the conceptual divisions of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages exist in those regions.
In all these regions, O best of the twice-born, there are seven principal mountain ranges each, and from them flow hundreds of rivers.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
That which lies north of the ocean and south of the Himālaya mountains—
That region is named Bhārata, where the lineage of Bharata resides.
O Great Sage, its extent is nine thousand yojanas;
this is the land of action for those who go to heaven and liberation.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these are the seven principal mountain ranges here.
Therefore, O Sage, from this [conduct] heaven is attained and from this they proceed to liberation; yet from this also men go to the state of animals or even to hell. (ViP 2.3.4)
From here, heaven, liberation, the intermediate state, and the end are reached;
indeed, for mortals, no other place than this land of action is ordained.
Listen now to the nine divisions of this land of Bhārata:
Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmraparṇa, and Gabhastimān; 2.3.6.
Likewise Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and Vāruṇa;
this, however, is the ninth among them, surrounded by the ocean.
This island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north;
the Kirātas dwell at its eastern edge, while the Yavanas are situated at its western end.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were established in their respective positions, subsisting through sacrifices, weapons, trade, and other such means.
O Sage, the Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, and others flow forth from the foothills of the Himavat; and the Vedasmṛti and other rivers originate from the Pāriyātra mountains.
The Narmadā, Surasā, and other rivers have issued from the Vindhya mountains;
while the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, and others originate from the Ṛkṣa mountains.
Likewise, the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and others—
these rivers originating from the foothills of the Sahya mountains— are remembered as destroyers of the fear of sin.
The rivers headed by the Kṛtamālā and Tāmraparṇī are known to originate from the Malaya mountains;
those beginning with the Trisāmā and Ṛṣikulyā are recorded as originating from the Mahendra mountain.
The Ṛṣikulyā, Kumārī, and others arise from the foot of Śuktimat;
there are also thousands of other rivers and tributaries belonging to them.
In them dwell these people— the Kurus, Pañcālas, and those from the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa),
as well as those from the Eastern regions and others who inhabit Kāmarūpa.
The Puṇḍras, Kaliṅgas, Magadhas, and all those from the southern regions,
as well as the Aparāntas, Saurāṣṭras, Śūras, Ābhīras, and Arbudas.
The Kārūṣas and Mālavas, the inhabitants of the Pāriyātra mountains,
the Sauvīras, the Saindhavas, the Hūṇas, the Śālvas, and the residents of Śākala.
The Madras, Rāmas, Ambaṣṭhas, Pārasis, and others—
these highly fortunate peoples, teeming with joyful and well-nourished folk, always dwell near and drink from the waters of these rivers.
O great sage, the four ages— the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— exist here in the land of Bhārata, but nowhere else.
There, ascetics perform austerities and sacrificers offer oblations;
and there, gifts are bestowed with devotion for the sake of the world beyond.
In Jambūdvīpa, the Lord of Sacrifice, Viṣṇu—who consists of sacrifice—is worshipped by men through sacrifices; in other dvīpas, he is worshipped in other ways.
In this regard also, O great sage, Bhārata is the most excellent within Jambūdvīpa;
for this is the land of action (karmabhūmi), whereas all others are lands of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi).
In this regard, O best of beings, even after thousands of thousands of births,
a living being may perhaps attain human birth through the accumulation of merit.

The gods indeed sing these songs: "Blessed are those men who, in the region of the land of Bhārata—which is the cause for attaining both heaven and liberation—become human beings once again after their celestial existence."
Having renounced their actions— devoid of any desire for their fruits— to Viṣṇu, who is the form of the Supreme Self,
those stainless ones attain that realm of action and go to dissolution in Him, the Infinite.
We do not know where we shall obtain a bodily bond once the merit that bestows heaven has dissolved; indeed, blessed are those men in Bhārata who are not deprived of their senses.
O Maitreya, I have thus briefly described to you this Jambūdvīpa, which is nine thousand yojanas in extent and one hundred thousand yojanas in width.
Surrounding Jambūdvīpa, O Maitreya, the salt-water ocean stands outside, one hundred thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a ring.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Just as the continent named Jambū is surrounded by the salt ocean (Kṣāroda), so too is it encompassed.
Plakṣadvīpa stands thus, having completely surrounded the salt-water ocean.
Then [the text] inserts: "Now, [he described] the islands beginning with Plakṣa, together with their regions, mountains, rivers, and oceans."
He describes [the world] from beginning to end through the distinctions of color, form, and so forth.
The extent of Jambūdvīpa is measured at one hundred thousand [yojanas];
O Brahmin, Plakṣadvīpa is declared to be twice that size.
Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa, had seven sons:
the eldest was named Śāntabhaya, and after him was Śiśira.
Sukhodaya, Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka,
and Dhruva as the seventh— these were indeed the lords of Plakṣadvīpa.
First was the age Śāntabhaya, then Śiśira which likewise bestows happiness;
then Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and Dhruva.
There are others, the boundary-forming mountain ranges of those [continents].
O best of sages, hear the names of those seven.
Gomeda, Candra, Nārada, Dundubhi,
Somaka, Sumanas, and Śaila— Vaibhrāja is the seventh.
O sinless ones, in these delightful mountain ranges of the Varṣas,
the inhabitants dwell constantly together with gods and Gandharvas.
In those regions, the districts are meritorious and people die only after a long time;
there are neither mental anxieties nor physical diseases, for that place is pleasant at all times.
Each of those seven regions has seven rivers that flow to the ocean;
I shall name them, for hearing their names removes all evil.
The Anutaptā, Śikhī, Vipāśā, Tridivā, Kramu,
Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā— these seven rivers flow there.
These mountains and principal rivers have thus been described to you;
there are also thousands of minor rivers and mountains there,
and the inhabitants of those regions always drink from those rivers with joy.
O twice-born one, for them there is indeed neither a period of decline (apasarpiṇī) nor a period of increase (utsarpiṇī);
in those seven regions, the state of the Yugas does not exist at all.
O high-minded one, O Brahmin, in Plakṣadvīpa and the other continents up to Śākadvīpa, time is always equal to the Tretā Yuga.
People live for five thousand years, free from disease; and during these [five periods], Dharma exists according to the divisions of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas).
And there are four castes therein; learn of them as I describe them to you.
The Āryakas, the Kuraras, the Viviṃśas, and those who are the Bhāvins— these,
O best of sages, were the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
In its center, O best of the twice-born, there is a very great tree equal in size to the Jambū tree; this island is named Plakṣa after that tree, and is thus called Plakṣadvīpa.
There, the Blessed Lord Hari— the creator of the universe, the all-pervading Lord of all— is worshipped by those castes beginning with the Āryakas in the form of Soma.
Plakṣadvīpa is surrounded by an ocean of sugarcane juice that conforms to its circumference, being equal in extent to Plakṣadvīpa itself.
Thus, Maitreya, this Plakṣadvīpa has been described by me to you in brief; now listen further from me concerning Śālmala.
The heroic lord of Śālmaladvīpa is Vapuṣmat; hear now of his sons, after whom those seven regions are indeed named.
Then Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha, O great sage. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.4.23)
This ocean of sugarcane juice is surrounded on all sides by the continent of Śālmaladvīpa, which is twice its extent in width.
Therein also, seven mountain ranges are to be known as the sources of jewels;
they likewise manifest seven regions and seven rivers.
Kumuda, Unnata, and the third, Balāhaka;
and where the great medicinal herbs dwell, that is the fourth mountain, Droṇa.
Kaṅka is the fifth, Mahiṣa the sixth, and likewise Kakudmān, the best of mountains, is the seventh; now hear from me the names of the rivers.
Yoni, Toyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, Vimocanī, and Nivṛtti is the seventh among them; these are remembered as bestowing the pacification of evil.
Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita,
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and the exceedingly beautiful Suprabha—
these seven regions are indeed endowed with the four social orders (cāturvarṇya).
O great sage, as for the castes who dwell in Śālmala,
they are— Kapilas, Āruṇas, Pītas, and Kṛṣṇas, each distinct from the others.

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras likewise worship that Blessed One— Viṣṇu, the imperishable Self of all— who has become the wind and is established in sacrifice through the most excellent of rituals performed by the sacrificers.
In this exceedingly beautiful place, there is the presence of the gods;
and there is a great tree named Śālmali, which brings about bliss.
This continent is surrounded on all sides by the Suroda ocean,
which is equal in extent to the Śālmala continent itself.
Surrounded on all sides by Kuśadvīpa, Surodaka is twice the extent of Śālmala in every direction.
Hear now of those seven sons of Jyotiṣmān in Kuśadvīpa.
Udbhida, Veṇumān, Svairatha, Lambana, Dhṛti,
Prabhākara, and Kapila— these are the regions named after them.
In that city dwell humans together with the Daityas and Dānavas,
as well as gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and others.
There too, O great sage, there were four castes devoted to their own duties:
the Damins, the Śuṣmins, the Snehas, and the Mandehas.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are declared in this sequential order.
Because they perform the duties as prescribed, they exhaust their own specific offices;
there, on Kuśadvīpa, worshipping Janārdana in the form of Brahmā,
they bring to an end that fierce office which yields its fruit.
Vidruma, Hemaśaila, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān,
Kuśeśaya, Hari, and Mandarācala as the seventh.
O great sage, these seven Varṣa mountains are located there on that island;
listen now to the names of the seven rivers in their proper order.
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, as well as Sammatis,
Vidyut, Ambhā, and Mahī— these others are the removers of all sins.
There are thousands of other small rivers and likewise mountains there;
because of a clump of *kuśa* grass, that island is known by the name Kuśadvīpa.
That island is surrounded by the Ghṛtoda ocean, which is equal in extent to it;
and the Ghṛtoda ocean is indeed encompassed by Krauñcadvīpa.
O highly fortunate one, hear now of another great island, Krauñcadvīpa,
whose extent is twice that of Kuśadvīpa.
In Krauñcadvīpa, the sons of the high-souled Dyutimat were seven;
the lord of the earth named the regions after them.
Kuśala, Manuṣya, Uṣṇa, Pīvaramat, Andhakāra,
Muni, and Dundubhi— these seven, O Sage, were his sons.
There too, O one of great intelligence, are the delightful mountain ranges frequented by gods and gandharvas; hear their names from me.
Krauñca, Vāmana, and the third, Andhakāraka;
the fourth was Ratnaśaila, whose army resembled a flood of horses.

In this regard, Divāvṛt is the fifth, and likewise another is Puṇḍarīkavat; Dundubhi is the great mountain [of the center]. These islands and the mountains within them are each double the size of the preceding one, just as the islands increase in size.
In these delightful regions and upon the excellent mountain ranges that divide them,
the subjects dwell free from fear together with hosts of gods.
O great sage, the Puṣkaras, Puṣkalas, Dhanyas,
and those called Tiṣyas were the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, respectively.
Listen, Maitreya, to those rivers which they drink there:
there are seven principal ones, and hundreds of other minor streams.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Saṃdhyā, Rātri, Manojavā,
Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā— these seven are the rivers of that region.
Here too, in the vicinity of the sacrifice, the Blessed Janārdana, abiding in the form of Rudra, is worshipped by the castes with sacrifices such as the Puṣkara.
Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of curd-cream water, which is equal to Krauñcadvīpa in measurement.
And the sea of curd-cream water is likewise surrounded by Śākadvīpa,
O great sage, with a breadth twice that of Krauñcadvīpa.
To the noble and great-souled Bhavya, the lord of Śākadvīpa,
he likewise gave seven sons and assigned those seven regions to them.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇīcaka,
Kusumoda, Sumodākin, and the seventh, Mahādruma.
There too, the seven regions are named after those very [mountains] in succession;
there likewise are seven mountains that serve to divide the regions.
There, O twice-born one, are Pūrva and Udayagiri, as well as Jaladhāra; likewise Raivataka, Śyāma, and Ambhogiri;
and also the delightful Āmbikeya and Kesarī, the best of mountains.
There dwell high-souled beings, free from fear and free from disease.
There stands a great tree called Śāka, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas;
from the touch of the wind blowing through its leaves, a supreme delight arises.
There, the districts are meritorious and inhabited by the four social orders;
and there are rivers of great merit that remove all sins and fears.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, and Nalinī; Veṇukā, Ikṣu, Dhenukā, and likewise Gabhastī as the seventh.
But there, O great sage, are other minor rivers by the tens of thousands,
as well as mountains by the hundreds and thousands.
Those inhabitants of the regions who dwell in places such as Jalada drink them with joy;
having come from heaven to the earth, they become those very districts.
In those seven regions, there was no decline of Dharma, nor mutual strife, nor any transgression of the bounds of propriety.
The Magas, the Māgadhas, the Mānasas, and the Mandagas;
among them, the Magas were mostly Brāhmaṇas, the Māgadhas were Kṣatriyas,
the Mānasas were Vaiśyas, and the Mandagas were Śūdras.
O Sage, in Śākadvīpa, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of the Sun,
is duly worshipped by those of self-restrained mind with the aforementioned rites.
But Śākadvīpa, O Maitreya, is surrounded on all sides by the Ocean of Milk,
encircling it like a bracelet with a circumference equal to the size of Śākadvīpa itself.
O Brahmin, the Ocean of Milk is surrounded on all sides by the continent named Puṣkara,
which is twice the size of Śākadvīpa on every side.
O Brahmin, it is surrounded on all sides by Puṣkara and also by the Ocean of Milk.
From Puṣkara, a son named Mahāvīra was also born; and from Savana, Dhātaki was born. There, two regions were marked by their names: one was Mahāvīra and the other was known as Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
And here, O illustrious one, there is one famous mountain range known as Mānasottara, which forms a circular belt right through the middle.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas in height and is just as wide, being perfectly circular on all sides.
O Sage, as if dividing the circular Puṣkaradvīpa through its center, that mountain stands; by it, the land has become split into two regions.
Each of those two regions is circular like a ring, and likewise is the mountain.
There, human beings live for ten thousand years;
they are free from disease and sorrow, and devoid of passion and hatred.
O twice-born one, among them there was neither high nor low status, nor were there the slain and the slayer;
there was no envy, malice, fear, anger, fault-finding, nor greed and the like.
Outside the Mahāvīra [ocean] is Dhātakīkhaṇḍa,
which extends as far as the Mānasottara mountain and is frequented by gods, Daityas, and others.
Neither truth nor falsehood exists there on that island known as Puṣkara;
nor are there rivers or mountains on that island which comprises two regions.
But there, the humans were identical in appearance to the gods, being of one and the same form.
O Maitreya, for two years this earth is like a supreme heaven;
it is a time that bestows happiness upon all and is free from old age, disease, and the like,
in Puṣkara, Dhātakīṣaṇḍa, and Mahāvīra, O Sage.
In Puṣkaradvīpa, there is a Nyagrodha tree, the supreme abode of Brahmā;
therein dwells Brahmā, being worshipped by gods and asuras alike.
Puṣkara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water;
it is equal to Puṣkara itself in both extent and circumference.
Thus, the continents are surrounded by seven oceans;
each successive continent and ocean is twice the size of the one preceding it.
The waters in all the oceans are indeed always equal;
no deficiency or excess ever arises among them.
Just as the water in a pot increases through contact with fire,
O best of sages, so does the water in the ocean increase when the moon waxes.
Neither decreasing nor increasing,
the waters swell and diminish during the rising and setting of the moon in its two phases, the bright and the dark.
O great sage, an increase and decrease of exactly five hundred and ten finger-breadths are observed in the waters of the oceans.
O Brahmin, in that Puṣkara-dvīpa, food endowed with the six flavors is always spontaneously provided there, and all the subjects indeed consume it at all times.
Beyond the ocean of sweet water, the arrangement of the world is seen:
a golden land twice its size, devoid of all living beings.
Beyond that is the mountain Lokāloka, ten thousand yojanas in width;
for that immovable mountain is likewise [ten thousand] thousands in height.
Then darkness, having enveloped that mountain situated on all sides,
was itself surrounded on every side by the shell of the cosmic egg.
If, in some places here and there, a contradiction is observed in the Purāṇas...
In that regard, the wise maintain that the established order is determined by the distinctions between kalpas and other such factors.
O great sage, this earth, together with its shell, its islands, oceans, and mountains, extends for fifty koṭis.
O Maitreya, she is the sustainer and the ordainer, superior to all beings in her qualities; she is the foundation of all the worlds.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
This detailed account of the earth has been narrated by me to you.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, the height of the mountain is said to be seventy thousand [yojanas].
Extending through seven levels, it stands like a palace above the lower regions.
The manifestation of the seven netherworlds (pātālas), however, is described upon the head of Ananta.
O best of sages, each of the netherworlds (pātālas) extends for ten thousand [yojanas]:
Aṭala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat,
the one called Mahātala, Sutala, and Pātāla as the seventh.
O Maitreya, the grounds there are white, black, reddish-brown, yellow, sandy, stony, and golden, and they are adorned with magnificent palaces.
O great sage, within those [mountains] dwell hundreds of tribes of Dānavas and Daityas, as well as various species of great serpents.
"Even more delightful than the world of the gods are the netherworlds (pātāla)," Nārada declared among the inhabitants of heaven while he was in the sky, having returned from the netherworlds.
Where the brilliant, radiant jewels that bring delight serve as ornaments for the Nagas, who could equal that Patala?
In Pātāla, which is beautified here and there by the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas, who would not feel delight— even one who is liberated?
There, the rays of the sun during the day spread forth radiance but not heat,
and the moon at night provides illumination alone, not cold.
There, amidst those great enjoyers who were delighted by various foods, edibles, and grand drinks,
even the passing of time was not noticed by the sons of Danu and the others.
O twice-born one, there were exceedingly brilliant ornaments, fragrant and richly scented unguents,
and the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums, as well as various musical instruments.
These and other vast and fortunate realms are enjoyed by the Dānavas,
Daityas, and Uragas who dwell within the depths of Pātāla.
And beneath the netherworlds dwells that tamasic form of Viṣṇu known as Śeṣa,
whose qualities even the Daityas and Dānavas are unable to describe.
He who is recited as infinite by the perfected ones, worshipped by gods and divine seers,
possessing a thousand heads, and manifest with the auspicious svastika as his stainless ornament.
He who, illuminating all directions with a thousand crest-jewels,
renders all the asuras powerless for the welfare of the world.
With eyes rolling from intoxication, always wearing a single earring,
a crown, and a garland, he shines like the white mountain [Kailāsa] enveloped in fire.
Clad in blue garments, intoxicated with pride, and adorned with white necklaces,
he was as lofty as Mount Kailāsa with its waterfall from the cloudy Gaṅgā.
With the tip of his hand resting on a plough and wielding an excellent mace,
he is himself worshipped by the goddess Vāruṇī through her own radiant form.
At the end of the eon, from whose mouths Rudra, in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa and blazing with the flames of the fire of poison, emerges and devours the three worlds.
Bearing the entire circle of the earth as his crest-jewel,
Śeṣa, who is worshipped by all the gods, remains stationed at the base of Pātāla.
Neither his valor nor his power, nor his true nature nor even his form, can be described or even known by the gods themselves.
Who can describe the prowess of him for whom this entire earth, reddened by the tips of the jewels on his hoods, rests like a garland of flowers?
When Ananta yawns, his eyes rolling with intoxication,
then this earth, together with its mountains, waters, and forests, trembles.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Kinnaras, Uragas, and Cāraṇas do not reach the end of his qualities; therefore, he is infinite and imperishable.
The yellow sandalwood paste, applied by the hands of Naga maidens,
is repeatedly scattered by his breath and becomes like a cloud in all directions.
By propitiating whom the ancient seer Garga came to know the luminaries in their true essence, as well as the entire fruit declared by the study of omens.
Therefore, this earth, supported on his head by that best of Nāgas,
bears the garland of the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: "And then, O Brahmin, [he described] the hells beneath the earth and below the waters."
O great sage, hear now of those [hells] into which sinners are cast.
Raurava, Sūkara, Rodha, Tāla, as well as Viśasana,
Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa, and Vilohita.
Rudhirāmbhas, Vaitaraṇī, Kṛmiśa, Kṛmibhojana,
Asipatravana, Kṛṣṇa, and the dreadful Lālābhakṣa.
Likewise, there are Pūyavaha, the sinful Vahnijvāla, Adhaḥśiras, Sandaṃśa, Kṛṣṇasūtra, Tamas, and Avīci.
Śvabhojana, Apratiṣṭha, and likewise Avīci—
these and other such hells are exceedingly terrible.
In the realm of Yama, those men who are devoted to evil deeds fall into these terrible places that inflict the fear of weapons and fire.
A false witness, as well as one who speaks improperly out of partiality,
and he who tells any other untruth— that man goes to Raurava.
O best of sages, the killer of a fetus, the slayer of a teacher, the killer of a cow,
and he who suppresses the breath— all these go to the Rodha hell.
The drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, the stealer of gold,
and he who associates with them— these indeed go to the Sūkara hell.

The killer of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya goes to Tāla; likewise, one who violates the teacher’s bed goes to Tapta-kumbha; as does one who has sexual intercourse with his own sister, and he who slays the king's soldiers.
The seller of a virtuous woman, the keeper of prisoners, the seller of lions,
and he who abandons his dependents— these fall into the Taptaloha hell.
Having gone to his daughter-in-law or even his own daughter, he is cast into Mahājvāla;
as is that lowest of men who treats his elders with contempt or who reviles them.
O twice-born one, he who reviles the Vedas, he who sells the Vedas,
and he who approaches those who should not be approached— these go to Lavaṇa.
A thief falls into delusion, as does one who violates the bounds of propriety.
He who hates the gods, the twice-born, and the ancestors, and he who defiles gems, goes indeed to the Kṛmibhakṣa hell; and he who performs improper sacrifices goes to the Kṛmiśa hell.
That lowest of men who eats before his ancestors, gods,
and guests goes to the fierce Lālābhakṣa hell, and the maker of arrows goes to the Vedhaka hell.
The man who makes ear-piercing weapons, as well as he who makes swords and the like,
both go to the extremely dreadful hell called Viśasana.
But one who accepts gifts from the unworthy goes to the Adhomukha hell,
as do one who officiates at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and likewise one who indicates the auspiciousness of constellations for gain.
One man, though eating sweet food, goes forth alone, carrying a burden of pus.
O twice-born one, a Brahmin who sells lac, meat, juices, sesame seeds, and salt goes to that very same hell.
O best of the twice-born, by rearing cats, chickens, goats, dogs, pigs, and birds, one goes to that very same hell.
And likewise from the sale of cakes and the sale of books. (ViP 2.6.21*)
One who lives by painting, a fisherman, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, a poisoner, a spy, a keeper of buffaloes, and that twice-born man who has sexual intercourse on sacred festival days; 22.
An arsonist, a betrayer of friends, a fowler, a village priest, and those who sell Soma—all these fall into the Rudhirāndha hell. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.6.23)
The man who steals honey and the destroyer of a village goes to the Vaitaraṇī river.
But those who, intoxicated by wealth and youth, violate the bounds of propriety, as well as those who live by deceit, go to the realm of Kṛṣṇa (the impure one).
He who cuts down forests goes to the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana);
the butcher of sheep and the hunter of deer indeed fall into the Blazing Fire (Vahnijvāla).
O twice-born one, these go to that very place, as does he who sets fire to uncooked food.
Both he who violates his vows and he who has fallen away from his own stage of life fall into the midst of the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs) hell.
Those men who, though practicing celibacy, emit semen during the day or in dreams,
and those who are taught by their own sons, fall into the Śvabhojana hell.
These and other hells exist by the hundreds and thousands,
wherein those who have performed evil deeds are cooked, having undergone their torments.
In the same way, these and thousands of other sins are experienced by men who dwell within the various hells.
Those men who perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life—
whether by deed, thought, or speech— fall into the hells.
The gods in heaven are seen by the denizens of hell with their heads downward;
and the gods, looking downward, see all the hell-beings below them.
Immobile beings, worms, aquatic creatures, birds, animals,
humans, the righteous gods, and likewise those seeking liberation, follow one another in this sequence.
O highly fortunate one, each subsequent stage is a thousandth part of the preceding one, continuing in this sequence until the final resort of liberation.
As many beings as there are in heaven, so many are the inhabitants of hell;
the doer of evil goes to hell if he is averse to performing expiation.
The supreme seers, having reflected upon them, have prescribed penances that correspond exactly to each respective sin, according as it is.
O Maitreya, those who know the truth— the Svāyambhuvas and others— have declared that for great sins there are great expiations, and for minor sins, minor ones.
Of all those various penances consisting of ascetic practices,
the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme one.
For that man in whom remorse indeed arises after a sin has been committed,
the one supreme expiation is the constant remembrance of Hari.
By constantly remembering Nārāyaṇa in the morning, at night, during the twilights, at midday, and so forth, a person immediately attains the destruction of all sins.
Through the constant remembrance of Viṣṇu, one whose entire accumulation of afflictions has been exhausted attains liberation; for him, the attainment of heaven is considered merely an obstacle.
O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth,
even the status of Indra or other such rewards are considered obstacles.
Where is the ascent to the vault of heaven, characterized by return once more;
and where is the recitation of "Vāsudeva," the unsurpassed seed of liberation?
Therefore, O sage, a person who constantly remembers Viṣṇu day and night becomes pure,
with all his sins completely destroyed, and does not go to hell.
Heaven is that which causes delight to the mind; hell is the opposite of that.
O best of the twice-born, merit and demerit are indeed designated as heaven and hell.
Since a single object leads to suffering, to pleasure, to the arising of envy,
and to anger, how can an object possess an inherent nature of its own?
That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, arises again as suffering;
for it arises both as anger and as serenity.
Therefore, there is nothing whose nature is suffering, nor is there anything whose nature is happiness;
this characteristic of pleasure, pain, and so forth is merely a transformation of the mind.
Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; yet knowledge is also held to lead to bondage.
This entire universe consists of knowledge; nothing exists beyond knowledge.
O Maitreya, understand that what are called "knowledge" and "ignorance" are in fact nothing other than wisdom itself.
Thus have I described to you this terrestrial mandala,
as well as all the subterranean realms and likewise the hells, O twice-born one.
The oceans, the mountains, the islands, the regions, and the rivers—everything has been described in brief. What more do you wish to hear?
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Brahmin, you have related all of this to me."
O Sage, I desire to hear about the worlds beginning with Bhuvarloka.
In that same manner, O illustrious one, please explain to me, who am questioning you, the true dimensions and the configurations of the planets.
Parāśara said: As far as the earth is illuminated by the rays of the sun and the moon— including its oceans, rivers, and mountains— that much is known as the earth.
O twice-born one, as great as the earth is in its extent and circumference,
so great indeed is the sky in its breadth and circumference.
O Maitreya, one hundred thousand yojanas from the earth is the solar orb; and one hundred thousand yojanas from the sun is situated the lunar orb.
At a full hundred thousand yojanas above the moon,
the entire circle of the lunar mansions shines forth.
O Brahmin, two hundred thousand yojanas above the circle of the stars is Mercury;
and at a distance equal to that same measure from Mercury stands Venus.
Aṅgāraka is also situated at that same distance from Śukra;
however, the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] from Bhauma.
O best of the twice-born, Saturn is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] above Jupiter,
and the circle of the Seven Sages is one hundred thousand [yojanas] beyond that.
Situated more than a hundred thousand yojanas above the ṛṣis,
Dhruva indeed stands as the central pivot of the entire circle of luminaries.
O great sage, this triple world has been described according to its height;
it is the ground for the fruit of sacrifice, and here sacrifice is established.
Above Dhruva is Maharloka, where those who dwell for an eon reside;
Maharloka is said to extend for one hundred million yojanas.
But there are two crores of people in that world where those sons of Brahmā—
Sanandana and the others— are said to dwell, O Maitreya, they whose minds are stainless.
Above Janaloka, at a distance four times greater, is said to be Tapoloka,
where those Vairāja gods reside, free from the affliction of burning heat.
Sixfold above the world of austerity (tapas), the world of truth (satya) shines forth;
for that is remembered as the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), where there is no more death.
Whatever object made of earth exists that can be traversed on foot is designated as the Bhūrloka; its full extent has been described by me.
That which lies between the earth and the sun, frequented by the Siddhas and other sages, is called Bhuvarloka; it is the second world, O best of sages.
That which lies between Dhruva and the Sun, measuring fourteen hundred thousand [yojanas],
is declared by those who contemplate the structure of the worlds to be the Svarloka.
O Maitreya, this triple world is taught to be "the created," while the triad consisting of Janas, Tapas, and Satya is the "uncreated."
Between the created and the uncreated, it is remembered as Maharloka;
it becomes empty at the end of a kalpa, yet it is never utterly destroyed.
O Maitreya, these seven worlds have been described by me to you, as well as the seven nether regions; such is the extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
This [egg] is enclosed on all sides— sideways, above, and below— by its shell, just as the seed of a wood-apple fruit is enclosed by its rind.
That egg of Maitreya is surrounded by ten times as much water;
this entire mass, encased in water, is enveloped on the outside by fire.
Fire is enveloped by wind, O Maitreya, and wind is enveloped by space;
space is surrounded by the *bhūtādi* (the source of the elements), and that too is encompassed by the Great Principle (*mahat*).
All these seven, O Maitreya, increase tenfold at each successive stage.
Encompassing the Great One (mahat), it exists as the Pradhāna;
for that infinite [Being], there is neither an end nor can it be numbered.
Since that [nature] is indeed infinite and of immeasurable extent,
and is the cause of everything without exception, O Sage, it is the supreme Prakṛti.
There were thousands, tens of thousands, and millions upon millions of such eggs there.
Just as fire resides in wood and oil in sesame seeds, so too does the pervasive Spirit (puruṣa),
whose nature is consciousness and who perceives itself, abide within Pradhāna.
O one of great intelligence, both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, having become the self of all beings, abide in a state of mutual dependence, enveloped by the power of Viṣṇu.
O Mahāmati, at the time of creation, that very [power] is the cause of their separation, the cause of their support, and the cause of their agitation.
Just as the wind, clinging to water, supports hundreds of droplets,
so too is that power of Viṣṇu, which consists of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
And just as a tree, endowed with roots, trunk, branches, and so forth, originates from its primary seed, and from it indeed other seeds [are produced]; ||| ViP_2,7.32 |||
From them, other trees arise and come into being;
O Sage, they too follow the same characteristics, substances, and causes as those [original trees].
Thus, from the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), Mahat and the others arise first;
from them, the specific elements (viśeṣa) emerge, and from those, the gods and other beings;
from them come their sons, and from those sons, yet other offspring.
Just as there is no depletion of a tree through the growth of new shoots from its seed,
so too there is no depletion of the primary elements through the creation of beings from those elements.
Just as space, time, and so forth are causes of a tree by virtue of their mere proximity,
even so is the Lord Hari the cause of the universe through non-transformation.
Just as in a grain of rice there is the root, the stalk, the leaf, and the sprout,
so too are the stem, the sheath, the flower, the milk, and likewise the grains of rice.
O best of sages, husks and chaff, though they exist [in a latent state], indeed manifest their own nature upon encountering the complete collection of causes for germination.
Likewise, within the manifold karmas, the gods and others,
having attained the power of Viṣṇu, indeed attain growth.
And that Viṣṇu is the Supreme Brahman, from whom this entire world proceeds,
who is the world, in whom this world exists, and into whom it shall go to its dissolution.
That is Brahman, that is the supreme abode, the highest state of both being and non-being,
from which this entire world of moving and unmoving things is not distinct.
He alone is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and he is the manifest form; he is the universe.
Everything goes to dissolution in him alone, and in him everything abides.
He is the agent of all actions; He is the sacrifice, and He alone is the fruit of that ritual act.
Even the sacrificial ladle and all other implements are entirely Hari; indeed, nothing exists apart from Him.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
"O observer of noble vows, this structure of the cosmic egg has been explained to you."
Next, hear from me regarding the dimensions and configurations of the sun and the other celestial bodies.
O best of sages, the chariot of the Sun measures nine thousand yojanas,
and its pole is twice that length.
Its axle, moreover, measures one and a half koṭis and seven additional niyutas of yojanas; upon it the wheel is established.
Upon the wheel of time, which consists of the year, which has three naves, five spokes, six rims, and is imperishable by nature, everything is established.
O Mahāmati, the second axle of Vivasvat’s chariot measures forty thousand [yojanas],
while the other five parts of the chariot measure an additional five and a half thousand.
The axle is the measure for both halves of that yoke;
the axle is short, and the half-yoke is likewise short, serving as the support for the chariot's pole.
That wheel, however, is fixed upon the second axle on Mount Mānasa.
And there are seven horses, which are the Vedic meters; hear their names from me:
Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh, and Paṅkti—these are said to be the meters that serve as the sun’s bay steeds.
On the Mānasottara mountain, however, there is the city of Vāsava to the east;
to the south is that of Yama, to the west that of Varuṇa,
and to the north that of Soma— listen to their names from me.
Vasvokasārā belongs to Śakra, Saṃyamanī likewise to Yama,
Sukhā to the Lord of Waters, and Vibhāvarī to Soma.
O Maitreya, the Blessed Lord Sun, accompanied by the circle of luminaries, has reached the southern limit and glides along like an arrow that has been shot.
The Blessed Sun is the cause for the establishment of day and night;
he is the supreme path of the gods for yogis who have exhausted their afflictions.
O Maitreya, at all times the sun is situated at the meridian of the day and facing the midpoint of the night across all the continents.
O Maitreya, at both sunrise and sunset, and indeed at all times, he is present face-to-face in all directions as well as in all intermediate points.
Wherever the radiant sun is seen by them, that is considered his rising;
and wherever he becomes invisible, right there occurs the setting of the sun.
For the sun that exists eternally, there is neither setting nor rising;
what are called "rising" and "setting" are merely the visibility and invisibility of the sun.
Abiding in the city of Śakra and the others, he touches three cities;
likewise, standing in Vikarṇa, he touches two corners and two cities.
Having risen, the sun shines with increasing rays until midday;
thereafter, as its rays diminish, it goes to its setting.
And by its rising and setting, the eastern and western directions are defined;
as far as it shines in front, so far does it shine behind and on both sides.
Except for the summit of Meru, the mountain of the immortals, upon which is the assembly hall of Brahmā—
whatever rays of the sun proceed toward that assembly hall of Brahmā,
they are all repelled by its brilliance and indeed return back.
Therefore, in that northern direction, day and night always exist;
for Meru lies to the north of all the continents and regions.
When the sun has set at night, the radiance of Vivasvat enters the fire;
therefore, the fire shines from afar during the night.
Likewise, O twice-born one, the foot of fire enters the sun during the days;
because of that intense conjunction with fire, the sun shines forth.
The two splendors—those of the sun and of fire—are of the nature of light and heat;
through their mutual interpenetration, they nourish one another day and night.
When the sun rises over the southern and northern halves of the earth,
day and night enter the waters, like darkness and lightness.
For the waters become slightly copper-colored by entering [the earth] during the day and night;
and when the sun has set, the water enters the earth during the day;
therefore, the waters become white at night due to the entry of the day.
Thus, when the sun moves through the center of Puṣkara,
its velocity at that time is such that it traverses a thirtieth part of the earth in one muhūrta.
O twice-born one, this sun, revolving like a potter's wheel until its limit,
creates day and likewise night as it traverses the earth.
At the beginning of the northern solstice, O twice-born one, the Sun enters Capricorn; from there he proceeds to Aquarius and Pisces, moving from one zodiac sign to another.
Then, when these three have been traversed,
the sun proceeds toward the equinoctial course (vaiṣuvatī gati), thereby making day and night equal.
Then the night comes to an end, and the day increases day by day.
Then, having reached the ultimate limit at the end of Gemini and entering the zodiac sign of Cancer, he initiates the southern solstice.
Just as the circumference of a potter’s wheel revolves rapidly,
so too does the sun move swiftly during its southern course.
Moving through time with extreme velocity, following the course of the wind's speed,
it traverses a vast distance in a very short period of time.
O twice-born one, during the southern course, the sun moves through thirteen and a half constellations in twelve swift muhūrtas by day;
it traverses the same number of constellations at night in eighteen muhūrtas.
Just as an object situated in the middle of a potter’s wheel moves slowly,
so the sun moves with slow progress during its northern course (udagayana).
Therefore, after a long period of time, he reaches a small portion of the earth—
that which lasts eighteen muhūrtas at the end of the northern course [of the sun].
Day becomes night there as well, and even there he moves with slow gait.
The sun moves through thirteen and a half constellations during the day,
and during the night it traverses as many constellations in twelve muhūrtas.
Just as a wheel revolves more slowly below the navel,
so indeed does Dhruva revolve, situated in the center like a lump of clay.
Just as the hub of a potter’s wheel remains fixed in that very place,
O Maitreya, so indeed does the Pole Star revolve in that very place.
And the circles described by the sun as it revolves between the two solstitial limits (kāṣṭhā) during day and night constitute its slow and swift motions respectively.
On whichever solstice his motion is slow during the day, it is then swift at night;
and when his motion is swift at night, it is then slow during the day.
O twice-born one, this sun-god travels along a single path, traversing all the zodiacal signs in the course of a day and night.
He consumes exactly six zodiac signs at night and the other six during the day.
During the day, the state of being long or short is produced by the measure of the zodiacal signs;
likewise, during the night, the brevity or length [of the day] is determined by the measures of the signs.
The lengthening and shortening of the day and so forth occurs precisely through that [sun's] movement;
at night its motion is swift during the northern course, while it is slow during the day.
But during the southern course of the sun, these are reversed for Vivasvat.
Uṣā is declared to be night, and vyuṣṭi is said to be day;
likewise, that which lies between uṣā and vyuṣṭi is called the twilight (saṃdhyā).
But when the twilight hour has arrived— fierce and most dreadful—
the terrible Mandeha Rākṣasas seek to devour the Sun.
O Maitreya, Prajāpati’s curse upon those Rākṣasas was that their bodies would be indestructible, yet they would die day after day.
Then a most terrible battle takes place between the Sun and them;
thereafter, O great sage, O best of the twice-born, they cast water [upon him].
Conjoined with the Brahman of the syllable Oṃ and consecrated by the Gāyatrī,
those sins are burnt away by that water which has become like a thunderbolt.
The first oblation that is offered with a mantra in the Agnihotra sacrifice is the sun;
by it the thousand-rayed Bhāskara shines.
The syllable *oṃ* is the Lord Viṣṇu, the abode of the three, the master of all speech;
by its utterance, those Rākṣasas go to their destruction.
The supreme Vaiṣṇava portion is the Sun, who is the internal light beyond all confusion;
the syllable Om is his designator, and he is the supreme impeller thereof.
Impelled by that, the radiant light, made luminous by the syllable Om,
indeed burns away all the sinful Rākṣasas known as Mandehas.
Therefore, one must not neglect the ritual of twilight worship;
for he who does not perform the twilight worship indeed slays the sun.
Then the Blessed One, intent upon the protection of the world, set forth, guarded by the Brāhmaṇas, the Vālakhilyas, and others.
After 58c, D3,4,T1,M0,4 insert: ... ...
[he was] even the lord of the Vaikhānasas.
Indeed, the Great-Souled One [was honored] by the Great-Souled Ones... // ViP_2.8.58*9:2 //
Fifteen nimeṣas make one kāṣṭhā, and one should count thirty such kāṣṭhās as one kalā;
thirty kalās make one muhūrta, and by thirty of those, night and day together are formed.
The decrease and increase of the days occur through their respective portions;
indeed, during both decrease and increase, the twilight is traditionally held to last for exactly one muhūrta.
Then, when three muhūrtas have passed from the appearance of the first line [of the sun] until the sun has risen, that time is known as morning; it constitutes the fifth part of the day.
From that morning time, the period of three muhūrtas is Saṅgava;
and from that Saṅgava time, the period of three muhūrtas is midday.
Therefore, the period following the midday hour is known as the afternoon;
it is recorded by the wise as consisting of exactly three muhūrtas, which constitute a division of time.
When the afternoon has passed, the time that follows is called the evening (sāyāhna);
it consists of five muhūrtas of the day and exactly three muhūrtas [of the night].
Indeed, the day of the equinox (vaiṣuvata) is recorded as consisting of fifteen muhūrtas.
The day increases and the night decreases during the northern and southern solstices;
during the former, the day swallows the night, and during the latter, the night swallows the day.
Between autumn and spring, the equinox is perceived;
when the sun has entered Libra and Aries, that is the time when day and night are equal.
When the sun is situated in Cancer, it is called the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana);
the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is likewise said to occur when the sun is in Capricorn.
O Brahmin, fifteen of those days and nights, each consisting of thirty muhūrtas as described by me, are designated as a *pakṣa* (fortnight).
A month is said to consist of two fortnights; two months, born of the sun, constitute a season (ṛtu);
three seasons likewise make an ayana, and two ayanas are designated as a year.
The five periods beginning with the year are each divided into four months;
this determination of all time is designated as a *yuga*.
The first is Saṃvatsara, the second is Parivatsara,
the third is Idvatsara, the fourth is Anuvatsara,
and the fifth here is Vatsara; this period of time is designated as a Yuga.
To the north of Śveta is the mountain renowned as Śṛṅgavān;
it has three peaks, by which it is known as Śṛṅgavān.

The sun reaches the southern, the northern, and likewise the central equinox; O Maitreya, it stands at the equinox at the beginning of Aries and at the beginning of Libra, situated between autumn and spring.
Then the dispeller of darkness makes day and night equal;
indeed, each of these two is known to consist of fifteen muhūrtas.
O Sage, when the sun is in the first quarter of Kṛttikā, the moon then undoubtedly stays in the fourth quarter of Viśākhā.
When the sun moves through the third quarter of the Viśākhās,
one should know that the moon is situated at the head of Kṛttikā.
At that very time, the period known as the equinox (viṣuva) is declared to be sacred;
at that time, gifts should be given to the gods by those of purified soul.
This mouth [of the sun] is born of gifts for the sake of the Brahmins and the ancestors;
one who has given a gift at the equinox (viṣuva) becomes one who has fulfilled his duty.
Day and night, the half-months, as well as the *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, and *kṣaṇas* should be known; likewise the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*),
as well as *sinīvālī*, *kuhū*, *rākā*, and *anumati*.
Tapas and tapasya, madhu and mādhava, śukra and śuci—these constitute the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
Nabhas and nabhasya, iṣa and ūrja, and saha and sahasya—these constitute the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
As for the mountain Lokāloka which was previously mentioned by me to you,
the four world-protectors (Lokapālas) of virtuous vows reside there.
O twice-born one, Sudhāmā and Śaṅkhapāda were the two sons of Kardama;
the others were Hiraṇyaroman and the fourth was Ketumān.
Free from dualities, free from pride, free from sloth, and free from possessions,
these guardians of the world stand in the four directions at the boundary between the world and the non-world.
That which lies north of Agastya’s region and south of the Ajavīthī is indeed the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), situated outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There dwell the high-souled sages who maintain the sacred fire;
praising the Brahman as the cause of the origin of beings, they stand ready as officiating priests and undertake the creation of the worlds. That is their southern path.
Furthermore, O Brahmā, they establish what has declined in every age through continuity,
austerity, the observance of boundaries, and sacred learning.
Indeed, those who were born previously are born here in the houses of those born later,
and those born later are born in the houses of those previously deceased.
Thus revolving, they remain until the dissolution of all beings,
for they abide in the southern path of the sun as long as the moon and stars exist.
That which lies north of the Nāgavīthī and south of the Seven Sages is known as the northern path of the sun, the path of the gods (devayāna).
There, those self-controlled perfected ones, pure and celibate, loathe progeny; therefore, death has been conquered by them.
Eighty-eight thousand ascetics of perpetual celibacy indeed take to the northern path of Aryaman until the dissolution of all beings.
They [attain this] through non-association with greed and the avoidance of sexual intercourse,
through the non-occurrence of desire and hatred, and through the renunciation of initiating new actions toward material elements.
Furthermore, because they were free from desire and because they perceived the defects in sound and the other sense objects,
through these causes they became pure and indeed attained immortality.
The state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings is considered immortality;
this duration of the existence of the three worlds is called "no further death."
O twice-born one, the rule regarding the performer of sin and the performer of merit— namely, the killing of a Brahmin and the horse sacrifice—
is said to have its fruit lasting until the end of the dissolution of all beings.
To whatever extent Maitreya remains established,
for that same extent the earth undergoes destruction at the dissolution of all beings.
Above the Ṛṣis, where Dhruva is established,
is this divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky.
O Brahmin, that is the supreme state for ascetics who have shaken off the mire of defects and whose selves are restrained, upon the exhaustion of both merit and sin.
When merit and demerit have ceased and all causes for rebirth are exhausted,
that place where one goes and no longer grieves is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
That place where Dhruva and the other world-witnesses abide,
ignited by the yoga produced through attaining equality with Him— that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
That in which this entire universe— the past, the present, and the future,
including all that is moving and unmoving— is woven like warp and woof, O Maitreya, is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Like an eye stretched across the sky, that which is spread out for the great-souled ones and perceived through the vision of discriminative knowledge— that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, upon that which is established, the radiant Dhruva himself stands as a central pivot; and upon Dhruva rest all the luminaries, and within the luminaries, the clouds.
O great sage, from the clouds comes continuous rain; from rain comes the creation [of crops], and from that, the nourishment and the satiation of all beings, beginning with the gods.
Then, nourished by means of oblations of clarified butter,
those consumers of sacrificial offerings once again become the cause of rain for the sustenance of living beings.
Thus is this third step of Viṣṇu, which is pure in nature,
the support of the three worlds, and the cause of rain.
From there, O Brahmin, flows the river Gaṅgā, which removes all sins and is tawny with the unguents from the bodies of the celestial nymphs.
Dhruva bears with devotion upon his head day and night that [stream] which has issued forth from the flow of the toenail of Viṣṇu’s left lotus-foot.
Beyond that is the river upon whose waters, carried by garlands of waves, the Seven Sages remain, devoted to the practice of breath control, their matted locks floating in the flow.
The lunar orb, which was flooded by her continuous streams of water,
now bears an even greater beauty despite its waning.
Having emerged from the lunar disc, she falls high upon the summit of Mount Meru;
for the sake of purifying the world, she proceeds in the four directions.
The Sītā, the Cālakanandā, the Cakṣus, and the Bhadrā are established as one and the same river,
which appears divided into four according to its course through the different directions.
And her branch known as Alakanandā,
even Śarva bore upon his head with affection for more than a hundred years.
And she who issued from the mass of Śambhu’s matted locks, having flooded the world with its bones and gravel,
led the sinful sons of Sagara to heaven.
O Maitreya, for one who has bathed in her waters, sin is instantly destroyed and the attainment of unprecedented merit arises immediately.
O Maitreya, the waters offered there by sons endowed with faith to their ancestors provide them with a satisfaction that is difficult to attain for three years.
Having sacrificed with great sacrifices to the Lord of Sacrifice, the Supreme Person, in that [city],
twice-born men and kings attained supreme prosperity both in heaven and here on earth.
And likewise, by bathing in its waters, ascetics whose sins were washed away and whose minds were fixed on Keśava attained supreme liberation.
Whether heard, longed for, seen, touched, drunk, or bathed in,
she purifies all beings when recited day after day.
Even if uttered by those standing hundreds of yojanas away, the name "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" destroys the sin accumulated over three lifetimes.
For that supreme third state of the Blessed One has arisen, which is capable of purifying even the three worlds.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The stellar form of the Lord, the Sovereign, in the shape of a porpoise—
That which is the form of Hari in the heavens—Dhruva is situated at its tail.
As he revolves, he causes the planets, such as the moon and the sun, to revolve;
and following him as he turns, the constellations move like a wheel.
The sun and moon, the stars, and the constellations together with the planets are indeed bound to Dhruva by bonds consisting of the hosts of winds.
The form of the luminaries in the sky is said to be shaped like a porpoise.
Thus, the seven winds carry along the three worlds.
Nārāyaṇa is the refuge of all abodes; he himself is the support within the heart.
But Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, having propitiated that Lord of the World,
became established at the tail of the stellar Śiśumāra.
Janārdana, the supervisor of all, is the support of the Śiśumāra;
the Śiśumāra is the support of Dhruva; and the sun is established upon Dhruva.
And this entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans, has that as its support.
O Brahmin, listen with an undivided mind to the procedure by which this occurs:
Vivasvat, having drawn up the waters charged with essence over eight months, rains down water; from that comes food, and from food, the entire world.
Vivasvat, having drawn up the water of the world with his sharp rays, releases it into the moon; and the moon, through channels consisting of the wind, disperses it in the clouds in the sky,
which are composed of smoke, fire, and air.

Because the waters do not fall away from them, they are therefore called *abhra* (clouds). O Maitreya, the pure waters, impelled by the wind while situated in the clouds, reach a transformation produced by time and then descend.
O Sage, the Blessed Sun draws up water of four kinds: that from rivers, from the ocean, from the earth, and that produced by living beings.
Likewise, having taken up the water of the celestial Gaṅgā,
the Sun immediately casts it upon the earth with his rays while still remaining in the cloudless sky.
O best of the twice-born, a mortal whose stain of sin has been shaken off by contact with that [water] does not go to hell; for that is remembered as a divine bath.
For that water which, having seen the sun, falls from the sky through the clouds without [the aid of] clouds—
that water of the celestial Gaṅgā— is cast down by the rays of the sun.
When water from the sky falls upon the odd-numbered lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā while the sun is visible, it should be known as the Gaṅgā water released by the elephants of the quarters.
But the water that falls from the sky upon the twin constellations,
released by the sun, is immediately drawn up and cast down again by the solar rays.
O twice-born one, O great sage, both are exceedingly meritorious and remove the sins of men: the water of the celestial Ganges and the divine bath [there]. ViP_2,9.17.
O twice-born one, that water which is released by the clouds nourishes all plants; for it is indeed the nectar of life for living beings.
O twice-born one, by that [water] the multitude of medicinal herbs is brought to supreme growth; it becomes a benefactor for all creatures until the ripening of their fruit.
Therefore, men who possess the eye of the scriptures perform the sacrifices as they have been prescribed day after day,
and by means of them, they nourish the gods.
In this way, the sacrifices, the Vedas, and the social classes headed by the twice-born, as well as all the hosts of gods and the multitudes of animals and spirits— ViP_2,9.21.
O best of sages, all this food is produced by rain; yet that rain itself is produced by the Sun.
O best of eminent sages, Dhruva is the support of Savitṛ;
that Śiśumāra is the support of Dhruva, and he too has Nārāyaṇa as his refuge.
Within the heart of that Śiśumāra resides Nārāyaṇa,
the eternal, primordial source, and the sustainer of all beings.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The interval between the two solstitial points (kāṣṭhā) is one hundred and eighty circles (maṇḍala).
The movement of the sun through its ascent and descent over the course of a year—
That chariot was presided over by the gods, the Ādityas, as well as the ṛṣis,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
Dhātṛ, Kṛtasthalā, Pulastya, Vāsuki,
Rathakṛt, Grāmaṇī, Heti, and Tumburu as the seventh.
O Maitreya, these seven indeed always reside in the month of Caitra, the month of honey, as the presiding deities of the Sun's chariot for that month.
Aryaman, Pulaha, Rathaujas, Puñjikasthalā,
Praheti, Kacchanīra, and Nārada were in the chariot of Ravi.
These dwell in Mādhava, which is known as Śuci; learn this from me.
Mitra, Atri, Takṣaka, Pauruṣeya Rakṣas, Menakā,
Hāhā, and Rathasvana— these, O Maitreya, indeed dwell there.
Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha, Rambhā, Sahajanyā, Huhū, and Rathacitra—
these dwell in the chariot during the month known as Āṣāḍha, when Śukra is present.
Indra, Viśvāvasu, Srotas, Elāpatra, as well as Aṅgiras,
Pramlocā, and Nabhas— these indeed dwell with the Serpent in the month of Ārka.
Vivasvān, Ugrasena, Bhṛgu, Āpūraṇa,
Umlocā, Śaṅkhapāla, and Vyāghra likewise [reigned] in the month of Bhādrapada.
Pūṣan, Suruci, Vāta, Gautama, Dhanañjaya,
another named Suṣeṇa, and Ghṛtācī dwell in the sun during the month of Āśvayuja.
Viśvāvasu, Bharadvāja, Parjanya, Airāvata,
as well as Viśvācī and Senajit, are the presiding deities in the month of Kārttika.
Aṃśuka, Āśyapa, Tārkṣya, Mahāpadma, Urvaśī, Citrasena, and Vidyun were the presiding deities of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Kratu, Bhaga, Urṇāyu, Sphūrja, Karkoṭaka,
Ariṣṭanemi, and another, the excellent Apsaras Pūrvacitti.
In the month of Pauṣa, these seven, acting as authorized officials, dwell within the solar orb for the purpose of illuminating the world, O best of Brahmins.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Jamadagni, Kambala, Tilottamā,
Brahmāpeta, Ṛtajit, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the seventh.
O Maitreya, these seven dwell in the sun during the month of Māgha;
now hear about those others who reside in the sun during Phālguna.
O great sage, Viṣṇu, Aśvatara, Rambhā, Sūryavarcas, Satyajit, Viśvāmitra, and likewise the Rākṣasa Yajñopeta [were born]. ViP_2.10.18.
O Maitreya, O Brahmin, during these months these seven dwell within the orb of the sun, empowered by the energy of Viṣṇu.
The sages praise the Sun; he is sung of by the Gandharvas before him;
the Apsarases dance, and the night-stalkers follow after the Sun.
The serpents carry it, and the Yakṣas hold the reins.
Likewise, the Vālakhilyas sit surrounding him on all sides.
Thus, O best of sages, this group of seven in the solar orb,
having reached its own appointed time, is the cause of cold, heat, and the falling of rain.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
Regarding that which the Blessed One has stated—that the host of the Sun is sevenfold—
I have heard from him the cause of the cold, heat, and so forth within the cosmic egg (maṇḍala).
O Teacher, the activities of the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as those of the Ṛṣis, the Vālakhilyas, and likewise the Apsarases, have also been described.
O Sage, you have described the chariots of the Yakṣas and of Bhānu, whose souls are sustained by the power of Viṣṇu; however, you have not yet told us here what the function of Āditya is.
If the seven groups of winds rain down water that is both cold and hot, then what is the role of the sun here, by virtue of which it is said that "the rain comes from the sun"?
Why does people say that Vivasvat rises in the middle [of the day] and goes to his setting? This would be the same action if it belonged to the group of seven [sages].
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to this which you ask:
how it is that among the group of seven, the Sun alone is preeminent by virtue of his superiority.
That supreme power of Viṣṇu which is designated as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—
this very triple Veda burns away sin and destroys whatever harms the world.
This very Viṣṇu, intent on the protection of the world, remains established in the act of preservation;
O twice-born one, he dwells within the Sun, having become the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Indeed, month after month, whichever sun is present in each respective location,
that supreme power of Viṣṇu, consisting of the three Vedas, truly establishes her abode there.
The Ṛg verses scorch during the forenoon, the Yajus formulas at midday, and the Sāman chants,
such as the Bṛhat and Rathantara, at the end of the day when the sun is setting.
This threefold Veda, known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, is a portion of Viṣṇu;
that power of Viṣṇu always abides within the sun.
That Vaiṣṇava power of the Sun is not only composed of the three Vedas;
for Brahmā, Puruṣa, and Rudra—this triad is likewise composed of the three Vedas.
At the beginning of creation, Brahmā consists of the Ṛgveda; for the maintenance of the world, Viṣṇu consists of the Yajurveda;
and Rudra consists of the Sāmaveda for the sake of dissolution. Therefore, his sound is impure.
Thus that Vaiṣṇavī power, which is of the nature of the three Vedas and characterized by sattva,
presides over that radiant one who abides within the seven groups of the self.
Empowered by her, he too blazes intensely with his own rays and brings about the destruction of all darkness throughout the entire world.
The sages indeed praise him; he is sung of before him by the Gandharvas;
the Apsarases dance, and the night-stalkers follow after him.
The serpents bear it, the Yakṣas hold the reins,
and the Vālakhilyas sit surrounding it on all sides.
Bearing the form of power, Viṣṇu never rises nor does he ever set; even this sevenfold host of his is not separate from Viṣṇu.
Just as a person who stands near a mirror mounted on a pillar attains the conjunction of seeing his own reflection, so it is with this [attainment].
In this way, O twice-born one, that Vaiṣṇava power never departs from him;
month after month, it dwells within him, remaining established there like the sun.
O twice-born one, the Lord Savitṛ, constantly nourishing the ancestors, gods, humans, and others,
revolves as the cause of day and night.
The sun's ray known as Suṣumṇā is that by which the moon is nourished;
during the dark fortnight, the gods constantly drink it, for it consists of nectar.
O twice-born one, at the end of the dark fortnight, the ancestors drink that yellow moon which has two phases; such is their gratification from the sun.
The Sun, with his rays, takes up the moisture situated upon the earth;
he releases it for the nourishment of living beings and for the growth of crops.
By that, the Blessed Lord Ravi gratifies all beings without exception;
in this way, he nourishes the ancestors, gods, humans, and others.
O Maitreya, the Sun bestows upon the gods satisfaction for a fortnight, upon the ancestors for a month, and eternal satisfaction upon mortals.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The chariot of Soma has three wheels; its horses have the luster of jasmine.
Joined by ten on the left and right, he moves along by means of them.
The constellations resting upon the celestial path are held by the swift Dhruva,
just as the rays of the sun undergo a process of decrease and increase.
For his horses, O best of sages, born from the womb of the waters, once yoked carry him for an entire kalpa, just like the horses of the Sun.
O Maitreya, the radiant sun causes the moon, which has been diminished and drunk by the gods until it remains as a single digit, to swell again by means of a single ray.
In the same sequence by which that [nectar] was drunk by the gods,
the sun, the stealer of waters, daily causes the moon to swell.

O Maitreya, the gods drink that nectar of immortality which is collected within the moon over the course of half a month; for this reason, they are called the "eaters of nectar" (sudhāhāra) and are therefore immortal.
Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred,
and thirty-three gods drink the maker of the night [the moon].
But when only two digits remain, he has entered the solar orb;
he dwells in the ray called Amā, and therefore it is known as Amāvāsyā.
During that day and night, the moon first enters the waters;
thereafter it dwells in the plants, and from there it proceeds to the sun in due order.
He who cuts down plants or causes even a single leaf to fall when the moon is situated in the lunar mansion of the Plants (Mṛgaśiras) incurs the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
When fifteen parts remain, with but a small portion of a *kalā* still left,
the hosts of ancestors wait upon [the sun] at the final hour of the afternoon.
O sage, the ancestors drink the Soma during two phases; as for that remaining digit of the moon which consists of sacred nectar, the Pitṛs drink that.
On the new moon day, that nectar of immortality flows forth from the rays;
having obtained supreme satisfaction for a month, the ancestors remain in a state of bliss.
They are of three kinds: the Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas.
In this way, he nourishes the gods during the bright fortnight and likewise the ancestors during the dark fortnight,
as well as the plants, with cool water-molecules consisting of nectar.
By means of the production of creepers and medicinal herbs, the cool-rayed moon nourishes humans, cattle, and insects; furthermore, it does so through its illumination and its gladdening power.
The chariot of the son of the Moon is composed of the substances of wind and fire;
it is yoked to eight tawny horses that possess the speed of the wind.
The great chariot of Śukra was also equipped with a protective fender and a chassis, yoked to horses born of the earth, and provided with quivers and banners.
The great chariot of Bhauma was also golden and magnificent, drawn by eight horses;
it was yoked with steeds as red as rubies, born from fire.
While Bṛhaspati stands upon that golden chariot yoked with eight white horses, he indeed remains for a year in each successive zodiac sign.
Having mounted a chariot joined with dappled horses born of space,
the slow-moving Śanaiścara proceeds gently.
Svarbhānu’s horses are eight in number, with the luster of bees; once yoked to his grey chariot, O Maitreya, they carry him perpetually and without ceasing.
Emerging from the Sun, Rāhu approaches the Moon during the lunar nodes;
and from the Moon he goes again to the Sun during the solar nodes.
Likewise, the eight horses of Keturatha possess the speed of the wind;
they have the hue of straw-smoke and are as ruddy as liquid lac.
O highly fortunate one, these nine chariots of the planets have been described by me to you; they are all bound to Dhruva by cords of wind.
O Maitreya, the planets, constellations, stars, and celestial mansions are all entirely bound to Dhruva and revolve in their proper courses by means of the reins of the wind.
As many as are the stars, so many are the cords of wind;
all of them are fastened to Dhruva, and as they revolve, they cause him to revolve.
Just as oil-pressers cause a wheel to revolve by their own spinning,
so too do the luminaries, impelled by the wind, revolve in every direction.
Driven by the wind-circles, the luminaries move like a whirling firebrand;
because it carries them along, it is therefore known as the Pravaha wind.
Now, O best of sages, hear also the configuration of that which is called the Śiśumāra, wherein Dhruva resides.
Whatever sin one commits by day, one is freed from it upon seeing him at night;
and for as many stars as there are situated upon the Śiśumāra in the sky,
for so many years, plus more, does he live.
Then Uttānapāda is to be known as his upper jaw, and Yajña is to be known as the lower; Dharma is to be understood as residing in the head.
Nārāyaṇa resides in his heart; the two Aśvins are in his two forefeet;
and Varuṇa and Aryaman are in his two hind-thighs.
The year is his penis; Mitra has taken refuge in his apāna.
In its tail are Agni, Mahendra, Kaśyapa, and then Dhruva;
these four stars of the Śiśumāra never set.
Thus has been described this configuration of the earth, as well as that of the luminaries, the islands, the oceans, and the mountains.
The nature of the rain-clouds, the rivers, and those who indeed dwell within them has been described; listen again as it is told once more in brief.
O Brahmin, from that water which was indeed the body of Viṣṇu,
the earth emerged in the form of a lotus, joined with mountains, oceans, and other features.
The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu, the forests, the mountains, and the quarters are Viṣṇu;
the rivers and the oceans—all that exists and all that does not exist is he alone, O best of brahmins.
Since the Blessed One is of the nature of consciousness and possesses an infinite form, yet is not a material entity,
you should therefore understand that the distinctions of mountains, oceans, the earth, and so forth, are merely the manifestations of consciousness.
But when, through the exhaustion of karma, all knowledge is pure, consisting of its own innate nature and free from defects,
then indeed the fruits of the tree of conceptual construction do not arise as distinctions between objects among things.
Is there anywhere any entity that is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and which remains eternally of one and the same form?
And since, O twice-born one, it undergoes change again and again, how can there be reality in that which is not as it was?
The earth becomes a jar; from the jar, shards; from the shards, powdered dust; and from that, atoms.
Tell me, what is the true reality here, perceived by people whose certainty regarding the self is fixed by their own karma?
