Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of objects whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, that exists apart from consciousness;
consciousness alone is accepted as manifold by minds differentiated by the distinctions of their own respective karmas.
Knowledge that is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, and devoid of all attachment such as greed—eternal, ever-one, and supreme—is Vāsudeva, the highest Lord; there is nothing other than He.

I have declared to you this true nature of yours, that knowledge which is truth and all else which is untruth; and even regarding that which constitutes worldly convention, I have explained to you that which pertains to the world.

The sacrifice, the animal, the fire, all the officiating priests, the Soma, the gods, and the desire consisting of heaven—these are seen as the paths dependent on ritual action; and their fruits are the enjoyments of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
Whatever has been told by me to you regarding this world, it is indeed the one who is subject to karma that wanders everywhere;
knowing this, one should perform that which is certain, immovable, and eternally uniform, by means of which one enters Vāsudeva.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, everything that you were asked by me has been correctly explained.
The configuration of the earth, oceans, and rivers, as well as the positions of the planets; 2.13.1.
Just as these three worlds are established with Viṣṇu as their support,
so too has the ultimate truth been declared to me, primarily through the perspective of knowledge.
However, regarding that which the Blessed One spoke concerning the deeds of King Bharata,
you should deign to relate that history to me.
That protector of the earth, Bharata, it is said, dwelt at Sālagrāma,
constantly engaged in yoga and fixing his mind upon Vāsudeva.
Given the power of that holy place and his constant meditation on Hari,
why did liberation not occur when he was born again as that twice-born man?
Furthermore, you ought to tell me what was done by that great-souled one while he was a Brahmin, according to the nature of his previous karma.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, that illustrious lord of the earth dwelt for a very long time at Sālagrāma, having fixed his mind upon the Blessed One.
The best among those possessed of virtues attained the highest perfection in all virtues, beginning with non-violence, as well as in the restraint of the mind.
"O Lord of Sacrifice, O Acyuta, O Govinda, O Mādhava, O Ananta, O Keśava,
O Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Hṛṣīkeśa"— this alone the king uttered.
After 9c, as edited by Veṅkaṭeśvara, the following is inserted:
... ... Vāsudeva, homage be to you! ViP 2.13.9*11:1.
Thus spoke King Bharata...
O Maitreya, he spoke nothing else even in his dreams;
apart from this state and its meaning, he thought of nothing else.
The ascetic yogin, free from attachment, performed the gathering of sacrificial wood, flowers, and *kuśa* grass for the sake of divine rites; he performed no other actions.
Once, he went to the great river for the purpose of ritual ablution;
he bathed there and then performed the rites that follow bathing.
Then, O Brahmin, a single doe, thirsty and near her time to give birth, came from the forest to that sacred bathing place to drink water.
Then, when the water had been mostly drunk by her,
there arose there a tremendous roar of a lion, terrifying to all living beings.
Then, suddenly leaping from the riverbank out of fear,
her fetus fell into the river because of that excessively high leap.
The king seized that young deer, which had fallen from her womb, as it was being carried away with great speed, tossed about by a garland of waves.
O Maitreya, due to the pain of the miscarriage of her fetus and from the intense shock, that doe fell down and died.
Then, having seen that doe fallen, the king-ascetic took the fawn and returned once more to the hermitage.
O Sage, that king performed the nourishment of the young deer day after day; and being thus nurtured by him, it grew up.
He grazed on grasses in the thickets at the edge of the hermitage;
and having gone far, he returned again out of fear of the tiger.
Having gone a very great distance in the morning, he returned to that hermitage in the evening;
and once again, Bharata arrived at the courtyard of the leaf-hut in the hermitage.
O twice-born one, as that deer moved about at a distance or nearby, his mind remained fixed upon it and did not go elsewhere.
Having renounced his kingdom and sons, and having abandoned all his kinsmen,
he felt an intense sense of possessiveness toward that young fawn.
"Has he been devoured by wolves? Has he been struck down by tigers? Or has he been killed by a lion?"—such was the thought in his mind as [Rāma] went out and delayed for a long time.
This earth is mottled by the wounds from the tips of his hooves.
"Where has that young fawn of mine gone, who used to come for my pleasure?
He was indeed intent on scratching my arms with the tips of his horns;
having returned safely from the forest, he will surely bring me joy."
With their tufts of hair recently shorn by his teeth,
these kuśa and kāśa grasses shine like young brahmin students chanting the Sāmaveda.
When he had thus departed for a long time, the sage, his face bright with joy, fixed his mind upon him and remained with the deer standing by his side.
Because his soul was absorbed in that [practice], there was no breaking of his concentration,
even though he was a king who had renounced royal power, enjoyments, prosperity, and his own kin.
Although that fawn was restless, far-reaching, and prone to wander afar,
the mind of that king became steadfast toward it.
Then, as time passed, that lord of the earth met his end,
watched with tears by his son like a young deer watching its father.
At that time, O Maitreya, he saw the deer; and even as he was giving up his life, being absorbed in that [deer], he thought of nothing else.
And then, having attained such a state of mental cultivation produced at that time,
he was born as a deer with the memory of his former births in the great forest of Jambūmārga.
O best of the twice-born, being distressed by the cycle of existence due to his recollection of past births,
he abandoned his mother and returned once more to Sālagrāma.
Sustaining himself with dry grass and leaves in that manner,
he attained the expiation for the karma that had caused his state as a deer.
And there, having cast off his body, he was born as a twice-born man who remembered his former births,
in a pure and preeminent family of yogis devoted to virtuous conduct.
Endowed with all forms of knowledge and knowing the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures,
O Maitreya, he beheld himself as transcendent to primordial nature (prakṛti).
O Great Sage, having attained knowledge of the Self, that high-minded one beheld all beings, beginning with the gods, as non-different from himself.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, he did not recite the Veda as taught by his guru;
nor did he observe the ritual acts, nor did he master the scriptures.
Although addressed many times, he spoke only a few words that were dull;
even those lacked the quality of refinement and relied upon the style of vulgar speech.
Then that brahmin, his body disfigured, wearing soiled garments,
with the gaps between his teeth wet, was treated with contempt by all the citizens.
Since honor causes the supreme ruin of the power of yoga,
the yogi who is disregarded by people attains the perfection of yoga.
Therefore, a yogi should indeed practice the dharma of the virtuous without causing offense, so that people do not despise him and do not avoid his company.
Reflecting thus upon the words of Hiraṇyagarbha, the high-minded one manifested himself among the people in the form of a dull-witted madman.
He eats groats, potherbs such as vāṭyāla, wild fruits, and grains;
whatever he obtains in great abundance, that he consumes while restraining himself according to the time.
When his father had passed away, he was then compelled by his brothers, rivals, and kinsmen to perform field labor and other such tasks, being nourished only on coarse food.
With coarse and stout limbs, he was dull-witted in his work;
he became a provider for all the world, receiving food as his wages.
The chamberlain considered that man— who was thus devoid of refinement and whose behavior was like that of a commoner— to be fit for manual labor for the king of Sauvīra.
After 48c, D₄, T₃, G₂,₃, and the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition insert: ... [he] yoked the animal for Kālyā.
Having adorned him at night according to the prescribed rules for execution, [he was led away].
Then Mahākālī, knowing that the Lord of Yoga was thus empowered, [acted].
Then, taking up a sharp sword at that time in the night, she [acted].
He severed the throat of the steward, who was a man of cruel deeds, right at its base.
With preparations for the sake of flesh, he drank the copious blood.
Then, as the high-souled king of Sauvīra set forth...
Then the overseer there [thought], "This man is indeed fit for forced labor."
The steward of the king of Sauvīra... // ViP_2,13.48*12:9 //
O twice-born one, that king, having set his mind on going, mounted his palanquin and proceeded toward the excellent hermitage of the seer Kapila on the banks of the Ikṣumatī.
"What is the highest good for men here in this cycle of existence, which is mostly suffering?"—
with these words he questioned that great sage named Kapila, who was a knower of the dharma of liberation.
Urged by the words of the steward, he carried the palanquin for him,
standing in the midst of other men who had been conscripted as forced laborers.
The Brahmin, who was the sole vessel for all knowledge, having been seized by forced labor,
remembered his former births and, desiring the destruction of his sins, carried her.
Then he, the best among the wise, proceeded with a slow gait, looking only the distance of a yoke ahead; but the others went quickly.
Observing that uneven motion of the palanquin, the king also said, "What is this? O bearers of the palanquin, proceed evenly!"
Again, looking at the palanquin in that same uneven state, the king laughed and said, "What is this? You are traveling in a different manner!"
Having heard these words spoken many times by the lord of the earth,
the bearers of the palanquin said, "He goes, but not with haste."
The King said:
"Are you tired? You have carried my palanquin only a short distance.
Are you not capable of enduring exertion? For you appear to be stout."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I am not fat, nor have I carried this palanquin of yours;
I am not weary, O lord of the earth, nor is there any fatigue for me to endure."
The King said:
"You appear visibly stout, and even now the palanquin is upon you;
for embodied beings certainly experience fatigue from carrying a burden."
The Brahmin said:
"O King, tell me what you have seen before your very eyes;
whether one is strong or weak is a qualification that should be stated afterwards."
"The palanquin was carried by you, and it remains with you even now;
this is false. In this matter, however, may your majesty hear my words."
The pair of feet was established upon the earth; the two shanks rested upon the two feet;
the two thighs were situated upon the two shanks; and the belly was likewise supported by them.
"The chest, the arms, and the shoulders are situated upon the belly;
this palanquin rests upon the shoulders. What burden has been placed upon me here?"
This body, which you perceive, is situated upon the palanquin;
yet there you are, and I am here as well—this is said to be otherwise [than what it appears].
"O King, you, I, and others as well are carried along by the elements;
even this entire collection of elements proceeds, fallen into the flow of the qualities."
O Lord of the Earth, these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are indeed subject to karma;
and that karma, accumulated through ignorance, exists in all living beings without exception.
The Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature;
it neither increases nor decreases, being one and the same within all living beings.
O King, since there was neither increase nor decrease for him, by what logic was it stated by you that he was "fat"? *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 2.13.68.
When this palanquin was placed upon your shoulder, with its weight distributed across your feet, shanks, hips, thighs, belly, and so forth, then the burden was indeed equal for you.
Likewise, O King, the chariot was produced not only by other creatures,
but also by mountains, trees, houses, or even the earth itself.
O King, when a man’s state is distinct from material causes, then what burden, O Lord of Men, is there for me to carry? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.13.71)
Of whatever substance this palanquin is made, of that same substance is this aggregate of elements;
it belongs to you and to all this world, yet it is magnified by your sense of "mine-ness."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, that twice-born man remained silent while carrying the palanquin;
the king, too, alighting from the ground, quickly grasped his feet.
The King said:
"O twice-born one, please set down the palanquin and show me favor;
tell me, who are you that stands here assuming the form of a commoner?"
O learned one, let all that— whether it be your purpose or the reason for your arrival— be told by you to me, who am eager to hear it.
The Brahmin said:
"O King, it is impossible to say who I am;
my movement everywhere is solely for the sake of experiencing objects of enjoyment."
The experience of pleasure and pain, which arise from merit and demerit and bring about the acquisition of a body and so forth,
leads the living being to assume a body and other such states in order to experience them.
For indeed, O protector of the earth, dharma and adharma are the cause for every living being in all circumstances; since this is so, why is the cause being questioned?
The King said:
"There is no doubt that dharma and adharma are the cause in all actions;
and the embodied soul's migration to another region is for the purpose of experiencing [the results]."
As for this which you have said—that "Who am I? regarding the self—it cannot be explained; yet, my desire to hear it is set in motion.
O Brahmin, how can it be impossible to say "I am he who exists"?
O twice-born one, for the word "I" used with respect to the Self alone entails no fault.
The Brahmin said:
"The notion 'I am sound' leads to error; it is not so with respect to the Self. The cognition of the Self in what is not the Self, or the word [expressing it], is characterized by delusion."
"The tongue says 'I am,' O King, as do the teeth, the lips, and the palate;
yet these are not 'I,' because they are all merely the instruments for producing speech."
"Does she speak thus by means of reasons, saying 'I am speech' herself?
Even so, it is not logical to say 'I am speech' in this manner."
Since this body, characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the person,
O King, why then do I apply this notion of "I" to it?
O best of kings, if there were anyone else superior to me,
then it would be appropriate to speak thus of both him and this other person.
When the one Puruṣa is established within all bodies, then indeed such speech as "Who are you? and "Who am I? is meaningless.
"You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers and those who go before;
and this world belongs to you"—O King, this which is said is not true.
From the tree comes the wood, and from that, O King, this palanquin occupied by you; where has the designation "tree" gone, or is it now the designation "wood"?
"The Great King is mounted upon a tree, yet this person does not speak to you;
nor does anyone say anything to you as you sit in the palanquin made of wood."
"O best of kings, search for the palanquin within the collection of wooden parts that constitutes its structure, arrangement, and stability; once it is dismantled, the palanquin is no longer found."
In this same way, consider the separation of the ribs of an umbrella;
where has the umbrella gone? This principle applies equally to you and to me.
"Man," "woman," "cow," "this horse," "elephant," "bird," and "tree"—these are worldly designations for bodies produced by the causes of karma; thus they should be understood.
The person (puruṣa) is neither god, nor man, nor beast, nor tree;
O King, these differences in bodily forms have their origin in karma.
Whatever in the world is designated as "king," whatever consists of the king's soldiers,
and likewise anything else, O King— it is thus not real, but is composed of mental construction.
O King, that which does not even over time acquire another designation, despite the occurrence of transformation and so forth— what indeed is that entity?
You are the king of the entire world; you are the son of your father and the enemy of your foe;
you are the husband of your wife and the father of your son—O King, whom among these may I call you?
"O Lord of the Earth, what is this head? Is it indeed your head? Likewise, what is the belly? And what indeed are the feet and so forth? Are these yours? ||| ViP_2,13.98 |||
O King, you exist as something distinct from all your constituent parts; becoming discerning, reflect deeply, O Ruler of the Earth, upon the question: "Who am I?"
Such being the established reality, O King, how could it be possible for me to speak of "I" as something to be accomplished through the process of differentiation?
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of his, which were endowed with the highest truth, [Maitreya spoke].
Bowing down with humility, the king spoke to that brahmin.
When the impossibility of valid means of knowledge has been established by the statement beginning with "I am not," etc., [Śiva spoke].
Then, suspecting that the object of knowledge might be impossible, he asks again and again.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, as for these words consisting of the supreme truth that you have spoken,
upon hearing them, the functions of my mind seem to whirl."
O Brahmin, this discriminative knowledge which you have shown regarding all living beings is supreme and greater than primordial nature.
"I do not carry the palanquin, nor does the palanquin rest upon me;
the body by which this palanquin is supported is distinct from us."
"The activity of beings proceeds from the operation of the *guṇas*, impelled by karma;
these *guṇas* themselves act—what concern is this of mine?"—this was said by you. (ViP 2.14.5)
When these words concerning the ultimate truth reached my ears,
my mind, seeking that very ultimate truth, fell into a state of agitation.
O twice-born one, previously I set out to go and question the illustrious seer Kapila, asking without doubt, "What indeed is the highest good? (ViP 2.14.7).
And during that interval, because of this very statement uttered by you,
my mind runs toward you for the sake of the ultimate truth.
The venerable sage Kapila was indeed a portion of the Blessed Viṣṇu, who pervades all beings; he descended to the earth for the purpose of destroying the delusion of the world.
Surely it is that very Blessed One who, out of a desire for our welfare,
has appeared here before our eyes, just as you have described him.
O twice-born one, you who are an ocean whose waves are the waters of all-encompassing knowledge, please tell me— that who am bowed before you— whatever is the supreme good.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, do you ask what is the highest good, or do you ask about the ultimate truth?
For all other forms of the good, O Lord of the Earth, are indeed not the ultimate truth."
Having performed the propitiation of the deities, he desires the attainment of wealth, sons, and a kingdom; that is the characteristic of attaining the highest good.
Action consisting of sacrifice is superior, as it bestows the fruit of the heavenly world;
yet that very action is the highest good when its fruit is not sought after.
O King, the Self and likewise the Supreme should always be meditated upon by those engaged in yoga;
for union with that very Self is the highest good, which is the supreme goal of the Supreme Self.
Thus, there are many hundreds and thousands of such superior things here; however, these are not the ultimate truths. Listen now to me as I explain them.
If wealth is for the sake of Dharma, why is it that the ultimate goal is abandoned?
And why is expenditure made for the mere purpose of attaining sensual desires?
O Lord of Men, if a son is called the ultimate reality (paramārtha), he too is the ultimate reality for another;
for that father is indeed the ultimate reality for him.
Thus, there is no ultimate reality in this world of the moving and the unmoving;
for the ultimate reality consists of the effects of causes in their entirety.
If the attainment of sovereignty and so forth mentioned here were [to be considered] from the perspective of ultimate reality,
then since things either exist or do not exist in this ultimate sense, they would [simply] cease to be.
In your view, the sacrificial rite is considered to be accomplished through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas;
even regarding that, hear from me as I speak of its ultimate reality.
O King, whatever effect is produced from clay as its material cause is known to be made of clay, because it follows the nature of its cause.
In this way, whatever ritual action is accomplished by means of perishable substances such as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and kuśa grass,
that action itself must be perishable.
The wise accept that the ultimate reality is imperishable;
however, that which is produced from perishable substances is certainly perishable, without a doubt.

Therefore, that very action which yields no fruit is considered by you to be the ultimate reality (paramārtha), because it serves as the means for liberation; yet the ultimate reality itself is not a means.
And meditation, O King, which is designated as the goal of the ultimate truth, creates a distinction from others; yet the ultimate truth itself is not characterized by distinction.
The union of the supreme self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality;
for this [union] is false, since one substance cannot become the nature of another substance.
Therefore, O King, all these are undoubtedly superior;
but as for the ultimate truth, O protector of the earth, hear it from me in brief.
The Self is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
free from birth, growth, and so forth, omnipresent, and immutable.

O King, the all-pervading Lord, who consists of supreme knowledge, has never been joined with, nor was he ever joined to, nor will he ever be joined to, unreal categories such as name, genus, and the like.
That consciousness which, though existing within the bodies of oneself and others, is indeed of a single nature—that is the ultimate reality; those who perceive duality are seers of unreality.
Just as the distinctions designated as *ṣaḍja* and so forth arise from the differences in the holes of a flute,
so too do the distinctions of that Great Soul arise from the air which pervades all without distinction.
Unity and the differentiation of forms arise from the engagement in external karma;
for when the distinctions such as "god" and so forth are destroyed, that obscuration simply does not exist.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
When this had been spoken, the king remained silent once more, lost in thought.
Then that brahmin replied with a discourse concerning non-duality.
The brāhmaṇa said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to that which was sung by Ṛbhu in the past,
producing awakening in the twice-born Nidāgha.
O King, the son of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was named Ṛbhu; he understood the true nature of reality from his very birth.
When both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge have been correctly ascertained through valid cognition and reasoning, [the goal is attained].
In ancient times, his disciple was Nidāgha, the son of Pulastya;
he bestowed upon him complete knowledge with supreme joy.
O Lord of Men, that Ṛbhu reflected upon the non-dualistic impression of Nidāgha, who had attained the reality of knowledge.
On the bank of the Devikā is a city named Vīranagara,
prosperous and exceedingly beautiful, which was established by Pulastya.
O best of kings, in former times a knower of yoga named Nidāgha, a disciple of Ṛbhu, lived there on the edge of that beautiful grove.
When a thousand divine years had passed,
that Ṛbhu went to see his disciple Nidāgha in that city.
At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he stood within the range of his vision at the doorway; having been offered the guest-offering (argha) by him, he was led into his own dwelling.
When he had washed his hands and feet and taken his seat,
that best of brahmins respectfully said to him, "Please eat."
Śr̥bhu said:
"O best of brahmins, let it be told what food is to be eaten in your house;
for I have no constant pleasure in poor-quality fare."
Nidāgha said:
"O best of the twice-born, whatever among the groats, barley-meal, pottage, and cakes in my house pleases you, please eat that according to your desire."
Śr̥bhu said:
"O twice-born one, these are but poor foods; give me sweet food—such as *saṃyāva*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and the like, along with honeyed drops and molasses."
Nidāgha said:
"O graceful lady, whatever excellent food-preparation there is in my house, prepare her meal with that sweet delicacy."
The Brahmin said:
Having been addressed thus by him, that wife, out of respect for her husband’s words, prepared the sweet food intended for the twice-born.
O King, when that great sage had finished eating the sweet food according to his desire,
Nidāgha, standing bowed with humility, spoke to him.
Nidāgha said:
"O twice-born one, has supreme satisfaction and contentment arisen within you? Has your mind been made healthy by this food?"
"O Brahmin, where is your residence, and whither are you prepared to go? O twice-born one, please tell us also from where you have come."
Śr̥bhu said: "O Brāhmaṇa, he who has hunger attains satisfaction after eating food.
I have had no hunger; why do you ask me about my satisfaction?"
When the earth element is consumed by fire, hunger arises;
and when the water element is diminished, thirst also arises in men.
"Hunger and thirst, O twice-born one, are known as properties of the body; since these do not belong to me, I am indeed always satisfied because of the absence of the occurrence of hunger."
"O twice-born one, composure of mind and contentment are these two qualities of the intellect;
ask about him whose mind possesses these, for such a man is not bound by these."
When it was asked, "Where is your residence? and "Where will you go?", as well as "From where have you come?", listen to my reply regarding all three of these.
Since this person is all-pervading and omnipresent like space, how could even such questions as "From where?", "Where?", or "Whither will you go? be meaningful?
Thus, I am neither a goer nor a comer, nor do I have a dwelling in any single place;
you and others are not you, nor are they others, and even I am not "I."
"Whether this is well-prepared or not—this inquiry was made by me concerning you.
O best of the twice-born, let it also be heard what he will say in that regard. (ViP 2.15.26)
O best of the twice-born, whether one eats food that is unpalatable or even delicious,
that which was once delicious becomes the very cause of distress when it turns unpalatable.
What is unrefined becomes refined; from the refined, people shrink away.
At its beginning, middle, and end, what food is truly pleasing?
Just as a house made of clay becomes stable when plastered with clay,
so too is this earthly body composed of earthly atoms.
For a person who is smeared [with sin] yet causes others to prosper, what enjoyment has been achieved in this world?
Barley, wheat, mung beans, and so forth; clarified butter, oil, milk, curd;
molasses, fruits, and the like, as well as the atoms of the earth—[all these were produced]. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15.30)
Having understood this, you should cause that mind—which discriminates between the pleasant and the unpleasant—to rest in equanimity; for equanimity leads to liberation.
The Brahmin said:
O King, having heard those words of his which were based on the ultimate truth, the illustrious Nidāgha prostrated himself and spoke these words. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 2.15.32.
Be gracious for my benefit; tell me who you are that have come here.
O twice-born one, my delusion has vanished upon hearing these words of yours.
Śr̥bhu said:
"I am Śr̥bhu, your teacher; O twice-born one, I have come here to bestow wisdom upon you.
I shall now depart; the supreme truth has been declared to you."
In this way, know that this entire world is one and without division;
it is the very nature of the Supreme Self, who is designated as Vāsudeva.
The Brahmin said:
Having said "So be it," and being honored with supreme devotion by Nidāgha preceded by prostrations, Ṛbhu departed according to his will.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O lord of men, when a thousand years had passed for Ṛbhu..."
He went to that very city in order to bestow the knowledge of Nidāgha.
Then, outside the city, that sage beheld Nidāgha as the king was entering the city with a vast retinue of great power.
He saw the illustrious one standing at a distance, avoiding the crush of people,
his throat parched with hunger, returning from the forest with sacrificial fuel and kuśa grass.
Having seen Nidāgha, Ṛbhu approached him, saluted him, and said:
"O twice-born one, why are you standing in this secluded spot?"
Nidāgha said:
"O Brahmin, this great crowd of people is gathered because the lord of men is about to enter the beautiful city; for that reason, I am staying here."
Śr̥bhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me who here is the lord of men and who is the other person; for you are considered by me to be one who possesses true knowledge."
Nidāgha said:
This king who has mounted the intoxicated lord of elephants, which is as lofty as a mountain peak— this world and the other [the next] are likewise dependent upon him.
Śr̥bhu said: "Indeed, these two king elephants were shown to me by you simultaneously;
they could not be distinguished by you through their individual characteristics."
Therefore, O illustrious one, let the distinction between these two be told by you;
I wish to know which here is the elephant and which is the lord of men.
Nidāgha said:
"O Brahmin, this elephant is below, and the king is right above it; who indeed, O twice-born one, does not know the relationship between the rider and the mount? (ViP 2.16.10)
Śr̥bhu said: "I know this, O Brahmin; therefore, instruct me accordingly:
what is designated by the word 'below,' and what is called 'above'?"
The Brahmin said:
Thus addressed, Nidāgha immediately climbed up and spoke to that Ṛbhu:
"Listen, I shall tell you that which you ask of me."
O Brahmin, I have shown you this illustration for the sake of your awakening: as I am the king above, so you are the elephant below.
Śr̥bhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, if you stand like a king and I am like an elephant, then tell me that very thing: who are you and who am I?"
The Brāhmaṇa said: Thus addressed, Nidāgha quickly grasped both his feet and said, "O Blessed One, you are certainly the preceptor Ṛbhu."
"The mind of no other person is so refined by the impressions of non-duality as that of the Teacher; therefore, I consider you to have attained the status of a Guru."
Ṛbhu said:
"O Nidāgha, out of respect for your previous service, I, Ṛbhu by name, have come as your guru to bestow instruction upon you."
This very essence of the ultimate truth, which is entirely non-dual, has been taught to you in brief, O Mahāmati.
The Brahmin said:
Having spoken thus, the learned Ṛbhu, his teacher, departed from Nidāgha;
and Nidāgha, through that instruction, became devoted to non-duality.
He beheld all beings as non-different from his own self;
thus, O twice-born one, that brahmin attained supreme liberation from Brahman.
In the same way, O knower of dharma, O lord of the earth, you too should become one for whom self, enemy, and kinsman are equal, knowing the Self to be all-pervading.
Just as the single sky is seen as divided by distinctions such as white and blue by those with deluded vision, so too the Self, though being one, appears as distinct and separate.
Whatever exists here in its entirety is the one Acyuta; there is nothing else beyond him.
He is I, he is you, and he is all this; abandon the delusion of duality regarding the nature of the Self.
Parāśara said:
Thus addressed by him, that best of kings, possessing the vision of ultimate reality, abandoned his sense of duality;
and he too, having attained awakening through the recollection of his former births, achieved liberation in that very life.
Thus, whoever narrates or listens with devotion to this essential account of the deeds of Bharata, the lord of men,
becomes pure-minded, does not fall into self-delusion, and becomes fit for liberation throughout the cycles of existence.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the second book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"The arrangement of the earth, the oceans, and so forth, has been correctly described by my preceptor."
And the configuration of the sun and other luminaries, as well as the celestial bodies in detail.
Likewise, the creation of the gods and others has been described, as well as that of the sages;
the origin of the fourfold caste system and of those belonging to the animal kingdom has also been told.
The life stories of Dhruva and Prahlāda have been related by you in detail;
now I wish to hear, in their proper sequence, all the Manvantaras without exception.
O Teacher, I desire to hear from you about these lords of the Manvantaras, headed by Śakra and the gods, as they have been described by you.
Parāśara said:
Those Manvantaras that have passed and those yet to come in this world,
I shall relate to you correctly and in their proper order.
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa Manu,
as well as Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
These six Manus have passed; but now this son of the Sun, Vaivasvata, is the one whose seventh interval is currently underway.
I have thus described to you the Svāyambhuva interval at the beginning of the Kalpa,
as well as the gods and sages therein, exactly as they were.
Hereafter, I shall duly proclaim the lords of the Manvantara of Svārociṣa Manu, as well as the divine sages and his sons.
In the Svārociṣa interval, the gods were the Pārāvatas along with the Tuṣitas;
there, O Maitreya, the mighty Vipaścit was the lord of the gods.
Ūrja, Stambha, Prāṇa, Dattoli, Ṛṣabha,
Niścara, and Cārvarīvat were the seven sages (saptarṣis) there.
Caitra, Kiṃpuruṣa, and others were the sons of Svārociṣa;
this second interval has been described—now hear the subsequent one.
In the third interval as well, O Brahmin, the Manu named Uttama appeared;
Maitreya, the lord of the gods, was then the Indra known as Suśānti.
The Sudhāmanas, the Satyas, the Śivas, and the Pratardanas,
as well as the Vaśavartins— these five groups are recorded as consisting of twelve each.
There, the seven sons of Vasiṣṭha became the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis);
likewise, Aja, Paraśu, Divya, and others were the sons of Uttama Manu.
Within the interval of Tāmasa, there were the gods known as Surūpas and Haris, as well as Satyas and Sudhis; these were the twenty-seven groups.
Śibi was Indra, characterized by the performance of a hundred sacrifices;
and there were the Seven Ṛṣis—now hear their names from me.
Jyotirdhāman, Pṛthu, Kāvya, Caitra, Agni, Vanaka,
and Pīvara— these seven sages were also there during that interval.
Nara, Khyāti, Śāntahaya, Jānu, Jaṅgha, and others were the sons of Tāmasa; they were kings of exceedingly great strength.
And in the fifth interval, O Maitreya, the Manu was named Raivata by name, and Vibhu was the Indra; hear now of the gods who were there as well.
The Amitābhas, Bhūtarayas, Vaikuṇṭhas, and Sasumedhas—
these are the fourteen groups of gods there, fourteen for each [of the seven worlds].
Hiraṇyaroman, Vedaśrī, the other named Ūrdhvabāhu,
Vedabāhu, Sudhāman, and the great sage Parjanya— these,
O Brahmin, were the seven ṛṣis during that Raivata Manvantara.
O best of sages, Balabandhu was highly esteemed, and his sons— Satyaka and the others— became kings of great prowess.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata—
these four Manus are remembered as belonging to the lineage of Priyavrata.
Having propitiated Viṣṇu through austerity, that royal sage Priyavrata obtained these lords of the Manvantaras born from his own lineage.
In the sixth Manvantara, there was likewise a Manu named Cākṣuṣa;
Indra was Manojava; and now learn from me about the gods as well.
The Āpyas, Prasūtas, Bhavyas, Pṛthagās, and Divaukasas,
as well as the Mahānubhāvas and Lekhas— these are the five groups of eight.
Sumedhas, Virajas, Haviṣmat, Uttama, Madhu,
Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu— these were the seven ṛṣis.
Ūru, Pūru, and others headed by Śatadyumna— these sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu, possessed of great strength, became lords of the earth.
O wise sage, the son of Vivasvat, the highly effulgent Manu Śrāddhadeva,
the intelligent one, is currently presiding over the seventh interval (manvantara).
O great sage, the gods beginning with the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras are here;
likewise, O Maitreya, Purandara, the lord of the thirty-three gods, is also here.
Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni along with Gautama,
Viśvāmitra, and Bharadvāja— these are the seven Ṛṣis here.
Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, the renowned Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, and Diṣṭa; ||| ViP_3.1.33 ||
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Vasumān, world-renowned—
these were the nine very righteous sons of Vaivasvata Manu.
The incomparable power of Viṣṇu, abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva), is established in the maintenance of the world;
throughout all the Manvantaras, she presides as the presiding deity.
In the first interval, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, this deity Yajña was born as a mental son from Ākūti by means of a portion of him.
Then again, when the Svārociṣa interval had arrived,
that very god was born in Tuṣitā together with the Tuṣita deities as Ajita.
Furthermore, in the interval between Auttama and Tāmasa, he was indeed Tuṣita;
in the Satya-manvantara, he was Satya, together with the most excellent gods who were themselves Satyas.
And when the interval of Tāmasa had arrived once again,
Hari himself indeed became Hari in Haryā together with the Haris.
In the Raivata period as well,
the god Hari, the best of deities, was born in Saṃbhūti as Mānasa, together with the gods who were characterized by the quality of passion (rājasa).
And in the Cākṣuṣa interval, the god Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
was born in the city of Vikuṇṭhā together with the deities known as the Vaikuṇṭhas.
But when the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived, O twice-born one,
Viṣṇu was born as Vāmana from Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Having conquered these worlds with three strides,
that Great-Souled One gave the triple-world, cleared of all thorns, to Purandara.
Thus, O Brahmin, these were his seven bodies during the seven Manvantaras, by which the progeny were protected.
Because all this has been pervaded by the power of that Great-Souled One,
he is therefore called Viṣṇu, from the root *viś*, meaning "to enter."
All the gods, all human beings, the seven ṛṣis, and those who are the sons of Manu,
as well as Indra who has become the lord of the thirty-three— these are indeed all the manifestations of Viṣṇu.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"These seven Manvantaras have indeed been described by you."
O brahmin-sage, you ought also to tell me about those that are yet to come.
Parāśara said:
O Sage, Saṃjñā, the daughter of Viśvakarman, was the wife of Sūrya;
Manu, Yama, and Yamī were indeed their offspring.
Unable to endure her husband’s splendor, she indeed assigned herself to his shadow;
while he remained in the forest for the sake of serving her husband, she herself departed for ascetic penance.
Thinking, "This is my wife," Arka then begot three sons upon Chāyā—
Śanaiścara, another named Manu, and also Tapatī.
When Chāyā, filled with anger, pronounced a curse upon Yama, both Yama and Sūrya then thought, "This is another [person], not she. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.2.5)
Then, when she had thus described her situation, Vivasvat beheld that mare established in asceticism within the forest by means of his vision gained through meditative concentration.
Then the two gods, the Aśvins, assuming the form of horses, begat Revanta upon her; and at the conclusion of that seminal emission, the Sun-god [beheld her].
And the Blessed One Ravi restored his consciousness and returned him to his own place;
furthermore, Viśvakarman performed the pacification of his fiery energy.
Having cast the sun into the whirlpool, he performed the destruction of its splendor;
yet he did not destroy that imperishable eighth part.
O best of sages, that Vaiṣṇava splendor which was severed from the sun by Viśvakarman fell blazing upon the earth.
With that very brilliance, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the discus of Viṣṇu,
the trident of Śarva, and the palanquin of Dhanada.
Viśvakarman increased with that splendor the spear of Guha and whatever weapons belonged to the other gods.
He who was called the second Manu, the son of Chāyāsaṃjñā, was of the same caste (savarṇa) as his predecessor; therefore, he is called Sāvarṇi.
This is indeed his eighth Manvantara, that of Sāvarṇika;
listen to that, O highly fortunate one, for I shall tell you what is to come.
O Maitreya, that Sāvarṇi who is to become the Manu thereafter, as well as the Suras Sutapas, Amitābhas, and Mukhyas, will then be the gods.
The host of each of those gods is recorded as consisting of twenty;
O best of sages, I shall now also describe the future seven ṛṣis.
Dīptimān, Gālava, Rāma, Kṛpa, and Drauṇi as another,
my son, as well as Vyāsa, and Ṛśyaśṛṅga as the seventh.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, the sinless Bali, son of Virocana, who dwells within the depths of Pātāla,
shall become their Indra.
Viraja, Cārvavaṃśa, Nirmoha, and others likewise will be the sons of Sāvarṇi Manu, who shall become lords of men.
O Maitreya, Dakṣasāvarṇi will be the ninth Manu.
At that time, there will be three classes of gods—the Pāras, the Marīcigarbhas, and the Sudharmans; each one shall consist of twelve groups.
O twice-born one, Indra will be their sovereign, possessing great heroism and being truly marvelous.
Savana, Dyutimat, Bhavya, Vasu, Medhātithi, Jyotiṣmat as the seventh, and Satya— these were the great ṛṣis there.
Dhṛtaketu, Dīptiketu, Pañcahasta, Nirāmaya,
Pṛthuśravas, and others were the sons of Dakṣasāvarṇi.
O Sage, the tenth Manu will be Brahmasāvarṇi;
the gods will be the Sudhāmans and the Viruddhas, numbering one hundred each.
Indra among them will be the one named Śānti, who shall be of great strength;
hear now also of those who will be the seven ṛṣis at that time.
Haviṣmān, Sukṛti, Satya, and another, Apāmūrti; Nābhāga of incomparable prowess, and likewise Satyaketu.
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, Bhūriṣeṇa, and the others— these ten sons of Brahmasāvarṇi shall protect the earth.
And the eleventh Manu will be Dharmasāvarṇika.
The birds, moving at will and delighting in their own emanations—
these shall then be the principal hosts of the future gods;
each of these groups consists of thirty, and their Indra shall indeed be Vṛṣa.
Niścara, Agnitejas, Vapuṣmat, Viṣṇu, Āruṇi, Haviṣmat, and Anagha—these were the seven Ṛṣis of that period. Thus, they were all destined for future greatness.
Sarvaga, Sarvadharmā, Devānīka, and others likewise,
shall be the sons of that Manu, lords of the earth.
The twelfth Manu will be Sāvarṇi, the son of Rudra;
Ṛtadhāman will be the Indra there; hear from me the names of the gods.
O twice-born one, the Haritas, the Lohitas, the Devas,
the Sumanasas, the Sukarmans, and the Supārās— these are indeed the five groups of ten.
Tapasvī, Sutapas, Tapomūrti,
Taporati, Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and another, the seventh, was Tapodhana.
Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and others—
these sons of that Manu will be kings of great heroism.
O Sage, the thirteenth Manu will be named Raucya.
The Sutrāmans, the Sukarmans, and likewise the Sudharmans—
these are the thirty-three distinct classes that constitute the hosts of gods.
The lord of the gods, Indra, possessed of great heroism, shall be their king.
Nirmoha, Tattvadarśin, Niṣprakampa, Nirutsuka,
Dhṛtimat, Avyaya, and the seventh, the sage Sutapas—
these were his sons; now learn from me about these seven ṛṣis as well.
Citrasena, Vicitra, and others will become rulers of the earth.
O Maitreya, Bhautya shall be the fourteenth Manu here;
Śuci will be the Indra, and there will be five hosts of gods—listen to them.
The Cākṣuṣas, the Pavitras, the Kaniṣṭhas, the Bhrājiras, and the Vācāvṛddhas were indeed the gods; now hear from me also concerning the seven Ṛṣis.
Agnibāhu, Śuci, Śukra, Māgadha, Agnīdhra, Yukta, and likewise Jita—these were others; now hear of the sons of Manu.
Ūrugambhīrabudhna and others were the sons of that Manu;
they have been described, O tiger among sages, as the kings who will protect the earth.
At the end of the four yugas, it is said that a dissolution of the Vedas occurs;
then the seven sages, descending from heaven, cause them to be promulgated again on earth.
O Brahmin, at the completion of each Kṛta age, Manu is born as the ordainer of memory;
and those gods who partake of the sacrifice remain for the duration of that Manvantara.
The earth is protected for the duration of a Manvantara by those who are the sons of Manu,
as well as by those born of their lineage.
In each Manvantara, these— the Manu, the seven ṛṣis, the gods, the kings who are the sons of the Manu, and Śakra— are the presiding authorities.
O twice-born one, when fourteen such manvantaras have passed,
it is said that a kalpa, consisting of a thousand yugas, has reached its conclusion without remainder.
O best of beings, the night thereafter is of that same duration;
then, assuming the form of Brahmā, he rests upon the serpent Śeṣa amidst the flood of waters.
O Brahmin, having swallowed the entire triple world, the Lord Ādikṛt, the omnipresent Janārdana, who is all beings, remains established in his own māyā.
Then, having awakened, the Blessed One, whose nature is imperishable and who possesses the quality of passion (rajas), creates once again in every aeon (kalpa) just as he did before.
The Manus, the kings, the gods including Indra, and likewise the seven ṛṣis—
O best of the twice-born, these are the sattvic portions that maintain the stability of the world.
O Maitreya, listen now to how this Viṣṇu, whose characteristic function is maintenance, establishes the order of the ages throughout the four yugas.
In the Kṛta age, the Self of all beings, who delights in the welfare of all beings, assumes the form of Kapila and others and bestows supreme knowledge.
In the Tretā age as well, that Lord, assuming the form of a universal monarch (cakravartin),
protects the three worlds while subduing the wicked.
Having divided this single Veda into four parts and further into hundreds of branches, the omnipresent Lord,
assuming the form of Vedavyāsa, makes it manifold once again.
Having divided the Vedas during the Dvāpara age, the Lord Hari, at the end of the Kali age, appearing in the form of Kalki, establishes those of wicked conduct back upon the right path.
Thus this infinite Self protects and creates this entire world, and at the end he destroys it; there is nothing that exists apart from him.
O Brahmin, the true nature of all great-souled beings— past, present, and future—
has been described to you here or elsewhere.
All the Manvantaras have been recounted by me to you, as well as the lords of those Manvantaras; what else shall I tell you?
[Thus ends the second chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"I have learned from you how this entire world [is composed]."
Viṣṇu is in Viṣṇu, and nothing exists that is beyond Viṣṇu.
But I wish to hear this: how the Vedas were divided by that Great-Souled One in each age, through his form as Vedavyāsa.
O great sage, tell me who was the Vyāsa in each particular age; O Blessed One, recount them to me and speak also of the divisions of the branches.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, it is not possible to state in detail the extent of the tree of the Vedas with its thousands of branches; listen to it in brief.
In every Dvāpara age, O great sage, Viṣṇu,
in the form of Vyāsa and for the welfare of the world, divides the single Veda into many parts.
And observing that the energy, brilliance, and strength of human beings were diminished,
he divided the Vedas for the benefit of all living creatures.
That body by which the Lord, as the master, makes the single Veda manifold is the form of the Slayer of Madhu known by the name Vedavyāsa.
Learn from me, O Sage, who those various Vyāsas were in each respective Manvantara,
and how the division of the Vedic branches was performed by each Vyāsa.
Indeed, during that Vaivasvata interval, in each of the Dvāpara ages, the Veda was divided twenty-eight times by the great seers again and again.
O best of men, twenty-eight Vedavyāsas have passed away,
by whom the Veda was divided into four parts again and again during the Dvāpara ages.
In the first Dvāpara age, the Vedas were divided by Svayambhū himself;
and in the second Dvāpara age, Prajāpati was the Vedavyāsa.
In the third [Manvantara] Uśanas was the Vyāsa, and in the fourth Bṛhaspati;
Savitṛ was the Vyāsa in the fifth, and the lord Mṛtyu is recorded as the Vyāsa in the sixth.
In the seventh [Manvantara], Indra was likewise [Vajra]; Vasiṣṭha is recorded as the lord in the eighth;
Sārasvata was in the ninth, and Tridhāman is recorded in the tenth.
In the eleventh [Manvantara] was Trivṛṣa Bhāradvāja;
after that, in the thirteenth, Antarikṣa; and in the fourteenth, Varṇin.
Trayyāruṇa was born in the fifteenth, Dhanañjaya in the sixteenth;
Kratujaya was born in the seventeenth, and Ṛṇajya is recorded as being in the eighteenth.
From him Vyāsa was born; from Bharadvāja came Gautama;
and from Gautama came Uttama Vyāsa, who is called Haryātmā.
Then Vena was born from Haryaśva; he who was Vājaśravas was Soma; and from him Śuṣmāyaṇa was born, who is known as Tṛṇabindu.
From him was born Bhārgava Ṛkṣa, from whom Valmīki is said to have descended; from him came our father Śakti, from him Vyāsa, and from him, O sage, I.
From me was born Jātukarṇa, and from him Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana;
these are the twenty-eight ancient Vedavyāsas.
The single Veda was divided into four parts by them during the Dvāpara age and subsequent periods.
In the future Dvāpara age as well, the son of Droṇa will become Vyāsa,
after this son of mine, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, has passed away.
The single-syllable Brahman, established as "Om," is eternal;
because of its vastness and its capacity for expansion, it is designated as "Brahman."
Eternal and abiding in the Praṇava, expressed as Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ,
consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas— to that Brahman, salutation.
Salutation to that Subrahman, who is designated as the cause of the dissolution and origin of the universe, and who is the supreme secret beyond the Great Principle (mahat).
The world is unfathomable, shoreless, and inexhaustible, a dwelling place for the delusion of beings;
it has as its purpose the attainment of the goals of human existence through both manifestation and activity.

The final goal and destination of those who possess the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and are devoted to tranquility and self-restraint is that which is unmanifest, immortal, the source of activity, and the eternal Brahman.
It is called Pradhāna, Ātmayoni, and Guhāsattva;
likewise, it is the undivided, pure, imperishable, and manifold essence.
Salutations again and again, eternally, to that Supreme Brahman,
whose form is that of Vāsudeva, the embodiment of the Supreme Self.
This Brahman is divided threefold, yet that Lord remains undivided;
though He is non-different from all beings, He is perceived as different by those with divided intellects.
He consists of the Ṛgveda, he consists of the Sāmaveda; he is the self of all, and he consists of the Yajurveda.
He is the essence of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman, and he alone is the self of all embodied beings.
He, who consists of the Veda, divides it; He creates the Veda with many divisions and its various branches.
He is the author of the branches, the Lord Ananta, whose very nature is the knowledge of all the branches.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The original Veda consisted of four quarters and was measured at one hundred thousand [verses].
Then this entire sacrifice, which grants all desires, is ten times greater than that.
Then, in this twenty-eighth interval, my son Vyāsa,
the lord, divided the single Veda with its four quarters into four parts.
Just as the Vedas were divided by that wise Vedavyāsa,
so too have they been divided by me through all those various Vyāsas.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, understand that by this very means the various branches of the Vedas were composed throughout all the cycles of four ages.
Know that Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa is the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself;
for who else on earth, O Maitreya, could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
O Maitreya, listen now to how the Vedas were divided by that high-souled son of mine during this Dvāpara age, exactly as it happened.
Urged by Brahmā, Vyāsa proceeded to divide the Vedas;
then he took four disciples who had mastered the Vedas.
That great sage took Paila as the reciter of the Ṛgveda,
and he accepted the one named Vaiśampāyana for the Yajurveda.
Jaimini was the [disciple] of the Sāmaveda, and likewise Sumantu, the knower of the Atharvaveda,
became the disciple of that wise Vedavyāsa.
The great sage took as his disciple for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas a man of great intelligence named Romaharṣaṇa, who was a Sūta.
The place [of the Purāṇa] is manifold, beginning with that of the Ṛṣis, and it has as its basis what was composed by the divine sages (devarṣi).
This is declared to be Itihāsa, joined with the most ancient and wonderful deeds.
There was once a single Yajurveda; he divided it into four parts. Within that [division], the Cāturhotra arose, and by means of it, he then performed the sacrifice.
The sage performed the duties of the Adhvaryu with the Yajus formulas, those of the Hotṛ with the Ṛcs, those of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmans, and likewise the office of the Brahman with the Atharvans.
Then that sage, having extracted the Ṛcas, composed the Ṛgveda;
likewise, he formed the Yajurveda from the Yajus formulas and the Sāmaveda from the Sāmans.

Furthermore, O Maitreya, that lord caused all the rites for the king to be performed according to the Atharvaveda, and likewise carried out the function of the Brahman priest as prescribed by tradition.
Thus, this single great tree of the Vedas was divided by him into four parts; from that, the forest of the Vedic trees was born.
O Brahmin, Paila first divided the tree of the Ṛgveda and gave the two Saṃhitās to Indrapramati and Bāṣkala.
Then that highly intelligent Bāṣkala divided his own Saṃhitā into four parts and gave them to his disciples, beginning with Baudhya.
Likewise, Baudhya and Āgnimāṭhara, as well as Yājñavalkya and Parāśara,
O Sage, received those sub-branches from that branch.
Then Indrapramati taught one *saṃhitā* to his own son,
the high-souled Māṇḍūkeya, at that time, O Maitreya.
From his disciples and grand-disciples, it passed in succession to his sons and disciples.
Vedamitra Śākalya, however, studied that Saṃhitā;
he composed five Saṃhitās and imparted them to his disciples.
Now hear from me the names of his five disciples:
Mudgala, Gālava, Vātsya, Śālīya,
and the great sage Śiśira, O Maitreya, who was the fifth.
These five names are based upon the *Saṃhitā*.
Śākapūṇi, another [son], composed a triad of Saṃhitās;
likewise, O best of sages, he made the Nirukta as the fourth.
Likewise, Krauñca, Vaitālaka, and the great sage Balāka were there;
and the fourth was Nirukta, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, these are the secondary branches even from the primary branches;
furthermore, O twice-born one, Bāṣkala composed three other Saṃhitās,
[taught] to his disciples Kālāyani, Gārgya, and the third, Java.
Thus have these Bahvṛcas been described, by whom the Saṃhitā was set forth.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The great-minded [Yājñavalkya] divided the branches of the Yajurveda tree into twenty-seven.
That disciple of Vyāsa named Vaiśampāyana indeed composed it.
He gave them to his disciples, and they too received them in due order.
Yājñavalkya, however, was his disciple, O twice-born one; he was the son of Brahmarāta, a supreme knower of dharma, and always devoted to the service of his guru.
"Whichever ṛṣi shall come today to the assembly on Mahāmeru,
he shall indeed incur the sin of killing a Brahmin after seven nights."
O twice-born one, previously a compact was thus made by the hosts of sages;
however, at that time, Vaiśampāyana alone transgressed it.
Then he killed his sister's young son, having touched him with his foot.
And he said to his disciples: "O disciples, all of you perform for my sake this vow which removes the sin of killing a Brahmin; this must not be questioned."
Then Yājñavalkya said to him: "O Blessed One, why should I practice this vow with these brahmins who have been troubled and possess little luster?"
Then the great-minded preceptor, enraged, said to Yājñavalkya:
"O despiser of brahmins, let that which was studied by you from me be relinquished!"
Since you speak disparagingly of these bulls among brahmins,
I have no need for such a disciple who violates my command.
Then Yājñavalkya said: "O twice-born one, this has been spoken by me to you out of devotion; enough of your learning from me—this which I have [taught] is now yours."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, that sage vomited up the blood-stained sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) identical in form to himself, gave them to him, and departed according to his own will.
Then, O twice-born one, when the Yajus formulas were released by Yājñavalkya, those who became partridges (tittiri) received them; therefore, they are known as the Taittirīyas.
O best of sages, those who, urged by their preceptors, performed the vow for the expiation of killing a Brahmin became the Carakādhvaryus because of that performance (caraṇa).
O Maitreya, Yājñavalkya also, devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
bowed down and praised the Sun, desiring thereby to obtain the Yajus formulas.
Yājñavalkya said:
Salutations to Savitṛ, the gateway to liberation, who possesses immeasurable splendor;
salutations to him who is the embodiment of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and who is the abode of the triple Veda.
Homage to the Sun, the supreme radiance, who bears the vast *sauṣumṇa* light, the cause of the world existing as Agni and Soma, and whose essence is the self of all beings.
Salutation to the self whose nature is the knowledge of time— consisting of *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *nimeṣas*, and so forth—
to the one who is to be meditated upon, who has the form of Viṣṇu, and who possesses the nature of the supreme imperishable.
Salutation to him whose essence is satisfaction, who nourishes the hosts of gods by swelling the moon with his own rays, and who satisfies the ancestors with the nectar of *svadhā*.
Homage to the one who has become Agni and Soma, and to the one who brings about all accomplishments.
Salutation to that Sūrya, the creator and the progenitor, the Lord who is the cause of snow, water, heat, and rain, and who exists throughout the three periods of time.
Salutations to that Vivasvat, the Lord of the world, who destroys the darkness of this universe and who is the deity who upholds the abode of pure being (sattva).
Salutations to that radiant God, without whose rising no person is fit for sacred rites and water itself is not a cause of purification.
Salutations to that Pure Self, by whose rays the world, when touched, becomes fit for ritual action; salutations to him who is the cause of purification.
Salutations to Savitṛ, to Sūrya, to Bhāskara, to Vivasvat, to Āditya, the primordial being; salutations again and again to the source of the gods and all others.
I bow to him whose golden chariot is borne by banners that carry nectar, and who is the eye for the illumination of the worlds.
Parāśara said: Being thus praised with these and other hymns by him, Ravi,
assuming the form of a horse, said, "Let that which is desired be chosen."
Then Yājñavalkya, having prostrated before the Sun, said:
"Grant me those Yajus formulas which were not present with my teacher."
Parāśara said:
Thus addressed, the blessed Sun-god gave him the Yajus formulas known as *ayātayāma*,
which even his own preceptor did not know.
O best of the twice-born, those brahmins by whom the *yajus* formulas were studied are designated as the *vājins*, because that horse was the Sun himself.
The branches of those Vājins are indeed fifteen;
the highly fortunate Kaṇva and others were established by Yājñavalkya.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
§ Parāśara said:
Jaimini, the disciple of Vyāsa, [divided] the branches of the Sāmaveda tree.
Listen to me, Maitreya, as to the sequence by which he divided them.
This [tree] has the Ṛg and Yajur Veda branches as its boughs; the number of its branches is explained in detail.
Now, the designations of the branches as described in the Sāma, Atharva, and Purāṇas are being stated.
Sumantu was his son, and Sukarman was his son as well;
those two great sages each studied one of the *saṃhitās*.
Then his son Sukarman divided that [Veda] into one thousand recensions (saṃhitā);
and two of his disciples, who observed great vows, received it.
Then Jaimini taught his son Sumantu.
And the sage Sumantu, while teaching his son Sumula, [said]:
O best of the twice-born, Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya and Pauṣpiñji were his disciples; fifteen Sāmavedic chanters from the north are recorded as his followers.
Those excellent twice-born ones by whom as many Saṃhitās were received from Hiraṇyanābha are also called by scholars "the Eastern Sāma-singers."
Lokākṣi, Kuthumi, Kuṣīdī, and likewise Lāṅgali—these were the disciples of Pauṣpiñji; through their various divisions, the Saṃhitās were multiplied.
And that highly intelligent one named Kṛti, the disciple of Hiraṇyanābha, proclaimed twenty-four Saṃhitās to his disciples.
And by them, that Sāmaveda was further expanded through many branches.
Now I shall describe the collection of the Atharvan Saṃhitās;
that sage Sumantu, of immeasurable luster, [expounded] the Atharvaveda.
He taught his disciple Kabandha; he, in turn, having divided him into two parts, gave them to Devadarśa and Pathya.
The disciples of Devadarśa were Maudga, Brahmabali,
Śaulkāyani, Pippalāda, and another, O best of sages.
O twice-born one, Pathya also had three disciples by whom the Saṃhitās were composed:
Jājali, Kumuda, and the third was Śaunaka, O twice-born one.
Śaunaka, however, having divided [the tradition] into two parts, gave one to Babhru and bestowed the second Saṃhitā upon Saindhava, who was named Sañjñin.
Saindhava and Muñjakeśa further divided the Veda into two parts,
as did Nakṣatrakalpa, and likewise [divided] the Saṃhitās of the Vedas.
The fourth would be the Āṅgirasa, and the fifth is the Śāntikalpa;
these are the most excellent alternative recensions (vikalpakas) of the Atharvaṇa Saṃhitās.
Skilled in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed a compendium of the Purāṇas by means of primary narratives, secondary episodes, verses, and accounts of the purification of the Kalpas.
The wise say that *ākhyānaka* is the narration of a matter after having seen it oneself.
The narration of the meaning of what has been heard is called an *upākhyāna*.
There was a famous Sūta named Romaharṣaṇa who was a disciple of Vyāsa;
to him the great sage Vyāsa gave the Purāṇasaṃhitā.
Sumati, Agnivarcas, Mitrāyu, Śāṃśapāyana,
Akṛtavraṇa, and Sāvarṇi were his six disciples.
Kāśyapa, Sāvarṇi, Śāṃśapāyana,
and another, Romaharṣaṇī— these are the four root-saṃhitās of the three [Vedas].
O Sage, this [work] consists of these four collections of joined verses.
The Brāhma is said to be the first among all Purāṇas;
those who know the Purāṇas declare that there are eighteen Purāṇas.
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Śaiva, as well as the Bhāgavata,
the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh.
The Āgneya is the eighth, and the Bhaviṣya is likewise the ninth;
the tenth is remembered as the Brahmavaivarta, and the Laiṅga as the eleventh.
The twelfth is indeed the Vārāha, and the thirteenth here is the Skānda;
the fourteenth is the Vāmana, and the fifteenth is remembered as the Kaurma;
then follow the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
O great sage, these eighteen are indeed the Mahāpurāṇas.
And likewise, the minor Purāṇas have been narrated by the sages.
In all these [books], primary creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the accounts of the dynasties' deeds are narrated.
O Maitreya, this ancient account which is being told by me to you is indeed known as the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, following immediately after the Pādma.
O best of beings, in all accounts of creation, secondary creation, genealogies, and the periods of the Manvantaras, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu alone is described.
The limbs [of knowledge] are the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra; for these are indeed the fourteen branches of learning.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these three,
together with Arthaśāstra as the fourth, constitute those eighteen branches of knowledge.
First, the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣis) are to be known; after them, the divine sages (devarṣis);
and after them, the royal sages (rājarṣis)—these are the three types of sages.
Thus the branches have been fully described, as well as the divisions of those branches;
the authors of the branches have also been named, and the cause of their division has likewise been declared.
In this same manner, it is traditionally held that there are equal divisions of branches in all the Manvantaras.
O twice-born one, the Śruti concerning Prajāpati is eternal, whereas these various alternatives are its modifications.
All this that was asked of me here by you has been told to you, O Maitreya, concerning the connection with the Vedas; what else shall I tell you?
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Guru, everything that you were asked by me has been explained exactly as it is."
I desire to hear one thing; may you explain that to me.
This boundless mass of the Vedas has been described according to its division into branches.
Now, the supreme dharma for those belonging to the various castes and so forth is being declared.
O great sage, the seven continents, the subterranean realms,
and the seven worlds situated within this entire cosmic egg on all sides— these are [contained therein].
This entire world is covered with living beings— some large, some small, some subtle, some subtler than the subtle, and some even larger than the large.
O best of sages, there is not even an eighth part of a finger’s breadth where there are no living beings bound by the fetters of karma.
"O Blessed One, it is said that all these indeed fall under the power of Yama;
at the end of their lifespan, they then undergo torments impelled by him."
"Having fallen away from the states of torment, living beings revolve through births such as those of gods; this is the conclusion of the scriptures."
Therefore, I desire to hear that stainless deed by which men do not come under the power of Yama; please tell it to me.
Parāśara said:
O Sage, this very same question was asked by the high-souled Nakula;
hear from me what the grandfather Bhīṣma replied when he was questioned.
Bhīṣma said:
"O child, in former times a Kalingan Brahmin, my friend, came to me;
that sage, who remembered his past lives, was questioned by me and spoke thus."
"Therefore, this was told by him, and this shall happen in this way;
and so it came to pass, my dear, exactly as it was spoken by that wise one."
And when that twice-born one was questioned by me again with faith,
whatever he said was never seen by me otherwise at any time.
Once, however, when I asked about that which you have mentioned,
the Kalinga Brahmin spoke, recollecting the words of that sage.
I shall relate to you that supreme secret told by one who remembers his past lives— the conversation that took place between Yama and his servant.
But being cooked in hell, he was rebuked by Yama:
Why was the god Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, not worshipped by you?
Kāliṅga said:
Beholding his own servant with noose in hand, Yama indeed whispers into his ear:
"Avoid those who have taken refuge in Madhusūdana; I am the lord of other mortals, but certainly not of the Vaiṣṇavas."
I have been appointed as Yama by the Creator, who is honored by the hosts of immortals, to determine what is beneficial and harmful for the world.
I shall punish those mortals who are averse to Hari and their gurus; I pay homage to those who bow at the feet of Hari.
With my inner self established in the Bhāgavatas, I too desire a happy rebirth from Vāsudeva.
I am subject to Hari and my preceptor; I am not independent, for Viṣṇu has power even over me to restrain me.
Even if it were heated here for a hundred years, iron never attains the state of gold;
for one who is averse to the Blessed One, there is no success— poison does not become nectar, for such a thing is not possible.
For the moon, with its pale and mottled luster, never undergoes defeat by darkness;
indeed, a man who has established his inner self in Hari shines brightly, even if he is utterly defiled.

Having thoroughly examined even the extensive systems of Vṛṣagaṇa, Kaṇabhakṣa, Śaṅkara, Daśabala, Pañcaśikha, and Akṣapāda, as well as the worldly treatises, there is no accomplishment apart from the worship of the Blessed One.

Salutations be to the Unborn, the primordial Lord of the world, whose lotus-feet are constantly worshipped by the lords of the gods with their hands folded like buds, who possesses unimpeded movement, and who is eternal.
Just as gold is considered to be one and undivided, despite the distinctions of bracelets, crowns, earrings, and so forth,
so too is Hari declared to be one, through all the conceptual constructions of gods, animals, humans, and the like.
Just as the atoms of earth and water return once more to oneness with the earth at the end of the wind,
so too do gods, animals, humans, and others [return] at the end to that eternal [principle] which is turbid with the qualities (guṇas).
O Vraja, avoid that mortal who bows down in truth to Hari, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the hosts of immortals,
for he is freed from the bonds of all sins, like a fire drenched with clarified butter.
Having heard these words of Yama, the noose-bearing servant of Yama spoke to that Lord of Dharma:
"Tell me, O All-pervading Lord, what kind of devotee this man is toward Hari, the creator of all beings."
Yama said:

Know him to be a devotee of Viṣṇu who does not deviate from the duties of his own caste, who is even-minded toward himself, friends, and enemies, who neither takes nor harms anything, and whose mind is exceedingly pure.

Know that man to be an exceedingly devoted follower of Hari, whose mind is constantly fixed upon Janārdana, and whose stainless intellect is not defiled by the impurity of the Kali age nor by the darkness of delusion.

Know that man to be a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu who, having perceived even gold in secret, regards it with his intellect as if it were a blade of grass, and whose mind is focused on no other than the Blessed Lord while regarding the property of others as such.

Where is Viṣṇu, as pure as a slab of crystal mountain, and where is the defect of envy and the like in the minds of men? Indeed, the scorching heat born of fire does not exist within the mass of rays of the moon made of frost.

Vāsudeva always dwells in the heart of that person who is pure-minded, free from envy, tranquil, of holy conduct, a friend to all beings, whose speech is pleasant and beneficial, and in whom pride and deceit have set.

When that eternal one dwells within his heart, a man becomes gentle in appearance toward this world; even a young *śāla* tree proclaims the exceedingly delightful essence of the earth within itself through its very beauty.

O Bhaṭa, go far away from those men whose sins have been shaken off by the observance of restraints and disciplines, whose minds are daily attached to Acyuta, and who are free from pride, arrogance, and envy.
If the Lord Hari, the beginningless and imperishable Self, who bears the sword, conch, and mace, resides within the heart,
then how can sin remain there when it has been shattered by Him, the destroyer of sins— just as darkness cannot exist when the sun is present?
In the heart of that man of impure mind, who steals the wealth of others, kills living beings, and speaks falsehoods and harsh words,
and who is intoxicated by the evil produced by his own inauspiciousness, there is no room for the Infinite One (Ananta).
The wicked man of defiled intellect cannot endure the prosperity of others and utters insults against the virtuous;
he neither performs sacrifice nor gives charity, and Janārdana does not dwell in the heart of such a base person.

Know that he who, being of deceitful mind, pursues thirst for wealth even toward his dearest friend, kinsman, wife, children, grandchildren, parents, and circle of servants, is one of base conduct; he has no devotion.
One whose mind is impure, who is addicted to evil conduct, who is constantly intoxicated by the company of the ignoble and the vulgar,
and who makes a daily effort to bind himself with sin— such a person is a mere beast, for he is not a devotee of Vāsudeva.
"This entire universe, and I myself, am Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, the one Supreme Lord"—
when this pure understanding arises regarding the Infinite One who has entered the heart, then, O Vraja, leave them far behind.
"O lotus-eyed Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, supporter of the earth, Acyuta, wielder of the conch and discus!
Be our refuge!"—those who indeed utter these words, O soldier, leave those sinless ones far behind.

O Discus, he in whose mind dwells that Imperishable Self—the Supreme Person—there is no path for you, nor for me, within the range of his vision; having seen him, his power and strength are thwarted, and he belongs to another world.
Kāliṅga said:
"Thus, indeed, did the god Yama, the son of the Sun, speak for the purpose of commanding his own soldiers;
and this was told to me by him, O best of the Kurus, and it has been correctly related by me to you as well."
Bhīṣma said:
"O Nakula, this was previously told to me by that twice-born man who,
having come from the land of Kaliṅga, was well-pleased with me, O great-souled one."
O child, I have also declared this correctly and according to the proper method to you:
that in the ocean of saṃsāra, there is no protection other than Viṣṇu.
Neither the servants, nor the staff and noose, nor Yama himself,
nor the torments of hell are capable of harming him whose soul always takes refuge in Keśava.
Parāśara said:
O sage, this which was sung by Vaivasvata has been fully related to you in accordance with your question; what else do you wish to hear?
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, by those who desire to conquer the cycle of worldly existence, [the Lord] is the divine Master."
O Lord of the World, please explain how Viṣṇu is to be propitiated.
D7 inserts:
"The mark of devotion to Viṣṇu and so forth, which is one's own duty as previously described."
To explain that very same matter with extreme clarity, this work in five chapters is composed.
O great sage, I desire to hear about that fruit which is obtained by men devoted to worship from Govinda when he has been propitiated.
Parāśara said:
Listen as I relate to you exactly what Aurva, when questioned, told the high-souled Sagara regarding that which you have asked.
Sagara, having prostrated himself, questioned Aurva of the Bhṛgu lineage regarding the means for the propitiation of Viṣṇu, O best of sages.
And hear from me, O Maitreya, all that he said when questioned regarding the fruit which arises for men when Viṣṇu has been propitiated.
Śaunaka said: When Viṣṇu is propitiated, one attains terrestrial desires, heaven, as well as that station which is praised even in heaven, and even the supreme liberation (nirvāṇa).
O Indra among kings, whatever one desires and to whatever extent the fruit may be— whether it be great or even small— one obtains all that when Acyuta has been propitiated.
As for what you ask, O protector of the earth—how indeed he is propitiated—I shall tell you all of that; listen to me.
By a person who follows the conduct prescribed for their social class and stage of life, the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, is propitiated; there is no other path that causes Him satisfaction.
O King, since Hari is all beings, when one sacrifices, he sacrifices to him; when one mutters prayers, he mutters them to him; and likewise, when one slays others, he slays him. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.8.10)
Therefore, Janārdana is propitiated by a man of good conduct who performs the duties prescribed for his own social class.
O Lord of the Earth, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, one who is devoted to his own duty worships Viṣṇu; it is not otherwise.
He does not speak slander, calumny, or falsehood, nor anything that causes distress to others; by this, Keśava is pleased.
O King, that man who does not set his mind upon another's wife, another's wealth, or the harming of others— by him Keśava is pleased.
O Lord of Men, that man who does not strike nor kill other living beings and embodied creatures— by him Keśava is pleased.
O lord of men, Govinda is pleased by that person who is always intent upon serving the gods, the twice-born, and their gurus.
He who desires the welfare of himself, his son, and all living beings in that same way— he, Hari, is always pleased by him and grants him constant happiness.
O King, he whose mind is not corrupted by defects such as passion and the like always pleases Viṣṇu with his pure heart.
O best of kings, a man who abides by those duties prescribed for the social classes and stages of life in the scriptures worships Viṣṇu; it cannot be otherwise.
Sagara said:
"O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear those duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) in their entirety, as well as the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma); please explain them to me."
Śaunaka said:
"Listen with a one-pointed mind to the duties proclaimed by me for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, in their respective order."
