A Brahmin should give gifts, worship the gods with sacrifices, be devoted to the study of the Vedas, remain constantly engaged in ritual ablutions, and maintain the sacred fires.
For the sake of his livelihood, a twice-born man may officiate at sacrifices for others, likewise teach others,
and accept gifts from others in accordance with the law, provided it is for the sake of his guru.
A twice-born man should act for the welfare of the entire world and never for the harm of anyone;
friendliness toward all beings is the supreme wealth of a Brāhmaṇa.
O King, a twice-born man should maintain an equal mind toward both a pressing-stone and a jewel belonging to another;
he is praised when he approaches his wife only during her season.
A Kṣatriya king should indeed give gifts to the twice-born according to his desire,
perform various sacrifices, and study the Vedas.
Living by the sword and protecting the earth was his preeminent livelihood;
even for him, the protection of the earth was practiced in the first kalpa.
A lord of men fulfills his duty solely by protecting the earth,
since the king is the share of the sacrificial rites and other religious acts.
By punishing the wicked and protecting the virtuous, the king who maintains the social order attains the worlds he desires. (ViP 3.8.29)
O lord of men, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, bestowed upon the Vaiśya the means of livelihood consisting of cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture.
For him as well, study, sacrifice, giving, and righteousness are praised,
as is the performance of obligatory and occasional rites and other actions.
For a Śūdra, humility, purity, and service to the master without guile [constitute his duty].
For this [sacrifice] consists of silent recitation; attachment to it is the protection of the Brahmins.
Even a Śūdra may give gifts and perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
indeed, by means of these, a Śūdra may perform all rites pertaining to the ancestors and so forth.
O Lord of the Earth, the acquisition of all things for the sake of maintaining servants and others, and approaching one's own wife during her fertile season; these are [the duties].
Compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from pride, truthfulness, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, and pleasant speech; ViP_3,8.35 //
And [she obtained] a body by means of even her own third auspicious deed.
One should not act to excess; that is called "effortlessness" (anāyāsa).
O Lord of Men, benevolence, lack of greed, likewise lack of miserliness,
and freedom from envy— these qualities are said to be common to all social classes.
These are the general characteristics of all the stages of life (āśramas).
Now hear these qualities and the duties for times of distress pertaining to the Brahmins and the other castes.
The duties of a Kṣatriya are prescribed for a twice-born man in times of distress, as are the duties of a Vaiśya;
likewise, the duties of a Vaiśya are prescribed for a Rājanya, but the duties of a Śūdra are not prescribed for either of these two.
O King, when one has the capacity, both [castes] should abandon that;
in times of distress, that very same thing may be done, but one must not practice the confusion of duties.
Thus, O King, these duties of the social classes have been described by me to you;
now listen as I correctly explain the dharma of those belonging to the stages of life.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Saurva said:
"A boy, having been initiated with the sacred thread, was intent upon acquiring the Vedas."
O King, he should dwell in the house of his guru as a celibate student, remaining composed in mind.
There, one who possesses purity and proper conduct, observing vows and possessing a disciplined intellect, should perform service to the guru and receive the Veda.
O King, with a concentrated mind, he should worship both twilights, as well as the sun and the fire;
likewise, he should perform the salutation to his guru.
O best of kings, while the teacher stands, the disciple should stand; when he walks, he should walk; and when he sits, the disciple should sit low; he should never act in opposition to his guru.
Instructed by him, he should recite the Veda with undistracted mind while standing before his teacher;
then, having been permitted by the guru, he may eat the food obtained as alms.
He should first immerse himself in the water where his teacher has already immersed;
he should also bring him fuel, water, and other such items every morning.
And having mastered what is to be grasped from that which has been grasped, and having obtained permission from him,
the wise man, having fulfilled his obligations toward the guru, should enter the state of a householder.
O protector of the earth, having obtained a wife according to the prescribed rite and having acquired wealth through his own efforts,
he should perform all the duties of a householder to the best of his ability.
One should worship the ancestors with funeral offerings (nivāpa), the gods with sacrifices, and likewise guests;
one should worship the sages with the study of sacred texts and Prajāpati with offspring.
Through the rite of offering to the ancestors (balikarman), one wins over the spirits; through affection, the entire world;
and by means of one's own performed actions, a person attains the worlds earned for themselves.
And whatever wandering mendicants or celibate students there may be, they too find their foundation in this very state; therefore, the householder's life is indeed supreme.
O Lord, for the purpose of recovering the Vedas, for bathing at sacred fords,
and for seeing the earth, the Brahmins wander across the world.
For those who are homeless, without provisions, and whose dwellings are wherever they find evening shelter—
the householder is the support and indeed the source of them all.
O King, one should speak sweet words of welcome and the like to them;
and to those who have come to the house, one should provide a bed, a seat, and food.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that person and taking away their merit.
For one who remains at home, contempt, egoism, and hypocrisy,
as well as causing distress, injury, and harshness, are not commended.
But that householder who correctly practices this supreme rule,
being liberated from all bonds, attains the unsurpassed worlds.
O King, when his age has advanced, a householder who has fulfilled his duties should entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
Subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, wearing his hair and beard in matted locks,
and sleeping upon the ground, the sage there, O King, should be hospitable to all guests.
He should make his lower garment and upper robe out of leather, kāśa, and kuśa grass;
likewise, O lord of men, bathing three times a day is prescribed for him.
O Lord of Men, the worship of the deities, the performance of fire-oblations, the honoring of all guests, and the giving of alms and offerings are prescribed for him.
O King of kings, for one performing austerities, anointing the limbs with forest oils is recommended,
as well as endurance of cold, heat, and other such conditions.
But the sage who, as a forest-dweller, practices this disciplined course of conduct,
burns away his defects like fire and conquers the eternal worlds.
The fourth stage of life, which is proclaimed by the wise as that of the mendicant (bhikṣu),—
you ought to hear from me, O King, as I describe its true nature.
O lord of men, having abandoned attachment to sons, wealth, and wife,
and having shaken off all envy, one should proceed to the fourth stage of life.
O Lord of the Earth, one should abandon all undertakings pertaining to the three aims of life;
one should be impartial toward friends and others, and friendly toward all living beings alike.

One who is disciplined should never commit an act of malice toward beings born from a womb, from an egg, and so forth, through speech, mind, or physical actions; furthermore, one should renounce all attachments.
One should stay one night in a village and five nights in a city,
remaining in such a way that neither attachment nor aversion arises within him.

And for the sake of sustaining life, he should wander from house to house at the proper time for alms among those of commendable appearance, when the embers have been extinguished and the people have already eaten.
Having abandoned those defects— namely desire, anger, as well as pride, delusion, greed, and the rest— the wandering mendicant should become free from the sense of "mine."
The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings never experiences any fear from any being whatsoever.
Having established the Agnihotra within his own body, the Brahmin offers the sacrificial oblation into the bodily fire through his own mouth;
with the oblations received from alms, he proceeds to the worlds by means of that kindled fire.
The twice-born who practices the stage of liberation as prescribed— pure, endowed with an intellect resolved upon its own goal, and tranquil like a flame without fuel— attains the world of Brahmā.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Sagara said:
"The four stages of life (cāturāśramya) and likewise the duties of the four castes (cāturvarṇya) have been described."
O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear about the ritual action of a man.
O best of the Bhṛgus, please describe in their entirety the daily, occasional, and optional rites for men; for in my opinion, you are omniscient.
Śaunaka said:
"O King, listen with an attentive mind as I shall explain that which has been mentioned by you regarding the obligatory and occasional rites."
The father should perform for his son, without omission, the entire cycle of rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), as well as the Śrāddha characterized by prosperity (ābhyudayika).
O lord of men, one should feed an even number of Brahmins facing the east;
one should perform the rites for the gods and the ancestors for the twice-born according to their respective status.
O King, filled with joy, one should offer balls of food mixed with curd, barley,
and jujube fruits to the Nāndīmukha ancestors by means of the Daiva-tīrtha.
Or, O Lord of the Earth, one should perform all the ritual services in a clockwise direction according to the Prajāpatya rite; likewise, one should do so during all times of prosperity.
Then, on the tenth day, the father himself should indeed bestow a name;
for it should be preceded by the word "deva," followed by a term denoting "man" (nara), and joined with such suffixes as "śarman" or "varman."
O King, some, however, desire that the naming ceremony take place on the tenth day.
Or on the twelfth day, O King, or when the month is full, or even later.
The suffix *śarman* is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, while *varman* pertains to the Kṣatriya;
names consisting of *gupta* or *dāsa* are indeed recommended for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.

One should not give a name that is devoid of meaning, nor one that is inauspicious, nor one containing incorrect words; likewise, one should not give a name that is inauspicious, loathsome, or of uneven syllables.
One should give him a name that is neither too long nor too short, not composed of excessively heavy syllables, easy to pronounce, and consisting of pleasant-sounding letters.
Thereafter, having been refined by the immediate preparatory rites in the teacher’s house,
he should undertake the acquisition of the Vidyā, following the prescribed rule.
O protector of the earth, having acquired knowledge and offered the teacher's fee to his guru,
one who desires the life of a householder should take a wife.
Or he may pass away while practicing celibacy according to his resolve;
or else, he should perform service to his guru, or even to the guru’s son or other heirs.
Or he may become a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), or a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) according to his wish;
O Lord of the Earth, he should act in whatever manner was previously resolved upon.
A man who is three times as old as his wife may marry her, provided she is one year younger than him;
he should not marry one with too much hair, nor one with no hair at all, nor one who is too dark, nor one who is tawny.
One should not marry a woman who is naturally deficient in limbs, nor one with extra limbs;
nor one who is impure, hairy, of low birth, or excessively diseased.

One should not marry a woman who is wicked, or one who is loquacious and foul-mouthed, or one who is physically deformed on account of her father or mother; nor one who has a beard or masculine characteristics, nor one whose appearance is that of a man.

One should not marry a woman with a gurgling voice, nor one whose speech is feeble, nor one with a voice like a crow's; likewise, one should not marry a woman with excessively squinting eyes, nor one with round eyes.
One should not marry a woman whose shanks are hairy, whose ankles are prominent,
or who has dimples on her cheeks when she laughs.
A wise man, skilled in his duties, should not marry such a girl.
A wise man should not marry a girl whose skin is too rough, whose hands and feet are jaundiced, whose eyes are reddish, or whose hands and feet are excessively swollen.
A man should not marry one who is short, nor one who is excessively tall, nor one whose eyebrows meet; nor one with teeth that have wide gaps, nor one with a gaping mouth.
O King, a householder should marry a maiden according to the lawful rite, one who is within five generations on the mother’s side and seven generations on the father’s side.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura; the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa are two others, and the Paiśāca is the eighth and lowest.
In sacrifices, the *daiva* [form of marriage] consists of giving [the bride] to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); the *ārṣa*, however, consists of taking two cows.
May those two together practice dharma; this is recorded as the *prājāpatya* rite.
Whichever duty has been prescribed for each of these castes by the great seers, one should take a wife according to that; one should avoid any other way.
Having obtained a wife who practices the same dharma, he should maintain the life of a householder together with her; he who gives this [gift] properly and remains well-concealed obtains great fruit.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Sagara said:
O Sage, I desire to hear about the virtuous conduct of a householder.
Abiding by which, one does not fall away from this world nor from the next.
Śaunaka said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to the characteristics of right conduct;
by a man who possesses right conduct, both worlds are conquered. (ViP 3.11.2)
The virtuous are those whose defects have been destroyed; the word "sat" (good/true) denotes them. Their conduct is what is called "sadācāra" (the conduct of the virtuous).
Furthermore, O lord of the earth, the seven ṛṣis, the Manus,
and the lords of creatures are both the exponents and the practitioners of right conduct.
O wise King, having awakened at the *brāhma-muhūrta* while the mind is composed,
one should contemplate dharma and that wealth which is not in conflict with it.
One should certainly consider the desires of both of them without causing them distress;
for the sake of avoiding the destruction of both the seen and the unseen, one should maintain an equal vision toward the three aims of life.
O King, one should abandon wealth and pleasure if they cause harm to dharma;
and one should also abandon dharma if it results in future suffering or is censured by the world.
Then, having risen at dawn, O Lord of Men, one should practice loving-kindness.
In the southwest direction, having gone beyond the range of an arrow-shot and further from his dwelling,
he should void urine and excrement at a distance.
One should not pour out the water used for washing the feet or other remnants into the courtyard of the house.

A wise man should never urinate upon his own shadow, the shadow of a tree, nor upon cows, the sun, fire, or wind; likewise, he should never urinate upon his teacher or members of the twice-born caste.
Not on ploughed land, nor in the midst of crops, nor in a cow-pen, nor in a gathering of people;
not on a path, nor at river-crossings and the like, O bull among men.
One should not perform the voiding of feces or the discharge of urine in water, nor on the bank of water, nor in a cremation ground. 3.11.13.
O King, a wise man should discharge urine facing north during the day, and facing the opposite direction at night, except in times of distress.
Having strewn the earth with grass and covered his head with a cloth,
he should stand there for no very long time and should not utter anything at all.
One should not take earth dug up by anthills or rats, nor earth from within water, nor that which remains after cleansing, nor that taken from a house, nor earth used for making a smear.
O King, one should avoid all these types of earth for the purpose of purification: earth inhabited by living creatures, and earth turned up by a plow.
One [application] on the penis, three on the anus, and ten on the left hand, O King.
After 18a, T2.3 and G2 insert:
... ... both of these are considered to be mild.
For a householder, [drinking] the five [kinds of] wine is a cause for loss of caste... // ViP_3.11.18a*19:2 //
And in both hands, there are seven other types of earth that bring about purification.
With water that is free from scum and froth, and devoid of bubbles, he should sip;
then, being composed, he should apply earth once again.
Having completed the washing of his feet, he should sprinkle water over them again;
he should then drink water three times with that [water] and likewise wipe his mouth twice.
Then one should touch the apertures of the head, the crown of the head,
the arms, the navel, and the heart with water.
Having washed his feet and hands, he should drink water that has been inspected three times.
Then, with the base of the thumb, he should wipe his face twice according to conventional practice.
Having first performed the three [libations] with the hands joined together, he should then touch [the water].
With the thumb and the forefinger... [lacuna] // ViP_3.11.21*20:4 //
And with the thumb and the ring finger, he should repeatedly touch the eyes and the ears.
From the little finger and the thumb [to the heart], and from the palm indeed to the navel.
One should touch all the limbs, and afterwards the head, with the edge [of the hand].
Then, having sipped water, a man should attend to his hair,
look into a mirror, apply collyrium, perform auspicious rites, and touch blades of dūrvā grass and other such items.
Thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, being endowed with faith, he should acquire wealth for the sake of his livelihood according to the duties of his own caste, and he should perform sacrifices.
Since the Soma-sacrifices, the Havis-sacrifices, and the Pāka-sacrifices are all established upon wealth for human beings, one should therefore strive for the acquisition of wealth.
One should bathe for the sake of daily rites in rivers, streams, and ponds, in waters excavated by the gods, and in mountain springs.
One should perform the bath with water drawn from wells, or on the ground;
or one may bathe with drawn water if it is not possible to do so on the ground.

Having bathed and wearing clean garments, one should, with a well-composed mind, perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors using the specific *tīrtha* (parts of the hand) belonging to each of them.
One should offer water three times for the gratification of the gods;
likewise, according to the rule, one should offer it once for the sages and once for Prajāpati.
O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of pleasing the ancestors, one should likewise offer water three times to the grandfathers and the great-grandfathers.

With a concentrated mind, one should offer [the water] through the *paitra* (paternal) *tīrtha* to the maternal grandfather, his father, and his father; now hear from me regarding other optional rites (*kāmya*).
O King, one may likewise offer it to one's mother, to one's maternal grandfather, to the wife of a guru,
to a guru, to the relatives of one's maternal uncles and others, to a dear friend, and to a sovereign.
And having performed the libations for the gods and others, O King, one who desires his own welfare should also recite this mantra and offer water for the benefit of all living beings.
May all creatures— those that move in water, those that dwell on land, and those that depend on the air—
quickly attain satisfaction through this water given by me.
"This water is offered by me for the nourishment of those who abide in all the hells and amidst their torments."
May those who were kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth,
as well as those who desire water from us, all attain complete satisfaction.
"Wherever beings dwell whose souls are afflicted by hunger and thirst,
may this water with sesame seeds, offered by me, become inexhaustible for them."
O King, I have thus described to you this ritual offering of water for the fulfillment of desires;
by giving this, a person gratifies the entire world and,
O sinless one, obtains the merit arising from the nourishment of the universe.
Having duly offered the water for the desired purpose to these with faith,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then offer a handful of water to the Sun.
Obration to Vivasvat, O Brahman, to the radiant one, to the splendor of Viṣṇu,
to the pure Savitṛ who brings forth the world and bestows the fruits of action!
Then one should perform the worship of the household deities and the adoration of one's chosen deity through offerings of water-sprinklings, flowers, incense, and other such items.
He should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice for the first time before offering it to the Brahmin thereafter.
One should reverently offer an oblation intended for Prajāpati;
then to the houses, to Kāśyapa, and thereafter to Anumati in due order.
Then he should throw the remainder of that [water] into the water-jars for the Parjanyas;
thereafter, he should pour it at the door for Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and in the center for Brahmā.
O tiger among men, hear from me also about the deities of the directions of the house.
A wise man should offer the bali consisting of the remnants of the oblation to Indra, Dharmarāja, Varuṇa, and likewise to Indu, in the eastern and other directions.
In the northeastern quarter, the wise man should offer the bali-oblation to Dhanvantari;
thereafter, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
In the northwest, he should offer a bali to Vāyu; then, in all the directions, to the Quarters (Diś);
and to Brahmā, to the Intermediate Space (Antarikṣa), and to the Sun, he should cast the offering.
O Lord of Men, one should offer a bali-oblation intended for the Viśvedevas, the Viśvabhūtas, the Pitṛs who are the lords of all, and for Yakṣman.
Then, having taken other food, the wise man, composed in mind, should according to his own desire give it upon a clean spot of ground to all beings without exception.
Gods, humans, animals, birds, Siddhas, along with hosts of Yakṣas, Uragas, and Daityas;
Pretas, Piśācas, and all trees—whatever beings desire food, let it be given by me.
May the ants, insects, moths, and the like, who are hungry and bound by the fetters of karma, attain satisfaction; this food has been released by me for them—may they be happy.

For those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and for whom there is neither the preparation nor the availability of food—may this food offered upon the earth for their satisfaction reach them; may they find contentment and be joyful.
All beings, as well as this food and I myself—Viṣṇu—are not other than this;
therefore, I offer this food, which is the very essence of the multitude of beings, for their sustenance.
This fourteenth class of spirits—whatever hosts of beings reside therein—for their satisfaction this food has been released by me; may they be joyful with it.
Having uttered this, a man endowed with faith should offer food upon the ground for the benefit of all beings, since the householder is the refuge of all.
Then the man should give [the food] on the ground to dogs, caṇḍālas, and birds,
as well as to any others who are outcasts or unworthy men on this earth.
Then he should remain in the courtyard of his house for the duration of a cow-milking,
or longer as he desires, for the purpose of receiving guests.
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other courtesies,
as well as by offering a seat and washing his feet.
With faith, by the gift of food, by pleasant inquiries and replies,
and by following them as they depart, the householder should generate affection [in his guests].
One should properly honor a guest who has arrived from elsewhere and whose family and name are unknown, but not one who dwells in the same village.
One who eats while failing to honor a guest— who possesses nothing, has no kin, and has arrived from another land— and who merely desires to satisfy his own appetite, goes to a state of degradation.
Without inquiring into his Vedic study, lineage, conduct, or family,
the householder should regard that guest with the thought that he is Hiraṇyagarbha himself.
O King, for the sake of the ancestors, he should also feed at least one other Brahmin who is a native of that region,
whose conduct and birth are well-known, and who performs the five daily sacrifices.
O protector of the earth, having set aside the first portion of the food prepared as the *hantakāra* offering,
one should present it to a *śrotriya* as a sacrificial oblation (*nirvāpa*).
And one should give three portions of alms to wandering mendicants and students;
and according to his desire, a wise man should give without restriction when he possesses the means.
Thus these guests have been declared, as well as those previously mentioned mendicants;
one should honor these four, and thereby one is released from the debt incurred by the sacrifice to men.
If a guest departs from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated and his face turned away,
he transfers his own misdeeds to that person and departs taking away their merit.
O lord of men, Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, Śakra, Vahni, the Vasu-gaṇa, and Aryaman—
these indeed enter the guest and consume the food.
And those who are eternally devoted to Viṣṇu, and those who belong to the Vikhānasa hermitage; D1,M1 insert this.
Those who know the ritual procedure for the Pañcarātra and those who are devoted to Viṣṇu.
Those who assume the form of Viṣṇu have taken refuge in Viṣṇu himself.
And those who remain, having realized that "the entire world is pervaded by Viṣṇu."
For all these are indeed guests who must always be tolerated.
By honoring even one of these as a guest, one becomes a partaker of the worlds of merit.
Therefore, a man should always strive to honor his guests;
he who eats without having honored a guest consumes only sin.
Then, the householder should first feed those women who have recently given birth, the distressed, pregnant women, the elderly, and children with consecrated food, and only afterwards [feed] himself.
If one eats while these [guests] have not yet eaten, one consumes a great evil deed;
and having died, that man goes to hell and is reborn as a consumer of phlegm.

One who eats without having bathed eats impurity; one who does not recite prayers eats pus and blood; one who eats unconsecrated food eats urine; and one who eats before children and others eats excrement. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.73)
One who utters false blessings eats worms; one who does not give receives poison.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, listen to how a householder should indeed eat,
so that while eating, no bond of sin arises for that man.
And here, O King, there is incomparable health, an increase in strength,
as well as the pacification of portents and the neutralization of the malevolent magic of enemy factions.
Having bathed according to the rules and performed the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors,
the disciplined householder, holding consecrated gems in his hands, should eat.
When the recitation is completed and the oblation offered into the fire, O King, wearing clean garments,
having given [gifts] to guests, Brahmins, teachers, and dependents,
and wearing auspicious fragrances and excellent garlands, O Lord of Men.
O Lord of Men, he should eat wearing only a single garment, with his hands and feet still moist, with a pure face and a joyful heart, and not facing an intermediate direction.
Facing either the east or the north, with his mind focused on nothing else,
a man should eat food that is commendable, wholesome, and sprinkled with consecrated water.
A householder, having given food that is not obtained through contempt, nor indeed anything loathsome or unrefined,
may then eat what remains from his hungry disciples.
O King, one should eat from vessels that are praised as pure, remaining free from anger.
O Lord of Men, a man should not give food from a vessel placed on a seat, nor in an improper place,
nor at an improper time, nor in a place that is too crowded, after first having offered a portion to the fire.
O King, food consecrated with mantras is recommended, provided it is not stale;
however, this excludes fruits, meat, dried vegetables, and the like.
Likewise, O lord of men, one should never eat the pith extracted from *bādari* fruits, nor from jujubes that have been baked with molasses.
O Lord of the World, a discerning person should not consume anything in its entirety, except for honey, water, curd, ghee, and roasted flour.
Having become single-minded, one should eat, beginning first with a sweet taste;
likewise, salt and sour in the middle, and then pungent, bitter, and so forth.
A person who eats liquid food first, solid food in the middle,
and liquid food again at the end does not lose his strength or health.
Restraining his speech and not disparaging it, he should thus eat blameless food;
taking five mouthfuls in great silence, that is for the nourishment of the vital breaths and the rest.
Having eaten properly and then sipped water (ācamana), facing either east or north,
one should again sip water in the prescribed manner after washing the hands from the base upwards.
But a man, established in himself with a tranquil mind and having assumed his seat,
should perform the remembrance of his chosen deity.
May Agni, impelled by the wind, cause the food of the earth to swell;
may he, granted space by the ether, digest it, and may there be happiness for me.
May this food serve for my strength from the earth, the waters, fire, and wind;
may there be unimpeded happiness for me upon its digestion.
May food be nourishing for the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna breaths; may there be unimpeded happiness for me.
May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) digest the food I have eaten without exception;
may they grant me the well-being arising from its digestion, and may I be free from disease in my body.
And just as the embodied soul [pervades] within all bodies... // ViP 3.11.94*23 //
Just as the Lord Viṣṇu is the single sovereign principle, the soul of all senses and bodies;
by that truth, may this entire food become a source of health and undergo its proper transformation for me.
"Viṣṇu is the eater, and likewise the food and its transformation;
by that truth, may this food which has been eaten be digested."
Having uttered this and rubbed his belly with his own hand,
he should perform his duties without weariness and with alertness, ensuring they cause him no exhaustion.

One should spend the day in the diversion of studying the true scriptures and other such activities that do not conflict with the path of the righteous; thereafter, one should perform the twilight worship with a concentrated mind.

O King, having properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the wise man should worship the evening twilight with the Sun and the morning twilight accompanied by the stars, according to the prescribed rule.
Attendance upon the king at all times, as well as during the two twilights, is required;
except, however, in cases of birth-impurity, ritual defilement, confusion, illness, or fear.
The man who is overtaken by the rising sun, or who sleeps while the sun is setting,
must perform penance, except in the case of illness.

Therefore, O lord of the earth, having risen before the sun has appeared, a man should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) belonging to the end of the day, and likewise that which belongs to the beginning of the day while still not asleep.
O King, those evil-minded ones who do not perform the twilight worship, neither the morning nor the evening, go to the Tāmisra hell.
Furthermore, O lord of the earth, having taken up the cooked food, even in the evening the wife should offer a *bali* for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*, though it may be without mantras.
Even there, one should likewise offer food to outcastes and others.
A wise man should honor a guest who has arrived there according to his own ability;
honoring consists of washing the feet, offering a seat, bowing low, and speaking words of welcome,
and then, O King, providing food and a place to sleep.
O King, whatever sin is incurred when a guest who has come for the day departs disappointed,
that very same sin is multiplied eightfold when the sun has risen and one who has come as a guest departs disappointed.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, a man should honor a guest who has arrived with the sun according to his own ability; when he is honored, all the deities are honored.
A person should gratify him according to their own ability by giving food, vegetables, and water,
or else by the gift of a bed, a grass mat, or land.
O King, having performed the purification of his feet and other limbs and having eaten in the evening, the householder should then go to a bed that is not cracked, even if it is made of wood.
One should not occupy a bed that is not spacious, nor one that is broken, uneven, dirty, infested with insects, or uncovered.
O King, for a man who is always sleeping with his head toward the eastern direction or toward the southern direction, it is auspicious; however, the opposite position brings about disease.
O Lord of the Earth, approaching one's own wife during her season is commended,
provided it is under a male asterism, at an auspicious time, and on the even nights of the four-night period beginning with Jyeṣṭhā.
One should not approach a woman who has not bathed, nor one who is ill, nor one who is menstruating;
nor one who is undesirable, nor one who is angry, nor one who is censured, nor one who is pregnant.
One should not approach a woman who has given her sacrificial fee, nor one who desires another man, nor one who is without desire, nor the wife of another;
nor one emaciated by hunger, nor one who has overeaten; and he himself should be endowed with these same qualities.
Having bathed, wearing garlands and perfumes, joyful, neither overfed nor hungry,
and full of desire and passion, a man should engage in sexual intercourse.
The fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, and the full moon— these, O King of kings, as well as the sun's transit into a new zodiac sign, are the sacred festival days (parvan).
A man who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these specific festival days goes,
upon death, to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana (Feeding on Excrement and Urine).
Therefore, on all these festival days, wise men who observe self-restraint should be devoted to the study of true scriptures, the worship of the gods, meditation, and the recitation of prayers.

He should not engage in sexual intercourse with one of another species, nor with one who is not a woman, nor when he has consumed medicinal herbs; likewise, he should not have intercourse in the presence of gods, twice-born men, or his guru.
O Lord of the Earth, one should never [discharge waste] at the bases of shrines, in courtyards, at crossroads, nor in cremation grounds, groves, or in bodies of water.
O protector of the earth, on all the aforementioned festival days, as well as during the two twilights,
a wise man should never engage in sexual intercourse, nor when oppressed by the urge to urinate or defecate.
O King, approaching [the water] on festival days is inauspicious; doing so during the day brings sin;
and doing so on the ground brings disease to men; it is not recommended at a reservoir of water.
One should never approach another's wife even in thought;
how much less so in speech? For those who engage in such misconduct, there is not even a bond of bone [to hold them together].
Having died, he goes to hell, and even here his life is diminished;
for men who take pleasure in another's wife, there is fear in both worlds.
Thinking thus, a wise man should approach his own wife when she is in her season, provided she is free from the aforementioned defects and is desirous; he may do so even outside the season.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Saurva said:
One should worship the gods, cows, and Brahmins, as well as the perfected ones (siddhas), elders, and teachers.
And he should perform the twilight devotions at the two times of day, as well as tend the sacred fires.
A self-restrained man should always wear unsoiled garments, as well as auspicious medicinal herbs and gems belonging to Garuda.
A man should always wear hair that is very glossy and free from dirt, be fragrant, dress elegantly, and carry beautiful white flowers that are pleasing to the heart.
One should not take even the slightest thing belonging to another, nor should one speak even a small unkindness;
one should not utter pleasant falsehoods, nor should one proclaim the faults of others.
O Lord of Men, one should not take pleasure in enmity toward another's wife;
one should not mount a faulty vehicle, nor should one rely on the shade of a riverbank.

[One should not associate] with those who are hostile, fallen, or insane; with those who have many enemies and the like; with insects; nor with harlots, the husbands of harlots, the base, or those who tell lies.
A wise man should not cultivate friendship with those who are excessively wasteful, those devoted to slander, or the deceitful; nor should he travel alone on a road.
O Lord of Men, one should not plunge into the force of a flood of water;
one should not enter a burning house, nor climb to the top of a tree. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.12.8)
One should not grind one's teeth, nor should one pinch the nose;
one should not yawn with the mouth uncovered, and one should avoid [noisy] breathing and coughing.
A wise man should not laugh loudly, nor should he emit wind with sound;
he should not bite his nails, nor should he tear grass or scratch the earth.
A wise man should not bite his beard, nor should he carry away clods of earth or soil;
O Lord, one who is impure should not gaze upon the luminaries.
One should not utter the sound "hum" toward a naked woman, another's wife, the sun at its rising or setting, or a corpse; for the odor of a corpse is born of Soma.
One should always avoid at night crossroads, sacred trees, cremation grounds, groves, and the company of wicked women.
A wise man should not step over the shadow of those worthy of worship, such as gods, brahmins, or luminaries;
he should not travel alone through a desolate forest, nor should he dwell in an empty house.
One should avoid from afar hair, bones, thorns, impurities, sacrificial offerings, ashes, chaff, as well as ground that is wet from bathing.
A wise man should not take refuge with any who are ignoble, nor should he find pleasure in crookedness;
he should not approach venomous beasts, nor should he remain standing for long once he has risen.
O Lord of Men, a wise man should likewise avoid excessive wakefulness and sleep, as well as standing and sitting; he should similarly avoid lying down and physical exertion.
A wise man should avoid from afar those with fangs and those with horns,
as well as dew, O Indra among kings, and likewise the morning breeze and the heat of the sun.

A wise man should not bathe, nor sleep naked, nor perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) while naked; he should not sip water with his lower garment hanging down, and he should avoid the worship of the gods and other deities [in such a state].
In rites such as the fire-oblation and the worship of deities, as well as in sipping water (ācamana),
in the recitation for Brahmins, and in silent prayer (japa), one should not proceed wearing only a single garment.
One should never sit together with those of improper conduct;
for even half a moment’s proximity to those of virtuous behavior is praised.
A wise man should never enter into conflict with those who are superior nor with those who are inferior;
both marriage alliances and disputes are desired by kings only with those of equal character.
A wise man should not initiate strife, and he should avoid groundless enmity;
even a small loss must be endured, for one should abandon the pursuit of wealth through hostility.
Having bathed, one should not wipe one's limbs with the bathing cloth nor with the hand;
one should not shake out one's hair, nor should one sip water for purification after having stood up.
One should not step over another's foot, nor should one lead it toward an object of worship;
endowed with humility, one should assume the vīrāsana posture before the guru.
One should not pass by temples, crossroads, auspicious objects, or those worthy of worship with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; one should not do so in the opposite manner toward these.
A wise man should not discharge phlegm, feces, or urine while facing the moon, fire, the sun, water, wind, or those worthy of worship.
One should not urinate while standing, nor should one urinate on a path;
one must never step over phlegm, feces, urine, or blood.
The discharge of phlegm or a sneeze at the time of eating is not commended;
nor is it appropriate during offerings, auspicious rites, recitations, burnt oblations, or in the presence of a great assembly.
A wise man should not despise women, nor should he place his full trust in them; he should not be envious toward them, nor should he ever entrust them with authority.
O King, a wise man devoted to right conduct should never leave his home without having paid homage to auspicious flowers, jewels, clarified butter, and those worthy of worship.
One should pay homage at crossroads, be intent on the fire-oblation at the proper time,
rescue the distressed, and attend upon virtuous men of great learning.
He who worships the gods and the sages, who properly offers funeral cakes and water to the ancestors,
and who honors guests— he shall go to the highest worlds.
For one whose mind is one-pointed, who is firm in his vows, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses,
who exerts himself in internal yoga, and who is ever non-violent, liberation is certain and eternal.
He who, having mastered his own self, speaks at the proper time words that are beneficial, measured, and pleasant,
goes to the imperishable worlds of kings, which are the cause of supreme joy.
The wise man, possessed of modesty, endowed with patience, faithful, and disciplined,
goes to the unsurpassed worlds of those who are advanced in learning and noble lineage.
A wise man should observe a suspension of study during unseasonable thunder and the like, on festival days, during periods of impurity, and likewise during eclipses and similar occasions.
For that virtuous man who brings peace to the angry, who is a kinsman to all and free from envy,
and who provides comfort to the frightened, heaven is but a meager reward.

In rain, heat, and similar conditions, one should always go with an umbrella and a staff; and when traveling at night or through forests, one desiring protection for the body should indeed go wearing sandals.
A wise man should wander about without looking upward, downward, or into the distance;
a person should walk while looking only at a span’s length of ground before him.
For one who, having mastered their own self, casts off all causes of defects without exception,
not even the slightest loss occurs in regard to dharma, artha, and kāma.
Devoted to the conduct of the virtuous, wise, and trained in learning and discipline. (ViP 3.12.40*25)
He whose inner being is melted with friendliness speaks pleasant words even to a sinner and even toward a man; for him, liberation rests in the palm of his hand.
Those who have transcended the sphere of desire, anger, and greed,
and who abide in right conduct— it is by their spiritual power that the earth is sustained.
Therefore, a wise person should speak the truth that causes joy to others;
regarding that truth which leads to the suffering of others, one should remain intent on silence.
Thinking that what is pleasant is not beneficial, one should not speak it;
rather, one should speak words that are for one's welfare, even if they are extremely unpleasant.
A wise person should devote themselves only to that which is beneficial for living beings both in this world and in the next, whether by deed, thought, or speech.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Saurva said:
"When a son is born, the ritual bathing of the father, along with his clothes, is prescribed."
One should likewise perform the birth-rite (jātakarma) as well as the śrāddha performed on auspicious occasions (abhyudaya).

With single-minded focus and no other thought in mind, one should properly worship and feed an even number of twice-born Brahmins representing both the gods and the ancestors, proceeding in the counter-clockwise direction (savya-krama).
O King, facing either the east or the north, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with curd, unbroken rice, and jujube fruits, using either the *devatīrtha* or the *kāya-tīrtha*.
O King, the host of ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas is gratified by that śrāddha;
therefore, it must be performed by men on all occasions of prosperity.
At the marriages of daughters and sons, at the entry into a new house, at the naming ceremony of children, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony and other such rites; ||| ViP_3,13.5 |||
At the parting of the hair during pregnancy, and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha group of ancestors.
The sequence for the worship of the ancestors has been briefly declared for occasions of prosperity;
now, O protector of the earth, hear the ritual procedure for the rites for the deceased.
Having bathed the corpse of the deceased with auspicious ablutions, adorned it with garlands and ornaments,
and cremated it outside the village, they should bathe with their clothes on in a body of water.
Reciting, "To such-and-such a person, standing here or there," the kinsmen, facing southward, should offer handfuls of water.
Having entered the village together with the cows at the appearance of the stars,
they should then observe the rules for a straw mat, sleeping upon a layer of grass on the ground.
O King, a morsel of food must be offered daily on the ground for the deceased spirit;
and during the day, O bull among men, one should eat a meal that is free of meat.
If those days are according to one's desire, the feeding of Brahmins must be performed;
thus the deceased attains satisfaction while the circle of kinsmen eats.
On the first, third, seventh, and likewise the ninth day,
having discarded one's clothes and bathed outside, one should offer water with sesame seeds.
Then the group of kinsmen should offer water with sesame seeds upon the ground.
And on the fourth day, O King, the collection of the ashes and bones must be performed;
after that, the touching of the limbs is also permitted for the sapinda relatives.
O King, they are fit for all ritual acts and share the same water [for funeral rites], except for the enjoyment of ointments, flowers, and other such luxuries.
The use of beds and seats is permitted even for the sapindas after the collection of ashes and bones; however, sexual union with women is not allowed.
In the case of an infant, one who has gone to another country, an ascetic who has fallen from his vows, or one who is dead;
likewise, in cases of death by water, fire, hanging, and so forth, purification is immediate according to one's wish.
For ten days after a kinsman has died, the food of that family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, sacrifice, and the private recitation of the Vedas are suspended.
This period of impurity lasts for twelve days for a Brahmin and likewise for a Kṣatriya;
it is half a month for a Vaiśya and one month for a Śūdra, for the sake of purification.
On that first day, he may at his pleasure feed an odd number of twice-born men;
then, on the following day, he should offer a rice-ball (piṇḍa) upon darbha grass near the remnants of the meal for the deceased.
However, water, weapons, goads, and staffs may be touched by the other castes immediately after a meal for Brahmins; they become pure from them in that respective order.
Then, a man should perform those duties of his own caste that have been prescribed for the Brahmins and the others, and likewise he should live by the earnings derived from his own specific duty.
After this, on the anniversary of the day of death, the ekoddiṣṭa rite must be performed;
for that is indeed devoid of the ritual acts such as the invitation (āvāhana) and the assignment of deities.
In that rite, a single arghya offering must be presented, and likewise a single purifying blade of grass (pavitraka);
a funeral cake (piṇḍa) must be offered for the deceased after the twice-born have finished eating.
There, the question and the delight of the sacrificer and the twice-born should be [expressed], and likewise, upon completion, it should be said: "May this be inexhaustible for so-and-so."
The dharma consisting of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites is thus prescribed for a year;
now hear, O Indra among kings, about the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* performed at that time.
O King, that too should be performed according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
After 27ab, D₃, G₂, and ed. Veṅk. insert:
"Or in the sixth year, or in the month, or on the twelfth day."
There, four bowls were prepared, filled with sesame seeds, perfumes, and water.
O King, there should be one vessel for the deceased (preta) and likewise three vessels for the ancestors (pitṛ);
one should pour the contents of the preta-vessel into the three ancestral vessels.
Then, O lord of the earth, once that deceased person has attained the status of a progenitor (pitṛ),
one should worship his ancestors with all the rites of the śrāddha.
O King, a son, a grandson, a great-grandson, a kinsman, the lineage of a brother,
or even the lineage of a *sapiṇḍa* becomes eligible to perform the funeral rites.
In the absence of all these,
the sapinda-kinship of the maternal side— those who are connected by the funeral cake (piṇḍa) or by water— is the recipient of the [water].
O King, when both families have been extinguished, the rites must be performed by women;

or else, those rites for the deceased which are to be performed should be carried out by members of a religious community (saṃgha). In the case of those whose kinsmen and heirs are extinct, the lord of the earth himself should cause the rites to be performed.
The preliminary rites, the intermediate ones, and likewise the subsequent rites—these rites are indeed of three kinds; hear from me their distinctions.

Those rites which begin with the touching of the fire, the water, the weapons, and so forth, and end with those same acts, are the preliminary ones; those performed month by month are known as the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

O King, those ancestral rites which are performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony once the deceased has attained the status of a *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) are called the "subsequent" (*uttara*) rites.
By the paternal and maternal sapindas, as well as by those who share the same water (samānodaka), by those belonging to their respective groups, or by the king who takes away the wealth; ||| 36 ||
The preliminary rites must be performed by the sons and others, while the subsequent ones,
O best of men, should be performed by the daughters' sons or likewise by their sons.
O King, the subsequent rites for women also must be performed on the anniversary of their death every year, according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* offering.
Therefore, O King, listen to those duties known as the *uttarasaṃjñā*, and at what times they should be performed and by what procedure, O sinless one. (ViP 3.13.39)
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Saurva said:
[He created] Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Nāsatyas, Sūrya, Agni, the Vasus, and the Maruts.
The Viśvedevas, the hosts of sages, birds, humans, and animals.
By performing the śrāddha rite with faith, one satisfies the crawling creatures, the hosts of ancestors, and whatever else is designated as a living being— indeed, the entire world.
O Lord of Men, one should perform [these rites] on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight every month, as well as on the Aṣṭakās; now hear from me the times for optional rites.

One should perform a śrāddha ceremony upon learning that material suitable for a śrāddha has arrived, or that a distinguished twice-born guest has come, or during the Vyatīpāta yoga, or at the solstices (ayana).
O protector of the earth, when the equinox has arrived, as well as during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
it occurs in all the zodiacal signs as the sun moves through them.
One should perform voluntary śrāddhas during afflictions caused by constellations and planets, upon seeing an evil dream, and likewise at the arrival of the new harvest.
When the new moon coincides with the conjunction of Anurādhā, Viśākhā, or Svātī,
the host of ancestors attains satisfaction through funeral rites for eight years.
When the new moon occurs under the asterism Puṣya, Raudra (Ārdrā), or Punarvasu,
then the ancestors, when honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.

The new moon day occurring under the asterisms of Vāsava (Jyeṣṭhā), Ajaikapād (Pūrvabhādrapadā), or the Pitṛs (Maghā), as well as that under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), is difficult to obtain even for the gods, for those who desire the satisfaction of the ancestors.
O Lord of the Earth, listen further: when the new moon occurs during these nine lunar mansions, the śrāddha then bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors. ViP 3.14.10.
This was the song sung by Sanatkumāra to the high-souled Ilā, who,
devoted to his father, questioned him with faith and humility.

Sanatkumāra said: The third day of the month of Vaiśākha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), and the fifteenth day of Māgha— ViP_3,14.12 //
O King, these four lunar days, which mark the beginnings of the Yugas, are declared to yield infinite merit.
The sages know that at the beginning of the Yuga, there are two white [ages] and likewise two black ones.
In the bright fortnight, it should be observed during the forenoon; in the dark fortnight, likewise during the afternoon.
That which is given at the beginning and at the end of the Yugas is held to be inexhaustible.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, on the three Aṣṭakās, and during the two solstices; ViP_3.14.13cd.

When the moon has waned in the month of Māgha, at the end of the day, when the two equinoxes occur, on the lunar days marking the beginnings of the Manvantaras, and likewise during the time of the Vyatīpāta yoga at the shadow of the elephant— Ś, D1.6.7 insert hereafter, and D5 inserts lines 1–2 after 13ab and lines 3–4 after 13: "When the moon has waned in the month of Māgha, at the end of the day, when the two equinoxes occur, on the lunar days marking the beginnings of the Manvantaras, and likewise during the time of the Vyatīpāta yoga at the shadow of the elephant."
A self-restrained man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors here;
by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years—this is a secret that the ancestors declare.

If the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha ever coincides with the lunar mansion Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), that time is supreme for the ancestors; indeed, O King, it is not attained by those of meager merit.
O protector of the earth, if the Dhaniṣṭhā asterism occurs at that time,
then water and food offered to the ancestors provides satisfaction for ten thousand years to the men born in that family.

If the Pūrva-Bhādrapadās fall upon that very same time, then the Śrāddha which is performed for the ancestors by means of that [offering] brings about supreme satisfaction, and through it the ancestors sleep peacefully for an entire Yuga.
Whether at the Gaṅgā, the Śatadrū, the Vipāśā, the Sarasvatī, or the Naimiṣa and Gomatī rivers—
having plunged into them and performed worship with devotion, one destroys the misdeeds of the ancestors.
And the ancestors always sing this, having attained further satisfaction from the water-offerings of Māgha:
"At the end of the dark fortnight of Māgha, we shall attain satisfaction through the waters of auspicious holy sites offered by our sons and others."
When the mind and wealth of men are pure, when the time is praised as auspicious, when the ritual procedure is declared,
when the recipient is as described, and when there is supreme devotion— these grant men their desired objects.
Likewise, hear from me those verses sung by the ancestors;
having heard them, you should remain there with a disciplined mind.
"May a wise man, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, be born into our family— one who will offer us funeral cakes (piṇḍas)."
Or, at this time, a man whose wealth is limited to that alone, with a mind bowed in devotion, shall feed the foremost of Brahmins according to his ability with food.
Being incapable of giving cooked food, he will give raw grain according to his ability to the foremost of the twice-born, or even a very small sacrificial fee.
Even there, O King, being devoid of strength, he will bow down and give some sesame seeds resting on the tips of his fingers to a certain eminent brahmin.
Bowing with devotion, he will offer handfuls of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds upon the ground, dedicating them to us.
Having obtained it from anywhere at all, or even from cattle for his daily cow-portion,
he will, being endowed with faith, give it to us while pleasing us in its absence.
In the absence of all else, having gone to the forest, displaying his armpits,
he shall recite this aloud to the Sun and the other world-protectors:
"I have no wealth, nor riches, nor anything else suitable for an act of faith; I bow only to my ancestors.
May my ancestors be satisfied through my devotion, as I raise these two arms upon the path of the wind."
Śaunaka said: "O King, he who acts according to this purpose regarding existence and non-existence, as sung by the ancestors,
by him the Śrāddha is truly performed."
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Saurva said:
Listen to me as I describe the qualities of those Brāhmaṇas whom one should feed at a Śrāddha ceremony. ViP_3.15.1.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who knows the Trimadhu, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, a knower of the Vedas, a learned śrotriya, a yogin, and likewise one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; [these are the ones who purify].
Likewise, the officiating priest, the sister’s son, the daughter’s son, the son-in-law, and the father-in-law;
the maternal uncle, one devoted to austerity, one intent upon the five fires,
disciples, kinsmen, and he who is devoted to his mother and father.

O King, one should first employ these previously mentioned Brāhmaṇas at the śrāddha for the sake of nourishing the ancestors; in the absence of these, one may employ those mentioned subsequently as substitutes.

A betrayer of friends, one with deformed nails, a eunuch, one with black teeth, a twice-born man who defiles a maiden, one who abandons the sacred fire and the Vedas, and a seller of Soma; ViP_3,15.5 //
Likewise, one who is falsely accused, a thief, a slanderer, a village priest, one who teaches for a fee, and he who is taught by one teaching for a fee; ||| ViP_3,15.6 |||
Likewise, the husband of a woman who previously had another husband, and one who abandons his mother or father; ViP 3.15.7ab.
Likewise, one who abandons his brother, a corrupter, and a reviler of all; ViP_3.15.7ab*30.
He was nourished by the offspring of a Śūdra woman and was indeed the husband of a Śūdra woman.
Likewise, a temple-priest (devalaka) is not worthy of an invitation to a śrāddha ceremony.
On the first day, the wise man should invite the learned priests and others who are praised for their knowledge,
and at that very time, he should explain to them the ritual duties pertaining to the ancestors and the deities.

Therefore, while performing the sacrifice together with the twice-born, the patron should not engage in anger, sexual intercourse, and the like, nor should he undergo physical exhaustion; for in such cases, there is this great fault.
One who engages in sexual intercourse after being appointed to a *śrāddha*, or after eating at one, or after having fed others, or after having appointed others,
causes his ancestors to sink into a pit of semen.
Therefore, the invitation of the foremost of the twice-born is prescribed here first;
one should feed the ascetics who have come to the house after having invited the twice-born.
One should honor the twice-born who have come to one's home by washing their feet and other such hospitable acts.
With the sacred grass (pavitra) in his hand, he should seat the twice-born who have sipped water on their seats— odd numbers for the ancestors and even numbers for the gods, according to his wish.
One should appoint either one deity at a time for the gods, and likewise for the ancestors.
Likewise, one endowed with devotion should perform the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva rite, or alternatively, follow the Vaiśvadeva procedure.
One should feed the Brahmins representing the gods facing the east;
and one should also feed those representing the ancestors and the paternal grandfathers facing the north.
Regarding these two, O King, some say that the performance of the *śrāddha* should be separate;
other great seers declare that it may be done together with a single cooking.
Having offered kuśa grass for a seat and having worshipped them with the arghya offering according to the rules,
the wise man should perform the invocation of the gods with their permission.
And one should offer the *arghya* to the gods with barley-water according to the prescribed rule;
having likewise offered garlands, perfumes, incense, and lamps to them in accordance with the ritual injunctions.
One should arrange all of that for the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
then, having obtained permission and having offered darbha grass cut in two, one should proceed.
O King, the wise man should perform the invocation of the ancestors preceded by mantras;
he should offer the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites with sesame-water while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
If at that time a guest arrives there seeking food— a traveler on the king's road—
he, being permitted by the Brahmins, should feed him as well according to his desire.
Yogins, who benefit human beings through various forms,
wander this earth with their true nature remaining unrecognized.
Therefore, a wise man should honor a guest who has arrived at the time of a śrāddha;
for a guest who is not honored, O King, destroys the fruit of the performance of the śrāddha.
Then, O bull among men, having been permitted by those twice-born ones, he should offer food into the fire three times, excluding condiments and salt.
"First, O King, an oblation is to be offered with the words, 'Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāha';
immediately after that, one should give an offering to Soma Pitṛmat."
Then another [portion] is offered to Vaivasvata as the third;
thereafter, one should pour out very small amounts of what remains from the oblation into the bowls of the Brahmins.
Then, having offered food that is delicious, exceedingly desirable, and well-prepared, one should say these non-harsh words: "Please enjoy it as you wish."
And they should eat that food happily with focused minds, remaining silent and with pleasant countenances; the giver, moreover, should give it with devotion, free from anger and haste.
Having recited mantras that destroy demons and having strewn the ground with sesame seeds,
those best of the twice-born should meditate upon their own ancestors.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
abiding today within the bodies of the Brahmins, attain satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
their forms nourished by the fire-oblation, attain satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by me upon the earth.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this devotion, which has been offered here by me.
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction, as well as his father and his other ancestors;
may the Viśvedevas reach supreme satisfaction, and may the malevolent spirits (yātudhānas) perish.
Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, the imperishable Self, the enjoyer of all sacrificial offerings and ancestral oblations, is the Sovereign here;
by His presence, may all demons and all Asuras immediately depart without exception.
When those brahmins have been satisfied, one should scatter food upon the ground;
and for the sake of sipping water, one should give them water once each.

Once they have been fully satisfied, he, being composed, should then properly offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) upon the ground with all the food mixed with sesame seeds, having received their permission.
One should offer water with the *pitṛtīrtha* and then a handful of water;
with that same *tīrtha*, one should present the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) to the maternal grandfathers.
And one should,
with great effort, ensure that the ground slopes toward the south.
Indeed, in open spaces that are clean, and likewise on the banks of water.
Upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, having honored it with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
he should first offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his own father near the remains of the meal.
He should satisfy the grandfather with another [portion], and likewise his father's father with yet another;
he should gratify those who consume the smears at the base of the *darbha* grass by rubbing them with the remnants of the smearings.
Having likewise honored the maternal grandfathers with rice-balls accompanied by perfumes, garlands, and other offerings,
he should then give water for sipping (ācamana) to the foremost of the twice-born.

O lord of men, with devotion and a focused mind, he should first offer [the oblation] to the ancestors, saying "May it be well-svadhā," and according to his ability, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
And having given the sacrificial fee to them, he should cause those representing the Viśvedevas to recite:
"May those who are the Viśvedevas be pleased by this. Thus he should say.
When those Brahmins have replied, "So be it," one should offer the requested blessings;
thereafter, O high-minded one, one should dismiss the gods first and the ancestors afterwards.
The same sequence is prescribed for the maternal grandfathers along with the gods;
likewise for the serving of food according to one's ability, for the giving of gifts, and for the dismissal.
Before the washing of the feet, one should perform the dismissal for the gods and the twice-born;
however, the dismissal for the ancestors should come first, and that for the maternal grandfathers follows.
Then, having honored them with respect and words of affection, he should dismiss them;
permitted to depart, he should follow them as far as the door.
Then the wise man should perform the daily rite known as Vaiśvadeva,
and he should eat together with those worthy of honor, his servants, and his kinsmen.
In this manner, a wise man should perform the *śrāddha* for his paternal ancestors as well as for his maternal ancestors;
nourished by these *śrāddhas*, the grandfathers shall grant all desires.
Three things are purifying at a śrāddha: a daughter’s son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds; likewise, the gift of silver, as well as the recounting and hearing of sacred stories.
O King of kings, for one performing a śrāddha who avoids forbidden things, anger, traveling on a road, and haste— these three are not recommended even for the eater there.
O King, for those men who perform the śrāddha rite, the Viśvedevas, the ancestors (pitṛs), as well as the maternal grandfathers, and their entire lineage are nourished.
The host of ancestors has the Soma as its support, and the Moon is the support of Yoga;
therefore, O protector of the earth, the application of Yoga during a Śrāddha ceremony is highly praised.
O King, if a yogi stands before even a thousand Brahmins,
he delivers all those who eat as well as the patron of the sacrifice.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Saurva said: "With sacrificial offerings, fish, meat, and the flesh of rabbits and birds..."
With the flesh of pigs, goats, lambs, Ruru deer, and gayals.
Likewise, the ancestors attain satisfaction through the flesh of sheep and cattle, increasing month by month;
they are eternally satisfied by the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa antelope.
O Lord of Men, in this rite, the flesh of the rhinoceros, kālaśāka greens, and honey are highly recommended; they provide extreme satisfaction.
O Lord of the Earth, for him who performs a śrāddha ceremony after reaching Gayā,
that birth becomes fruitful, granting satisfaction to the ancestors.
O bull among men, *prasātikā*, *sanīvāra*, and the two kinds of *śyāmāka*— these,
being the foremost of wild herbs, are fit for the *śrāddha*.
Barley, millet, mung beans, wheat, rice, sesame seeds,
flat beans, kovidāra, and mustard seeds are excellent for this purpose.
O Lord of Men, one should avoid all kinds of grain for which the *āgrayaṇa* offering has not been performed, as well as kidney beans,
millet, and lentils.
The bottle-gourd, the garlic, the onion, the carrot, the scallion, fermented gruel, and salts from saline soil; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.16.8.
Resins that are reddish, visible salts,
these indeed must be avoided at a śrāddha, as well as anything that is not commended by word.
O King, water brought at night that has not been offered, where a cow does not find satisfaction, and water that is foul-smelling or frothy, is not fit for use in a Śrāddha ceremony.
One should avoid the milk of one-hoofed animals, as well as that of camels and sheep, and likewise the milk of does and buffaloes, in the performance of a śrāddha rite.
[The ground] is [defiled] by eunuchs, outcasts, Caṇḍālas, heretics, the insane, and the diseased;
by cocks, dogs, the naked, monkeys, and village pigs.

O bull among men, when a *śrāddha* is looked upon by a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, one who is impure due to death, or a carrier of corpses, the ancestors do not partake of the offerings.
Therefore, endowed with faith, one should perform the Śrāddha in an enclosed space;
and by scattering sesame seeds upon the ground, one should ward off the Yātudhānas.
O King, food that is putrid, or infested with hair, insects,
and the like, as well as food mixed with fermented liquors or that has become stale, must not be offered.
Whatever is given by those endowed with faith to the ancestors according to their names and lineages,
that becomes the very food of whatever kind of sustenance those ancestors have become.
Moreover, O Lord of the Earth, verses sung by the ancestors in the grove of Kalāpa in ancient times concerning Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu, are still heard.
"Will there be those in our family who, having gone to Gayā, will out of reverence offer us funeral cakes (piṇḍas), being disciplined in the ways of the righteous path?"
"May he be born in our family who would give us milk-rice with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism."
Or he may marry a Gaurī maiden, or set free a dark-colored bull,
or perform the horse sacrifice according to the rules with the prescribed sacrificial fees.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Thus spoke the venerable Aurva to the high-souled Sagara.
O Maitreya, [this was] previously asked by you correctly regarding the practices of the virtuous.
Thus, by means of these nine chapters, the dharma of the three Vedas has been expounded in detail.
The subsequent two chapters are for the purpose of censuring the abandonment of that [dharma].
I have also explained this to you in its entirety, O twice-born one:
no one who transgresses the conduct of the virtuous ever attains prosperity.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, I have learned about those headed by the *ṣaṇḍha* and the *apaviddha*, as well as all those such as the *udakyā*; now I wish to know about the *nagna*."
Who is naked, what is his conduct, and how may a man receive the designation "naked"? I wish to hear the true nature of the naked as it is accurately described by you.
O best among the upholders of dharma, there is indeed nothing unknown to you that we wish to hear.
Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, this triad known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma is the covering for the social classes (varṇa).
He who abandons it out of delusion is considered naked and a sinner.
O twice-born one, since the triple Veda is the covering for all social classes,
one becomes naked, without a doubt, when it is abandoned.
And hear this other [account] which our grandfather Vasiṣṭha, the knower of dharma, related to the great-souled Bhīṣma.
O Maitreya, I too have heard this account concerning Nagna from that great-souled one as he spoke it, which I have been asked about here by you.
Long ago, O twice-born one, there was a divine battle between the gods and the asuras lasting for a year;
in that conflict, the gods were defeated by the Daityas led by Hrāda.
Having gone to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, they performed austerities and then sang this hymn for the purpose of propitiating Viṣṇu.
The gods said:
"May the primordial Lord Viṣṇu be pleased by that speech which we shall utter for the propitiation of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds."
Nevertheless, those who seek worldly existence, their own vigor destroyed by the destruction wrought by enemies,
shall praise you— even though the true nature of your words is not within the scope of their perception.
You are the earth, the waters, fire, wind, and space;
you are the entire internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), primordial matter (pradhāna), and the Puruṣa who transcends it.
O Soul of all beings, this single body of yours consists of both the formed and the formless,
extending from Brahma down to a blade of grass, and is distinguished by various states and times.
O Lord, salutation to that form of yours in the nature of Brahmā, which previously arose from the lotus of your navel for the sake of assisting creation.
Obeisance to that divine Self, whose nature is such as ours, yet who appears divided according to the distinctions of Śakra, Arka, Rudra, Vasu, Aśvin, Marut, Soma, and the rest.

O Govinda, salutation to that form of yours which consists primarily of deceit, lacks awakening, and is devoid of patience and self-restraint; salutation to that which is the very essence of the Daityas.

Salutations to you, whose nature is that of a Yakṣa, in whom the channels do not carry excessive consciousness, whose splendor is motionless, and who is yet attracted by sound and other sense objects.
O Supreme Person, salutations to you in that terrible, dark form of yours, which consists of cruelty and illusion, and belongs to the nature of a night-stalker.
O Janārdana, salutations to you, whose form is called Dharma, which serves as the instrument for the fruit of the true dharma of those residing in heaven.
Salutations to that Siddhātman, whose nature consists primarily of joy, who is unattached, and who moves with speed in acts such as going and coming, O you whose self is perfected.
O Hari, salutations to that form of yours which is of the nature of a serpent—cruel, possessing the wealth of extreme endurance, capable of bearing [all] enjoyments, and double-tongued. ViP 3.17.23.
And salutation to you, O Viṣṇu, whose form is that of the Sage, who has realized that which is peaceful, faultless, and stainless.
O lotus-eyed one, salutation to You, the soul of Time, whose form is unrestrained as it devours all beings at the end of the eon.
Salutation to that one whose nature is Rudra, who, having consumed all beings without distinction, including the gods and others, dances at the end of time.
O Janārdana, salutations to that form of yours which is the self of all actions arising from the activity of *rajas*, and which is the essence of the human being.

O Soul of All, salutation to that form of yours which is characterized by darkness (tāmasa), endowed with twenty-eight types of slaughter, which follows the wrong path, and whose nature is that of a beast.

Salutation to that primary Self, who is the very form that constitutes the limbs of sacrifice and is the means for the accomplishment of the world, yet who appears divided through various distinctions such as trees and other entities.
Salutation to You, the soul of all, who are the form of everything— from animals, humans, and gods, to space, sound, and so forth— beginning with that which is first.

O Supreme Self, salutation to You, the cause of all causes, whose primordial form is distinct from this entire universe consisting of primary matter, intellect, and the rest— a form which has no equal and nothing else like it.

To that form of yours, O Blessed One, which is devoid of white and other colors, as well as length and other dimensions or density; which is beyond the range of qualifiers; which is pure and utterly stainless; and which is visible only to the supreme sages—we bow down.

To that whose nature is Brahman we bow— the unborn and undecaying which exists within our bodies, within other bodies, and within all things without exception, and from which nothing else distinct exists.
We bow down to that stainless Lord Vāsudeva, who is the unborn, eternal, and supreme Self, whose form is this entire universe; he is the deathless one, the seed of all things without exception.
Parāśara said: At the conclusion of this hymn, the gods beheld Hari, the Supreme Lord, mounted upon Garuḍa and holding in his hands the conch, the discus, and the mace.
All the gods, seeking refuge, spoke to him with prostrations: "Be gracious, O Lord; protect us from the Daityas! ViP 3.17.36.
O Supreme Lord, the three worlds and the sacrificial portions have been seized by the Daityas led by Hrada,
