who have transgressed even the command of Brahmā.
Although we and they are all portions of you, who are the entirety of all beings, nevertheless,
due to the differentiation caused by ignorance, we perceive the world as divided.
Delighting in the duties of their own respective castes and following the path of the Vedas,
those enemies, endowed with ascetic power, cannot be slain by us.
O Soul of All, you ought to grant us that means by which,
O Blessed One, we may become capable of slaying those Asuras.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Lord Viṣṇu produced Māyāmoha from his body and gave him to them, saying this to the best of the gods: Viṣṇu spoke these words to the foremost of the gods.
This Māyāmoha will delude all those Daityas;
consequently, having been cast outside the path of the Vedas, they shall become fit for slaughter.
While I am established in my station, all those who are my adversaries— the gods, Daityas, and other deities— are to be slain by me, for they obstruct the authority of Brahmā.
Therefore, go; you should have no fear. This Māyāmoha is before you; O gods, he shall go today for the sake of your benefit.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the gods prostrated before him and departed as they had come;
Māyāmoha also went with them to where the great Asuras were.
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Then Māyāmoha [approached] those great Asuras who were devoted to asceticism.
Maitreya went and saw those who were dwelling on the banks of the Narmadā.
Then, O twice-born one, Māyāmoha—naked, shaven-headed, and wearing peacock feathers—spoke these gentle words to the Asuras: ||| ViP_3.18.2 |||
Māyāmoha said:
"O lords of the Daityas, tell me for what purpose you perform this austerity;
do you desire the fruit of your penance to be of this world or of the next?"
The Asuras said:
"O high-minded one, this practice of austerity has been undertaken by us for the sake of attaining rewards in the next world; what is it that you wish to say regarding this?"
Māyāmoha said: "If you desire liberation, carry out my words;
you ought to practice this dharma, which is the unobstructed gateway to liberation."
This Dharma is worthy of liberation; there is nothing higher than this. Abiding in this very [Dharma], you shall go to heaven or to liberation.
And you all, who possess great strength, must accept this Dharma as authoritative.
Parāśara said: By many such means, augmented by the display of reasoning,
those Daityas were led away from the path of the Vedas through the delusion of Māyā.
"This is for dharma, this is for adharma; this is existent, this is non-existent";
"this leads to liberation, but this does not bestow liberation. ||| ViP_3,18.9 |||
This is the ultimate truth, yet it is exceedingly beyond the ultimate; nor indeed is this [the ultimate].
"This is what ought to be done, and this is not to be done"—this is not at all clear;
for this is the duty of those who go naked, while this is the duty of those who wear many garments.
Thus, O twice-born one, by that Māyāmoha, who displayed the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) in many ways, the Daityas were made to abandon their own duties.
"Receive this great Dharma, for you have been declared by Māyāmoha to be Arhats; because they rely upon that Dharma, they became Arhats."
"Those Asuras were made by you to abandon the dharma of the three Vedas through the delusion of Māyā;
for they became absorbed in that, as did others who were incited by them."
By them others were defeated, and by those others still more; and by those yet others, until in a few days the triple Veda was for the most part abandoned by those Daityas.
Furthermore, wearing red garments, Māyāmoha, with unconquered eyes, went to the other Asuras and spoke to them in soft, gentle, and sweet words: Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.18.16.
Māyāmoha said:
"O Asuras, if you desire heaven or even the state of Nirvāṇa, then enough of this wicked dharma consisting of the slaughter of animals and the like; understand this!"
Understand that all this without exception consists of consciousness alone;
comprehend my words correctly, as they have been thus uttered by the wise.
This world, being without support and devoted solely to the objects of deluded cognition,
is excessively corrupted by passion and other vices, and thus wanders in the perils of cyclic existence.
Parāśara said: Speaking thus—"Understand this! Understand!
Understand this!"—that Māyāmoha caused the sons of the Daityas to abandon their own dharma.
He spoke various kinds of words to them, joined with logical reasoning; in such and such a manner he taught the Dharma that they gradually abandoned [their former views].
They too spoke in the same way to others, and others were likewise addressed by them;
O Maitreya, they abandoned the supreme Dharma proclaimed in the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
O twice-born one, Māyāmoha, the creator of extreme delusion, also deluded other Daityas through many various forms of false doctrines.
For in a very short time, those Asuras were deluded by Māyāmoha and abandoned all discourse based on the path of the three Vedas.
O twice-born one, some reviled the Vedas, others the gods,
still others the entire collection of sacrificial rites, and likewise others the brahmins.
This statement is not tenable to reason: that violence is intended for the sake of dharma, while oblations consumed by fire lead to fruit—this is the talk of a child.
If Indra enjoys the status of a god attained through numerous sacrifices merely because of a wooden sacrificial post (śamyā) and the like, then it is better to be an animal that feeds on leaves.
After 27c, M₁ inserts:
... ... may it become the means for accomplishing the sacrifice.
Then his food was constant... // ViP_3,18.27*34:2 //
If it is held that an animal slain in a sacrifice attains heaven,
why then does the sacrificer not likewise slay his own father?
If food eaten by another person results in satisfaction for a man, then one should offer food with faith at a śrāddha; otherwise, those who have gone abroad would not carry [the burden of the rite].
Understanding that this is merely a matter of popular belief, indifference toward it is best for you; may the words spoken by me be pleasing to you.
For the words of the authoritative do not fall from the sky, O great Asuras;
speech endowed with reason is what should be accepted by me and by others like you.
Parāśara said:
By means of Māyāmoha, those Daityas were thus distracted in many ways,
so that not one among them took any pleasure in the Triple Veda (trayī).
When those Daityas had thus gone astray, the immortals,
having made a supreme effort, stood ready for battle.
Then, O twice-born one, the battle between the gods and the asuras broke out once again;
and those asuras, who were obstacles on the path of the righteous, were slain by the gods.
O twice-born one, they first possessed the armor of the True Dharma;
by that they were previously protected, but when that was lost, they perished.
Then, O Maitreya, those people who followed that path became naked, because they had pointlessly abandoned the covering of the three Vedas.
And those Asuras, who reviled the various Vedas, were defeated by the gods. (Veṅk. ed. inserts this line)
The stages of life are the student, the householder, and likewise the forest-dweller;
the wandering mendicant is the fourth here, and a fifth does not exist.
But he who, having abandoned the life of a householder, does not become a forest-dweller or a wandering mendicant,
O Maitreya, is a naked man and a doer of evil.
O Brahmin, for one who is capable, there is a daily lapse in the performance of obligatory rites;
by failing to perform the prescribed duty on that day, he falls.
O Maitreya, in times of non-distress, a man who neglects his daily obligatory rites for a fortnight attains purification through a great expiation.
If a man’s performance of religious rites fails for a year,
virtuous people should always look upon the sun after first looking at him.
O great sage, bathing with one's clothes on is the cause of purification for a man who has touched [such a person];
however, no purification is declared for that man of sinful deeds.
In whose house the gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits depart unhonored after merely breathing upon it, no man is more sinful than he.
One should not create a mixture of impurity with the house, seat, or furnishings of one whose body and dwelling have been struck by the breath of a god or similar beings.
O twice-born one, for a man who engages in conversation, inquiry, and the like with laughter, equality with that very person arises within a year.
Then, if one eats in his house, occupies his seat, or likewise his couch,
and even sleeps on his bed, he would immediately become equal to him.
He who eats without having first honored the deities, the ancestors, the spirits, and likewise the guests, eats sin; what kind of atonement can there be for him?
And those castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who turn their faces away from their own duty and remain established in degraded actions, they indeed receive the designation of "naked ones" (nagna).
O Maitreya, wherever there is an extreme intermingling of the four castes,
it arises there for the destruction of those who follow virtuous conduct.
Those men who eat without first having worshipped the sages, the gods, the ancestors, the spirits, and guests,
fall into hell by merely conversing with them.
Therefore, a wise man should always avoid these naked ones, who are defiled by their abandonment of the three Vedas, in matters such as conversation and physical contact.
That śrāddha, even if performed with effort by those possessed of faith, does not gratify the gods, the fathers, or the grandfathers, if it is looked upon by these [evil beings].
It is heard that in ancient times there was a famous king on earth named Śatadhanu,
and his wife was Śaibyā, who was exceedingly devoted to dharma.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, endowed with truthfulness, purity,
and compassion, she was possessed of all auspicious marks and perfected in modesty.
That king, together with her, propitiated the omnipresent Janārdana, the god of gods, through supreme meditative concentration.
With devotion, with his mind fixed on Him and no other, he should perform daily offerings of oblations, recitations, gifts, fasts, and worship.
Once, O twice-born one, that husband and wife, having fasted on the full moon day of Kārttika, bathed together in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī and emerged,
when they saw a heretic approaching toward them.
He was a friend of that high-souled king, who was a master of archery;
therefore, out of respect for him, he engaged in conversation with him.
Having come together according to the rule and in accordance with the prescribed rites, O best of the twice-born, that couple performed all the worship and other services for Viṣṇu.
As time passed, that king, the conqueror of his enemies, died;
the queen ascended the funeral pyre after her husband, the lord of the earth.
But due to that transgression— namely, the conversation he held with heretics while fasting— that lord of the earth was born as a dog.
She too was born as the auspicious daughter of the King of Kāśī, endowed with the memory of her former births,
perfected in all branches of knowledge, and adorned with all the auspicious marks.
Her father desired to give her away, but was dissuaded by the suitor;
the king himself desisted from the commencement of the marriage due to that very slender maiden.
Then, having perceived her own husband, the dog, with her divine vision,
she went to the city named Vaidiśa and beheld him in that condition.
As soon as she saw her husband in that state, having become a dog, the illustrious woman gave him excellent food, prepared with great hospitality and auspiciously.
While eating the food given by her, which was exceedingly delicious and desired,
he indeed performed many flatteries, behaving like one of his own canine species.
Deeply ashamed by him as he offered such flattery, the young woman spoke these words with a bow to her beloved, that one born of a base womb.
The wife said:
"O Great King, let that courtesy of yours be remembered,
by which you, though having entered the womb of a dog, have become a flatterer of mine."
"O Lord, having conversed with a heretic immediately after bathing at a sacred ford, you have entered a contemptible womb; do you not remember that?"
Parāśara said:
When he had been thus reminded there of his deeds in a previous birth,
he meditated for a long time and then attained an exceedingly rare state of world-weariness.
With a mind full of world-weariness, he departed from that city and,
by casting himself down from a mountain peak, entered the womb of a jackal.
When the second year had arrived, she too, having perceived that jackal with her divine eye, went to Mount Kolāhala to see him.
There too, having seen her husband who had entered the womb of a jackal, the daughter of the king, with her beautiful limbs, spoke to him.
The wife said:
"O Indra among kings, do you remember that former deed of yours which was told by me while you were dwelling in the womb of a dog— a discourse based on the talk of heretics?"
Parāśara said:
Having learned from her that it was true, he who was the best among the truthful abandoned his own body in the forest while remaining without food.
Then, having gone once more to that wolf born in the lonely forest,
the blameless woman reminded her husband of their former history.
O illustrious one, you are not a wolf; you are King Śatadhanu.
Having first become a dog and then a jackal, you have now attained the state of a wolf.
Parāśara said:
Just as he had been reminded, his self manifested and returned to its state as a vulture;
then that blameless, beautiful woman awakened him once again.
"O King, remember your true self; indeed, enough of this vulture-like behavior!
This defect that has caused you to become a vulture was born from the talk of heretics."
Then, having perceived through her own yogic power that he had attained the state of a crow in his immediately following birth, the slender lady spoke to her husband:
O Lord, you who were formerly the one to whom all kings without exception submitted and offered tribute,
have now fallen into the state of a crow and become a consumer of offerings.
And in this very way, being reminded of his former state as a crow,
that king gave up his life-breaths and attained the form of a peacock.
Then that auspicious young woman, having become a peahen, indeed attended to him, providing at every moment food appropriate for his species.
Then King Janaka performed the great horse sacrifice (vājimedha),
and at its concluding bath (avabhṛtha), he then caused him to be sprinkled with water.
The slender-limbed woman bathed herself and also reminded him how that king had taken birth in wombs such as those of dogs and jackals.
Then, remembering the sequence of his births, he cast off his own body and was born as the son of the great-souled Janaka.
Then that slender maiden urged her father to arrange her marriage; and so her father caused a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice ceremony) to be held for her.
When the svayaṃvara had been performed, that beautiful woman chose him once again as her husband, having obtained him as her own lord.
And the prince enjoyed pleasures together with her;
when his father had passed away, he ruled the kingdom over the Videhas.
He performed many sacrifices, gave gifts to those who sought them,
begot sons, and fought with his enemies.
Having ruled the kingdom according to justice and having protected the earth,
that king righteously gave up his dear life in battle.
Then that lady of auspicious eyes, filled with joy, ascended once more onto her husband who lay upon the funeral pyre, according to the prescribed rite and just as before.
Then that king, together with the princess,
attained worlds beyond those of Indra— indestructible worlds that yield all desires.
O best of the twice-born, having attained that purification, you have obtained the fruit of merit: imperishable heaven and a most rare, incomparable conjugal union.
O twice-born one, I have thus declared to you the fault of conversing with heretics,
as well as the majesty of the purificatory bath at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice.
Therefore, one should avoid conversation and touch with sinful heretics;
especially so during the performance of rites, such as sacrifices and when one has been initiated.
If the neglect of religious rites occurs in anyone's household for even one month,
a wise man should look upon the sun after first beholding that person.
How much more so, O twice-born one, for those who have completely abandoned the threefold Veda,
who eat the food of others, who are sinful, and who oppose the teachings of the Vedas?
After verse 99, the edition by Veṅkaṭeśvara inserts:
"But association [with such a woman] consists of conversation with her, and laughter with her is exceedingly sinful."
Therefore, one should avoid those heretics of wicked conduct.
One should not honor, even with mere words, heretics, those engaged in improper acts, those who act like cats, the deceitful, rationalists, and those who behave like herons.
One who has fallen from his own duty is a heretic, one who persists in improper actions, and one who performs what is forbidden.
Of whatever dharma he was always the upholder, standing as high as the banner of the gods.
And when evil deeds are concealed, that is indeed called the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratam).
She speaks pleasant words in one's presence, yet elsewhere she acts most harshly to cause displeasure.
And having abandoned all offensive conduct, this person is called "shameless" (śaṭha) by the wise.
He who creates doubt regarding virtuous deeds by means of fallacious arguments is a *haituka*.
They were short-sighted, deceitful, and solely intent on accomplishing their own self-interest.
The deceitful one who is falsely disciplined is described as having the conduct of a heron.
Contact even with those who laugh with him—sinners, heretics, and those of evil conduct—is cast away from afar; therefore, one should avoid them completely.
These naked ones have been described to you; by sight they are destroyers of faith, and by conversing with them, the merit of men for the day perishes.
These are sinful heretics; a wise man should not speak with them, for by conversing with them, the merit arising from that very day is destroyed.
By even conversing with those men who wear matted hair yet are shaven-headed, who eat in vain and have abandoned all purity,
and who are excluded from the offering of water and funeral cakes for the ancestors, other men go to hell.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, that which ought to be performed by men established in virtuous action—
That [dharma], consisting of the obligatory and the occasional, was declared to me by my preceptor.
The duties of the social classes have been thus declared, as well as those duties pertaining to the stages of life;
O Guru, I wish to hear about the genealogies—please explain them to me.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to this lineage of Manu, beginning with Brahmā, which is adorned by kings who were performers of many sacrifices and heroes among warriors.
And so it has been said:
"He who remembers day after day the lineage of Manu, beginning with Brahmā, for him there shall never be an extinction of his lineage. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.1.4)
Therefore, O Maitreya, listen to that lineage of his in its proper sequence for the sake of washing away all sins without exception.
For example, Hiraṇyagarbha Brahmā— the beginningless primordial source of all worlds, consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and other Vedas, and being the embodied form of Lord Viṣṇu—
first came forth from the cosmic egg as the venerable Brahmā.
From the right thumb of Brahmā was born Dakṣa Prajāpati; from Dakṣa came Aditi; from Aditi came Vivasvat; and from Vivasvat came Manu.
Manu had ten sons named Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Prāṃśu, Nābhāga, Nediṣṭha, Karūṣa, and Pṛṣadhra.
And Manu, desiring a son, performed a sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa.
There, due to the transgression of the Hotṛ priest, a daughter named Ilā was born.
And by the grace of Mitra and Varuṇa, Maitreya, he became the son of Manu named Sudyumna.
Furthermore, due to the wrath of Īśvara, the woman, though virtuous, wandered near the hermitage of Budha, the son of Soma.
And being filled with passion for her, Budha begot a son, Purūravas, upon her.
And when he was born, the supreme ṛṣis of immeasurable splendor— desiring manhood for Sudyumna— performed a sacrifice according to the rules, consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas,

composed of all things, of mind, and of knowledge, yet not consisting of anything at all; the Lord, whose nature is that of the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa), being propitiated, by His grace Ilā became Sudyumna once again.
He, too, had three sons named Utkala, Gaya, and Vinata.
But Sudyumna, because he had previously been a woman, did not obtain a share of the kingdom.
His father, however, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, gave the city named Pratiṣṭhāna to Sudyumna, and he in turn bestowed it upon Purūravas.
But Pṛṣadhra, the son of Manu, became a Śūdra due to the slaughter of his guru’s cow.
From Karūṣa were born the Kārūṣas, Kṣatriyas of great strength and prowess.
Nābhāga, the son of Nediṣṭha, attained the status of a Vaiśya;
from him was born a son named Bhalandana.
From Bhalandana was born Vatsaprī, of noble fame.
Vatsapri became Prāṃśu.
And Prajāni was the only one born of Prāṃśu.
And from that Cakṣuṣa was born Khanitra, and from Cakṣuṣa was born Viṃśa, who possessed exceedingly great strength and prowess.
From him came Viviṃśa, from him Khaninetra, and from him Ativibhūti.

From Ativibhūti was born a son, Karaṃdhama, who possessed great strength and prowess; from him came Avikṣit, and from Avikṣit was born a son, Marutta, of exceeding strength, concerning whom these two verses are sung even today: [The verses follow.]
Whose sacrifice on earth was like that of Marutta,
in which every sacrificial implement was made of gold and was exceedingly beautiful?
Indra was exhilarated by the Soma, the twice-born by the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
and the Maruts, the attendants, and the celestial dwellers of the assembly hall were likewise delighted.
Marutta, the universal monarch, obtained a son named Nariṣyanta.
And from that Dama was born Rājyavardhana, the son of Dama.
From Rājyavardhana was born Sudhṛti; from him, Nara; from him, Kevala; from Kevala, Bandhumān; from Bandhumān, Vegavān; from Vegavān, Budha; and from him, Tṛṇabindu.
He also had one daughter named Ilavilā.
And the excellent Apsaras named Ālambuṣā attended upon that Tṛṇabindu.
From him was born Viśāla, who indeed founded the city named Vaiśālī.
Hemacandra was the son of Viśāla.
From him was born Sucandra; his son was Dhūmrāśva, and his son was Sṛñjaya.
From Sṛñjaya was born Sahadeva;
from him there was a son named Kṛśāśva.
Somadatta was born from Kṛśāśva; he performed ten horse-sacrifices.
His son was Janamejaya,
and from Janamejaya came Sumati;
these were the kings of Vaiśālī.
A verse is also sung in this regard:
"By the grace of Tṛṇabindu, all the kings of Vaiśālī were long-lived, high-souled, heroic, and exceedingly righteous."
Śaryāti had a daughter named Sukanyā, whom Cyavana married.
And there was a righteous son of Śaryāti named Ānarta.
To Ānarta also was born a son named Revata, who ruled over the territory of Ānarta and dwelt in the city of Kuśasthalī.
Revata’s son was also named Raivata; he was a righteous soul called Kakudmin, who became the eldest of a hundred brothers.
He had a daughter named Revatī;
taking her with him, he went to the world of Brahmā to ask the Lord who was born from the lotus, "To whom is she worthy to belong?"
And at that moment, in the presence of Brahmā, two Gandharvas known as Hāhā and Hūhū sang a divine Gandharva melody called Atitāna.
And during that time, although Raivata remained for many cycles of ages through the revolutions of the three paths, he felt as if it were but a single moment while listening.
And at the conclusion of the song, Raivata, having bowed to the Lord who is the lotus-born Brahmā, asked for a bridegroom suitable for his daughter.
And the Blessed One said to him, "Speak the boon that is desired by you."
And bowing once more to that Blessed One, he stated the boons desired by himself as they pleased him:
"Which among these is favored by the Blessed One, to whom shall I give this maiden?"
Then, with his head slightly bowed, the Lord born from the lotus spoke with a smile.
Those whom you consider [your ancestors]—even their lineage of descendants does not currently exist upon the surface of the earth.
For indeed, while you have been listening right here to the Gāndharva, many cycles of four yugas have passed away.
For now, on the surface of the earth, the fourth age of the twenty-eighth Manu is almost passed; indeed, the Kali age is close at hand there.
This jewel of a daughter must be given by you alone to someone else.
For you as well, all these—friends, ministers, servants, wives, kinsmen, forces, and treasuries—have utterly passed away by means of this very time.
Then, his agitation arising once more, the king bowed to the Blessed One and asked:
"Blessed One, this being the case, to whom should I give her?"
Then the Blessed One, the Preceptor of all the worlds, spoke to the lotus-born Brahmā, who had slightly bent his neck and joined his palms in reverence.
Brahmā said:
"Indeed, we do not know the beginning, middle, or end of that unborn Creator who consists of all things;
nor do we know the true nature, the supreme essence, or even the core reality of the Supreme Lord."
And time, consisting of moments, muhūrtas, and so forth, is not the cause of transformation for His manifestation—
He who is without birth or death, whose form is everything, who is nameless and formless, and who is eternal.
Through the grace of that Acyuta, I have become the creator of beings and the bringer of their end;
and from his wrath Rudra arose, while from him as the supreme source, the Puruṣa exists as the cause of maintenance in the midst.
Assuming my own form, the Unborn creates; he who exists in the form of Puruṣa maintains [the world];
and in the form of Rudra, he devours the universe; likewise, with his infinite body, he sustains everything.
Assuming the form of Śakra and others, he protects the universe; in the form of the sun and moon, he destroys darkness.
Having entered the state of fire for the sake of ripening, he sustains the worlds as the imperishable self in the body of the earth.
In the form of breath, he performs the vital activity; in the form of water and food, he provides satisfaction to the world;
and abiding as the support of the universe's stability, in the form of space, he grants room for all things.
He who is created by himself as the creator of the creation, who is protected as the protector of the gods, and who,
as the soul of the universe, withdraws all as the bringer of the end— he is the imperishable self who stands apart from these three.

O King, He in whom this world exists, who is the primordial source of this world, and who as the Self-born One has taken refuge within this world— that Viṣṇu, the source of all beings, has descended upon the earth by means of His own portion.
O King, that delightful city of yours which formerly was Kuśasthalī, like Amarāvatī, is now Dvārakā; and there dwells he who is a portion of Keśava, named Baladeva.
Therefore, O lord of men, bestow this daughter of yours as a wife upon that illusory Māyāmānuja;
he is a praiseworthy suitor and she is your daughter—a jewel among women—and indeed, this union is a fitting one.
Parāśara said: Thus addressed by the Lotus-born One, that Lord of Creatures, having reached the earth,
beheld all men as short in stature, possessing little vitality, and deficient in discernment and vigor.
Having approached that city of Kuśasthalī and seeing it transformed into another form,
the king of incomparable intellect gave his daughter to Sīradhvaja, whose chest resembled a mountain of crystal.
Beholding her to be of such great height, Tālaketu then bent her down with the tip of his own plow;
and immediately she became like any other woman.
That wielder of the plow-wielded weapon married that Revatī, the daughter of King Raivata, according to the prescribed rites;
and having given away his daughter, the king, his mind fixed on austerity, departed for the Himalayas.
Thus ends the first chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
While Kakudmin Raivata had not yet returned from the world of Brahmā, the Rākṣasas known as Puṇyajanas destroyed his city, Kuśasthalī.
And his hundred brothers fled in all directions out of fear of the Puṇyajanas.
And the Kṣatriyas descended from him came to exist in all directions.
From Dhṛṣṭa also was born the Kṣatriya Dhārṣṭaka.
The son of Nabhaga was named Nābhāga;
his son was Ambarīṣa,
and the son of Ambarīṣa was Virūpa.
From Virūpa was born Pṛṣadaśva, and from him was born Rathītara.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"These, born indeed from Kṣatriyas, are further remembered as Aṅgirases;
they are the foremost among the Rathītaras, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas."
And from the nose of Manu as he was sneezing, a son named Ikṣvāku was born.
Of him there were three sons, the most eminent among his hundred sons, named Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍa;
and fifty sons, headed by Śakuni, became the protectors of the northern region (Uttarāpatha),
while forty-eight became the rulers of the southern region (Dakṣiṇāpatha).
On the occasion of the Aṣṭakā festival, that descendant of Ikṣvāku commanded Vikukṣi, saying, "Bring meat fit for the śrāddha.
Having accepted the command with "So be it," he went into the forest, slew many deer, and being extremely exhausted and overcome by hunger, Vikukṣi ate a single hare.
He then brought the remaining meat and presented it to his father.
Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor of the Ikṣvāku clan, being urged to consecrate it, said:
"Enough with this impure meat, for this flesh has been defiled by your wicked son because he ate the hare."
Then, having been addressed thus by his preceptor and abandoned by his father, that Vikukṣi received the name Śaśāda.
And when his father had passed away, he ruled this entire earth according to dharma.
To Śaśāda was born a son named Purañjaya.
Furthermore, in ancient times, during the Tretā age, there was an exceedingly terrifying war between the gods and the asuras.
There, the immortals, having been defeated by the exceedingly powerful asuras, propitiated the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.
And the gracious Nārāyaṇa—the god who is without beginning or end, the supreme refuge of the entire world—spoke:
"I already know what you desire; listen to this for that purpose.
There shall be a son of the royal sage Śaśāda named Purañjaya, a preeminent Kṣatriya, and I shall enter his body with a portion of myself."

"I myself, having descended, shall slay all those Asuras without exception; therefore, you must make an effort toward the conquest of the city for the sake of destroying the Asuras. Having heard this and bowed to the Blessed Viṣṇu, the immortals went into the presence of Purañjaya.
And they said to him:
"O best of Kṣatriyas, we desire that you, being entreated by us, grant assistance to us who are intent on slaying our enemies.
Therefore, you must not cause a breach of the affection shown to us who have come to you as supplicants."
Thus addressed, Purañjaya said:
"If I, mounted upon the shoulder of this Śatakratu, who is the lord of all the three worlds and your Indra, shall fight against your enemies, then I will be your ally.
Having heard this, all the gods and Indra likewise agreed, saying, "So be it."

Then Kakutstha, filled with great joy, having been invigorated by the splendor of the blessed Acyuta— the teacher of all things moving and unmoving— slew all the asuras in the battle between the gods and the asuras, [the latter] having assumed the form of a bull under Śatakratu.
And because the army of the Asuras was destroyed by King Vṛṣabhakakutstha, he therefore obtained the name Kakutstha.
From Kakutstha was born Anenas; from Anenas came Pṛthu; from Pṛthu came Viśvagaśva; his son was Candra, whose son was Yuvanāśva;
and from that Yuvanāśva was born Śrāvasta, who founded the city of Śrāvastī.

Śravasta’s son was Bṛhadaśva, and his son was Kuvalayāśva; he, empowered by the Vaiṣṇava splendor, slew the Asura named Dhundhu— who had wronged the great seer Uttaṅka— and, surrounded by twenty-one thousand sons,
he acquired the name Dhundhumāra.
And all of his sons perished, consumed by the fire of the breath emitted from Dhundhu’s mouth.
Only three remained: Dṛḍhāśva, Candrāśva, and Kapilāśva.
From Dṛḍhāśva came Haryaśva; from him, Nikumbha; from Nikumbha, Saṃhitāśva; from him, Kṛśāśva;
and from him, Prasenajit; from him, Yuvanāśva was born.
While he, being childless, was living in a circle of hermitages belonging to sages out of extreme despondency, those compassionate sages performed a sacrifice for the sake of procreating offspring.
When the middle of the night had passed, those sages placed a jar filled with water consecrated by mantras in the center of the altar and fell asleep.
And while they were asleep, that king, overcome by extreme thirst, entered the hermitage.
He did not wake those sages who were asleep;
instead, he drank that water from the jar, which was purified by mantras and possessed immeasurable majesty.
And the awakened sages asked: "By whom was this water, purified by mantras, drunk?"
For, having heard that the wife of King Yuvanāśva would give birth to a son of great strength and prowess once this [milk] was drunk, the king said, "I drank it unknowingly."
And the embryo of Yuvanāśva was within her womb, and it grew in due course.
And when the time had arrived, he emerged by bursting through the right side of the lord of the earth, yet that king did not die.
"Once born, whom will he suckle? the sages asked.
Then the king of the gods, having arrived, said to me, "He shall sustain this."
From that he became known by the name Māndhātṛ.
And the King of the Gods placed his index finger in his mouth;
having tasted it, which flowed with nectar, he grew in a single day.
That universal monarch Māndhātṛ, however, enjoyed sovereignty over the earth consisting of the seven continents.
And there is a verse on this point:
"From where the sun rises until where it sets—
all that is said to be the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva."
Māndhātṛ married Bindumatī, the daughter of Śaśabindu, and begot upon her three sons: Purukutsa, Ambarīṣa, and Mucukunda.
And that king had fifty daughters.
And there was a seer named Saubhari, a master of the Rigveda, who dwelt within the water for a period of twelve years.
And there, within the water, lived a lord of fish named Sammada, who had an immense brood and was of extraordinary size.

His sons, grandsons, and daughters’ sons swam around him—by his sides, behind him, in front of him, and even above his chest, tail, and head—and together with him, they sported day and night in great contentment.
He too, his joy intensified by their touch, delighted in many ways every day with those sons, grandsons, and daughters’ sons, even as that sage looked on.

Then, while staying within the water, Saubhari abandoned his one-pointed meditative concentration and, observing day after day that most delightful and graceful sport of the fish together with its sons, grandsons, daughters, and so forth, thought:
"Aha! Blessed is this one; even having attained such an undesirable other birth, he sports here with these sons, grandsons, and others, and he inspires great longing in us.
We too shall sport in this way with our own sons and others."
Having reflected thus, he emerged from that water and, desiring to be released, went to King Māndhātṛ for the sake of the maiden.
Immediately upon hearing of his arrival, King [Kalmāṣapāda] rose, honored him properly with water for the feet and other offerings, and once Saubhari had accepted a seat, he spoke.
Saubhari said:

"O lord of men, I desire to marry; grant me a maiden, do not destroy my affection. For those who come as supplicants driven by necessity never depart disappointed from one born of the lineage of Kakutstha."
O protector of the earth, there are indeed other kings on this earth whose sons have been born;
however, this lineage of yours is praiseworthy for having undertaken the vow of the initiation into the giving of what is requested by supplicants.
"O King, you have daughters numbering fifty; grant one of them to me.
For I fear the pain that comes from the rejection of my request, O best of kings, more than anything else."
Parāśara said:

Having heard these words of the sage, the king, beholding that seer whose body was worn out by old age, became distressed at the prospect of being refused and, fearing the curse of the venerable one, reflected for a long time with his face cast slightly downward.
Saubhari said:
"O lord of men, why do you fall into such anxiety? Nothing impossible has been said by me here.
Since our daughter must necessarily be given away, we have achieved our purpose through her alone; if so, what is not already gained?"
Parāśara said:
Then, fearing his curse, that king spoke to him with humility.
The king said:

"O Blessed One, this is the established custom of our family: whichever bridegroom of noble lineage is pleasing to the maiden, to him the maiden is given. Your command, O Blessed One, lies beyond even the reach of our desires."
"How has this come about? Now that such a situation has arisen, we do not know what to do"—this is what I am reflecting upon.

When he had spoken thus, the king thought to himself: "Aha! This is another means of rejecting me; he is old and undesirable even to women, how much more so to maidens. Having reflected thus, the sage spoke as follows:
Thinking, "So be it; I shall do accordingly," he spoke to Māndhātṛ.
"If that is so, then let the eunuch of the maiden's inner apartments be commanded to admit us.
If any maiden indeed desires me, then I shall take her as my wife; otherwise, enough of this undertaking of ours which has begun at a past time," he said, and then he ceased.
Parāśara said:
Then Māndhātṛ, fearing the sage’s curse, commanded the superintendent of the maidens’ inner apartments.
As soon as the Blessed One entered the maiden’s inner apartments, he assumed a form of such surpassing loveliness that it exceeded even that of all the siddhas, gandharvas, and humans.
And having ushered that sage into the inner apartments, the eunuch spoke to those maidens:
"Your father, the Great King, issues this command:

'This Brahman seer has come to us seeking a maiden, and I have made a promise to him that if any of my daughters chooses the Blessed One, I shall not place any obstacle in the maiden's way according to her desire. Having heard this—"
All those maidens, filled with passion and stirred by love, vied with one another to choose that sage as their husband, just as female elephants seek the leader of a herd.
And they said:
"Enough, sisters! I choose him; he has been chosen by me. He is not suitable for you;
he was created by Fate as my husband alone. I have been created for him, so go and seek peace."

"He was chosen by me first! He is being obstructed by me as he enters the house!"—thus did an excessive quarrel arise among the daughters of the king over him, each crying "By me! By me!"* *Note: The asterisk indicates that the original Sanskrit text contains a play on words (śleṣa) where "mayā" can mean both "by me" and "by Maya," the architect of the gods. The commentary clarifies this pun.*
But when that prince of irreproachable fame was chosen by all the maidens out of intense affection,
then the official in charge of the maidens, with a bowed body, reported the matter duly to the king.
Parāśara said:

Upon understanding that, with his mind agitated as to what this might be and what he should do, the king—though unwilling—somehow gave his consent when asked, "Tell me what this is; what shall I do? and "What was spoken by me? (ViP 4.2.59).
Having performed a marriage befitting his status, the great seer led all those maidens back to his own hermitage.

And there, having summoned Viśvakarman— another creator like Dhātṛ, the master of all arts and crafts— he commanded: "Let palaces be constructed for each one of all these maidens, complete with gardens and open courtyards, furnished with excellent beds and furnishings, and containing delightful reservoirs with blooming lotuses and the warbling of kalahamsas, kāraṇḍavas, and other water-birds."
And Tvaṣṭṛ, the master teacher of all specialized crafts, showed that it had been executed exactly in that manner.
Then, commanded by the supreme seer Saubhari, a great treasure named Nandana, which never perishes, took up residence in those houses.

Then, with a continuous supply of various foods—edibles, soft foods, lickables, and so forth—those daughters of the king fed their attendants, followers, and servants day and night throughout all the houses.
Once, however, his heart drawn by affection for his daughters, that lord of the earth, wondering whether they were very miserable or happy,
approached the hermitage of that great seer and beheld a series of crystal palaces shimmering with garlands of rays, together with most delightful groves and ponds.
Having entered a certain palace and embraced his daughter, he took his seat; with eyes filled with tears born of overflowing affection, he spoke.

"O child, is there happiness here for you, or is there some unhappiness? Is that great seer still affectionate toward you, and do you remember our dwelling in his house? Having been thus addressed, his daughter said to her father:

O dear one, here is a palace exceedingly delightful, a most charming grove, ponds with water-lilies in full bloom resounding with the sweet warbling of birds, and enjoyments consisting of food, drink, ointments, garments, ornaments, and other luxuries that are pleasing to the mind; there are soft beds, and this state of household life is endowed with every prosperity— nevertheless, by whom is one's birthplace not remembered?
Through your grace, all this has become exceedingly beautiful in its entirety.

"But there is this one cause of sorrow for me: that this great seer, my husband, does not leave our house; because of his excessive affection for me alone, he remains by my side and not with our other sisters.
Thus, my own sister is distressed"—having said this, which was a source of extreme grief, she approached the second palace, embraced her daughter, and sat down, asking her exactly the same questions.
She too described all these pleasures of enjoying the palace and so forth, saying, "It is for me alone, out of excessive affection."
Having heard such words as, "She is not among our sisters," and so forth, the king entered all the palaces, and his sons likewise questioned her.

Addressed by all of them in that manner, his heart overwhelmed with an abundance of satisfaction and wonder, he approached the Blessed Saubhari as he sat in a secluded spot; having offered him worship, he said:
"O Blessed One, this very great power of accomplishment has been seen by you. We have never observed such a display of majesty belonging to anyone else."
"How great is this fruit of asceticism, O Blessed One? Having thus honored that seer, he enjoyed desired pleasures for some time right there with that best of seers;
and as time passed, a hundred sons were born to him by his royal daughters.
And as his flow of affection increased day by day, his heart became exceedingly drawn toward him by a sense of possessiveness.
"Would that these sons of mine, speaking so sweetly, might walk on their own feet; would that they might reach the prime of youth;
and would that I might see them married with wives."
"May they have sons;
may I see their sons endowed with sons"—perceiving that such desires proceed from the fulfillment of time day after day, he reflected thus:
"Alas! How vast is the extent of my delusion! (ViP 4.2.77)
There is no end to desires even in ten thousand years, nor even in hundreds of thousands of years;
for as each desire is fulfilled, new desires arise once again.
Those who were young have grown old and walked with their feet; they have entered into union with wives and brought forth offspring.
I have seen my sons, and yet my inner self desires once more to behold the birth of their children.
If I should even behold their progeny, my desire would be for something else beyond that;
for when that is fulfilled, by whom can the birth of yet another desire be prevented?
"Until death, there is truly no end to desires; this has been understood by me today.
The mind of one who is intent on attachment to desires never becomes joined with the ultimate truth."

That samādhi of mine was suddenly destroyed by association with the company of fish, like a fish's dwelling in the water; this attachment of mine was caused by that association, and from that attachment arose a great desire to possess.
The suffering that arises from the birth of a single body, numbering fifty-fold,
has been multiplied many times over by the possession of daughters of kings and their numerous sons.
Through their sons, grandsons, and the descendants of those sons, this attachment—
which is the cause of extreme suffering and the very repository of the sense of "mine"— will expand ever further through their continued possession of property.
The power that resulted from the austerity I performed while dwelling in the water has become an obstacle to that very austerity;
through association with this fish, a passion for my daughter and others arose within me, and by that I have been robbed.
Freedom from attachment is the state of liberation for ascetics; from attachment, all defects arise.
Even a yogi who has ascended to the highest yoga is cast down by attachment, let alone one of minor accomplishment.
I shall act for my own sake with a mind seized by the grasping of possessions, so that,
having further diminished my faults, I may not suffer through the miseries of people.

I shall worship with asceticism alone Viṣṇu, the Lord of lords, the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, and who is both white and black.

In that Viṣṇu, who possesses inexhaustible energy, who assumes all forms, whose body is both unmanifest and clearly manifest, and who is infinite— may my mind remain forever unwavering, free from defects, for the sake of perpetual liberation.
Since there is nothing whatsoever other than him— who is pure, infinite, the Lord of all, and without beginning or middle— I take refuge in that Viṣṇu, the supreme teacher among teachers.
Parāśara said:
Having thus addressed himself by means of his own self, that Saubhari abandoned his son, house, seat, belongings, and the entirety of his wealth; accompanied by all his wives, he entered the forest.

There too, having daily performed the entire range of ritual acts to be accomplished by forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*), he exhausted all his sins. With his mental dispositions fully matured, he internalized the sacred fires within himself and became a mendicant (*bhikṣu*).

Having entrusted the entire multitude of his ritual duties to the Blessed One, he attained the supreme, immutable state of Acyuta—the unborn, changeless, and deathless condition that transcends all other beings.
Thus has this account of Māndhātṛ been told, beginning from his connection with his daughter.

Whoever recollects, reads, hears, comprehends, or causes this account of Saubhari’s life to be written— such a person shall, throughout eight births, possess neither wrong-mindedness nor false dharma, nor any practice of an evil path by the mind, nor any sense of "mine" toward anything that is to be utterly abandoned.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the fourth part of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: Hereafter, the lineage of Māndhātṛ’s sons is described.
Yuvanāśva was the son of Māndhātṛ, the son of Ambarīṣa.
Therefore, because they were descended from Aṅgiras, the descendants of Hari are called Hārītas.
And in the netherworld (rasātala), the Gandharvas named Mauneyas, numbering sixty million, deprived all the Naga clans of their sovereignty over their most precious jewels.

And by those lords of serpents, shaken by the power of the *gandharvas*, the Blessed One—the Lord of all gods, whose lotus-eyes were opened and blossomed upon hearing his praise, who reclines upon the waters—awoke from the end of his sleep; having prostrated themselves, they said to him: "O Blessed One, will our fear of these *gandharvas* also come to an end? The Blessed One replied: *Note: The term "puṇḍarīka" refers to a white lotus, often used as a metaphor for the eye in classical Indian literature.*
I am the beginningless Puruṣa, the Supreme Person; having entered into that son of Māndhātṛ, Yauvanāśva, named Purukutsa, I shall bring those wicked Gandharvas entirely to subdual.
Having heard this and offered their salutations to the Blessed One, the lords of the serpents returned once more to the world of the Nagas and urged Narmada to go with Purukutsa.
And she led him down to Rasātala.
Having gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala), his own strength invigorated by the splendor of the Blessed One, he slew all the gandharvas and returned once more to his own abode.
And all the lords of the serpents granted a boon to Narmadā:
"He who shall utter your name accompanied by mindfulness of you shall have no fear of the poison of snakes."
And here is a verse on this subject:
"Homage to Narmadā in the morning; homage to Narmadā at night. Homage be to you, O Narmadā; protect me from poisonous serpents. (ViP 4.3.10)

Having uttered this day and night, whether entering into darkness or not, one shall not be bitten by serpents; nor shall even the poison consumed by one who possesses the power of recollecting this mantra lead to any harm. And the lords of the serpents granted a boon to Purukutsa, saying, "There shall be no interruption of your lineage."
Purukutsa begot Trasadasyu upon Narmadā.
From Trasadasyu was born Saṃbhūta, and from him came Anaraṇya, whom Rāvaṇa slew during his conquest of the quarters.
Pṛṣadaśva was the son of Anaraṇya, and Haryaśva was the son of Pṛṣadaśva. From him came Vasumanas; his son was Tridhanvan, and the son of Tridhanvan was Trayyāruṇa.
Therefore, he who was Satyavrata acquired the name Triśaṅku and fell into the state of a Caṇḍāla.
During a twelve-year drought, for the sake of nourishing his wife and children and to avoid accepting gifts from a *caṇḍāla*, he hung deer meat daily on a banyan tree on the bank of the Ganges;
being thoroughly satisfied, Viśvāmitra raised him bodily to heaven.
From Triśaṅku came Hariścandra; from him, Rohitāśva; from him, Harita; from Harita, Cañcu; from Cañcu, Vijaya and Sudeva; from Vijaya, Ruruka; and from Ruruka, Vṛka.
Then Bāhu, who had been defeated by the Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, and others, entered the forest together with his pregnant queen.
And poison was administered by that co-wife in order to arrest the development of her fetus.
Because of that, her fetus remained within her womb for seven years;
and that son, due to his advanced age, died near the hermitage of Aurva.
His wife, having prepared a funeral pyre and placed him upon it, became resolved to follow him in death.
Then the Blessed Aurva, who knows the past, future, and present times, emerged from his own hermitage and said:

"Enough with this false obsession! A universal monarch—lord of the entire earth, possessed of extreme heroism and prowess, performer of many sacrifices, and destroyer of the enemy faction—resides within your womb."
When he said, "Not so, not so! Do not resolve upon such a rash act," she desisted from her insistence on following him in death.
He was brought to his own hermitage by that very Blessed One;
and within a few days, a child of exceeding brilliance was born together with that poison.
Having performed the birth rites and other ceremonies for him, Aurva gave him the name Sagara.
And once his initiation had been performed, Aurva taught him the Vedic scriptures, as well as the weapon known as the Bhārgava, which was of fiery nature.
Having conceived the thought [of his origin], he asked his mother:
"Mother, how did we come to be here? Where is our father? To him who asked such things, his mother told everything.
Then, incensed by the seizure of his father’s kingdom, he made a vow to slay the Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, and others;
and for the most part, he did indeed slaughter the Haihayas.
The Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas, being struck down, sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor of that lineage.
Then Vasiṣṭha, having rendered these [sons] living corpses, said to Sagara:
"My child, enough with these living corpses who have followed you in death."
And it was by me alone that these were made to abandon their own dharma and their association with the twice-born, for the sake of fulfilling your vow.

Saying "So be it," he welcomed those words of his preceptor and caused them to change their dress: the Yavanas with shaven heads, the Śakas with half-shaven heads, the Pāradas with long hair, and the Pahlavas with beards; he made these and other Kṣatriyas devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call.
And having abandoned their own dharma and being forsaken by the Brahmins, they fell into the state of barbarians (mlecchas).
Sagara also, having returned to his own capital, ruled this earth consisting of seven continents with unimpeded sovereignty.
Thus ends the third chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Parāśara said:
Sagara had two wives: Sumati, the daughter of Kaśyapa, and Keśinī, the daughter of the King of Vidarbha.
And Aurva, propitiated by those two for the sake of offspring through supreme meditative concentration, granted them a boon.
One shall give birth to one son who will uphold the lineage, while another shall give birth to sixty thousand sons.
When it was said, "Let each take whatever she desires according to her wish," Keśinī chose one son, while Sumati chose sixty thousand sons.
When the sage had replied, "So be it," Keśinī, after only a few days, gave birth to a single son named Asamañjasa, the upholder of the lineage;
whereas Sumati, the daughter of Vinatā, had sixty thousand sons.
From him was born an ill-omened prince named Aṃśumān.
But that Asamañja had already turned away from virtue since his childhood; his father, however, thought: "Once he has passed his childhood, he will become wise."
Then, when that period had also passed, his father abandoned him for that very same conduct.
Those sixty thousand youths also imitated the conduct of Asamañjas.
Then, when the world had been cast away from the true path of sacrifice and other duties by the oceans that followed the improper conduct [of their progenitor], the gods,
having bowed down to Kapila— who was a portion of the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama, who consisted of all knowledge, and who was untouched by any defects— spoke for the sake of that purpose.
"O Blessed One, these sons of Sagara are following the conduct of Asamañja;

how will the world fare with them following in such a manner? And for the sake of protecting the distressed world, the Blessed One has assumed a body here. Having heard this, the Blessed One said, "In just a few days, these shall perish."
In the meantime, Sagara commenced a horse sacrifice; however, someone stole his horse—which was being supervised by his sons—and entered a subterranean cavity in the earth.

Then he appointed his sons to search for the horse; thereupon those sons, following the tracks of the horse's hooves, each one dug into the surface of the earth for a league after league with great persistence.
And in the netherworld (pātāla), those daughters of the lords of the earth beheld that horse wandering about.

And seeing the venerable Kapila Rishi standing not far away—like the sun in the cloudless autumn season incessantly illuminating the zenith, the nadir, and all directions with its splendors—they cried out, "This evil-souled one, who harms us, who obstructs the sacrifice, and who has stolen the horse, let him be slain! Let him be slain! Thereupon, they were looked upon by that Blessed One with eyes turned slightly, and being consumed by a fire arising from his own body, they perished.

Sagara, having learned that his entire army of sons who were following the horse had been consumed by the fiery splendor of the supreme rishi Kapila, urged Aṃśumat, the son of Asamañjas, to bring back the horse.

Having approached Kapila by the path dug by the sons of Sagara, he praised him with such devotion and humility that the Blessed One said to him: "Go, deliver this horse to your grandfather; choose a boon, and your son and grandson shall bring the Gaṅgā from heaven."
Then Aṃśumān replied, "May the Blessed One grant us a boon that will cause our ancestors—who have been struck by the Brahmanical staff and are thus unfit for heaven—to attain the celestial realm.
The Blessed One said to him, "O grandson, this has already been stated by me: 'Your descendant shall bring Gaṅgā from the third heaven to the earth.
When their bones and ashes are touched by her waters, they shall ascend to heaven."
For such is the majesty of that water which has issued forth from the big toe of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.

It was said that not only is the body beneficial when used intentionally for purposes such as bathing and so forth, but even when abandoned by one whose life has departed— consisting of bones, skin, sinews, hair, and the like,
and fallen upon the earth— it immediately leads the embodied being to heaven; having paid homage to the Blessed One and taken the horse, he returned to the sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Sagara, having recovered the horse, completed that sacrifice.
And out of affection for his son, he regarded the ocean as his own son.
Dilīpa was the son of that Aṃśumat.
From Dilīpa came Bhagīratha, who, having brought the Gaṅgā here from heaven, gave her the name Bhāgīrathī.
From Bhagīratha, Nābhāga was heard; from him, Ambarīṣa; from him, Sindhudvīpa;
from Sindhudvīpa, Ayutāyus; and his son was Ṛtuparṇa, who was an associate of Nala and knew the secret of dice.
R̥tuparṇa’s son was Sarvakāma; his son was Sudāsa; from Sudāsa came Saudāsa, named Mitrasaha.
And he, having gone hunting in the forest, saw two tigers.
And by those two, that forest was cleared of wild animals; yet he struck one of them with an arrow.
And as he was dying, he became a Rākṣasa of most terrifying appearance and an exceedingly hideous countenance.
The second one also, having said, "I shall perform a counter-action against you," vanished from sight.
As time passed, that Saudāsa performed a sacrifice.

When the sacrifice was completed and the preceptor Vasiṣṭha had departed, that Rākṣasa assumed the form of Vasiṣṭha and said, "At the conclusion of the sacrifice, my meal of human flesh must be provided; let it be prepared, and I shall return here in a moment," and having spoken thus, he went out.
Furthermore, having assumed the guise of a cook and prepared human flesh by the king's command, he presented it to the king.
He too, taking the meat placed in a golden vessel, waited for Vasiṣṭha’s arrival,
and when Vasiṣṭha had come, he presented it to him.
He too thought, "Alas, what wickedness is this king's, that he gives us this meat! What kind of substance is this? and became absorbed in meditation.
He saw that it was human flesh;
then, his mind clouded by anger, he cast a curse upon the king.

"Since you give this to me even though you know it is unfit for ascetics like us, your own mind will surely become greedy for it. Immediately after that, when the Blessed One said, "I have been addressed by him," the sage remained in meditative absorption, reflecting, "What was it that I said? ||| ViP_4,4.35-36 ||| Please provide the text you would like me to translate. Having understood the matter through his meditative concentration, he showed him favor, saying:
"This food of yours shall last for twelve years, but it will not be permanent."

But even he, having raised his joined palms of water and being intent on pronouncing a sage’s curse, was pacified by his own wife Madayantī, who said, "O Blessed One, our teacher does not deserve to be cursed; he is the family deity. For the sake of protecting the crops and the rain-clouds, he did not cast that water of the curse upon the earth nor into the sky, but instead sprinkled it upon his own feet.
By that water infused with his wrath, the shadows of his feet were burnt and became mottled;
consequently, he acquired the name Kalmāṣapāda.
And due to Vasiṣṭha’s curse, having assumed the nature of a Rākṣasa at the sixth mealtime, he wandered through the forest and devoured many human beings.
Once, however, he saw a certain sage united with his wife during her fertile period;
and as the couple fled in terror upon beholding that most terrifying Rākṣasa, he seized the Brāhmaṇa.

Then that Brahmin woman entreated him many times: "Be gracious, O Great King! You are the ornament of the Ikṣvāku lineage, Mitrasaha, not a Rākṣasa. Knowing the happiness that is the duty of a wife, you ought not to devour my husband while I have yet to fulfill my purpose. As she was thus lamenting in many ways, [the king spoke].
Like a tiger devouring a beast, he devoured that Brāhmaṇa.

Then the Brahmin woman, filled with extreme rage, cursed that king, saying: "Since you have devoured this husband of mine while I was still unsated, therefore you too shall meet your end while engaged in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. She then entered the fire.
Then, at the end of twelve years, once he was released from the curse and had developed a longing for women, Madayantī reminded him [of his past].
Thereafter, he renounced the enjoyment of women.

And Vasiṣṭha, being requested by the childless king for the sake of a son, performed the impregnation ceremony upon Madayantī. When that embryo did not manifest for seven years, the queen then struck it with a stone.
A son was born to him, and his name was Aśmaka alone.

Aśmaka had a son named Mūlaka, who, when this earth was being cleared of the Kṣatriya caste, was surrounded and protected by naked women; therefore, they call him Nārīkavaca (the one whose armor is women).

From Mūlaka came Daśaratha; from him, Ilivila; and from him, Viśvasaha. From him came Khaṭvāṅga, whose son was Dilīpa. This Dilīpa, having been requested by the gods in the battle between the gods and the asuras, slew the asuras.
And when he had performed his service for the gods in heaven, he was urged by them to choose a boon, whereupon he spoke:
"If a boon must certainly be accepted, then let my lifespan be told.

Immediately thereafter, they said, "Your lifespan is but the measure of a single muhūrta. Having been told this, he then descended to the world of mortals by means of a celestial chariot moving with unimpeded speed and possessed of the quality of lightness, and said this:
"Just as I have no one dearer to me than myself, even so [I hold] nothing dearer than the Brahmins."
Nor have I ever transgressed my own duty;
nor has my vision ever wavered from the Imperishable Lord, even toward any god, human, animal, tree, or other being.

Thus, with unswerving resolve, I shall reach that very Lord, the Blessed One remembered by the sages, the Teacher of all gods, whose form is indefinable and whose essence is pure existence. [I offer myself] to the Blessed One...
He united himself with the Supreme Self known as Vāsudeva,
and in that very place he attained dissolution.
In this regard, a verse sung by the Seven Sages in ancient times is also heard:
"There shall be no one else on earth equal to Khaṭvāṅga."
Having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment,
he indeed secured the three worlds through his intellect and his generosity.
From Khaṭvāṅga was born a son named Dīrghabāhu;
from him came Raghu, and from him, Aja.

From Aja came Daśaratha, and into the womb of Daśaratha, the Blessed One whose navel is a lotus (Viṣṇu), for the sake of the world's preservation, entered as his own portion, assuming the form of four sons: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna.
Rāma, too, while still a mere boy, went to protect Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice and slew Tāṭakā.
And at the sacrifice, he cast Mārīca far away, struck by the flight of his arrow, and brought Subāhu and the others to their destruction;
by a mere glance, he rendered Ahalyā free from sin;
and in the house of Janaka, he broke the bow of Maheśvara without any effort.
And he obtained Sītā, the daughter of King Janaka, who was not born from a womb and whose bride-price was valor.
He rendered Paraśurāma—who had caused the destruction of all the kṣatriyas and had become a comet to the entire Haihaya clan—devoid of the arrogance born of his prowess and strength.
And at his father's word, disregarding all desire for the kingdom, he entered the forest accompanied by his brother and his wife.
He slew Virādha, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and others, as well as Kabandha and Vālin.

Having bound the ocean and brought about the destruction of the entire race of Rākṣasas, he brought Sītā— the daughter of King Janaka, who had been abducted by the Ten-faced One— to Ayodhyā; she was freed from the stain [of suspicion] by his slaying of that demon, purified by her entry into the fire, and praised by all the lords of the gods.
Praised by the foremost sages, such as Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and Agastya, with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas;

and amidst all the kings, the son of Daśaratha was duly consecrated for the protection of the entire world, accompanied by the sounds of dance, song, instrumental music, and all auspicious instruments of the world— such as the lute, flute, mṛdaṅga, bherī, paṭaha, conch, kāhala, gomukha, and others, which produced beautiful melodies.
The lord of Kosala, the ornament of the Raghu dynasty, the beloved of Jānakī and his three brothers, sat upon the throne and ruled the kingdom for twelve thousand years.
Bharata also slew three crores of fierce Gandharvas who were intent on seizing the realm of the Gandharvas.
By Śatrughna, too, the lord of the Rākṣasas named Lavaṇa—the son of Madhu, possessed of exceeding strength and prowess—was slain, and Madhurā was established as his capital.

Thus, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna—whose stability for this entire world had been established by those of incomparable strength and prowess who utterly destroy the most wicked—ascended once again to heaven;
and those inhabitants of the city and countryside of Kosala who were devoted to those portions of the Blessed One, with their minds fixed on them, attained residence in the same world as them.

Rāma’s sons were Kuśa and Lava; Lakṣmaṇa’s were Aṅgada and Candraketu; Bharata’s were Takṣa and Puṣkara; Śatrughna’s were Subāhu and Śūrasena. Kuśa’s son was Atithi, and Atithi’s son was Niṣadha. Niṣadha’s son was Nala, his son was Nabha, and Nabha’s son was Puṇḍarīka.

His son was Kṣemadhanvan; his son was Devānīka; his son was Ahīnagu; from him came Ruru; his son was Pāriyātra; from Pāriyātra came Dala; from Dala came Śala; his son was Uktha; from Uktha came Vajranābha; from him came Śaṅkhanābha;
from him came Vyutthitāśva; and from him, Viśvasaha was born.
From him, Hiraṇyanābha, the great lord of yogins and disciple of Jaimini, Yājñavalkya obtained yoga.
The son of Hiraṇyanābha was Puṣya; from him came Dhruvasandhi, from him Sudarśana, and from him Agnivarṇa. From him came Śīghraga, whose son was Maru.
This Maru, having resorted to yoga, remains even today dwelling in the village of Kalāpa;
he will be the one who initiates the Kṣatra lineage of the Solar dynasty in a future age.
Prasuśruta was his son; his son was Susaṃdhi; from him came Amarṣa; his son was Mahasvān;
from him came Viśrutavat; and from him came Bṛhadbala, who was brought to his destruction in the Bhārata war by Abhimanyu, the son of Arjuna.
These kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty have been described by me according to their importance;
hearing of their deeds, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Parāśara said:
That son of Ikṣvāku named Nimi commenced a sacrificial session (*sattra*) lasting for a thousand years, and he chose Vasiṣṭha as his officiating priest (*hotṛ*).

Vasiṣṭha said to him, "I was chosen first by Indra for the sake of a sacrifice lasting five hundred years; after he has departed, I shall become your officiating priest as well. When this was said, the lord of the earth said nothing at all.
Vasiṣṭha also performed a sacrifice for the Lord of the Immortals, as he had been requested by him.
He too, at that very time, had the sacrifice performed by others such as Gautama and the rest.
When the sacrifice of the Lord of the Immortals was completed, Vasiṣṭha arrived in haste, thinking, "I shall perform the ritual for Nimi.
Seeing that Gautama was the performer of that ritual there, he then said to that sleeping king: "Without having refused me for this..."
"Because he has entrusted another task to Gautama, therefore he shall become 'Videha' (the bodiless one)," thus he pronounced a curse.
And when the king awoke, he also said:

"Since that wicked preceptor has cast a curse upon me while I was sleeping, without even addressing me and out of sheer ignorance, therefore his body too shall fall. Having thus uttered this counter-curse, he cast off his body.
And because of that curse, the splendor of Mitra and Varuṇa entered the splendor of Vasiṣṭha;
from the presence of those two, whose seed had fallen upon seeing Urvaśī, Vasiṣṭha obtained another body.

Even Nimi’s body, though being treated with highly enchanting oils, perfumes, and other substances, did not suffer any defect such as putrefaction; it remained as if he had just died. When the sacrifice was completed, the priests said to the gods who had arrived to receive their shares, "Let a boon be granted to the patron of the sacrifice. Being thus entreated by the gods, that Nimi spoke: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.5.7: "Let me have the power to enter another body at will, and let my kingdom be restored to its former state. The gods granted him these two boons. Then, having entered the body of King Daṇḍaka, Nimi performed a great sacrifice. Having completed that sacrifice, he returned to his own body and ascended to heaven. There he saw the gods seated on their thrones, and he asked them, "Why have you all come here? They replied, "We have come for the sake of your body. He said, "I am not dead; I have merely entered another body. I shall return to this body when I have finished my sacrifice. The gods said, "This body of yours has already been consumed by the fire of the sacrificial altar. He said, "If this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of the altar, then let the merit of this sacrifice go to whoever is present here. The gods said, "It is so. Then, having entered the body of King Daṇḍaka, Nimi performed a great sacrifice. Having completed that sacrifice, he returned to his own body and ascended to heaven. There he saw the gods seated on their thrones, and he asked them, "Why have you all come here? They replied, "We have come for the sake of your body. He said, "I am not dead; I have merely entered another body. I shall return to this body when I have finished my sacrifice. The gods said, "This body of yours has already been consumed by the fire of the sacrificial altar. He said, "If this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of the altar, then let the merit of this sacrifice go to whoever is present here. The gods said, "It is so. Then, having entered the body of King Daṇḍaka, Nimi performed a great sacrifice. Having completed that sacrifice, he returned to his own body and ascended to heaven. There he saw the gods seated on their thrones, and he asked them, "Why have you all come here? They replied, "We have come for the sake of your body. He said, "I am not dead; I have merely entered another body. I shall return to this body when I have finished my sacrifice. The gods said, "This body of yours has already been consumed by the fire of the sacrificial altar. He said, "If this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of the altar, then let the merit of this sacrifice go to whoever is present here. The gods said, "It is so. Then, having entered the body of King Daṇḍaka, Nimi performed a great sacrifice. Having completed that sacrifice, he returned to his own body and ascended to heaven. There he saw the gods seated on their thrones, and he asked them, "Why have you all come here? They replied, "We have come for the sake of your body. He said, "I am not dead; I have merely entered another body. I shall return to this body when I have finished my sacrifice. The gods said, "This body of yours has already been consumed by the fire of the sacrificial altar. He said, "If this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of the altar, then let the merit of this sacrifice go to whoever is present here. The gods said, "It is so. Then, having entered the body of King Daṇḍaka, Nimi performed a great sacrifice. Having completed that sacrifice, he returned to his own body and ascended to heaven. There he saw the gods seated on their thrones, and he asked them, "Why have you all come here? They replied, "We have come for the sake of your body. He said, "I am not dead; I have merely entered another body. I shall return to this body when I have finished my sacrifice. The gods said, "This body of yours has already been consumed by the fire of the sacrificial altar. He said, "If this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of the altar, then let the merit of this sacrifice go to whoever is present here. The gods said, "It is so. Then, having entered the body of King Daṇḍaka, Nimi performed a
"The Blessed Ones are the destroyers of the entire mass of suffering in saṃsāra; indeed, there is no other suffering in this world like that which occurs upon the separation of the body and the self.

Therefore, I desire to dwell within the eyes of all people, and not to undergo the taking up of a body again. When the gods had spoken thus, he was introduced into the eyes of all living beings. Thereupon, the beings performed the opening and closing of their eyes.
Fearing that the realm would be without a king, those sages churned the body of that childless monarch in the forest.
And there a prince was born, and he received the name Janaka from his birth.
His father was Videha, from whom he was called Vaideha; from Mathana, Mithi was born.
His son was Udāvasu;
from Udāvasu came Nandivardhana; from him, Suketu; from him, Devarāta; and from him, Bṛhaduktha. His [son]—

And from Mahāvīrya was born Satyadhṛti; from him was born Dhṛti; and from him Dhṛṣṭaketu was born. From Dhṛṣṭaketu came Haryaśva; his son was Maru; from Maru came Pratibandhaka; from him Kṛtaratha; from him Kṛti; his son was Vibudha; from him also came Mahādhṛti; and from him Kṛtirāta; and from him Mahāromā.
His son was Suvarṇaroman; his son was Hrasvaroman; from him was born Sīradhvaja.
While Sīradhvaja was plowing the sacrificial ground for the sake of obtaining a son, a daughter named Sītā was produced from the furrow.
Sīradhvaja’s brother was named Kuśadhvaja, the lord of Sāṃkāśya.
Sīradhvaja’s offspring was Bhānumat; from Bhānumat came Śatadyumna; his son was Śuci, and from him was born a son named Ūrjavaha.

His son was Śatadhvaja; from him came Kuṇi; from Kuṇi came Añjana; his son was Ṛtujit; from him came Ariṣṭanemi; from him Śrutāyus; from Śrutāyus Supārva; from him Saṃjaya; from him Kṣemāri; from him Anenas;
from him Mīnaratha; his son was Satyaratha; his son was Sātyarathi; from Sātyarathi came Upagu; and from him came Śāśvata.

From him came Sudhanvan; from him, Subhāṣa; from him, Suśruta; from him, Jaya; Jaya’s son was Vijaya; his [son] was one named Ṛta, who was a learned physician (suśruta); from that Suśruta came Jaya; his son was Vijaya;
Vijaya’s son was Ṛta; from Ṛta came Sunaya; from him, Vītahavya; from him, Dhṛti; from Dhṛti, Bahulāśva; his son was Kṛti. In Kṛti this lineage of Janaka comes to an end.
Thus, these Maithilas shall for the most part be kings who take refuge in the knowledge of the Self.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, you have narrated to me the lineage of Sūrya."
I wish to hear about all the kings in the lineage of Soma.
O Brahmin, you whose countenance is gracious through your favor, it behoves you to relate to me that which is proclaimed among those of steadfast fame, whose lineage persists even today.
Parāśara said:
Listen, O tiger among sages, to the lineage of Soma, whose splendor is far-renowned,
in which there arose kings celebrated in succession.

For this lineage has been adorned by kings such as Nahuṣa, Yayāti, and Kārtavīryārjuna, who were endowed with supreme virtues and possessed of exceeding strength, prowess, splendor, virtue, and noble conduct;
I shall relate it—let it be heard.
Atri was the son of Brahmā—the lotus-born one who emerged from the navel-lotus of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the entire world; and Soma was the son of Atri.
And the Blessed One, whose origin is the lotus, consecrated him in the sovereignty over all medicinal herbs, birds, and constellations.
And he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice;
through its power and because of his presiding over an exceedingly exalted sovereignty, intoxication took possession of him.
And out of the arrogance of his pride, he abducted Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of all the gods.
Although urged many times by the venerable Brahmā at the instigation of Bṛhaspati, and entreated by all the celestial sages, he did not release her.
And because of his hatred for Bṛhaspati, Uśanas became his rear-guard ally.
Having acquired knowledge from Aṅgiras, the blessed Rudra rendered assistance to Bṛhaspati.
Where Uśanas was, there all the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, headed by Jambha and Kumbha, made a great effort;
and Śakra, accompanied by the entire army of the gods, took his stand against Bṛhaspati.
Thus, between those two, there occurred an exceedingly fierce battle known as the Tāraka-war, caused by Tārā;
then the gods, led by Rudra, discharged all their weapons upon the Asuras, and the Dānavas did likewise against the gods.
And thus the entire world, its hearts agitated by the agitation caused by the battle between the gods and the asuras, went to Brahmā for refuge.
Then the Blessed One, having restrained both Uśanas and Śaṅkara, as well as the Asuras and the Devas, gave Tārā back to Bṛhaspati.
And seeing that she was pregnant, Bṛhaspati said:
"This son of another must not be kept by you in my field; cast him out, enough of this excessive audacity! thus he spoke.
And she, being exceedingly devoted to her husband, having been thus addressed by him, released that embryo into a clump of reeds at her husband's word.
And as soon as it was cast forth, by its exceeding brilliance, it overwhelmed the splendors of the gods.
Seeing both Bṛhaspati and Indu looking at that boy with longing due to his extreme beauty, the gods, their suspicions aroused, questioned Tārā.
