"Tell us the truth, O most beautiful one: whose son is this? Is he the son of Soma or of Bṛhaspati?
Though addressed in this way, Tārā said nothing out of shame.
When she did not disclose the matter to the gods even after being questioned many times, the prince, intent on cursing her, spoke:

"O wicked girl, why do you not tell my father? This very day, I shall inflict such punishment upon you, who are possessed of false modesty, that no other woman shall ever again speak with such excessive slowness. Then the Blessed One, the Grandfather, restrained the prince and himself questioned Tārā.
"Tell me, child, whose son is this—is he the son of Soma or of Bṛhaspati? When she was thus addressed, she replied, "Of Soma," her speech rendered sluggish by shame.

Then the Blessed Lord, the Lord of the Stars (the Moon), his pure cheeks radiant with a throbbing smile, embraced the youth and said, "Excellent, excellent, my son! You are wise," and thus he gave him the name Budha.
It has already been told how he begot upon Ilā a son named Purūravas.

Purūravas, however, was exceedingly generous, a great sacrificer, and possessed of supreme splendor; while he was resolved that he must dwell in the world of men due to a curse from Mitra and Varuṇa, saying, "I must live in the human realm," Urvaśī beheld him as one who was truthful and of surpassing beauty.
And as soon as he was seen, [the people] abandoned their pride, cast aside all desire for heaven, and with their minds fixed solely upon him, waited upon him alone.

And he too, beholding her—whose qualities of loveliness, delicacy, grace, gait, charm, laughter, and other attributes surpassed those of all women in the world—became one whose mental state was entirely dependent upon her.
Both of them became focused on that alone, with no other gaze, having abandoned all other purposes.
But the king, out of boldness, said to her:
"O fair-browed one, I am filled with intense desire for you;
be gracious and return my love. Thus addressed, Urvaśī spoke, her speech broken by bashfulness.
"Let it be so, provided that you fulfill my agreement."
"Tell me your agreement," she was asked, and she replied once more:
"The two gerbils near my bed, who have become like sons to me, must not be removed;
and you must not be seen by me naked."
"And my food shall consist of nothing but ghee," the lord of the earth replied, "it shall be exactly so.

And together with her, the ruler of the world spent sixty-one years in Alakā, delighting in the Caitraratha and other groves, and in lakes filled with clusters of stainless lotuses; his joy increased day by day, and Urvaśī, her passion growing daily through that enjoyment, felt no longing even for residence in the realm of the immortals.
Without the celestial nymph Urvaśī, the world of the gods was no longer particularly delightful to the Apsarases, Siddhas, and Gandharvas.
Then, at night, Viśvāvasu, who was conversant with their agreement and accompanied by a host of Gandharvas, stole a single ram from the vicinity of Urvaśī and Purūravas as they lay in bed.

As he was being carried through the sky, Urvaśī heard his voice and said, "Someone is carrying away my son while I am left protectorless; to whom shall I go for refuge? Hearing this, the king did not go, thinking, "The queen will see me naked.
Then the Gandharvas departed, taking another ram as well.
Hearing the sound of that [jewel] being carried away through the sky, she again cried out in distress: "I am once more without a protector, without a husband, and dependent on a wicked man!"
The king also, out of indignation, thinking "this is darkness," took up his sword and rushed forward, crying out, "Wicked one! Wicked one! You are slain!"
At that moment, the Gandharvas produced an exceedingly brilliant flash of lightning;
by its light, Urvaśī saw that the king was without clothing, and her agreement having been violated, she departed from that very instant.
Having abandoned those two rams, the Gandharvas departed for the world of the gods.
And the king, having taken those two rams, returned to his own bed with a joyful mind, but he did not see Urvaśī.
Not seeing her and being naked, he wandered about like one mad.

In Kurukṣetra, at a lotus lake, he beheld Urvaśī together with four other apsarases; thereupon, appearing mad, he spoke many kinds of well-spoken words: "O wife! Stay! O terrible mind, stay! O speech, stay! etc.
Urvaśī said:

"O Great King, enough of this undiscriminating behavior! I am pregnant; you must come here at the end of the year, for a son shall be born to you, and I shall dwell with you for one night. Having been told this, he returned to his own city greatly delighted.
He departed.

And among those *apsarases*, Urvaśī said, "This is that preeminent man with whom I lived for so long, my mind drawn by passion. When she had spoken thus, the *apsarases* said to her, "Excellent, excellent! His form is wonderful; we too would desire to sport with him at all times."
Thus, when the year was complete, the king came there,
and Urvaśī then gave the long-lived Kumāra to him.
Having stayed with that king for one night, she conceived a child for the sake of giving birth to five sons.
And he said to that king, "Out of affection for us, all the Gandharvas have become granters of boons to the great king; let a boon be chosen."
The king said:

"Having conquered all enemies, with the power of my senses unimpaired, possessing kinsmen and immeasurable strength and treasure, there is nothing else unattainable for us except co-residence in the same world as Urvaśī. Therefore, I desire to spend my time together with this Urvaśī."
When this was said, the Gandharvas gave a vessel of fire to the king.

They said to him, "Having become one who follows the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), divide this fire into three parts and perform the sacrifice properly, aiming for the desire of attaining the same world as Urvaśī; then you will certainly obtain what you long for. Having been told this, he took that fire-vessel and departed.
In the middle of the forest, he thought, "Alas! What great folly is mine, that I have brought the fire-vessel and not Urvaśī!"
Then, he abandoned that fire-vessel right there in the forest and returned to his own city.
At the time when midnight had passed, he woke up and thought:
"For the sake of attaining union with Urvaśī in the same world, the Gandharvas gave me a fire-vessel, and that was abandoned by me in the forest.
Therefore, I shall go there to retrieve it. Having risen, he went there as well, but he did not see the fire-vessel.
Seeing an *aśvattha* tree with a *śamī* tree at its core in the place where the fire-vessel had been, he thought:
"I deposited the vessel here, and it has become this *aśvattha* tree with a *śamī* core.

Therefore, taking this very thing as the form of the fire, I shall go to my own city, fashion it into an *araṇi*, and perform the worship of the fire produced from it. Thinking thus, he went to his own city and fashioned the *araṇi*.
Measuring that [fire-pit] with his fingers while reciting the Gāyatrī,
the fire-wood (araṇi) became exactly as many finger-breadths in length as there were syllables in the verse he was reciting.
Having churned the fire there, he offered oblations into the three sacred fires in accordance with the Vedic injunctions, aiming for the fruit of attaining the same world as Urvaśī.
Having performed various kinds of sacrifices according to that very ritual of the fire, he attained the worlds of the Gandharvas and did not suffer separation from Urvaśī.
"In the beginning there was but one fire; however, in this Manvantara of Aila, it has been set forth in a threefold manner."
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Parāśara said:
To him also were born six sons known as Āyus, Dhīmān, Amāvasu, Viśvāvasu, Śatāyus, and Śrutāyus.
To Amāvasu was born a son named Bhīma.
Bhīma’s son was Kāñcana; from Kāñcana came Suhotra, and his son was Jahnu.

It was he who, seeing the entire sacrificial enclosure flooded by the waters of the Gaṅgā, his eyes bloodshot with rage, fixed the Blessed Lord of Sacrifice within himself through supreme meditative concentration and drank up the entire Gaṅgā.
Then the celestial sages propitiated him and brought Gaṅgā to be his daughter.
And Jahnu had a son named Sumantu;
his son was Ajaka, from whom came Balākāśva, and from him Kuśa. Kuśa had four sons: Kuśāmba, Kuśanābha, Mūrtarayas, and Āvasu.
Among them, Kuśāmba performed austerities, thinking, "May I have a son equal to Śakra.
Observing him engaged in such fierce penance, Indra thought, "Let there be no one else of power equal to us," and so he himself became his son.
He became the Kauśika named Gādhi;
and Gādhi begot a daughter, Satyavatī,
whom Ṛcīka, a descendant of Bhṛgu, chose as his wife.

Gādhi, however, being unwilling to give her to a Brahmin who was excessively irascible and very old, demanded as the bride-price for the maiden a thousand horses, each with one ear black, possessing the luster of the moon and the speed of the wind.
That sage, having obtained from Varuṇa a thousand such horses born at Aśvatīrtha, gave them [to Ṛcīka].
Then Ṛcīka married that maiden;
and for the sake of offspring, Ṛcīka prepared a sacrificial pap (caru) for her.
And being propitiated by him, he prepared another *caru* for the sake of producing a son of the best of the Kṣatriyas from that very woman alone.
"This is the sacrificial pap; this other one must be consumed by you in its entirety," he said, and then departed for the forest.
And at the time of the consultation, her mother Satyavatī said to her:
"Daughter, everyone desires their own son to possess extraordinary virtues; one does not generally pay excessive regard for the qualities of one's daughter's brothers."
Therefore, you ought to give me your sacrificial oblation and consume my own oblation yourself.
"Indeed, my son must protect the entire circle of the earth; what indeed is the wealth of strength and valor for a Brahmin? Having said this, she gave her own sacrificial oblation to her mother.
Then, having returned even from the forest, the seer beheld Satyavatī.
And he said to her: "O most wicked woman, what is this improper act you have committed?
Your body appears exceedingly fierce;
surely you have consumed the sacrificial oblation intended for your own mother—this was not right."
For I have placed the entirety of the excellence of heroism, valor, and strength into this *caru*;
whereas in yours, I have placed the entire excellence of a Brahmin, such as peace, knowledge, and forbearance.
Since you are acting in this contrary manner, your son shall possess the conduct of a Kṣatriya, being intent on wielding most terrible weapons and on killing.
Upon hearing that his conduct was Brahmanical and that he delighted in tranquility, she immediately grasped his feet.
Having prostrated before him, he said:
"O Blessed One, this was performed by me out of ignorance;
please grant me your grace."
"Let not such a son be born;
rather, let there be a grandson of this kind," he said; and the sage replied, "So be it."
Immediately thereafter, she gave birth to Jamadagni;
her mother gave birth to Viśvāmitra;
and Satyavatī became the river named Kauśikī.
Jamadagni married Reṇukā, the daughter of Reṇu who was born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
Upon her, Jamadagni begot Paraśurāma, known as the destroyer of the entire warrior class (kṣatra), who was a portion of the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of all the worlds.
Śunaḥśepa, however, was indeed a Bhārgava who had been given by the gods to Viśvāmitra;
consequently, he became known by the name Devarāta.
Furthermore, there were other sons of Viśvāmitra named Madhucchandas, Jaya, Kṛtadeva, Aṣṭaka, Kakṣepa, and Hārīta.
And among them, O Kauśika, many lineages became intermarried with those of other sages.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The eldest son of Purūravas, named Āyu, married the daughter of Rāhu.
Upon her he begot five sons:
Nahuṣa, Kṣatravṛddha, Raṃbha, Raji, and likewise Anenā was the fifth son.
From Kṣatravṛddha, Suhotra was born as a son.
Kāśya, Leśa, and Gṛtsamada were his three sons;
of Gṛtsamada was born Śaunaka, who was the promulgator of the fourfold social order.
From Kāśya was born Dīrghatamas, the king of Kāśī;

from Dīrghatamas was born Dhanvantari. For he was one who had accomplished his tasks and possessed complete knowledge regarding all forms of existence; indeed, a boon was granted to him by the Blessed Nārāyaṇa in a past birth.
"You shall descend into the lineage of the King of Kāśī and properly divide the Ayurveda into eight parts; you shall also be a partaker in the sacrificial offerings," he was thus addressed.
The son of that Dhanvantari was Ketumān; from Ketumān came Bhīmaratha; his son was Divodāsa, and from him came Pratardana.
Because he conquered all his enemies following the destruction of the lineage of Bhadraśreṇya, he became known as Śatrujit (the Conqueror of Enemies).
And because his joyful father addressed him as "Vatsa, Vatsa," he thereafter became known as Vatsa.
Through his devotion to truth, he obtained the name Ṛtadhvaja.
Furthermore, he received a horse named Kuvalaya; thus he became celebrated throughout this earth as Kuvalayāśva.
And that Vatsa had a son named Alarka,
about whom this verse is sung even today:
"For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years..."
No other youth besides Alarka enjoyed the earth.
That Alarka also had a son named Sannati;
from him came Sunītha, from him Suketu, from him Dharmaketu,
from him Satyaketu, from him Vibhu, his son was Suvibhu, from him Sukumāra, and his son was Dṛṣṭaketu.
From him came Vainahotra, from him Bharga, from Bharga came Bhārgabhūmi,
and from him arose the manifestation of the four castes; these are declared to be the Kāśa kings.
Now, let the lineage of Raji be heard.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
§ Parāśara said:
Raja had five hundred sons, whose essence was incomparable valor.
At the commencement of the battle between the gods and the asuras, both the gods and the asuras, desiring to slay one another, questioned Brahmā.
"O Blessed One, in this dispute between us, which side will be the victor?"
Then the Blessed One said, "For whose sake will Raji fight, having taken up his weapons?

Thereupon, the Daityas approached Raji and requested him to provide them with his assistance; he replied, "I shall fight for your sake, provided that through my victory over the immortals I shall become your Indra. Having heard this, [they agreed].

Addressed by them, he said, "We shall not speak one way and act another; our Indra is Prahlāda, and this endeavor is for his sake. When the Asuras had departed after saying this, the gods likewise addressed that lord of the earth in the same manner.
And when he had spoken accordingly, the gods requested, "You shall become Indra."
Raji, aided by the divine army, destroyed that entire host of Asuras with numerous great weapons.
And Indra, having conquered the faction of his enemies, pressed the pair of Your dust-covered feet against his own head and said:
"By granting protection from fear, You have become the supreme father of all the worlds; I am Your son, the lord of the three realms."

And that king, laughing, said: "Let it be so; for even from the side of an enemy, a prostration containing various kinds of flattering words is not to be disregarded. Having said this, he went to his own city.
Even Śatakratu attained the status of Indra.
When Raji had ascended to heaven, the sons of Raji, urged by the sage Nārada, requested the kingdom from Śatakratu according to custom, as he was both their father’s son and their own son.
And when he did not grant it, those exceedingly powerful ones defeated Indra himself and assumed the sovereignty of Indra.
Then, after a long period of time had passed, Śatakratu, having been deprived of his share of the sacrifices of the three worlds, saw Bṛhaspati in private and said:
When told, "You ought to give me even a piece of the sacrificial cake the size of a jujube fruit for my nourishment," Bṛhaspati replied:
"If you had urged me to this earlier, what would I not have done for your sake?
In just a few days, I shall lead you to your own position. Having said this, he performed daily oblations intended to bewilder their intellects and to increase the splendor of Śakra.
And they too, being overcome by that delusion of intellect, became haters of Brahman, abandoners of dharma, and turned their backs on the declarations of the Vedas.
Then Indra struck down those who had strayed from righteous conduct;
his splendor nourished by his domestic priest, he ascended to the third heaven.
Having heard this account of Indra’s fall from his own station and his subsequent ascent, a person does not suffer the loss of their own position nor the consequences of wickedness.
Rambha, however, was childless;
Pratikṣatra was the son of Kṣatravṛddha.

His son was Saṃjaya; his son was Jaya; from him was born Vijaya; and from him was born Kṛta. His son was Harṣavardhana; the son of Harṣavardhana was Sahadeva; from him came Adīna; his son was Jayatsena; and from him was born Saṃkṛti, whose son was Kṣatradharmā. These were the descendants of Kṣatravṛddha; now I shall proclaim the lineage of Nahuṣa.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Parāśara said:
Nahuṣa had six sons named Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Viyāti, and Kṛti; they were all possessed of great strength and prowess.
Yati, however, did not desire the kingdom;
Yayāti, on the other hand, became the ruler of the earth.
He married Uśanas’s daughter Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.

Regarding this, there is a genealogical verse: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.10.3: "Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, having obtained the two daughters of Śukra—Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā—ruled the earth for many thousands of years."
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu,
while Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
And due to the curse of a poet, Yayāti attained old age prematurely.
And because of the words of the pure Śukra, he spoke to his eldest son Yadu in order to transfer his own old age upon him.

"Due to the curse of your maternal grandfather, this premature old age has come upon me. By his very grace, I shall transfer it to you for one thousand years; I am not yet satiated with sense-objects and wish to enjoy them through your youth. You must not refuse me. Thus addressed, he did not wish to take that old age.
And his father also cursed him, saying:
"Your offspring shall not be worthy of the kingdom."
Thereafter, the lord of the earth requested Durvasu, Druhyu, and Anu to accept his old age in exchange for giving them his own youth;
but when he was rejected by each of them one by one, he cursed them.
Then she spoke in the same manner to Pūru, the youngest son of Śarmiṣṭhā.

He, whose mind was exceedingly devoted, bowed to his father and said with great respect, "This is a great favor for us," and having spoken thus nobly, he accepted the old age and gave his own youth to his father.
Having attained his youth, he too enjoyed the objects of the senses according to his desire, according to the season, and according to his energy, without violating dharma;
and he performed the protection of his subjects correctly.
Having experienced enjoyment with both Viśvācī and Devayānī, he became daily intent on that thought: "I shall reach the end of my desires."
And day by day, through his enjoyment of them, he considered those desires to be exceedingly delightful.
And then he sang this song:
"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more."
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth are not enough for even one person; therefore, one should abandon craving.
When a man harbors no evil intent toward any living being,
then, for that person of equal vision, all directions are filled with happiness.
The wise man should utterly abandon that craving which is so difficult for the foolish to give up, and which does not age even as one ages; by doing so, he is filled with happiness.
The hair of an aging man decays; the teeth of an aging man decay.
But the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay, even as one ages.
For a full thousand years my mind has been attached to sense-objects;
nevertheless, my thirst for these very things arises day after day.
Therefore, having abandoned this [world] and fixed my mind upon Brahman,
I shall become free from dualities and free from the sense of "mine," and wander with the deer.
Parāśara said: Having taken the old age from Pūru and given him his youth,
and having consecrated Pūru upon the throne, he departed for the forest to practice asceticism.
Then he assigned Turvasu to the south-eastern direction,
Druhyu to the west, and Yadu to the south.
Having likewise subdued the sovereign kings of the north,
he consecrated Pūru as the lord of the entire earth and retired to the forest.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the lineage of Yadu, the first son of Yayāti.

Therein, the Lord Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, descended by means of an inconceivable portion of his majesty— [a portion] which is eternally praised for the sake of attaining various fruits by all the inhabitants of the world: humans, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, guhyakas, kiṃpuruṣas, apsarases, uragas, birds, daityas, dānavas, rudras, vasus, aśvins, maruts, divine seers, brahminical seers, and those seeking liberation, all of whom desire dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
And on this point there is a verse: "When a person hears of the lineage of Yadu, he is liberated from all sins— the lineage in which the supreme Brahman, called Viṣṇu, who is formless, descended."
There were four sons of Yadu named Sahasrajit, Kroṣṭu, Nala, and Raghu.
Sahasrajit’s son was Śatajit. He had three sons: Haihaya, Haya, and Veṇuhaya.
The son of Haihaya was Dharma; his son was Dharmanetra. From him came Kunti, and from Kunti came Sāhañjit. His son was Mahiṣmān.
From him came Bhadraśreṇya; from him, Durdama; from him, Dhanaka.
Dhanaka had four sons: Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, Kṛtadharma, and Kṛtaujas.
From Kṛtavīrya was born Arjuna, the lord of the seven continents, who possessed a thousand arms.

He who, having propitiated Dattātreya— the portion of the Blessed One born in the Atri lineage— desired and obtained these boons: a thousand arms, the prevention of the practice of unrighteousness, the conquest of the earth through dharma, its protection according to dharma, invincibility against enemies, and death at the hands of a man renowned throughout the entire world.
By him this entire earth, comprising all its continents, was properly protected;
he performed ten thousand sacrifices.
And a verse concerning him is still sung even today:
"Surely no kings shall ever equal the destiny of Kārtavīrya,
whether by sacrifices, gifts, austerities, humility, or sacred learning."
And in his kingdom, there was no loss of property;
thus, for eighty-five thousand years, he ruled the realm with unimpeded health, prosperity, strength, and valor.

In Māhiṣmatī, Rāvaṇa— who, though possessed of the intoxicating pride born from his victory over all the lords of the gods, demons, and gandharvas, was effortlessly bound like a beast and stationed in a corner of his own city by him (Kṛtavarman), who was agitated by the intoxication of excessive drinking during his sport of plunging into the waters of the Narmadā upon arriving there on his world-conquest— [was thus subdued].
And he who was destroyed at the end of the period characterized by eighty-five thousand years by Paraśurāma— an incarnation of Lord Nārāyaṇa—
had five sons who were the chief among his hundred sons,
known by the names Śūra, Śūrasena, Vṛṣaṇa, Madhu, and Jayadhvaja.
From Jayadhvaja was born a son named Tālajaṅgha.
Tālajaṅgha had a hundred sons known as the Tālajaṅghas,
the eldest of whom was Vītihotra, and another was Bharata.
From Bharata were born Vṛṣa and Sujāta. Madhu was the son of Vṛṣa,
and he too had a hundred sons, the foremost of whom was Vṛṣṇi.
From that time on, this lineage acquired the name Vṛṣṇi.
And Madhu became the cause for the name "Madhu," and the Yādavas were so called because they were characterized by the name Yadu.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
And the son of Kroṣṭu, the son of Yadu, was Vṛjinīvān.
From him came Svahi; from him, Ruṣaṅku;
from Ruṣaṅku, Citraratha. His son was Śaśabindu, who became a universal monarch (cakravartin) possessing the fourteen great jewels.
He had one hundred thousand wives and sons numbering one million.
And they had six principal sons: Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthukarman, Pṛthujaya, Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthudāna, and Pṛthuśravas.
And Pṛthuśravas’s son was Tamas;
from him came Uśanas, who performed a hundred horse-sacrifices.
And his son was named Śitapu.
His son was Rukmakavaca.
From him came Parāvṛt, and from Parāvṛt was born Parāvṛta. His five sons were Rukmeṣu, Pṛthu, Jyāmagha, Pālita, and Harita by name.
Regarding this, even today this verse concerning Jyāmagha is sung:
"Among all those who will exist or have existed as husbands subject to their wives,
King Jyāmagha, the husband of Śaibyā, was the most excellent."
His wife, named Śaibyā, was childless;
nevertheless, although he desired offspring, he did not take another wife out of fear.
Once, however, while fighting in a most terrible great battle crowded with an immense throng of elephants, horses, and chariots, he conquered the entire circle of his enemies.
That hostile host, having been deprived of its sons, wives, kinsmen, forces, and treasury, abandoned its own capital and fled in all directions.

And as he fled, he beheld that jewel among princesses, distressed by agitated lamentations, crying out, "Save me, save me, father! Mother! Brother! with her pair of large eyes trembling with extreme terror.
Upon seeing her, his inner soul filled with passion for her, the king thought:
"This jewel of a daughter has been provided by Fate at this very moment as a cause for offspring for me, who am childless and the husband of a barren wife."
Therefore, I shall carry her away; then, having placed her upon a chariot, I will lead her to my own abode.
"Permitted by that very queen Śaibyā, I shall marry her"; having said this, he placed her upon the chariot and went to his own city.
And Śaibyā, accompanied by all the citizens, servants, attendants, and ministers, came to the gate of the palace to see King Vijayin.

Having looked toward the maiden standing on the king’s left side, her sprout-like lower lip quivering with a slight surge of indignation, she said to the king: "Who is this exceedingly fickle-minded woman who has been placed here in the chariot? Without considering his reply, the king, out of extreme fear, said to her: "She is my daughter-in-law."
Then Śaibya said to him:
"I was not delivered by you as a son, nor did any other wife exist for you;
by which of your sons, then, does this relationship of daughter-in-law arise?"
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words, which were defiled by self-interest, envy, and anger, and which had robbed her of her discernment, the king spoke this in order to avoid the harshness of her speech:

"This girl has been designated as the wife for that son who shall be born to you, even before he has come into being. Upon hearing this, she broke into a gentle smile and said, "So be it," and entered the royal palace together with the king.

Immediately thereafter, due to the merit of the conversation regarding the birth of a son— which had been determined by the most pure *lagna*, *horā*, degrees, and subdivisions— Śaibyā, although having reached the decline of her age, conceived a child in just a few days and,
in due time, gave birth to a boy;
and his father gave him the name Vidarbha.
And he married that daughter-in-law.
And upon her he begot two sons named Kratha and Kaiśika;
furthermore, he fathered a third prince named Romapāda.
From Romapāda came Babhru, and the son of Babhru was Dhṛti.
Dhṛti’s son was Kaiśika, and Kaiśika’s son was Cedi; in his lineage were born the Caidya kings. Kratha’s son was Kunti, who was the son of a daughter-in-law.
From Kunti came Vṛṣṇi; from Vṛṣṇi came Nirvṛti; from Nirvṛti came Daśārha, and from him Vyoma;
from him also came Jīmūta, from him Vikṛti, and from him Bhīmaratha.

From him came Navaratha, from him Daśaratha, and from him Śakuni; his son was Karambhi, from Karambhi came Devarāta, and from him Devakṣatra; from Devakṣatra came Madhu, from Madhu Anavaratha, from Anavaratha Kuruvatsa, and from him Anuratha; from him Puruhotra was born. From him came Aṃśu, and from him Satvata; from Satvata came these Sātvatas. Having heard this lineage of Jyāmagha with perfect faith, one is liberated from all sins.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Bhajana, Bhajamāna, Divya, Andhaka, Devāvṛdha, Mahābhoja, and Vṛṣṇi were the sons of Satvata.
To Bhajamāna were born Nimi, Kṛkaṇa, and Vṛṣṇi, as well as others who were his half-brothers known by the names Śatajit, Sahasrajit, and Ayutajit.
Devāvṛdha’s son was Babhru;
concerning these two, this verse is sung:
Just as we hear him from afar, so do we behold him from nearby:
the tawny one, the best among men, equal to the gods who increase the divine power.
Sixty-six thousand and eight men attained immortality through Babhru Devāvṛdha as well.
Mahābhoja was exceedingly righteous; in his lineage, the Bhojas of Mārtikāvata arose.
Vṛṣṇi had two sons, Sumitra and Yudhājit.
From them were born Anamitra and Śini; likewise, from Anamitra came Nighna, and from Nighna came Prasena and Satrājit.
The blessed Āditya was the friend of that Satrājit.
Once, while staying on the shore of the ocean, Satrājit praised the Sun with single-minded devotion; and being thus extolled, the Radiant One stood before him.
Beholding him there, yet bearing an indistinct form, Satrājit said to the Sun:
"Just as I saw you in the sky like a mass of fire, even so today, though you have come before me, I do not perceive any particular favor bestowed by your lordship."
When the Blessed One Sūrya had spoken thus, he unfastened from his own neck the great jewel named Syamantaka, took it down, and placed it aside.
Then he beheld the Sun-god, whose body was slightly coppery, radiant, and short, and whose eyes were somewhat reddish-brown.
Having performed prostrations, hymns of praise, and other rites, Satrājit said to him,
"O Blessed One, choose from me whatever boon you desire."
And he requested that very same jewel;
and having given it to him, he ascended into the sky to his own celestial abode.
Satrājit also, his neck adorned with that spotless jewel-gem, entered Dvārakā, illuminating the interiors of all directions with his splendors like the sun.

But the inhabitants of the region around Dvārakā, seeing the Blessed One—the Primeval Person, the Supreme Person—who had assumed a human form as a partial incarnation for the purpose of removing the earth's burden, prostrated themselves and said:
"O Blessed One, surely this is the Sun-god who has come to see the Blessed One. Hearing this, the Blessed One laughed and said to them:
"This is not the Sun-god; this is Satrājit, who approaches here bearing the great jewel named Syamantaka, which was given to him by the Sun."
Having been told, "Therefore, look at him with confidence," they departed;
and he placed that great jewel named Syamantaka in his own dwelling.
And that most excellent jewel-gem flows eight loads of gold every day;
and by its power, no fear of calamities—such as drought, predatory beasts, fire, water, or famine—arises for the entire kingdom.
Acyuta also desired that jewel, thinking it was suitable for King Ugrasena;
yet, though he was capable of taking it, he did not seize it out of fear of causing a schism in the lineage.
Thinking, "Acyuta will surely ask me for this," Satrājit, having become aware of the greed for the jewel, gave that gem to his own brother Prasena.
And when worn by one who is pure, it produces its full range of qualities, such as the flowing of gold;
otherwise, it kills the very person who wears it.
Prasena, too, having fastened the Syamantaka jewel to his neck, mounted his horse and went into the forest to hunt.
There he met his death at the hands of a lion.
Having slain him along with his horse, the lion was about to depart taking that pure jewel in its mouth when it was seen and killed by Jāmbavān, the lord of the bears.
Jāmbavān also, taking that stainless jewel-gem,
entered his own cave and made it a plaything for the boy named Sukumāra.
And while Prasena was away, Kṛṣṇa coveted that jewel; yet he did not obtain it.
"Surely this must be his own deed," the entire Yadu clan said to one another, passing the word from ear to ear.
Having learned the circumstances of the public scandal, the Blessed One, accompanied by the Yadu army, followed the tracks of Prasena’s horse.
He saw Prasena slain by a lion amidst the midst of the entire populace, along with his horse; having established his innocence by observing the lion's tracks, he followed those lion tracks.
Having seen even a lion slain by a bear on a small patch of ground, he followed the tracks of the bear out of reverence for that jewel.
Having stationed the entire Yadu army on the mountain slope, he entered the bear's cave following its footprints.
Having entered halfway, he heard the voice of a nurse lulling a delicate infant to sleep.
"The lion slew Prasena; the lion was killed by Jāmbavān.
Do not weep, my dear child; for this Syamantaka belongs to you."
Having heard this and obtained news of the Syamantaka, he entered and saw the Syamantaka—blazing with splendors—held in the hand of his nurse as a plaything for the prince.
Beholding that unprecedented man who had arrived with eyes longing for the Syamantaka, the nurse cried out, "Save me! Save me! (ViP 4.13.16–17).
Immediately after hearing that cry of distress, Jāmbavat arrived with a heart full of indignation.
As those two fought with one another, their battle lasted for twenty-one days.
Meanwhile, the Yādava soldiers remained there for seven or eight days, waiting for their emergence.
And since Madhuripu had not emerged, they concluded with certainty that he must have met his end within this cave;
otherwise, how could he have been so distracted by the conquest of his enemy for so many days? Having reached Dvārakā with this resolve, they proclaimed, "Kṛṣṇa has been slain."
And his kinsmen performed the entire range of funeral rites appropriate for that occasion.
During that time, as he fought, Kṛṣṣṇa’s strength and vital energy were nourished by the food, water, and other offerings provided with great faith to distinguished recipients.

The other, however, suffered a loss of strength due to fasting, his entire body being tormented by exceedingly cruel blows from a most powerful man day after day. And having been defeated by the Blessed One, Jāmbavān prostrated himself and spoke:
"The Blessed One cannot be conquered even by all the asuras, suras, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others combined."
"How much less so for men who range only upon the earth and possess little vigor, who are merely limbs of a man, and follow the path of animal births—how much more so for those like us?

Surely the Blessed One must be an emanation of our Lord Nārāyaṇa, the ultimate refuge of the entire world. Having been addressed thus, the Blessed One explained to him his descent to relieve the burden of the whole earth.
And by the touch of his palm, anointed with affection, he dispelled the fatigue of battle from him.
Having prostrated before him and once again propitiated him, he caused a maiden named Jāmbavatī to be accepted as an offering of hospitality for his arrival at the house.
He too, having prostrated, gave the Syamantaka jewel to him;
and Acyuta, though it was something that should not have been accepted from one who had bowed so excessively, took that precious gem for the sake of his own purification.
Accompanied by Jāmbavatī, he arrived at Dvārakā.
For the inhabitants of Dvārakā, whose joy was at its peak due to the Lord’s arrival, the very moment they beheld Kṛṣṇa, even those of advanced age seemed as if they had attained fresh youth.
And all the Yādavas and their women honored Ānakadundubhi, exclaiming, "By good fortune! By good fortune!"
The Blessed One also related everything exactly as it had occurred to the assembly of Yadus;
and by giving the Syamantaka jewel to Satrājit, he attained purification from his false accusation.
And he established Jāmbavatī in the inner apartments.
Satrājit, however, became terrified, thinking, "I have been falsely accused by him of a crime," and gave his daughter Satyabhāmā to the Blessed One as a wife.
Previously, the Yādavas—headed by Akrūra, Kṛtavarman, and Śatadhanvan—had sought her hand in marriage.
Then, considering themselves as if insulted by that gift, they conceived a persistent enmity toward Satrājit.
And Akrūra, Kṛtavarman, and the others said to Śatadhanvan:
"This man is exceedingly wicked-souled; although Satrājit was entreated by us and by you, he disregarded both us and you and gave his daughter to Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, enough with him living! Why do you not have him killed and take that great jewel for yourself?"
"We shall provide assistance if Acyuta should maintain a persistent enmity toward you."
Having been addressed thus, he replied, "So be it.

Although the Blessed One knew the ultimate truth regarding the sons of Pāṇḍu who had been burned in the house of lac, he went to Vāraṇāvata in order to cause Duryodhana’s efforts to slacken, or perhaps to act in accordance with [the Pandavas' needs].

When he had departed, Śatadhanvan killed Satrājit while he was still asleep and took the precious jewel. Filled with indignation at her father’s murder, Satyabhāmā quickly mounted a chariot, went to Vāraṇāvata, and said to the Blessed One: "My father has been slain by the intolerant Śatadhanvan, who has also carried off that Syamantaka jewel."
"Therefore, this is his dismissal;
having considered this, let that which is appropriate here be done," he said to Kṛṣṇa.
Although his heart was thus satisfied by her words, Kṛṣṇa, his eyes copper-red with indignation, said to Satyabhāmā: "Satyā, this is merely a mockery directed at me;
I shall not tolerate this from that wicked-souled one."
"For birds that dwell in nests built upon an excellent tree are not slain as long as they do not leap over it.
Therefore, enough with this elaborate display of words prompted by grief before us. Having said this, Vāsudeva went to Dvārakā and spoke to Baladeva in private:
"While Prasena was out hunting in the forest, the lord of beasts (the lion) slew him."
Satrājit, too, has now been brought to his death by Śatadhanvan;
therefore, due to the destruction of both, that jewel shall become common property for us two.
"Rise then! Mount the chariot and make an effort to slay Śatadhanvan. Being thus addressed, he agreed, saying "So be it," and prepared accordingly.
Perceiving that both of them had made their preparations, Śatadhanvan approached Kṛtavarman and urged him to fulfill his duty as a rear-guard.
Kṛtavarman said to him:
Having been told, "I am not capable of opposing Balarāma and Vāsudeva," he urged Akrūra;
and the latter replied, "Indeed,
no one [is capable] against the Blessed One, by whom the three worlds were made to tremble by the strike of his foot and who brought widowhood to the women of the cities of the asuras."

He is capable of fighting even the foremost of the immortals, who are worshipped by the entire world—namely, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), whose discus is unimpeded by the circle of powerful enemies, who destroys the enemy forces with a glance from eyes gladdened by joy, and the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), whose great strength is manifested by the dragging away of the most formidable enemy elephants;
how much more so, then, can he fight others? Therefore, let someone other than him be sought as a refuge.
Thus addressed, Śatadhanvan said:
"If you consider yourself incapable of protecting us, then let this jewel of ours be taken and guarded. Being thus told, he replied:
"If you will not tell anyone of this, even in the final extremity of your state, then I shall accept it."
When he had said "So be it," Akrūra took that jewel-gem.
Śatadhanvan, having mounted a mare of incomparable speed that could travel a hundred yojanas, fled;
Baladeva and Vāsudeva, stationed in a chariot yoked with the four horses Śaibya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka, pursued him.
And that mare, having traversed a path measuring a hundred yojanas, gave up her life in the region of the Mithilā forest while still being driven on;
Śatadhanvan, too, abandoning her, fled on foot alone.
Kṛṣṇa also said to Balabhadra:
"You must remain right here on this chariot while I follow this man of base conduct on foot and slay him;
for in this region, horses have been known to suffer harm."
"These horses must not be led beyond this portion of the earth."
Having said, "So be it," Balabhadra remained right there on the chariot.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having followed the ground for a distance of two *krośas*, hurled his discus while still standing at a distance and severed the head of Śatadhanvan.
When he searched extensively through that body, the garments, and other belongings, yet did not find the Syamantaka jewel, he approached Balabhadra and said:
"Śatadhanvan has been slain by us in vain;
that jewel-gem, which is the very essence of the entire world, has not been obtained.
Hearing this, Balabhadra, his anger aroused, said to Vāsudeva:
"Fie on you, who thus desire wealth! And because you are my brother, I tolerate this;
therefore, take this path and go as you please.

I have no need for Dvārakā nor for these kinsmen; enough of these false oaths in my presence! Having thus rebuked him, he did not stay, even though he was being entreated with some difficulty to remain.
He entered the city of Videha.
Janaka, having first offered him the guest-offering (arghya), caused him to enter his home and remained right there;
Vāsudeva, for his part, returned to Dvārakā.

And for as long as Balabhadra remained in the palace of King Janaka, Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, learned the art of mace-fighting from him. At the end of three years, the Yādavas, led by Babhru and Ugrasena—who had come to the conclusion that the jewel had not been stolen by Kṛṣṇa—went to the city of Videha; having reassured Baladeva, they brought him back to Dvārakā.
Akrūra, too, intent on meditating upon the gold produced from that supreme jewel, performed sacrifices.

For it is said that one who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya while they are engaged in a Soma sacrifice becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, he remained there having entered the armor of initiation.
Thus, for sixty-two years, by the power of that jewel, no calamities, famines, or pestilences occurred there.
Then, when Śatrughna had slain Akrūra’s great-grandson on behalf of the Bhojas who were hostile to him, Akrūra abandoned Dvārakā and fled along with the Bhojas.
From the day he departed, calamities such as portents, predatory beasts, drought, and pestilence occurred there.
Then the Blessed One, whose banner bears the enemy of serpents, together with the Yādava Balabhadra and Ugrasena, deliberated:
"Let this be considered—why is it that these numerous calamities have arrived all at once?"
When this was said, the elder of the Yadus named Andhaka spoke:
"Wherever this Akrūra’s father, Śvaphalka, was present, there famine, pestilence, drought, and the like did not occur."
When there was a severe drought in the territory of the King of Kāśī, Śvaphalka was brought there;
immediately thereafter, the rain-god sent down rain,
and in the womb of the King of Kāśī’s queen, a daughter was first conceived.
Even when the time for birth was fulfilled, she did not emerge at all;
and so twelve years passed while that fetus remained without coming forth.
And the King of Kāśī spoke to his daughter who was still within the womb.

"Daughter, why are you not born? Come forth! I wish to see your face and my own mother; why will you cause us such long-lasting distress? When he had spoken thus, she, while still within the womb, replied:
"Father, if you give one cow each day to the Brahmins, then after three more years I shall certainly emerge from this womb.
Having heard these words of hers, the king gave a cow to a Brahmin every single day.
She too was born after that same amount of time;
therefore, her father gave her the name Gāndinī.
And he gave that maiden Gāndinī as an *argha* offering to Śvaphalka, who had come to his house as a benefactor.
In her, this Akrūra was born from Śvaphalka;
thus his birth was from such a pair of excellent qualities.
"How is it that when he has departed, calamities such as pestilence and famine will not occur?
Therefore, let him be brought back; enough with searching for faults in one who possesses such great virtues. (ViP 4.13.43)

Having heard these words of the elder Andhaka, Keśava, Ugrasena, Balabhadra, and the other Yadus granted him an assurance of safety born of their forgiveness for his offense; thus Śvāphalki was brought back to his own city.
As soon as he arrived there, by the power of that jewel remaining with him, the calamities of drought, pestilence, famine, wild beasts, and other such afflictions were pacified.
And Kṛṣṇa reflected:
"The reason why this Akrūra was born to Gāndinī by Śvaphalka is quite insignificant;
yet his power is truly great, for he brings about the pacification of calamities such as drought, famine, and pestilence."
Therefore, that great jewel named Syamantaka must surely be with him;
for such are the powers of it that are heard of.
Moreover, he performs another sacrifice immediately after this one, and yet another sacrifice immediately after that.

Having formed the firm conviction that the excellent jewel remained there within it, with only a small portion taken out and no further doubt remaining, he convened the entire assembly of the Yādavas at his own residence under the pretext of some other purpose.
When all the Yādavas were seated there, Janārdana presented his original purpose; and when that was concluded, having engaged in a conversation of incidental jesting with Akrūra, he spoke to him.

"O Lord of Generosity, we already know how Śatadhanvan surrendered to you that Syamantaka jewel, which is the very essence of the entire world; thus it remains with you for the benefit of the realm. Let all of us remain here enjoying the fruits of its power. However, this Balabhadra has become suspicious of us; therefore, show it to us for our pleasure. Being thus addressed, he [Satrājit], along with the jewel, reflected:
"What should be done here? If I speak otherwise, they will think that while searching for this jewel, they will find only the concealment by my garment;
thus, their search would not be secure. Having reflected thus, Akrūra spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the cause of the entire world:
"O Blessed One, this Syamantaka jewel was entrusted to me by Śatadhanvan."
Thinking, "Now that he has departed, the Blessed One will request [the gift] from me today, tomorrow, or the day after," I have maintained this for so long with great hardship.
And through the pain of maintaining it, my mind has become unattached to all enjoyments; I do not perceive even a fraction of my own happiness.
"I have not urged this myself, thinking that you might consider me incapable of sustaining even this much for the benefit of the entire kingdom."
"Therefore, let this Syamantaka jewel be taken; let it be handed over to whomever desires it.
Then he revealed a very small golden casket concealed within his lower garment.
Then, having stepped out, he released the Syamantaka jewel into that assembly of the Yadus; and as soon as it was released, that entire hall was illuminated by its exceeding brilliance.
Then Akrūra said, "This is that very jewel which was entrusted to us by Śatadhanvan; let its rightful owner take it.
Upon seeing it, the voices of all the Yādavas were heard crying out in amazement, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Beholding him who was not subject to death and who was sought after by Acyuta as his own equal, Balabhadra became filled with longing.

Satyabhāmā felt an intense longing, thinking, "This is my father’s wealth. And because of Balabhadra and Satyabhāmā looking at his face, Kṛṣṇa also felt as if he were situated inside a discus. Then, in the presence of all the Yādavas, he spoke to Akrūra:
For this jewel was shown to these Yadus for the sake of their own purification; it is the common paternal inheritance of both myself and Balabhadra, and belongs to Satyabhāmā and no other.
This [fire], when maintained at all times by one who is pure and chaste, is beneficial to the entire kingdom; however, when maintained by one who is impure, it destroys even its own support.
Therefore, I am unable to maintain this retinue of sixteen thousand women;
how could Satyabhāmā accept this?
Furthermore, how is it possible for the noble Balabhadra to renounce the drinking of wine and all other forms of sensual enjoyment?
Therefore, O Lord of Generosity, this world, myself as Balabhadra, and Satyabhāmā entreat you:
you alone are capable of upholding this.
And since it will be beneficial to this kingdom when it rests with you, may you uphold it as before for the sake of benefiting the entire realm.
Having been told by him, "You must not speak of this to anyone else," the lord of the sacrifice replied, "So be it," and took that great jewel.
From that time forward, Akrūra moved about like the sun garlanded with rays, with that jewel blazing with its exceedingly brilliant luster clearly visible, fastened around his own neck.
Whoever remembers this cleansing of the Blessed One’s false accusation will never suffer even the slightest false accusation;
with unimpaired faculties, he shall attain liberation from all sins.
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The son of Anamitra was named Śini.
From him [Satrājit] was born Satyaka; from Satyaka came Sātyaki, whose name is Yuyudhāna. From him also came Asaṅga, his son Tūṇi, and from Tūṇi, Yugandhara—these are the descendants of Śini.
In the lineage of Anamitra himself was Vṛṣṇi;
from him came Śvaphalka, whose power has already been described.
Śvaphalka had a younger brother named Citraka.
From Śvaphalka and Gāndinī was born Akrūra.

Likewise, from Upamadgu were born sons named Mṛdu, Aviśārin, Mejayagiri, Kṣatra, Upakṣatra, Śatrughna, Arimardana, Dharmadṛk, Dṛṣṭavarma, Gandhamoja, Vāha, and Prativāha, as well as a daughter named Sutārā.
Devavān and Upadeva were the two sons of Akrūra.
Citraka had many sons, headed by Pṛthu and Vipṛthu;
likewise, Andhaka had four sons named Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śuci, and Kambalabarhiṣat.
From Kukura was born Dhṛṣṭa; from him, Kapotaroman; and from him, Viloman.
From him also was born Bhava by name, the friend of Tumburu, who possessed sandalwood water and the sound of drums.
From him came Abhijit, and from him, Punarvasu.
His son was Āhuka, and his daughter was Āhukī.
Āhuka had two sons, Devaka and Ugrasena.
Devaka also had four sons: Devavān, Upadeva, Sahadeva, and Devarakṣita.
They had seven sisters: Vṛkadevā, Upadevā, Devarakṣitā, Śrīdevā, Śāntidevā, Sahadevā, and Devakī.
Vasudeva married all of them as well.
Ugrasena also had sons named Kaṃsa, Nyagrodha, Sunāman, Aṅka, Śaṅku, Subhūmi, Rāṣṭrapāla, Yuddhamuṣṭi, Tuṣṭimat, and Matsya;
and daughters named Kaṃsā, Kaṃsavatī, Sutanū, Rāṣṭrapālī, and Kaṅkī—these were the offspring of Ugrasena.
From Bhajamāna was born a son, Vidūratha; from Vidūratha came Śūra; from Śūra came Śami; from Śami came Pratikṣatra;
from him [was born] Svayaṃbhoja, and from him Hṛdika.
He, too, had sons named Kṛtavarman, Śatadhanu, and Devamīḍhuṣa.
The wife of the heroic Devamīḍhuṣa was named Māriṣā.
And she bore him ten sons, headed by Vasudeva.

As soon as Vasudeva was born, the gods—who beheld with unimpeded vision the descent of a portion of the Blessed One into that house—sounded divine drums (*divyānakadundubhi*). Consequently, he received the name *Anakadundubhi* at that very moment.
He, too, had nine brothers known by the names Devabhāga, Devaśravas, Ānadhṛṣṭi, Karundhaka, Vatsabālaka, Sṛñjaya, Śyāma, Śamīka, and Gaṇḍūṣa;
and Pṛthā, Śrutadevā, Śrutakīrti, Śrutaśravā, and Rājādhidevī were the five sisters of Vasudeva and the others.
Śūra had a friend named Kunti;
to him, being childless, Śūra gave his daughter Pṛthā according to the prescribed rites. And Pāṇḍu married her.
And upon her, through Dharmarāja, Vāyu, and Śakra, three sons were begotten named Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and Arjuna;
furthermore, while she was still unmarried, a son named Karṇa was born to her by the divine Sun as her maiden-child.
And she had a co-wife named Mādrī;
upon her also were begotten two sons of Pāṇḍu, Nakula and Sahadeva, by the Nāsatyas and Dasras.
Furthermore, Śrutadevā was married by a Karūṣa king named Vṛddhaśarman.
From her was born a great asura named Dantavakra.
King Kaikeya also married Śrutakīrti;
from her were born five sons, the Kaikeyas, headed by Saṃtardana.
Vinda and Anuvinda, the two princes of Avanti, were born of Rājādhidevī.
Furthermore, the King of Cedi, named Damaghoṣa, married Śrutaśravas;
through her, he begot Śiśupāla.
For he was formerly Hiraṇyakaśipu, the first among the Daityas, who was endowed with both improper conduct and prowess.
And he who had been struck down by the Blessed One, the Teacher of the Entire World,
once again became the Ten-faced One, possessing the qualities of unimpaired vigor, heroism, excellence, and prowess, and having surpassed the majesty of the Lord of the Three Worlds.

Having long enjoyed the proximity of the Blessed One and thereby obtained the fruit of merit arising from the fall of his body, he too was brought to his end by the Blessed One himself in the form of Rāghava.
The son of Damaghoṣa, the king of Cedi, became the lord of Cedi named Śiśupāla.
Even while in the state of Śiśupāla, he maintained an exceedingly persistent enmity toward the Lord named Puṇḍarīkākṣa, who had descended as a partial incarnation to remove the burden of the earth;
and when brought to his death by the Lord, he attained union (*sāyujya*) with Him alone, through one-pointed concentration of the mind upon that very Supreme Self.
For the Blessed One, when pleased, grants whatever is desired; yet even when displeased, he bestows a divine and incomparable station upon those he strikes down.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"In his births as Hiraṇyakaśipu and as Rāvaṇa, by Viṣṇu..."
Slain, he attained enjoyments that were unattainable even for the immortals.
How could he, who had been struck down by that very [Viṣṇu] and had not attained absorption (laya) therein,
have again reached union (sāyujya) with the eternal Hari in the form of Śiśupāla?
I desire to hear this, O best among all upholders of the Dharma;
being filled with curiosity, you ought to speak to me who have thus questioned you.
Parāśara said:
For the sake of slaying the lord of the Daityas, he who effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all the worlds previously assumed a body and manifested the form of Nṛsiṃha;
however, at that time, the thought "This is Viṣṇu" did not occur to Hiraṇyakaśipu's mind.
Thinking, "This being has arisen from a mass of unsurpassed merit," his one-pointed mind was impelled by an excess of passion; through the application of that meditation,
he obtained, as the cause for his death, an unsurpassed abundance of enjoyments in the state of having ten faces— an excellence surpassing the entire three worlds.
Therefore, when that Blessed One—who is the supreme Brahman, without beginning or end—is not taken as an object of focus, the mind does not attain absorption in Him.

Even though he possessed ten faces, because his heart was dependent on the bodiless god of love and fixed upon Jānakī, he assumed the form of the son of Daśaratha; thus, for this [Rāvaṇa], the mere sight of that form led to the conviction "this is not Acyuta. This was merely a human perception arising from an internal organ that had fallen away from its true state.
This occurred for him.

Furthermore, he obtained as his fruit merely the avoidance of falling into ruin, a birth in the royal family of Cedi—which is praised throughout the entire circle of the earth—and unimpeded sovereignty in the state of Śiśupāla.
In that regard, however, all the names of the Blessed One became the very causes for him;

consequently, with a mind whose persistent enmity had been nurtured through many births, he incessantly uttered all those names of Acyuta— names produced by those very causes— in acts such as reviling and threatening.
And that form— with eyes as pure as the petals of a full-blown lotus, wearing exceedingly brilliant yellow garments, adorned with a stainless crown, armlets,

and bracelets, possessing four noble and stout arms bearing the conch, discus, and mace— never departed from his own mind due to the power of his intense devotion, throughout all states such as walking, eating, bathing, sitting, and lying down.

Uttering those very insults and holding him fast in his heart, he beheld the Blessed One— the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is imperishable splendor, who is radiant with the garland of rays from the discus-weapon, who has transcended defects such as passion and hatred, and who exists for the sake of his own destruction.

At that very moment, he was swiftly slain by the discus of the Blessed One; with the entire accumulation of his sins burnt away by the remembrance of Him, he was brought to his end by the Blessed One himself and attained absorption into Him alone.
All of this has been related to you by me.

For this Blessed One, when praised or remembered—even through a continuous attachment of hatred—bestows a fruit difficult for all gods and asuras to attain, let alone for those possessed of perfect devotion.
Vasudeva Ānakadundubhi had many wives, headed by Pauravī, Rohiṇī, Madirā, Bhadrā, and Devakī.
Ānakadundubhi begot Balabhadra, Sāraṇa, Śaṭha, Durmada, and other sons upon Rohiṇī.
Balabhadra, in turn, fathered two sons, Niśaṭha and Ulmuka, upon Revatī.
Mārṣṭi, Mārṣi, Macchi, Śiśu, Satyadhṛti, and others were the offspring of Sāraṇa.
Bhadrāśva, Bhadrabāhu, Durdama, Bhūta, and others were born into the lineage of Rohiṇī.
Nandopananda and Kṛtakādya were the sons of Madirā; Upanidhi, Gadā, and others were the sons of Bhadrā;
and he begot one son, Kauśika, upon Vaiśālī.
To Devakī, Ānakadundubhi also begot six sons named Kīrtimat, Suṣeṇa, Udāyin, Bhadrasena, Arjuna, and Bhadradeva.
Kaṃsa killed all of them;
and immediately thereafter, at midnight, Yoganidrā, sent by the Blessed One, drew the seventh embryo from the womb of Rohiṇī and carried it away.
And because of his power of attraction, he also obtained the name Saṃkarṣaṇa.

Thereupon, the Blessed One Vāsudeva— the root of the great tree of the entire world, beyond the reach of the minds of all gods, asuras, sages, and men, past, present, and future; he who was propitiated by Brahmā and the others, led by Agni, for the removal of the earth’s burden— descended into the womb of Devakī, he who is without beginning or middle.
And Yoganidrā, her pride and self-conceit increased by his grace, entered the womb of Yaśodā, the wife of the cowherd Nanda.

While that lotus-eyed one was being born and after he had been born, this entire world became free from unrighteousness, with its sun, moon, and planets perfectly serene, its minds composed and free from fear of serpents and other dangers. Furthermore, when the Blessed One descended here into the mortal world, he had sixteen thousand one hundred wives.
Among them, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Jāmbavatī, Cāruhāsinī, and others were the eight principal wives;
and into them the Lord, whose form is the whole and who is without beginning, begot one hundred and eighty thousand sons.
Among them, Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, Sāmba, and others were the thirteen principal sons. Pradyumna also married Rukmiṇī’s daughter, named Kakudvatī;
by her, Aniruddha was born to him.
Aniruddha also married Subhadrā by name, the granddaughter of Rukmin; from her was born his son Vajra;
Vajra’s son was Pratibāhu, and his son was Sucāru.
Thus, even in hundreds of years, it is impossible to know the number of persons in the Yādava clan, which consists of many hundreds of thousands of men.
For indeed, these two verses here have fulfilled their purpose.
There were thirty-eight million eight hundred thousand young men who served as household teachers and were devoted to the practice of archery.
Who could possibly count the high-souled Yādavas,
among whom ten thousand times ten thousand Āyutas are always present, along with a hundred thousand Āhukas?
Those Daityas of immense strength who were slain by the gods and Asuras have been reborn among human beings as those who cause affliction to people.
O twice-born one, for the sake of their destruction, gods descended upon earth into the lineage of Yadu,
where there were one hundred and one families.
Viṣṇu was established in their authority and sovereignty;
all the Yādavas remained obedient to his command.
The man who constantly hears this account of the lineage of the Vṛṣṇi heroes is liberated from all sins and attains the world of Viṣṇu.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Thus has this lineage of Yadu been described to you in brief.
Now, take note of the lineage of Turvasu.
The son of Turvasu was Vahni; from Vahni came Gobhānu; from him, Traiśānu; and from him, Karaṃdhama. His son was Marutta, who remained childless.
And thereafter, he adopted Duṣyanta, the son of Puru, as his own son;
thus, due to the curse of Yayāti, his lineage came to rely upon the Paurava dynasty.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The son of Druhyu was Babhru.
From him came Setu; Setu’s son was named Āradvān;
his son was Gāndhāra.
From him came Dharma; from Dharma was born Dhṛta; from Dhṛta, Durdama; and from him, Pracetas.
The hundred sons of Pracetas exercised sovereignty over the Mlecchas of the north, who were largely characterized by unrighteousness.
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
To Anu, the fourth son of Yayāti, there were three sons named Sabhānara, Cakṣupa, and Paramēkṣu.
Sabhānara was the son of Anara; from Kālānara came Sṛñjaya; from Sṛñjaya came Purañjaya.
From him was born Janamejaya, from whom came Mahāśāla, and from him Mahāmanas. From him, too, two sons were born: Uśīnara and Titikṣu.
Uśīnara also had five sons named Śibi, Nṛga, Nara, Kṛmi, and Darva.
The four sons of Śibi were Vṛṣadarbha, Suvīra, Kaikeya, and Madra.
Titikṣu also had a son named Ruśadratha.
From him also came Hema; from Hema, Sutapas; and from him, Bali.
In Bali’s lineage, within his own field, Dīrghatamas begot the Kṣatriyas known as Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Suhya, and Pauṇḍra, who were the descendants of Bali.
And there were five objects known by the names of his lineage:
Aṅga’s son was Anapāna; his son was Diviratha; from him came Dharmaratha; and from him, Citraratha, who was also known as Romapāda.
He whose son was Daśaratha;
for him, the sonless Daśaratha, who was himself the son of Aja, bestowed his daughter named Śāntā in the status of a daughter.

From Romapāda came Caturaṅga, and from him Pṛthulākṣa; from him came Campa, who founded the city of Campā. The son of Campa was Haryaṅga; from him Bhadraratha; from him Bṛhadratha; from him Bṛhatkarman; from Bṛhatkarman came Bṛhadbhānu; from him Bṛhanmanas; and from him Jayadratha.
Jayadratha begot a son named Vijaya upon his wife, who was born from the union between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya woman.
And Vijaya obtained a son named Dhṛti;
his son was Dhṛtavrata;
from Dhṛtavrata came Satyakarman, and from Satyakarman came Adhiratha.
He who went to the Gaṅgā and obtained as a son Karṇa, who had been cast into a basket and abandoned by Pṛthā—from Karṇa was born Vṛṣasena; these were the Aṅgas.
Therefore, you ought to hear the lineage of Puru.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Janamejaya was the son of Pūru; his son was Pracinvān, and from Pracinvān came Pravīra.
From him [Raudrāśva] came Manasyu; from Manasyu came Abhayada; from him also came Sudyu; from Sudyu came Bahugava; from him also came Saṃyāti; from Saṃyāti came Ahaṃyāti; from him came Raudrāśva.
Raudrāśva had ten sons named Ṛteyu, Kakṣeyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, Dhṛteyu, Jaleyu, Sthaleyu, Dharmeyu, Saṃnateyu, Dhaneyu, and Vaneyu. These were his sons.
Rantināra was the son of Ṛteyu;
Rantināra obtained three sons: Sumati, Apratiratha, and Dhruva.
From Apratiratha came Kaṇva, and his son was Medhātithi.
From whom the Kaṇvāyana brahmins originated.
Apratiratha had another son, Ailīna;
from him were born four sons, beginning with Duṣyanta.
From Duṣyanta was born the universal emperor Bharata, concerning whose name a verse is sung by the gods:
"The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very one by whom he was begotten.
Support your son, O Duṣyanta; do not despise Śakuntalā."
"O god among men, the son who has conceived the seed leads [his father] from the abode of Yama;
you are the progenitor of this child—Śakuntalā has spoken the truth."
Bharata had nine sons by his three wives;
thinking, "These are not worthy of me," their mothers killed them for fear of being abandoned.

Then, when his birth of sons was thus rendered fruitless, Bharata, desiring sons and performing the Marutsoma sacrifice, [obtained offspring] from the seed of Bṛhaspati, which had been cast aside by Dīrghatamas with his heel.
A son named Bharadvāja, born from Amata, the wife of Utathya, was granted by the Maruts.
For him as well, a verse explaining the etymology of his name is recited: // ViP_4.19.4 //
"O deluded one, support this Bhāradvāja; support this Bhāradvāja, O Bṛhaspati!
Since his parents, having spoken thus, departed, therefore he is called Bhāradvāja."
Thus, because the birth of his son had been rendered futile by the Maruts, Bharadvāja thereafter received the name Vitatha.
From Vitatha was born a son named Manyu.
The sons of Manyu were Bṛhatkṣatra, Mahāvīrya, and Naragarga.
From Nara was born Saṃkṛti; from Saṃkṛti were born Ruci and Dhīra, and Antideva.
From Garga came Śini; from him were born the Gārgyas and Śainyas, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
From Mahāvīrya was born a son named Durukṣaya; he had three sons— Trayyāruṇa, Puṣkariṇa, and Kapi—
and all three of them later attained the status of Brahmins.
From Bṛhatkṣatra came Suhotra; from Suhotra came Hastin, who founded this city of Hastināpura. Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and Purumīḍha were the three sons of Hastin.
From Ajamīḍha came Kaṇva, and from Kaṇva came Medhātithi.
From whom the Kaṇvāyana twice-born ones [descended].
Another son of Ajamīḍha was Bṛhadiṣu; from him came Bṛhaddhanus, from him Bṛhatkarmā, from him Jayadratha, from him Viśvajit,
and from him Senajit.
Rucirāśva, Kāśya, Dṛḍhahanu, Vatsahanu, and Saṃjña were the sons of Senajit.
From Rucirāśva came Pṛthusena;
from him came Pāra; and from Pāra came Nīpa.
He had one hundred sons;
among them, the eldest was Samara, the lord of Kāmpilya.
Samaras also had three sons: Pāra, Supāra, and Sadāśva.
From Pāra came Pṛthu; from Pṛthu came Sukṛti; and from Sukṛti came Vibhrāja.
From him was born Aṇuha, who married Kṛtvi by name, the daughter of Śuka.
From Aṇuha came Brahmadatta;
from him, Viṣvaksena; his son was Udaksena; his son was Bhallāṭa.
The son of Dvimīḍha was named Yavīnara; his son was Dhṛtimān; from him came Satyadhṛti; from him, Dṛḍhanemi; from him, Supārśva; from him, Sumati; from him, Sannatimān;
and from Sannatimān was born Kṛta, whom Hiraṇyanābha instructed in yoga.
He who composed the twenty-four Saṃhitās of the Prācya Sāmagas.
And by him, Ugrāyudha was slain, who had extensively brought about the destruction of the Nīpas.
From Ugrāyudha came Kṣemya; from Kṣemya, Suvīra; from him, Ripuñjaya; and from him, Bahuratha—these were the Pauravas.
Ajamīḍha had a wife named Nalinī, and by her a son named Nīla was born. From him also came Śānti; from Śānti, Suśānti; and from Suśānti, Purujānu.
From him came Cakṣu, from him Haryaśva;
from Haryaśva came Mudgala, Sṛñjaya, Bṛhadiṣu, Pravīra, and Kāmpilya.
"These sons of mine are capable of protecting the territories of these five [kingdoms]," so it was said by their father.
From him came the Pāñcālas.
From Mudgala were born the Maudgalyas, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
From Mudgala came Vadhyaśva; from Vadhyaśva was born a pair consisting of Divodāsa and Ahalyā. From Śaradvat and Ahalyā was born Śatānanda.
From Śatānanda was born Satyadhṛti, who reached the furthest limit of the science of archery (dhanurveda).
Upon seeing the beautiful Apsaras Urvaśī, however, the seed of Satyadhṛti fell, discharged, into a clump of reeds.
That [seed] developed into two offspring, a boy and a girl;
having gone out on a hunt, Śāntanu saw them and took them out of compassion.
Then that prince Kṛpa and the maiden Kṛpī became the mother of Aśvatthāman and the wife of Droṇa.
Mitrāyu was the son of Divodāsa; from Mitrāyu came the king named Cyavana, and from Cyavana came Sudāsa. From him came Saudāsa, then Sahadeva, and his son was Somaka.
From him, Jantu was born as the eldest of a hundred sons. Among them, the youngest was Pṛṣata; from Pṛṣata came Drupada, from him Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and from him Dhṛṣṭaketu.
Ajamīḍha had another son named Ṛkṣa.
From Ṛkṣa came Saṃvaraṇa, and from Saṃvaraṇa came Kuru,
who made this field of dharma known as Kurukṣetra.
Sudhanus, Jahnu, Parīkṣit, and others were the sons of Kuru.
Sudhanus’s son was Suhotra; from him came Cyavana, and from Cyavana came Kṛtaka.
From him was born Uparicara Vasu.
Seven sons were born to Vasu, headed by Bṛhadratha, Pratyagra, Kuśāmba, Māvellaka, and Matsya.
From Bṛhadratha came Kuśāgra; from him, Ṛṣabha; and from him, Puṣpavān.

From him [Bṛhadratha] was born Satyahita; from him, Sudhanvan; and his son was Jantu. Another son of Bṛhadratha was born from two fragments of flesh joined together by Jarā (Old Age), and thus he was named Jarāsandha.
From him came Sahadeva; from him, Somapi; and from him, Śrutaśravas.
These were the kings of Magadha.
[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
The venerable Parāśara said:
Parīkṣit had four sons: Janamejaya, Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
Jahnu, however, had a son named Suratha.
And his son was Vidūratha;
Vidūratha’s son was Sārvabhauma; from Sārvabhauma came Jayatsena; from him, Ārādhita; from him, Ayutāyu; from Ayutāyu, Akrodhana;
and from him, Devātithi.
From him was born Ṛkṣa.
From Ṛkṣa came Bhīmasena, and from him Dilīpa; from Dilīpa came Pratīpa. He, too, had three sons named Devāpi, Śāṃtanu, and Bāhlīka.
Devāpi entered the forest while still a child.
Śāntanu became the protector of the earth,
and this verse concerning him is sung throughout the world:
"Whomever he touches with his two hands, though aged, he attains youth."
Because he attained supreme peace through that action, he was called Śāṃtanu.
In the kingdom of that Śāntanu, the god did not send rain for twelve years.
Then, perceiving the impending destruction of his entire kingdom, the king questioned the brahmins:
"Why does the rain-god not send rain upon our kingdom? What is my transgression?
They said to him:
"You are consuming this earth which belongs to your elder brother; you are a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother). Thus addressed, he asked them again, "What should I do?
They spoke once more:

"As long as Devāpi is not overcome by defects such as falling from his status, so long shall the kingdom rightfully belong to him; therefore, enough of this—let it be given to him. When this was said, Aśmasārin, the foremost of his ministers, dispatched ascetics in that forest who were speakers of words contradicting the Vedic injunctions.
By them, the intellect of that prince of straightforward mind was led onto a path that followed a course contrary to the Vedas.
King Śāntanu, his grief and lamentation aroused by the words of the twice-born, went to the forest with those brahmins at his head to bestow the kingdom upon his elder brother.
Upon arriving at that hermitage, they approached Devāpi, the son of the lord of the earth.
Those brahmins, whose speech was bound to the declarations of the Vedas, spoke to him words full of meaning, saying that the kingdom must be ruled by the elder brother.
Devāpi, for his part, addressed them with many kinds of arguments that were contrary to the teachings of the Vedas and refuted by logic.
Thereupon, those Brahmins said to Śāntanu:

"Come, O King, enough of this excessive persistence; the fault of the drought has already been pacified, brought about by the utterance of these harmful words that defile the Vedic injunctions from time immemorial."

Since it was declared that there is no offense of "marrying before the elder brother" (*pārivedya*) when the elder has fallen [from his status], Śāntanu returned to his own city and ruled the kingdom.
While he was thus defiled by uttering words contrary to the Vedic injunctions, the divine rain-god Parjanya sent down rain for the completion of all things.
To Bāhlīka, a son named Somadatta was born.
Somadatta also had three sons named Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śalya.
To Śāntanu, moreover, was born a son named Bhīṣma, of noble fame and a knower of the meaning of all the scriptures, by the immortal river Gaṅgā.
And upon Satyavatī, Śāntanu begot two sons, Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya.
Citrāṅgada, however, was slain in battle by the Gandharva Citrāṅgada while still a youth.
Vicitravīrya also married Ambikā and Ambālikā, the two daughters of the King of Kāśī;
but from the exhaustion caused by excessive indulgence with them, he was seized by consumption and passed away.
And by the command of Satyavatī, her son Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, considering his mother’s word to be not to be transgressed, begot Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu in the wives of Vicitravīrya,
and Vidura upon the maidservant sent by them.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra also begot a hundred sons, the chief of whom were Duryodhana and Duḥśāsana.

Furthermore, when Pāṇḍu’s capacity for procreation had been destroyed by a sage’s curse in the forest, five sons— Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and Arjuna— were begotten upon Kuntī by Dharma, Vāyu, and Śakra, and Nakula and Sahadeva upon Mādrī by the two Aśvins.
And they had five sons by Draupadī:
Prativindhya from Yudhiṣṭhira, Śrutasoma from Bhīmasena, Śrutakīrti from Arjuna, Śatānīka from Nakula, and Śrutakarman from Sahadeva.
Furthermore, there were other sons of the Pāṇḍavas as follows:
Yaudheyī obtained a son, Devaka, from Yudhiṣṭhira;
Hiḍimbā received a son, Ghaṭotkaca, from Bhīmasena;
and Kāśī likewise obtained a son, Sarvatraga, from Bhīmasena alone.
And from Sahadeva, Vijayā obtained a son named Suhotra;
and Nakula also begot Niramitra upon Kareṇumatī.
Arjuna also had a son named Irāvān by Ulūpī, the daughter of the Nāgas;
and by the daughter of the lord of Maṇipura, according to the custom of a "daughter-son" (*putrikā-dharma*), Arjuna begot a son named Babhruvāhana.
And from Subhadrā, even while still a child, was born that Abhimanyu, who possessed exceeding strength and prowess and was the conqueror of all enemy chariot-warriors;
he was born to Uttarā from Abhimanyu, when the Kurus were nearly extinct, having been reduced to ashes even in the womb by the Brahmāstra weapon discharged by Aśvatthāman—
the Lord whose pair of feet are worshipped by all gods and asuras, who had assumed a human form by his own will.
Through that power, Parīkṣit regained his life and was born as he who now protects this circle of the earth with a dharma of unimpaired continuity. 420.13 //
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
§ Parāśara said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the kings who are yet to come.
Of this present lord of the earth, Parīkṣit, there will also be four sons: Janamejaya, Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
His successor will be Śatānīka,

who, having studied the Vedas under Yājñavalkya and acquired weapons from Kṛpa, will— with the mental disposition detached from sense objects and proficient in the knowledge of the Self through the instruction of Śaunaka— attain supreme Nirvāṇa;
and after Śatānīka, there will be Aśvamedhadatta.
For that reason as well, they brought forth Adhisīmakṛṣṇa from among the Adhisīmakṛṣṇas,
[saying]: "He who shall dwell in Kauśāmbī when Hastināpura has been swept away by the Gaṅgā,
he too shall have a son named Uṣṇa."

From Uṣṇa came Citraratha; from him, Śuciratha; from him, Vṛṣṇimān; from him, Suṣeṇa; from him, Sunītha; from Sunītha, Ṛca; from him, Nṛcakṣus; his son was Sukhibala; from him, Pariplava; from him, Sunaya; from him, Medhāvī;
from him, Pañjaya; from him, Mṛdu; from him, Tigma; and from Tigma came Bṛhadratha.
From him came Vasudāna; after him was Śatānīka;
from him Udayana; from Udayana came Ahīnara; from him Daṇḍapāṇi; from him Niramitra; and from him Kṣemaka.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
This lineage of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, honored by royal sages,
shall reach its end in the Kali age upon reaching King Kṣemaka.
[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Hereafter, the future kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty are described.
Bṛhatkṣaṇa was the son of Bṛhadbala.
From him came Urukṣaya; from him, Vatsa; from Vatsa, Vatsavyūha; from him, Prativyoma; his son was Divākara; and from him, Sahadeva.
From him came Bṛhadaśva; his son was Bhānuratha; his son was Pratītāśva; his son was Supratīka.
From him came Marudeva; from Marudeva came Sunakṣatra; from him came Kiṃnara; from Kiṃnara came Antarikṣa; from him came Suvarṇa; and from him came Amitrajit.
And after him came Bṛhadrāja; his son was Dharmī; from Dharmī came Kṛtañjaya;
from Kṛtañjaya came Raṇañjaya; from Raṇañjaya came Sañjaya; from him came Śākya;
from Śākya came Śuddhodana; from him came Rāhula; and from him, Prasenajit.
From him came Kṣudraka, from him Kuṇḍaka, and from him Suratha;
his son was Sumitra, the last of this line. These were the Ikṣvākus of the lineage of Bṛhadbala.
Regarding this, there is a genealogical verse:
"This lineage of the Ikṣvākus shall end with Sumitra;
for upon reaching him as king, it will come to its conclusion in the Kali age."
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the fourth book of the glorious *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Parāśara said: I shall now relate the succession of the future Bārhadratha kings of Magadha.
For in this lineage there were those of great strength, of whom Jarāsaṃdha was the foremost.

From Sahadeva, the son of Jarāsandha, will come Somāpi; from him, Śrutavān; from him, Ayutāyus; and from him, Niramitra. His son will be Sukṣatra, and from him, Bṛhatkarman. From him, Senajit; from him, Śrutañjaya; from him, Vipra; his son will be named Śuci. From him, Kṣemya; from him, Suvrata; from Suvrata, Dharma; and from him, Suśrama.
