From him will come Dṛḍhasena, from him Sumati, from him Subala, and his son will be Sunīta. From him will come Satyajit, from Satyajit Viśvajit, and his son will be Ripuñjaya.
These shall be the Bārhadratha kings, and they will rule for one thousand years.
[Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Of this last descendant of Bṛhadratha, named Ripuñjaya, there will be a minister named Munika.
And having killed that master, he will consecrate his own son named Pradyota.
His son will be named Pālaka;
after him will come Viśākhayūpa, his son Janaka, and his son Nandivardhana.
Thus, these five Pradyotas shall enjoy the earth for one hundred and thirty-eight years.
Then Śiśunāga will arise, and his son will be Kākavarṇa;
his son will be Kṣemadharmā, and his son will be Kṣatraujas; his son will be Vidhisāra, and from him Ajātaśatru will come.
From him [Darbhaka] came Darbhaka, and from Darbhaka, Udayana; from him came Nandivardhana, and from him, Mahānandin.
Thus, these ten Śaiśunāga kings will rule for three hundred and sixty-two years.
The son of Mahānandin, born from the womb of a Śūdra woman, will be the exceedingly greedy Mahāpadma Nanda; like another Paraśurāma, he will be the destroyer of all the Kṣatriyas.
From that time forward, the protectors of the earth shall be Śūdras;
and that Mahāpadma, whose command remains unchallenged, shall rule the earth under a single umbrella.
He too will have eight sons, beginning with Sumālya, who will rule the earth after that Mahāpadma. Mahāpadma and his sons will be lords of the earth for one hundred years.
The Brahmin Kauṭilya will rescue these nine Nandas.
In their absence, the Mauryas shall enjoy the earth;
Kautilya himself shall consecrate Candragupta in the kingdom.
His son will be Bindusāra; his son will be Aśokavardhana; from him Suyaśas; from him Daśaratha; from him Saṅgata; from him Śāliśūka; from him Somaśarmā; from him Śatadhanvan;
and after him, one named Bṛhadratha will arise.
Thus there will be ten Maurya kings for one hundred and thirty-seven years; at the end of their reign, the Śuṅgas shall rule the earth.
The commander-in-chief Puṣyamitra, having slain his master, will rule the kingdom.
His son will be Agnimitra; from him, Sujyeṣṭha; from him, Vasumitra; from him, Ardraka; from him, Pulindaka; from him, Ghoṣavasu; from him, Vajramitra; from him, Bhāgavata; and from him, Devabhūti.
These ten Śuṅgas shall enjoy the earth for one hundred and twelve years.
Then this earth shall go to the Kaṇvas.
But when King Devabhūti of the Śuṅga dynasty falls into misfortune, his own minister named Kaṇva, known as Vasudeva, will overthrow him and enjoy the earth himself.
His son will be Bhūmitra, and his son will be Nārāyaṇa. The son of Nārāyaṇa will be Suśarman.
These four Kāṇvāyanas shall be lords of the earth for forty-five years. But having forcibly killed Suśarman, the Kāṇva, his own servant named Śipraka, born of the Andhra caste, will enjoy the earth;
thereafter, his brother named Kṛṣṇa will become the king.

His son was Śrī-Śātakarṇi; his [son] was Pūrṇotsaṅga; and his son was Śātakarṇi. From him came Lambodara; from him, Divīlaka; from him, Meghasvāti; from him, Paṭumān; from him, Ariṣṭakarman; from him, Hāla; from Hāla, Pattalaka; from him, Pravillasena; from him, Sundara Śātakarṇi; from him, Cakora Śātakarṇi; from him, Śivasvāti; and from him, Gomatīputra; his son was Pulimān.
His son will be Śātakarṇī; from him, Śivaśrī; from him, Śivaskandha;
from him, Yajñaśrī; from him, Vijaya; and from him, Candraśrī; his son will be Pulomāvin.
Thus these Andhrabhṛtyas shall enjoy the earth for three hundred and fifty-six years.
There will be seven Ābhīras and ten Gardabhilas as rulers;
after that, sixteen Śakas will become kings;
then eight Yavanas, fourteen Tuṣāras, thirteen Muṇḍas, and eleven Maunas.
These shall rule the earth for thirteen hundred and ninety-nine years.

Then the Pauras and eleven kings will enjoy the earth for three hundred years. When they have perished, the Kailakila Yavanas will become kings, though they are not consecrated with the royal aspersion (*amūrdhābhiṣikta*). Among them, Vindhyaśakti [will be the first].

From him will come Purañjaya, from him Rāmacandra, from him Dharma, from Dharma Vaṅgara, Kṛtanandana, Suṣinandin, his brother Nandiyaśas, and the two heroes Śiśuka and Pravīra; these shall rule for one hundred and six years.
Then there will be his thirteen sons and three Bāhlikas.
Then there will be thirteen Puṣyamitras and Paṭumitras, seven Mekalas, and seven Andhras;
in Kosala, however, there will be exactly nine kings,
and as many Naisadhas as well.
In Magadha, however, one known as Viśvasphaṭika will establish other castes;
he will place fishermen, artisans, Pulindas, and Brahmins in the kingdom,
having utterly destroyed the entire Kṣatriya lineage.
The nine Nāgas shall enjoy the city named Padmāvatī, Mathurā, and the region along the Ganges up to Prayāga; the Māgadhas and the Guptas shall enjoy [the rest].
Devarakṣita shall protect Kośala, Oḍra, Puṇḍra, Tāmralipta, and the coastal cities. Kaliṅga, Māhiṣaka, and Mahendra shall enjoy the mountain cave of Bhūmi.
The descendants of Maṇidhānaka will rule over the provinces of Naiṣadha, Naimiṣika, and Kālatoyā;
those called Kanaka will rule over the Trairājya and the Mūṣika provinces;
and the Vrātyas, along with the twice-born, Ābhīras, Śūdras, and others, will rule over Saurāṣṭra, Avanti, the Śūdra lands, and the regions of Arbuda and Marubhūmi.
The Vrātyas, Mlecchas, and others who are Śūdras will enjoy the lands along the banks of the Indus, the Dāvikā, the Candrabhāgā, and the regions of Kaśmīra.
All these kings on earth will be contemporaries;

they will be of little grace and great wrath, always delighting in falsehood and unrighteousness, committing the slaughter of women, children, and cows, and taking pleasure in seizing the property of others.
They will be of little worth, mostly risen and fallen, short-lived, possessed of great desires, and having little dharma.
And the people, intermingled with them, following their conduct and flourishing under the patronage of kings, along with the Mleccha teachers acting in opposition, will destroy the subjects.
Consequently, through a daily decrease that becomes ever more minute until its cessation, there will be the destruction of the world’s dharma and artha.
Therefore, wealth alone is the cause of noble lineage; wealth alone is the cause of all religious duties;
and mutual affection alone is the cause of the bond of marriage.
Womanhood itself is the cause of enjoyment;
falsehood alone is the cause of victory in legal proceedings;
and the possession of jewels and copper alone is the cause of [obtaining] land.
The sacred thread alone is the cause of Brahminhood; the wearing of the marks alone is the cause of the stage of life;
and improper conduct alone is the cause of livelihood.
Weakness alone is the cause of non-return;
utterance born of fear alone is the cause of scholarship;
and wealth alone is the cause of goodness.
Bathing alone is the cause of adornment;
giving alone is the cause of dharma;
taking as one's own alone is the cause of marriage.
"The body itself shall be the vessel;
the water from afar shall be the sacred ford.
Thus, on this earth-mandala abounding in manifold defects, whoever among all the social orders is powerful shall become the sovereign.
And thus, those who are exceedingly greedy and unable to endure the burden of taxes will take refuge in the inner valleys of the mountains;
they will subsist on honey, vegetables, roots, fruits, leaves, flowers, and the like;
and clothing themselves in garments made of tree bark and rags, they will have very large families and endure cold, wind, heat, and rain.
No one shall live for twenty-three years; and here in this Kali Yuga, this entire population will incessantly undergo decline and reach its end.

When the Vedic and Smārta dharma had fallen into extreme disorder and the Kali age was nearly exhausted, an incarnation of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— the creator of the entire universe, the teacher of all moving and unmoving beings, the primordial, the final, the all-pervading, the embodiment of Brahman, and whose form is the Self— endowed with the eightfold divine perfections, appeared in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas, the preeminent Brāhmaṇa of Śambalagrāma.
Having descended here upon this earth in the form of Kalki, he—whose power and majesty are limitless—will bring to destruction all those barbarians, bandits, and those of wicked conduct and mind.
He will then establish the entire world in its own respective duties.
Immediately thereafter, at the conclusion of the entire Kali age, the minds of the very same people who have awakened at the end of the night will become as pure as stainless crystal.
And from those seeds of all those humans, even though they have been transformed by the conditions of that time, there will be the procreation of offspring;
and those children shall indeed follow the dharma of the Kṛta Yuga.
To this it is replied:
When the Moon and the Sun, and Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati,
shall come together in a single zodiacal sign, then the Kṛta age will begin.
O best of sages, those kings who have passed away, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come, have all been described within these genealogies.
From the birth of Parīkṣit until the consecration of Nanda,
this period of one thousand and fifteen years is to be known.
Of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), those two who are first seen risen in the sky—
between them, whichever constellation is seen level at night,
with that [constellation] the Seven Sages remain conjoined for a hundred years of men.
O best of the twice-born, at that time during the reign of Pārīkṣita, the moon was in the Maghā constellation;
then the Kali age commenced, consisting of twelve hundred years.
O twice-born one, at the very moment when the portion of the Blessed Viṣṇu born in the lineage of Vasudeva ascended to heaven, Kali arrived here.
As long as he touched this earth with his two lotus-feet,
Kali was not able to embrace the world.
When that portion of the eternal Viṣṇu had departed from there,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, together with his younger brothers, abandoned the kingdom and went from earth to heaven.
Having seen those adverse omens after Kṛṣṇa had departed, that Pāṇḍava, Parīkṣit, then performed his consecration.
And when these great seers depart for Pūrvāṣāḍhā,
then this Kali age shall begin to increase from the time of Nanda onward.
On that very day when Kṛṣṇa ascended to heaven, the Kali Yuga began; learn from me its duration.
O twice-born one, by human calculation, this Kali age will indeed last for three hundred and sixty thousand years.
Then, by calculation, those seven hundred and five divine years will have passed in their entirety, and the Kṛta age shall begin once again.
O best of the twice-born, in age after age, thousands of high-souled Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras have passed away.
Because the names [of the lineages] are so numerous, a complete enumeration for each family has not been recited by me, as it would involve excessive repetition.
King Devāpi, the descendant of Puru, and Maru, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
were both endowed with the power of great yoga and took refuge in the village of Kalāpa.
Having come here at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, those two will indeed become the founders of the Kṣatriya order; established as the seeds of Manu’s lineage, they shall prevail.
By this sequential process, the sons of Manu enjoyed the earth throughout three ages known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth.
But in the Kali age, some who have become like seeds remain upon the earth,
just as Devāpi and Māru are currently situated.
This genealogy of kings has been recounted by me to you only in brief;
it is not possible to recount it in its entirety even in hundreds of lifetimes.
These and other kings, blinded by delusion, have established a sense of ownership over this earthly realm with their impermanent bodies as if they were eternal.
"How shall this earth remain unshakable for me? How shall it belong to my son?
How shall it belong to my lineage?"—afflicted by such thoughts, these kings met their end.
There were others even earlier than them, and likewise others after them;
those yet to come shall pass away, as will others who follow after them.
Beholding the lords of men busily engaged in expeditions for the conquest of their own sons,
the earth seems to laugh in autumn with the blossoming of flowers.
O Maitreya, learn here these verses sung by the Earth,
which the sage Asita spoke to Janaka Dharmadhvaja.
The Earth said:
How is it that this delusion exists even among wise kings, by which their minds become so excessively trusting, though they are as fragile as foam?
Having first achieved victory over themselves, counselors desire to conquer;
thereafter, they seek to conquer their servants, the citizens, and likewise their enemies.
"In this sequence we shall conquer the earth together with its oceans"—
with minds thus attached, they do not perceive that death is close at hand.
Then his own circle of vassals, bounded by the ocean, comes under his control.
To what extent does this result from self-conquest? The fruit of self-conquest is liberation.
"Having abandoned her, my ancestors departed, and even my father did not take her when he went;
yet, out of delusion, these kings desire to win her, thinking, 'She is mine.'"
On my account, conflicts arise among fathers and sons, as well as among brothers,
for those whose minds are possessed by extreme delusion and attached to the sense of "mine."
"This entire earth is mine; it is mine, and it belongs eternally to my lineage as well.
For whatever king has died here, he was surely possessed of evil intellect. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.24.53)
Having seen me alone, with a mind devoid of the sense of "mine," departing for the path of death,
how can that sense of "mine" arising from me still find a foothold in the heart of one who stands as my descendant?

When kings speak through the mouths of their messengers to their own enemy, saying, "This earth is mine; abandon it quickly," I feel great laughter toward them, yet I also approach those fools with compassion.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, these are the verses sung by the Earth;
when heard, they cause the sense of "mine-ness" to dissolve, just as snow is melted by heat.
Thus, this lineage of Manu has been correctly described by me to you,
in which the kings were portions of the portions of Viṣṇu engaged in the maintenance of the world.
Whoever listens with devotion to this lineage of Manu in its proper sequence,
all the sins of that pure-souled person are indeed utterly destroyed.

Having heard this entire, praiseworthy lineage of the Moon and the Sun— namely Ikṣvāku, Jahnu, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Aṅga, and the Raghus— one whose senses are unimpeded attains incomparable abundance of wealth and grain.
Having learned that Yayāti, Nahuṣa, and others—
who possessed great strength, great heroism, and infinite stores of wealth— had reached their ultimate end;
The lords of men, who had been rendered mere subjects of legend by powerful Time, [were restored].
Having heard this, a man of perfected wisdom does not cultivate a sense of "mine" toward his children, wife, and so forth, nor toward houses, fields, or wealth.
By those heroic men, with upraised arms, austerities were performed for many groups of years;
and sacrifices were offered by those powerful and exceedingly valiant ones, yet they have all been reduced to mere legends by the power of time.
Pṛthu, who moved unhindered through all the worlds and whose circle of enemies was destroyed,
perished when struck by the wind of Time, like the cotton-wool of a silk-cotton tree cast into a fire.
Kārtavīrya, who, having subdued all the continents and destroyed the circle of his enemies, enjoyed [the earth]— he,
of whom one speaks in the course of conversations, is himself the cause of conceptual construction and discursive thought.

Alas for the power of Death! How could the sovereignty of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa—who had illuminated the quarters with his splendor and had never even beheld the descendants of Raghu—not be reduced to ashes in an instant by the mere casting down of a frown?
Since even the universal monarch named Māndhātṛ on earth has become merely the body of a story,
what virtuous person, having heard this, would still harbor a sense of "mine" toward their own self, even if they are dull-witted?
Bhagīratha and others, Sagara, Kakutstha, Daśānana, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as Yudhiṣṭhira and the rest—these have truly existed; it is not false. Yet, we do not know where they are now.
Those kings who exist now and those who are yet to come, O best of Brahmins, whom I have described as possessing fierce valor—
whether they be these or others who are to be named in that manner— all shall become exactly like those of former times.
Having understood this, a wise man should not cultivate a sense of "mine-ness" even toward his own self;
let alone children, wives, fields, and so forth, which are other than the body.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. V inserts:
Homage to the venerable Rāmānuja.
Maitreya said: You have related the entire expansion of the dynasties of kings,
and the accounts of their deeds within those lineages have been described exactly as they occurred.
"O Brahman-sage, I wish to hear in full detail and without omission about this partial incarnation (aṃśāvatāra) of Viṣṇu who was born in the Yadu lineage."
O Sage, tell me those deeds which the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, performed after descending upon the earth through his various portions.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to this which I have been asked by you here—
the account of the birth of those born from portions of portions of Viṣṇu, which is for the benefit of the world.
O great sage, in former times Vasudeva married the highly fortunate Devakī, the daughter of Devaka, who was like a goddess.
Kaṃsa, the enhancer of the Bhojas, acting as their charioteer, urged on that excellent chariot for the union of Vasudeva and Devakī.
"O fool, this woman whom you carry on the chariot together with her husband—
the eighth child she bears shall take away your life."
Parāśara said:
Having heard this, the mighty Kaṃsa took up his sword and began to kill Devakī; then Vasudeva spoke these words.
"O illustrious one, Devakī must not be slain by you;
I shall deliver to you all the children born from her womb."
Parāśara said:
"O best of the twice-born, Kaṃsa said 'So be it' to Vasudeva;
and out of respect for him, he did not have Devakī executed."
At that very time, however, the earth, oppressed by an excessive burden,
went to Mount Meru at the assembly of the inhabitants of heaven.
Then the Earth, speaking with piteous words out of distress, bowed down to all the gods including Brahmā and related everything that had occurred.
The Earth said:
Fire is the preceptor of gold, and the Sun is the supreme preceptor of cows;
for me, as well as for all the worlds, Nārāyaṇa is the preceptor.
Brahmā, the Lord of Prajāpati, is the first-born even of the ancients;
he is Time, whose nature consists of kalās, kāṣṭhās, and nimeṣas, and who possesses an unmanifest form.
O best of gods, this assembly of you all is a portion of that [Supreme Being].
The Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Rudras, Vasus, Aśvins, and Vahnis, as well as the Pitṛs who are the creators of the worlds, with Atri at their head; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.1.17.
This is the form of that immeasurable, great-souled Viṣṇu.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, daityas, piśācas, uragas, dānavas,
gandharvas, and apsarases are indeed the form of the high-souled Viṣṇu.
The planets, constellations, and stars; the variegated sky, fire, water, and wind;
myself, and the objects of the senses—all this world is composed of Viṣṇu.
Nevertheless, the various forms of that [universe], which possesses manifold aspects, day and night undergo the state of being the oppressor and the oppressed, like the waves in the ocean.
Therefore, at present, these Daityas, led by Kālanemi,
having invaded the world of mortals, oppress the subjects day and night.
That great asura Kālanemi, who was slain by the powerful Viṣṇu,
has been born as Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena.
Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, Keśin, Pralamba, and likewise Naraka; the very fierce Asura Sunda, and Bāṇa, the son of Bali.
Likewise, there were others of great prowess who were born in the palaces of kings; I do not venture to enumerate those evil-minded ones.
"Here there are numerous Akṣauhiṇī divisions of gods possessing divine forms,
and of the haughty lords of the Daityas who are endowed with great strength, all directed against me."
"O lords of the immortals, afflicted by the pain of that heavy burden, I am unable to sustain myself;
thus do I inform you."
O highly fortunate ones, let that which will relieve my burden be performed,
so that I, utterly overwhelmed, may not go to the netherworld (rasātala).
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of the Earth in their entirety, Brahmā was then urged by the gods and spoke for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
Brahmā said: "O dwellers of heaven, everything that the Earth has said is true;
I, Bhava, and you—all are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa."
But as for those manifestations of his, among them alone there exists a state of mutual superiority and inferiority by way of being the sublated and the sublator.
Therefore, come, let us go to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk;
having propitiated Hari there, we shall indeed inform him of everything.
At all times, for the sake of the world, he who is the soul of all and consists of the universe descends to earth with even a small portion of himself and establishes the dharma.
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, the Grandfather (Brahmā) departed from there together with the gods;
and with a concentrated mind, he praised the one who has Garuḍa as his banner (Viṣṇu).

Brahmā said: "There are two kinds of knowledge, O Lord, which you have not described—the higher (parā) and likewise the lower (aparā). These indeed are your two forms, consisting of the manifest (mūrta) and the unmanifest (amūrta)."
O you whose self is exceedingly subtle and beyond the gross, O knower of all things, there are indeed two Brahmans:
the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman) and the Supreme Brahman which belongs to Him who consists of Brahman.
You are the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda;
you are phonetics, ritual procedure, etymology, prosody, and astronomy.
Likewise, O Lord Adhokṣaja, there are the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as grammar,
Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and the Dharmaśāstras.
O Primordial Lord, even that speech which investigates the self, the body, and the qualities—
its practice is not different from the nature of the inner self itself.
You are the unmanifest, indefinable, inconceivable, and without color; you are without hands, feet, or form—Viṣṇu, eternally higher than the highest.
Though earless, you hear; though eyeless, you see; though one, you take on many forms.
Without feet or hands, you are swift and a grasper; you know everything, yet you are not an object of universal knowledge.
O Supreme Self, for one who beholds You—who are subtler than the subtle and whose nature is non-existent—the cessation of ignorance is supreme;
his intellect, O Worthy One, bears nothing other than that which is higher than the highest, Your most excellent form.

You are the origin of the universe and its protector; all beings dwell within you. That which was and that which is to be is subtler than the subtlest; you alone are the Supreme Person beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
The one Lord, the sacrificial fire, being fourfold, bestows upon the world an abundance of splendor;
O Creator of infinite form, you whose eye is everywhere, you have established your station in three ways.
Just as fire, though single and of an unchanging nature, is kindled in many ways through various modifications of its fuel,
so too do you, O Lord, who are omnipresent and of a single form, manifest manifold forms in succession.
You alone are that which is the foremost and supreme state, which the wise perceive as visible through knowledge;
O Supreme Self, there is no other essential nature whatsoever than you—neither what has been nor what is yet to be.

You are the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest; you possess the forms of both the collective totality and the individual; you are all-knowing, all-seeing, and endowed with all power, knowledge, strength, and spiritual perfection.
Neither diminished nor increasing, he is self-dependent, beginningless, and the master of himself;
he is untouched by fatigue, sloth, fear, anger, desire, and the like.
He is faultless, supreme, peaceful, without support, and the imperishable sequence;
he is the Lord of all, the ultimate substratum, the essence of all abodes, and the undecaying.
O You who have transcended all veils, O You whose meditation is without support,
O Abode of great majesty, salutations to You, the Supreme Person!
O all-pervading one, your supreme assumption of a body is not for no reason, nor for a [mere] cause, nor from both cause and non-cause; it is solely for the protection of dharma.
Parāśara said:
Having heard this praise in his mind,
the unborn Lord Hari, the soul of the universe who assumes all forms, spoke to Brahmā.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmā, whatever you desire from me along with the gods, let that be spoken in its entirety; consider it as already accomplished."
Parāśara said:
Then Brahmā, having beheld that divine universal form of Hari,
praised him again while the gods stood with their bodies bowed down in awe.
Brahmā said:
Homage, homage be unto you, O thousand-formed one, with a thousand arms and many faces and feet!
Homage, homage to you, O immeasurable one, who effects the activity, destruction, and maintenance of the world.

O Blessed One, supreme Self, who are subtler than the subtlest, greater than the greatest in measure, and possessed of a nature more weighty than even the most weighty; O Supreme One, who are the primary source like the primordial matter (pradhāna) of the intellect and the senses, be gracious!
O God, this earth, whose mountain fastenings are oppressed by the great asuras born from the earth,
approaches you— the boundless shore of the shoreless— for refuge, in order that her burden may be removed.
"Here we are, as well as this enemy of Vṛtra (Indra), these two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins), and Varuṇa;
and here are the Rudras, the Vasus together with Sūrya, and others headed by Samīraṇa (Vāyu) and Agni."
"O Lord of the Gods, all these gods and whatever task has been assigned to them by me, O Master—all that we shall carry out while obeying your command; we shall remain ever thus, free from fault."
Parāśara said:
While being thus praised, O great sage, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, plucked out two hairs from himself, one white and one black.
And he said to the gods: "These two, my sons, having descended upon the surface of the earth, will effect the removal of the burden and the suffering of the world."
And let all the gods descend to the surface of the earth with their own portions and wage war against the intoxicated great asuras who were born in former times.
Then, crushed by the fall of my gaze, all those Daityas will undoubtedly go to their destruction upon the surface of the earth.
O gods, this eighth embryo of Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva who is like a goddess, shall be my hair.
Having descended there, Hari said, "He will slay Kaṃsa on earth and bring about the destruction of Kālanemi," and then he vanished.
Then, having prostrated before that invisible Great Soul,
those gods departed for the summit of Mount Meru and descended once more to the surface of the earth.
The venerable sage Nārada declared: "In his eighth conception from Devakī, the Supporter of the Earth shall be born for Kaṃsa."
Having heard that from Nārada, Kaṃsa then became enraged and imprisoned Devakī and Vasudeva within his own house.
O twice-born one, as he had previously declared to Kaṃsa regarding every child born,
Vasudeva likewise delivered each son to him.
The sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu were renowned as the Ṣaḍgarbhas;
at the command of Viṣṇu, Nidrā (Sleep) placed them successively within the womb.
The Blessed Lord Hari spoke to that Yoganidrā Mahāmāyā Vaiṣṇavī, by whom— through ignorance— the entire world is deluded.
The Blessed One said: "O Sleep, go at my command to those residing in the depths of Pātāla;
one by one, lead the six embryos into the womb of Devakī."
When those haters have been slain by Kaṃsa, then my portion known as Śeṣa shall arise from a fraction of a fraction within her womb as the seventh [incarnation].
O Goddess, while Vasudeva’s wife Rohiṇī remains in Gokula,
you must carry this child in your womb until his birth.
"Out of fear of King Bhoja, people will say that the seventh embryo of Devakī has fallen due to the obstruction of her confinement."
Then, because he draws forth the embryo, that hero— who resembles the peak of a white mountain— shall indeed obtain the name Saṃkarṣaṇa in the world.
Then I shall be born in the auspicious womb of Devakī;
you must enter the womb of Yaśodā without delay.
And during the rainy season, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhas, I shall be born at night;
and on the ninth day, you shall obtain my birth.
O blameless one, Vasudeva, his mind impelled by my power, will carry me from Yaśodā’s bed to you on Devakī’s.
And Kaṃsa, O Goddess, having taken you up, will throw you onto the surface of a mountain rock; and you shall attain a station in the intermediate space.
Then Śakra, the hundred-eyed one, bowing out of respect for me with his head bent low in prostration, will accept you as his sister.
Then, having slain Śumbha, Niśumbha, and thousands of other Daityas,
you shall adorn the entire earth with many sacred sites.
You are prosperity, humility, fame, forbearance, heaven, earth, and fortitude; you are modesty, nourishment, and the dawn—and whatever else exists, that too is you alone.
And whatever knowledge there may be, that too is yours alone through my grace.
Those who address you as Āryā, Durgā, Vedagarbhā, Ambikā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Kṣemyā, and Kṣemakarī; ||| ViP_5.1.84 ||
In the morning and in the afternoon, they shall offer praise with bodies bowed low;
for by my grace, everything they desire shall come to pass.
Worshipped with offerings of liquor and meat, as well as various kinds of food and edibles,
you, being pleased, shall bestow upon men the fulfillment of all their desires without exception.
"O auspicious lady, by my grace, all of them shall at all times undoubtedly become free from doubt; go, O Goddess, as has been instructed."
[Thus ends the first chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
"Just as it was told by the God of gods at that time, so did she, the sustainer of the world..."
He performed the ritual placement of the six embryos and the drawing forth of another.
When the seventh month had arrived and Rohiṇī was reached, Hari then entered Devakī’s womb for the benefit of the three worlds.
On that very same day, Yoganidrā likewise entered the womb of Yaśodā,
exactly as had been declared by the Supreme Lord.
Then, O twice-born one, the host of planets moved properly in the sky,
and auspicious seasons prevailed once Viṣṇu’s portion had descended to earth.
No one was able to look upon Devakī because of her excessive splendor;
seeing her blazing so brightly, the minds of all were shaken with agitation.
Unseen by men or women, the hosts of deities praised Devakī day and night as she bore Viṣṇu within her body.
The deities said:
"In ancient times, you were the supreme, subtle Prakṛti, whose womb was Brahman;
from her, O most beautiful one, you were born as Vāṇī, the womb of the Vedas for the Creator of the World."
Containing within her the nature of all that is to be created, she became the eternal source of creation;
indeed, the threefold Veda (Trayī) became the womb of sacrifice and the seed of everything.
You alone are the sacrifice that contains the fruit, just as the fire-drill contains the fire;
you are Aditi who bears the gods within her, and likewise Diti who bears the Daityas within her.

You are moonlight containing the essence of day; you are humility containing the essence of knowledge; you are statesmanship bearing the essence of policy; and you are modesty carrying the essence of deference.
You are Desire, whose womb is sensual pleasure; you are Contentment, pregnant with satisfaction;
you are Intelligence, whose womb is awakening; and you are Fortitude, who bears the womb of steadfastness.
The sky, containing the planets, constellations, and stars, is composed of all causes;
these, O Goddess, are your manifestations, as are thousands of others.

O auspicious Mother of the World, in this manner, the entire earth— adorned with oceans, rivers, islands, forests, and cities, and rich in villages, hamlets, and market towns— is currently contained within your womb in an incalculable number.
All the fires, all the waters, and all the winds;
Likewise, the Mahoragas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and Guhyakas [were present].
Variegated with planets, lunar mansions, and stars, it was crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots.
And that which provides space for everything without exception is the sky.
The world of the earth (bhūrloka), then the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the world of heaven (svarloka), then mahar, jana,
tapa, and the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka)— all this is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), O auspicious lady.
Within that space dwell the gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as Mahoragas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and Guhyakas.
O illustrious lady, humans, animals, and whatever other living beings there may be—all these abide within him; he is that infinite one, the Lord of all, the creator of all things.
He whose true nature as form and action is not within the scope of any means of valid cognition— that Viṣṇu is the one dwelling in your womb.
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you are knowledge, and you are nectar; you are the light in the sky.
For the sake of protecting all the worlds, you have descended upon the surface of the earth.
Be gracious, O Goddess; O auspicious one, bestow welfare upon the entire world.
Out of love, support that Īśāna by whom the whole universe is sustained.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Being thus praised by the gods, she conceived the God.
By means of his embryo, he [beheld] the lotus-eyed one, the cause of protection for the worlds.
Then, for the sake of awakening the lotus of the entire world, the sun-like Great Soul Acyuta manifested from Devakī, who was like the morning twilight.
The day of his birth became exceedingly delightful for all the world, making the quarters of the sky pure, just as the moonlight of the full moon does.
When Janārdana was being born, the winds became exceedingly calm, the rivers attained tranquility, and the fierce storms reached a state of serenity.
The rivers produced enchanting music with their own sounds;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The gods dwelling on earth and in the intermediate space showered rains of flowers;
and the fires, though normally blazing, became tranquil as Janārdana was being born.
O twice-born one, as Janārdana was being born at midnight— the support of all—
clouds thundered softly while releasing showers of flowers.
Beholding him who had appeared, possessing four arms with the luster of the petals of a full-blown blue lotus and the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, Ānakadundubhi offered praise.
Having praised him with pleasing words, that high-minded one,
O best of the twice-born, then made his request out of fear of Kaṃsa.
Vasudeva said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you are known; O God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, withdraw this divine form by your grace."
"O Lord, this very day Kaṃsa inflicts torment upon me, having learned that you have descended into my palace. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.3.11)
Devakī said:

May that God of gods be gracious—he who is of infinite form, whose body is the entire universe, and who even within the womb sustains the worlds with his own person; he who has manifested the form of a child through his own divine power.
O All-pervading One, assume this four-armed form so that Kamsa,
the son of a Daitya, may not recognize you as an incarnation.
The Blessed One said:
"O Goddess, that which was previously praised by you while desiring a son has today become fruitful for you, since I have been born from your womb."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, the Blessed One became silent;
Vasudeva also, taking him with him at night, went outside.
And while Ānakadundubhi was departing, the guards there and the gatekeepers of Mathurā were rendered unconscious by yogic sleep.
And as the clouds rained down exceedingly copious water at night,
Śeṣa followed Ānakadundubhi, shielding him with his hoods.
Carrying Viṣṇu, Vasudeva proceeded along the Yamunā, which was exceedingly deep, agitated by hundreds of various whirlpools, and flowing only knee-deep.
Taking Kaṃsa’s hand, he beheld Nanda and the other elder cowherds who had arrived right there on the bank of the Yamunā.
At that time, O Maitreya, while the people were deluded, Yaśodā too was stupefied by yogic sleep (yoganidrā), and she gave birth to that very same girl while her kin remained in a state of confusion.
Vasudeva, of immeasurable splendor, having placed the boy down and taken the girl,
quickly returned to Yaśodā’s bedchamber.
And having awakened, Yaśodā beheld her newborn son, dark as the petal of a blue lotus; thereupon, she attained exceeding joy.
Vasudeva also, having taken the girl to his own residence,
placed her upon Devakī’s bed and remained there as before.
Then, O twice-born one, hearing the cry of a child, the guards rose up suddenly and informed Kaṃsa of Devakī’s delivery.
Kaṃsa then quickly approached and seized the girl; he was stopped by Devakī, who, with her voice choked with grief, cried out, "Release her! Release her! (ViP 5.3.25).
And she hurled it onto the surface of a rock; once hurled, it remained suspended in the sky and assumed a massive form with eight great arms bearing weapons.
She laughed loudly in that same manner and, filled with wrath, said to Kaṃsa:
"Kaṃsa, what is the use of this child born of me whom you have cast away? He is the one who will slay you."
In former times, Death was the very self of the gods;
therefore, having reflected well upon this, act quickly for your own welfare.
Having spoken thus, the goddess, adorned with divine garlands and perfumes,
departed through the sky while being praised by the Siddhas, even as the King of the Bhojas looked on.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Then Kaṃsa, with an agitated mind, spoke to all the great Asuras.
He summoned the foremost among the asuras, headed by Pralambakeśin.
Kaṃsa said:
"O Pralamba, O mighty-armed Keśin, Dhenuka, Pūtanā,
Ariṣṭa, and all you others, listen to my words."
"Indeed, an effort was made by the wicked immortals to kill me;
yet, O heroes, scorched by my prowess, I do not take them into account."
What is to be accomplished by Indra, who possesses little prowess; or by Hara, who wanders alone;
or even by Hari, the slayer of demons, who strikes only at vulnerabilities?
What need is there for the Ādityas with their limited power, or for the Vasus, or for the Agnis,
or for all the other immortals who have been conquered by the strength of my arms?
Have you not seen how that Lord of the Immortals, having entered into combat with me,
fled away carrying the arrows on his back alone, and not upon his chest?

Why is it that all the rulers on earth, terrified by the strength of my arms,
have not submitted, with the sole exception of their preceptor Jarāsandha?
O best of Daityas, contempt for mortals arises within me;
O heroes, even when they are intent on their efforts, laughter arises in me toward them.
Nevertheless, O lords of the Daityas, I must indeed strive even more to bring about the harm of those wicked and evil-minded ones.
Therefore, whatever ascetics there may be on earth, and those who perform sacrifices—
their slaughter must be carried out with all one's soul for the sake of harming the gods.
"Death has indeed arisen for me, and it has occurred before as well," thus spoke the young girl born from the womb of Devakī.
Therefore, the greatest effort must be exerted against the foolish on this earth;
wherever a fool possesses excessive power, he must be slain with diligent care.
Having thus commanded the Asuras, Kaṃsa then entered his own palace and released Vasudeva and Devakī from their confinement.
Kaṃsa said:
"The embryos of you two have now been slain by me in vain;
for some other boy entirely has arisen for my destruction."
Therefore, enough with this grief; for that was surely destined for you.
Who indeed is not destroyed at the end of their lifespan, even if they are but children?
Parāśara said:
Having thus consoled and released them, Kaṃsa, filled with apprehension,
O best of the twice-born, entered his own inner apartments once again.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having been released, Vasudeva also went to Nanda’s cart.
He saw Nanda greatly rejoiced, thinking, "A son has indeed been born to me."
Vasudeva also said to him respectfully, "By good fortune! By good fortune!
since a son has now been born to you even in your old age.
"O wealthy ones, you have indeed paid the king's entire annual tax;
therefore, since you have come for that purpose, you should not remain here."
"The purpose for which you have come has been accomplished; why do you remain?
O Nanda, you should go quickly now to your own Gokula."
My own young son, who was born of Rohiṇī,
must also be protected by you, just as this is your own biological son.
Having been addressed thus, the mighty cowherds, led by Nandagopa, departed after paying the tax, with their goods loaded upon carts.
While they were dwelling in Gokula, Pūtanā, the slayer of children,
took the sleeping Kṛṣṇa at night and gave her breast to him.
To whichever child Pūtanā offers her breast at night,
that child’s body is destroyed in an instant.
Filled with rage, Kṛṣṇa seized her breast, which was being pressed firmly by her hands, and drank from it along with her very life-breath.
With her great shrieks silenced and the bonds of her sinews severed,
the most terrifying Pūtanā fell to the ground while dying.
Awakened by the terror of hearing that roar,
the inhabitants of Vraja saw Kṛṣṇa in Pūtanā’s lap and her herself cast down.
O best of the twice-born, Yaśodā, filled with terror, took Kṛṣṇa and,
whirling a cow’s tail with her hand, removed the infant's affliction.
Taking cow dung, Nanda the cowherd also placed it upon Kṛṣṇa’s head, providing protection while uttering this: Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.5.13.
Nandagopa said: May Hari, the source of all beings without exception, protect you—
he from whose navel-born lotus the universe arose.
May that Lord Keśava, who assumed the form of a boar and by whom the earth— the support of the world— is held up, supported by the tip of his tusk, protect you.
May that omnipresent Keśava, who in the form of Nṛsiṃha tore open the chest of his enemy with the tips of his claws, protect you everywhere.
May Vāmana protect you always— he who in an instant became Trivikrama, having traversed the three worlds with his strides and brandishing his flashing weapons.
May Govinda protect your head; may Keśava guard your throat; may Viṣṇu protect your private parts along with your belly; and may Janārdana protect your shanks and feet.
May the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, whose sovereignty is unimpeded, protect your face, arms, forearms, mind, and all your senses.
May those preta-s, kūṣmāṇḍa-s, and rākṣasa-s who are hostile to you go to their destruction at the sound of the conch of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace.
May Vaikuṇṭha protect you in the cardinal directions, Madhusūdana in the intermediate directions,
Hṛṣīkeśa in the sky, and Mahīdhara protect you upon the earth.
Parāśara said:
Thus, having had the rites for his well-being performed by Nanda the cowherd,
the boy was laid beneath the cart on the surface of a small cradle.
And those cowherds, seeing the massive corpse of the dead Pūtanā, then experienced supreme terror and amazement.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Once, Madhusūdana was lying beneath a cart.
Desiring milk, she raised her feet upward and wept.
By the blow of his foot, the cart was overturned;
its jars and vessels were shattered, and it fell upside down.
Then, O twice-born one, all the cowherds and cowherdesses, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", arrived and beheld the child lying on his back.
"O cowherds, by whom was this cart overturned? "By this boy," the children there replied, "it was knocked down. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.6.4)
"While we were crying, we saw a cart overturned by the trampling of a footstep; this was certainly not the work of anyone else."
Then once again the cowherds were filled with extreme wonder;
Nanda Gopa too, utterly amazed, took up the child.
Yaśodā, seeing the fragments and shards of the pots broken upon the cart,
nevertheless honored the cart with curd, flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice.
And Garga, urged by Vasudeva, remained concealed there in Gokula and performed the sacramental rites for the two of them among the cowherds.
The highly intelligent Garga, the best among the wise, gave them names, calling the eldest Rāma and the other Kṛṣṇa.
O Brahmin, in a very short time, both of those boys became covered in dust in Vraja, with their knees and hands rubbed raw.
With their limbs smeared with cow-dung and ashes, wandering here and there,
neither Yaśodā nor Rohiṇī was able to restrain them.
Playing within the cow-pen and having entered the calf-pen once more,
they were intent on pulling the tails of the calves born on that very day.
When Yaśodā was unable to restrain those two boys, who were both extremely restless as they played together in one place, [she bound them].
Yaśodā, taking up a staff, pursued him in anger.
Then, in her rage, she threatened Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals.
There is no external covering for that by which this [universe] is covered.
He proceeded to bind that lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa with a rope.
Then, having bound him with a rope, she fastened Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, to the middle of a mortar; and being indignant, she said this to him: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.6.14.
"If you are able, go, O you of most fickle behavior!
Having said this, the housewife performed her own duties.
Then, while she was thus distracted, the lotus-eyed one, dragging the mortar along, passed between the twin *arjuna* trees.
By pulling the mortar sideways between the two trees,
he broke those two Yamalārjuna trees, whose lofty branch-tips had been interlocked.
Then, alarmed by the sound of the creaking,
the people of Vraja arrived and beheld the two great trees.
With their shoulders broken and their branches shattered, they lay fallen upon the earth;
between them stood a young calf, its smile-like radiance white with the light of its newly sprouted small teeth,
its belly bound tightly with a rope.
And from that, he attained the state of Dāmodara because of his binding with ropes.
Then all the elder cowherds, led by Nanda Gopa,
being anxious and terrified of the great portents, held a consultation.
"We have no need to remain here; let us go to another great forest, for many portents are seen here that are causes of destruction."
The destruction of Pūtanā, the overturning of the cart, and likewise the falling of the two trees without any fault such as wind; ||| ViP_5.6.23 |||
"Let us go from this place to Vṛndāvana without delay, before the calamity caused by the great terrestrial portents overcomes Vraja."
Having thus resolved upon their departure, all those inhabitants of Vraja said to each of their own families, "Let us go quickly; do not delay."
Then, in an instant, the inhabitants of Vraja set out with their wagons and herds of cattle,
driving the cowherd boys along in groups.
O twice-born one, at that moment, the cow-pen was instantly cleared of all its material parts and became filled with crows and vultures.
Vṛndāvana was meditated upon with an auspicious mind by the Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, as he desired the increase of the cows.
Then, O best of the twice-born, even during that exceedingly harsh summer season,
fresh grass sprouted everywhere as if it were the rainy season.
Then the entire settlement of Vraja was encamped in Vṛndāvana,
extending as far as the wagon-paths and arranged in the shape of a half-moon.
Thereupon Rāma and Dāmodara became cowherd boys;
staying together in one place in the cow-pen, they engaged in the play of childhood.
They wore chaplets fashioned from *barhi* grass and ear-ornaments made of wild flowers;
they played musical instruments made from cowherds' flutes and produced sounds with leaf-instruments.
Wearing side-locks like young boys, the two princes, like the sons of Agni,
wandered through that great forest laughing and playing.
In some places they wandered about, laughing with one another and playing with other cowherd boys, while tending the calves.
As time passed, those two, having reached the age of seven years, became protectors of the entire world as cowherds in Mahāvraja.
Then the rainy season arrived, with the sky completely shrouded by masses of clouds,
as if making all the quarters of the horizon one through torrents of rain.
At that time, the earth, rich with lush new grass and strewn with *śakragopa* insects,
appeared as if made of emerald and adorned with rubies.
The waters of the rivers flowing out of their courses were swept away in every direction,
just as the minds of the ill-behaved are carried off upon attaining new fortune.
The spotless moon, obscured by dark clouds, did not shine,
just as the discourse of the virtuous does not shine when confronted by the boastful speeches of fools.
Even by a bow devoid of string, the position in the sky was attained by Śakra,
just as it is obtained through the patronage of a king who lacks discernment.
Upon the back of the cloud, the pure row of cranes shone like the exceedingly beautiful conduct and gestures of a man of noble birth toward one of wicked character.
The lightning, being exceedingly fickle, did not find stability in the sky,
just as friendship extended by a wicked person finds no firm footing in an excellent man.
The paths became indistinct,
covered with a fresh growth of young grass, like the words of the dull-witted that have reached a different meaning.
At that time, in that great forest filled with wild peacocks and deer,
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma wandered about joyfully together with the cowherds.
In some places, both of them, delighting in singing and rhythmic measures, wandered together with the cows; in other places, they took refuge beneath the shade of trees that were exceedingly cool.

In some places they were variegated with garlands of kadamba flowers, in others they wore peacock garlands; in various places they appeared wonderful, adorned with the diverse minerals of the mountain.
In some places they slept soundly on beds of leaves, seeking intervals of rest; in others, while the clouds thundered, they were filled with cries of "Alas! Alas! at the sight of the rain.
While the other cowherds were singing, the two players of the cowherd flutes occasionally excelled in their praise, accompanied by the cries of peacocks.
Thus, filled with various emotions and joined by supreme affection,
the two of them wandered through that forest with contented minds as they played.
And at the wrong time of day, they returned together with the cattle, accompanied by a herd of cowherds.
After 50ab, Ś₁, V₁, B insert:
"Both Kṛṣṇa and Bala arrived, wearing the dress of cowherds."
And at the improper time, having returned to the cow-pen according to their pleasure, the two of great strength—
Accompanied by their peers, the cowherds, they played like two immortals.
After verse 51, the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition inserts:
"In this manner, the two highly resplendent Rāma and Kṛṣṇa dwelt there."
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Paraśara said:
Once, Kṛṣṇa went to Vṛndāvana without Rāma.
Surrounded by cowherds and radiant with garlands of wild flowers, he wandered about.
Then he went to the Kālindī, which was graced by rolling waves and seemed to laugh on all sides with masses of foam clinging to its banks.
And there he beheld the exceedingly terrifying lake of the naga Kāliya, filled with water from which poison and fire issued forth, and which was most fearsome to behold.
Its great trees on the banks were scorched by the spreading fire of poison,
and the birds were burnt by the touch of the spray of water driven by the wind.
Beholding him, who was exceedingly fierce and like another mouth of Death,
the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana reflected.
In this place dwells that evil-minded Kāliya, whose weapon is poison;
he who was defeated by me fled to the ocean, abandoning his wickedness.
Thus, this entire Yamunā, the consort of the ocean, has been defiled;
she is no longer utilized by men or even by herds of cattle afflicted by thirst.
Therefore, I must subdue this king of the nagas,
so that the inhabitants of Vraja may dwell here in happiness for a long time.
For this purpose I have taken incarnation in this world of men:
that peace should be established for these evil-minded ones who stand upon the wrong path.
Climbing this broad-branched kadamba tree standing not far from here, I shall leap into this lake inhabited by the wind-eater.
Parāśara said: Having reflected thus and having tightly girded his loins,
he then swiftly plunged into that lake belonging to the king of serpents.
As it fell there, that great lake was so violently agitated by it that it drenched those trees which stood at a very great distance.
Sprinkled by the water and wind heated by the flames of that malignant poison,
those trees immediately burst into flame, their fire spreading across the quarters of the sky.
Then Kṛṣṇa slapped his arm upon the serpent-pool;
and hearing that sound, the king of the serpents quickly approached.
With eyes copper-red from anger, he was surrounded by other air-eating serpents of great venom whose hoods were filled with the flames of poison.
And hundreds of Naga wives, adorned with captivating necklaces,
shone with the beauty of earrings swaying as their trembling bodies moved.
Then Kṛṣṇa was cast into a confinement of serpents by them;
and they bit Kṛṣṇa with mouths filled with the flames of poison.
Seeing him fallen there, crushed by the coils of the serpent,
the cowherds returned to Vraja and wailed, overcome with grief.
The cowherds said:
"Kṛṣṇa has fallen into a swoon, submerged in the lake of Kāliya;
he is being devoured by the king of serpents. Come, let us go and see!"
Having heard those words, which were like the falling of a thunderbolt, the cowherds and the cowherd women, led by Yaśodā, then went quickly to the lake.
"Alas, alas! Where is he? crying thus, the people of the cowherds, overcome with extreme agitation, wandered together with Yaśodā and went forth quickly, stumbling at every step.
Nandagopa, the cowherds, and Rāma of wondrous prowess,
longing for a sight of Kṛṣṇa, quickly went to the Yamunā.
And there they also saw Kṛṣṇa, fallen under the power of the king of serpents, rendered motionless and entwined by the coils of the serpent.
And Nanda Gopa, O best of sages, became motionless, fixing his gaze upon his son’s face; and the highly fortunate Yaśodā likewise became so.
But other cowherd women, weeping and overcome with grief, beheld him and spoke to Keśava with affection, their voices faltering from fear and distress: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.7.25.
"Let us all enter this great lake together with Yaśodā; it is not proper for us to go back to Vraja, O King of Nagas."
What is day without the sun? What is night without the moon? What are cows without a bull? And what is Vraja without Kṛṣṇa?
"Separated from this Kṛṣṇa, we shall not go to Gokula;
it would be like a lake devoid of water that cannot be resorted to in the forest."
Where this Hari, whose splendor resembles the petals of a blue lotus, does not exist.
By whom was this man born, who does not possess human behavior?
It is a marvel that even he finds delight in dwelling among mortals.
Not seeing Hari, whose eyes possess the clear beauty of the petals of a full-blown lotus, how will you remain in the cowherd settlement, O wretched ones?
"Without the lotus-eyed one, whose exceedingly sweet speech has captivated all our wealth of minds, we shall not go to Nanda’s Gokula."
Behold, O cowherd girls, even though he was encircled by the king of serpents,
Kṛṣṇa’s face was beautiful with a smile as he looked toward us.
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of the cowherd women, and seeing the cowherds distressed with fear, the mighty son of Rohiṇī stood with a fixed gaze.
He saw Nanda, who was exceedingly dejected and had fixed his gaze upon his son’s face,
and Yaśodā, who was overwhelmed by fainting due to her realization of Kṛṣṇa’s greatness.
Balabhadra said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, for what purpose is this human state manifested by you? Do you not know yourself to be truly infinite?"
You are the navel of this world, the support for all things like the hub of spokes;
you are the creator, the destroyer, and the protector of the three worlds, composed of the triple Veda.
O You of inconceivable nature, You are meditated upon by Śaṇmukha, Rudra, the Aśvins, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the Maruts, and Agni, as well as by all the yogis.
O Lord of the World, for the sake of the world and with the desire to remove its burden, you have descended here among mortals; and I am your elder brother, born from a portion of yourself.
O Blessed One, while you were engaged in human pastimes, all the gods remained there constantly, imitating your very play.
O Eternal One, having first caused the celestial damsels to descend here in Gokula for your own sport, you yourself subsequently descended.
O Kṛṣṇa, for those two of you who have descended here, the cowherds and the cowherd women are indeed your kinsmen;
why do you neglect your kin as they languish?
The human nature has been displayed, and the fickleness of a child has been shown;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, let this evil-minded one whose weapons are his fangs now be subdued.
Parāśara said: Thus reminded, Kṛṣṇa, his lips parted with a smile,
slapped his arms and released his own body from the bondage of the serpent's coils.
Having bent down his middle hood with both hands and climbed upon it, he of great prowess danced upon its curved head.
Wounds appeared on his hood from Kṛṣṇa’s trampling with his feet; wherever he raised his head, Kṛṣṇa’s head bowed down there.
The serpent fell into a swoon from the whirling, piercing blows of Kṛṣṇa;
struck by the falling of the staff, he vomited much blood.
Beholding him with his head and neck bent back and blood flowing from his mouths,
his wives sought refuge with Madhusūdana.
The wives of the Nāgas said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you are known; you are the Lord of all, the unsurpassed.
You are that supreme, inconceivable light, of which the Supreme Lord is a portion."
The gods are not capable of praising that Lord who has no other source of birth;
how then shall a woman describe his true nature?
How shall we praise him, of whom the entire universe— composed of earth, sky, water, fire, and air— is but a minute fraction of a fraction?
We bow to Him whose true nature yogis, though striving constantly, do not know;
who is the ultimate reality, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
Salutation always to Him, whose birth the Creator does not bring about, whose end the Destroyer does not effect, and for whom there is no other maker of his duration.
Not even the slightest anger exists in you; your sole purpose is the preservation of stability.
Therefore, hear the reason for this subduing of Kāliya.
Women are objects of compassion for the virtuous, as are foolish and wretched beings; therefore, O bestower of boons, let this wretched man be forgiven.
"You are the support of the entire world, yet this serpent is of little strength;
if he were to be oppressed by your foot, he would lose his life within half a moment."
Where is this serpent of little power, and where are you, the refuge of the world?
For joy and hatred have as their objects those who are equal or superior, O Imperishable One.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, show favor to this one who is despondent;
this serpent is giving up his life—grant him the boon of his master's life.
After verse 57, the editor adds:
O Lord of gods, who is to be known through the Vedānta, the destroyer of the wicked Daityas!
Parāśara said:
When they had spoken thus, the serpent, though his body was exhausted, took heart and slowly spoke these words: "Be gracious, O God of gods! *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 5.7.58.
Kāliya said:
O Lord, Your supreme sovereignty possesses the eightfold qualities and is innate;
for one in whom all excellence has been surpassed, what indeed shall I praise?
You are the beyond, you are the first of that which is beyond; the supreme essence is beyond you, yet you are the highest even beyond that. How then could I possibly praise you?
Since Brahmā, Rudra, Candra, Indra, the Maruts, and the Aśvins,
as well as the Vasus together with the Ādityas [are his], what indeed shall I praise?
How can I praise Him, of whom this entire universe is but a minute portion of a single limb, while [the world] is but a portion of a limb of His conceptual construction?
After verse 62, Ś₂ and D₇ insert:
"While Kāliya was thus being praised by the wives of the Nāgas..."
Having prostrated with a hymn of praise and having joined his palms in reverence, he should speak.
Homage to you, O Protector, Blessed One, Lord of the Yellow-Robed and of the Unfallen!
Be gracious to me, O Lord of the World; what was it, O Master, that I did not understand?
How indeed shall I praise him, whose ultimate reality even the foremost of the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know, for he possesses both the nature of existence and non-existence?
And how can he, who is worshipped by Brahmā and others with divine flowers and unguents produced in the Nandana grove and other celestial realms, be worshipped by me?
How can he, whose forms of incarnation the King of the Gods always worships,
yet does not know his supreme form, be worshipped by me?
Having withdrawn all the senses from their objects,
whom the yogis worship through meditation— how can he be worshipped by me?
How can that Lord, whose form yogis conceive in their hearts and worship through meditation with the flowers of their own being, be worshipped by me?
Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, I am not capable of worship, praise, or the like; my mental activity consists solely of compassion for you. Be gracious to me!
"O Keśava, this serpent race is cruel, and I was born into it;
this is its inherent nature here, O Acyuta, and not my fault."
Everything in this world is created by you, and likewise it is withdrawn;
and birth, form, and essential nature are all created by you as the creator.
O Lord, just as I have been created by you with my birth, my form,
and my inherent nature, so too has this action been performed by me.
O God of gods, if I were to act otherwise than this,
then the infliction of punishment upon me would indeed be just, according to your own word.
Nevertheless, this punishment which the Lord of the World has inflicted upon me has been endured;
it is better that I receive this punishment from you than any other.
My vigor destroyed, my poison neutralized, I have been subdued by you, O Acyuta;
let one life be granted to me—command me, what shall I do?
The Blessed One said: "O serpent, you must never remain here in the waters of the Yamunā;
go with your servants and retinue to the waters of the ocean."
And seeing my footprints upon your head in the ocean, O serpent,
Garuḍa, the enemy of the pannagas, will not strike you.
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus to the king of serpents, the Blessed Lord Hari released him;
and he too, having bowed down to Kṛṣṇa, departed for the ocean, the reservoir of waters.
While all living beings looked on, together with his servants, children, and kinsmen,
and accompanied by all his wives, he abandoned his own lake.
Having embraced the serpent that had departed only to return as if dead,
the cowherds drenched Govinda on the head with tears born from their eyes.
Seeing the river of auspicious waters, other cowherds, their minds filled with wonder, joyfully praised Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are untiring.
He, whose charming deeds were celebrated through his exploits, was being sung of by the cowherd girls.
Accompanied by Baladeva, Nanda, and Yaśodā. (ViP 5.7.81ab*10)
Being praised by the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa returned to Vraja.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
And Baladeva and Keśava, once again together, were tending the cows.
Wandering through that forest, they came upon a delightful grove of palm trees.
That palm grove was constantly inhabited by a Dānava named Dhenuka,
who had the form of a donkey and subsisted on the flesh of men and cattle.
Seeing that palm grove endowed with an abundance of ripe fruit, the cowherds were filled with longing and spoke these words regarding the gathering of the fruit: *Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.8.3*
The cowherds said:
"O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, this region is always protected by Dhenuka; therefore, these [fruits] are indeed ripe."
"Behold the fruits of the palmyra trees, which perfume the quarters with their fragrance;
we desire these—if it pleases you, let them be felled."
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of the cowherd boys, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa indeed caused the palmyra fruits to fall upon the ground.
Having said, "This must be told," he indeed caused them to fall.
Hearing the sound of the falling fruits, that evil-minded Dānava-donkey, who was difficult to approach, arrived there in a rage.
Then that powerful one struck him on the chest with both his hind legs; he was seized by those two, and he too was seized by him.
Having seized him and whirled him around, he cast him, now lifeless, with great force right there upon that king of grasses (the palm tree) in the sky.
Then, leaping from the tops of the palm trees, Khara caused many fruits to fall upon the earth,
just as a great wind causes clouds to descend.
Kṛṣṇa and Balabhadra also effortlessly cast down other Daityas who had arrived there disguised as donkeys, hurling them onto the tops of palm trees.
O Maitreya, in an instant the earth was adorned with ripe palm fruits and by the carcasses of the donkey-like Daityas, and thus it shone even more brilliantly.
Then, O twice-born one, the cows, free from affliction, grazed happily on the fresh grass in that palm grove— grass that had never been eaten before.
Bala, having entered, shook the palm trees with his two arms. (ViP 5.8.13*12:1)
He caused the fruits to fall by his might, like a mighty elephant.
Hearing the sound of the falling fruits, the asura-donkey [cried out].
He rushed toward the surface of the earth, making the mountain tremble all around.
Having swiftly approached from behind, the powerful one struck Bala with both his feet.
Striking them on their chests and letting out a cry, Khara roamed about.
Approaching him once more, the enraged jackal stood nearby, intent on reviling him.
O King, in his rage, he cast his other two feet toward Bala.
Having seized it and whirled it around with one hand, he cast it forth.
He hurled it at the tip of the king of grass (the *śara*), having abandoned his life by whirling it around.
Struck by him, the great palm tree, massive in its trunk, trembled violently.
He struck one standing at his side, and he was broken; he [in turn] struck another, and that one also [was broken].
Slain by the blows from his own body as it was cast off in play by the child.
All the palm trees trembled, as if shaken by a great wind.
This is not surprising in the Blessed One, the infinite Lord of the World.
This [universe] is woven warp and woof within that, just as a cloth is woven upon its threads.
Then the kinsmen of Dhenuka [attacked] both Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
All the jackals, their kinsmen having been slain, fled away in a state of agitation.
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma [received] those various [weapons] as they fell upon them with the ease of a king's sport.
He sent those who had grasped his hind feet among the lords of grass (the lions).
Having heard of their exceedingly great deed, the gods and others—
They released showers of flowers, played musical instruments, and offered hymns of praise.
Then, having eaten the palmyra fruits, the men were freed from their trepidation.
And the cattle grazed upon the grass in the forest where the cow had been slain.
Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious.
Being praised by his followers and the cowherds, he entered Vraja together with his elder brother.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
When that Daitya Rāsabha had been struck down along with his followers,
The beautiful Tālavana forest, frequented by cows, cowherds, and cowherd-maidens, shone forth.
Then, their joy having been restored, both sons of Vasudeva,
after slaying the Daitya Dhenuka, arrived at the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree.
They were playing, singing aloud, searching among the trees,
driving the cows to a distance, and calling them by their names.
With their yoke-ropes and halters removed from their shoulders and adorned with forest garlands,
those two great-souled ones shone like two young bulls with fresh horns.
Then, with their garments dyed by the powders of gold and collyrium,
those two appeared like white and black clouds accompanied by Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
Having descended to earth, those two who were the lords of all the lords of the world sported with one another in games well-known among people.
Delighting in human virtues and honoring their humanity,
they roamed the forest with diversions suited to their kind and qualities.
Then those two of great strength engaged in physical exercise there by means of swings, wrestling matches, projectiles, and likewise stones.
While the two were thus enjoying themselves, an Asura named Pralamba, desiring to seize them and disguised in the dress of a cowherd, arrived there.
Assuming a human form, that supreme Dānava Pralamba, a non-human being, fearlessly plunged into their midst.
Seeking a vulnerability between the two of them, he considered Kṛṣṇa to be unbearable; then he set his heart on killing the son of Rohiṇī.
Then, performing the childhood game called "The Deer's Play," they all leaped up simultaneously in pairs.
Govinda leaped with Śrīdāman, Balarāma with Pralamba,
and the other cowherds leaped together with their respective companions.
For verses 1–13ab, Ś₂ and D₇ substitute the following:
"Then, when the summer season had arrived at the place known as Bhāṇḍīraka..."
While Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were tending the cattle with cowherds in that forest, [the following occurred].
The Asura Pralamba, assuming the form of a cow, went there with the desire to seize him.
Even though he was all-knowing and the Blessed One who perceives everything, the descendant of Daśārha knew that.
He approved of that friendship, while contemplating his own destruction.
There, having summoned the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa, who knows the ways of sport, spoke to them.
"O cowherds, we shall sport in pairs, each according to his own inclination."
There, the cowherd Cakru, the lord of the herdsmen, [honored] Rāma and Janārdana.
Some were joined with Kṛṣṇa, and others were with Rāma.
They engaged in various sports characterized by riding and being ridden.
There, the victors mount [the chariots], and the defeated are carried away.
Carrying, driving, and tending the wealth of cattle.
Led by Kṛṣṇa, they went to the banyan tree named Bhāṇḍiraka.
For those such as Śrīdāman, Vṛṣabha, and others were indeed the companions of Rāma.
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa and the others carried those various victors in their play.
The defeated [demons] carried Kṛṣṇa and the blessed Śrīdāman.
Bhadrasena [attacked] Ṛṣabha, while Pralamba [attacked] the son of Rohiṇī.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rohiṇī, defeated Śrīdāman and Pralamba;
the other cowherds who sided with Kṛṣṇa were victorious, while the others were defeated.
Driving one another along, they all who had been defeated there reached the trunk of the Bhāṇḍīra tree and indeed turned back again.
But the Dānava, having quickly lifted Saṃkarṣaṇa onto his shoulder,
did not remain still but moved away, like a rain-cloud carrying the moon.
Unable to bear the burden of the son of Rohiṇī,
that best of Dānavas grew to a truly massive body, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
But Saṃkarṣaṇa, seeing him with a form like a scorched mountain,
adorned with hanging garlands and ornaments, and with a head towering with a crown, [was amazed].
Fierce, with eyes like the wheels of a cart, he made the earth tremble with the placement of his feet.
With a fearless mind, that Rākṣasa [attacked] the son of Rohiṇī. (ViP 5.9.19ab*)14)
Then, as he was being carried away, he spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa:
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Look! I am being carried away by some Daitya in the guise of a cowherd, with a form as lofty as a mountain!"
"O Slayer of Madhu, tell me what must be done by me here at this moment;
for this evil-souled one is departing with extreme haste."
Parāśara said: Govinda, the Great Soul who knew the measure of the strength and heroism of Rauhineya’s son, spoke to that Rāma with his lips parted by a smile.
The Blessed One said: Why is this human state being so clearly assumed by you, O Soul of All, whose nature is the secret of all secrets? (ViP 5.9.23)
O Lord of the entire world, remember yourself— the sole cause, the first-born of all causes—
who existed as that One even when the world was a single ocean.
"Do you not know how both you and I have come to this mortal world as a single cause for the purpose of removing the earth's burden? (ViP 5.9.25)
The sky is your head, and your body consists of water; the earth is your feet, and the infinite fire is your mouth.
The moon is your mind, the wind is your breath, and the four directions, O Imperishable One, are your arms.
For you are the Great-Souled One with a thousand faces, possessing a body with a thousand hands and feet;
you are the primordial source born from a thousand lotuses, whom sages praise in a thousand ways.
For no one other than yourself knows your divine form, which is the form of your incarnations among all the gods;
do you not know that you are worshipped because, in the end, the entire universe attains dissolution within you alone?
Supported by you, O one of infinite forms, this earth sustains the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings;
yet you, O Unborn One, in the form of Time divided into the Kṛta and other ages, consume this world beginning with a mere blink of an eye.
Just as water, having been turned to stone by the submarine fire,
returns to its state of fluidity upon reaching the Himalayas through contact with the rays of the sun, so too does the self [attain its true nature].
O Lord, in this very manner, when you have withdrawn this entire world,
it must necessarily once again become the world as it was before, as you exert yourself for its creation at the beginning of every kalpa.
O Soul of the Universe, you and I are indeed the single cause of this world;
for the sake of the world, we are established as two distinct entities.
Therefore, O immeasurable one, remember your true self; slay the Dānava, and by assuming merely human form, bring about the welfare of your kinsmen.
Parāśara said:
Thus reminded by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, O Brahmin,
the powerful Balarāma laughed and began to crush Pralamba.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he struck him on the head with his fist;
by that blow, his two eyes were knocked out.
With his brain forced out and vomiting blood from his mouth,
that best of Daityas fell upon the surface of the earth and died.
Seeing Pralamba slain by Bala of wondrous deeds, the cowherds were delighted; they praised him and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (ViP 5.9.37).
While being praised by the cowherds after the demon Pralamba had been struck down, Rāma,
together with Kṛṣṇa, returned once more to Gokula.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
While Rāma and Keśava were thus sporting in Vraja,
The rainy season passed away, and autumn arrived with its blossoming lotuses.
The small fish in the water of the pond experienced extreme distress,
just as a householder does through his sense of possessiveness attached to sons, fields, and other such things.
In the forest, the peacocks stood silent, having abandoned their pride,
just as yogis do upon realizing the essencelessness of worldly existence.
Having surrendered their entire essence as water, the clouds— now pure and white in form— abandoned the sky, just as men of wisdom abandon their homes.
And the lakes, scorched by the rays of the autumn sun, went to desiccation,
like the hearts of embodied beings due to their excessive attachment to worldly objects.
The autumn waters attained a state of fitness with the white water-lilies,
just as the minds of pure-souled beings attain a connection through spiritual awakenings.
In the sky, stainless with stars, the full-orbed moon shone like a yogi of noble lineage in his final body.
And very gradually the reservoirs abandoned their banks,
just as the wise abandon the deep-seated sense of "mine-ness" regarding fields, sons, and other possessions.

The swans reunited with the waters of the lake they had previously abandoned, just as practitioners of false yoga, struck down by obstacles, are eventually reunited with all their afflictions once they have been completely eliminated.
The ocean became exceedingly tranquil, its waters still,
like an ascetic who has attained great yoga through gradual practice and whose soul is motionless.
Then the waters became exceedingly clear everywhere,
like the minds of the wise when the all-pervading Viṣṇu has been known.
The sky became stainless, its clouds dispelled by autumn,
like the minds of yogis whose flood of afflictions has been consumed by the fire of yoga.
The lord of the stars brought to an end the heat produced by the sun's rays,
just as great discernment brings to an end the suffering born of egoism.

Autumn, as if through the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), removed the clouds from the sky, the mud from the earth, and the turbidity from the waters; it likewise withdrew the senses from the objects of the senses.

Like the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), it is practiced daily by means of the waters of the lakes, which have been filled to capacity and then discharged through the processes of exhalation (recaka) and retention (kumbhaka).
When the time had arrived during which the stars shone in a cloudless sky,
he saw those inhabitants of Vraja preparing for the great festival of Indra.
