Seeing those cowherds eager and longing for the festival, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa spoke these words out of curiosity to the elders: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.10.17.
"What is this so-called festival of Śakra, because of which joy has come upon you?
Nandagopa replied with great respect to him who was asking thus.
The Lord of the clouds and of the waters is Śatakratu, the King of the Gods;
impelled by him, the clouds rain down the essence consisting of water.
We and other embodied beings subsist by consuming that grain produced by rain,
and we satisfy the deities [with offerings].
"These cows are full of milk and accompanied by their calves, living in peace;
indeed, they become satisfied and well-nourished by the crops raised by him."
In that place, the earth was not devoid of grain nor lacking in grass; no person was seen afflicted by hunger, and only rain-bearing clouds were visible.
This terrestrial water was milked from the sun by the rays;
Parjanya, the giver of rain, pours it down upon the earth for the welfare of all the world.
Therefore, during the rainy season, all kings, filled with joy,
worship Śakra, the lord of the gods, with great festivals— both we and other men.
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of Nanda Gopa regarding the worship of Śakra,
Dāmodara then spoke so as to provoke the anger of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
"We are neither farmers nor do we live by trade;
O dear one, cows are our deity, for we are forest-dwellers."
Through *ānvīkṣikī*, there is the knowledge of the self; through the *trayī* (the three Vedas), the nature of dharma and adharma is established.
In the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), which follows after profit and loss, victory and defeat [are determined].
Logic, the three Vedas, economics, and likewise the science of government—this is the fourfold system of knowledge; now hear from me concerning economics.

Agriculture, trade, and likewise thirdly, animal husbandry—these, O highly fortunate one, are the sciences; for this livelihood, which rests upon these three occupations, is indeed the science of subsistence.

Agriculture is the livelihood of farmers, trade for those who live by the marketplace, and the cow is our supreme livelihood; thus, this [economy] consists of these three distinct branches of economic activity.
Whichever knowledge a person is endowed with, that alone is his great deity;
it alone is to be honored and worshipped, and it alone is his benefactor.
O dear one, that man who, while enjoying the fruit of one woman, honors another both in this world and after death, does not obtain anything auspicious.
The cultivated fields are well-known as our boundaries, and beyond the boundaries lies the forest;
the mountains mark the limits of the forest, and they all constitute our ultimate refuge.
They have no obstruction from the closing of doors, nor do they possess houses or fields;
indeed, they are happy throughout the entire world just like those who move by means of a wheel.
It is heard that these mountains in this forest can assume any form at will; taking on various shapes, they take their pleasure upon their own ridges.
And when these [people] commit offenses against those who dwell in the forests,
then the mountains cause them to be slain by means of lions and other such forms.
"Therefore, let this mountain sacrifice and the cow sacrifice be inaugurated;
what need have we for Mahendra? Cows and mountains are our deities."
The Brahmins are devoted to sacrifices with mantras, the farmers to sacrifices with the plow,
and we, who dwell in mountains and forests, are habituated to sacrifices with the mountain and the cow.
Therefore, let Mount Govardhana be honored and worshipped by you with various offerings, having slain a sacrificial animal according to the prescribed rite.
"Let the collection of all sounds be gathered; let it not be deliberated upon.
Let the Brahmins be fed with it, as well as those who desire it."
When the worship has been performed, the oblation offered, and the twice-born have been fed,
let the herds of cows, adorned with wreaths of autumnal flowers, roam about.
O cowherds, if this which is my opinion is carried out with affection,
then the pleasure of the cows, of the mountain, and likewise of myself will have been achieved.
Parāśara said:
Having heard these words of his, O Brahmin, Nanda and the other inhabitants of Vraja, their faces blossoming with joy, then exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"* *Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.10.42*
"Your thought is excellent, my child, that which has been spoken by you;
we shall do all of that. Let the sacrifice on the mountain be commenced."
Parāśara said:
And so, having performed the mountain-sacrifice (giri-yajña), those inhabitants of Vraja then offered the mountain-oblation with curds, milk-rice, meat, and other foods.
And they fed the twice-born by the hundreds and by the thousands.
After verse 45, Ś₁ and M₄ insert:
"Having spoken thus to the others who had also arrived, just as he had done before, Kṛṣṇa said: [ViP 5.10.45*16]
Then those cows, having been honored, circumambulated the mountain clockwise;
and the bulls bellowed like water-laden clouds.
O twice-born one, at that time Kṛṣṇa also, manifesting his form on the mountain peak as "I am the mountain," consumed a great deal of food brought by the best of the cowherds.
In that very same form, Kṛṣṇa, having ascended the summit of the mountain together with the cowherds,
worshipped his own second manifestation.
When he had vanished, the cowherds, having received those boons, celebrated the mountain festival and returned once more to their own cow-pen.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, when his power was thus thwarted, Śakra was filled with extreme rage.
Then he spoke to the host of clouds known as the Saṃvartakas.
O clouds, listen to these words of mine as I speak;
immediately after this command, let it be carried out swiftly and without hesitation.
The foolish Nandagopa, supported by other cowherds and puffed up by the strength derived from Kṛṣṇa's protection, brought about the destruction of the great festival.
"Let those cows, whose livelihood depends on others and who are the cause of my state as a cowherd, be afflicted by a downpour of rain at my command."
I too, having mounted a lofty elephant that resembles a mountain peak,
shall provide you assistance by discharging wind and water.
Parāśara said:
Thus commanded by the lord of the gods,
O twice-born one, those clouds released a most terrifying wind and rain for the destruction of the cows.
Then, in an instant, O Sage, the earth, the quarters of the sky, and the firmament itself became one through the filling of a great downpour of rain.
As if terrified by the lash-strokes of the lightning-vines, the clouds,
filling the circle of the quarters with their roar, rained down a torrential downpour.
When the world was enveloped in darkness by clouds raining incessantly,
the universe— below, above, and across— became as if entirely composed of water.
But the cows, shaken by that swift, falling rain-wind,
gave up their lives, their flanks, thighs, and necks collapsing.
O great sage, some cows stood having seized their calves with their chests,
while others were deprived of their calves by the flood of water.
And the calves, with dejected faces and necks trembling in the wind, seemed to cry out to Kṛṣṇa in their distress with soft voices, "Save us! Save us!"
Then, O Maitreya, seeing that entire Gokula crowded with cows, cowherd women, and cowherds, and being exceedingly distressed, Hari reflected upon it.
This was accomplished by Mahendra, who is opposed to the destruction of the great;
therefore, this entire cow-pen must now be protected by me.
"By my fortitude, I shall uproot this mountain, thick with massive boulders, and hold it above the cow-pen like a broad parasol."
Parāśara said:
Having thus resolved his mind, Kṛṣṇa uprooted the Govardhana mountain with a single hand and held it up as if in play.
Having lifted up the mountain, the Lord of the World said to the cowherds:
"Enter here together; a protection against the rain has been prepared."
"Stay here as you please in these windless places;
enter without fear, for you have no dread of a mountain collapse."
Thus addressed by him, those cowherds entered together with their herds of cattle, and the cowherd women,
oppressed by the downpour, entered with their goods loaded upon carts.
Kṛṣṇa also held that mountain perfectly motionless,
while he was gazed upon by the inhabitants of Vraja with eyes wide with joy and wonder.
While his deeds were being praised by the joyful cowherds and cowherd girls, whose eyes were wide with affection, Kṛṣṇa supported the mountain.
O Brahmin, for seven nights great clouds, impelled by Indra and intent on the destruction of the cowherds, rained down upon Nanda’s cow-pen.
Then, once the great mountain had been held up and Gokula had been rescued,
the breaker of forces (Indra), his vow having failed, restrained those clouds.
Then, while the lord of the gods stood in a cloudless sky with his words proven false,
the joyful Gokula emerged and returned once more to its own place.
Then Kṛṣṇa also released the great mountain Govardhana;
it was seen by those inhabitants of Vraja with astonished faces as it returned to its own place.
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
When Mount Govardhana had been held up and Gokula had been protected,
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, desired a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Having mounted the great elephant Airāvata, the conqueror of enemies,
the lord of the thirty gods beheld Kṛṣṇa on Mount Govardhana.
He was tending the cows with great vigor, assuming the form of a cowherd;
he was the protector of the entire world, surrounded by the sons of cowherds.
And he saw Garuḍa, the bull among birds, who had become invisible and high above, O twice-born one,
casting a shadow over Hari’s head with his two wings.
Having descended from the king of serpents, Śakra, his eyes wide with joy, spoke these words with a smile to Madhusūdana in a secluded spot.
Indra said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, listen to this for which purpose I have come into your presence, O illustrious one; this must not be considered by you otherwise."
O support of all, you alone are the Supreme Lord who has descended to the surface of the earth for the purpose of relieving the burden of the world.
By me, acting in opposition to Mahābhaṅga, great clouds were commanded to destroy Gokula; by them, this slaughter was carried out.
"And those cows were rescued by you after you uprooted the great mountain;
therefore, O hero, I am gratified by this most wonderful deed of yours."
O Kṛṣṇa, I believe the purpose of the gods has been accomplished,
since this best of mountains was held by you with a single hand.
Urged by the cows, O Kṛṣṇa, I have come here into your presence;
I have been exceedingly protected by you who were rescued for the sake of honoring you.
Impelled by the words of the cows, I shall consecrate you as Kṛṣṇa;
as Indra among the cows in the capacity of Upendra, you shall become Govinda.
Parāśara said: Then, taking the bell from his mount, the elephant Airāvata,
he performed the consecration for her with it, which was filled with pure water.
While the consecration was being performed, at that very moment, the cows of Kṛṣṇa immediately made the earth wet with the milk flowing from their udders.
Having consecrated Janārdana at the word of the cows, the Lord of the Gods,
the husband of Śacī, spoke again to Kṛṣṇa with affection and humility.
This speech was made by the cows; hear from me another as well, O illustrious one, which I speak with the desire to bring down the burden of the earth.
"O tiger among men, a portion of myself has descended upon the surface of the earth as Arjuna, born of Pṛthā; he must always be protected by you."
O Madhusūdana, that hero will assist you in relieving the burden; he must be protected by you just as you protect yourself.
The Blessed One said:
"I know Pārtha, born in the lineage of Bharata, who is a portion of you;
I shall protect him as long as I remain upon the earth."
O Śakra, subduer of enemies, as long as I remain upon the surface of the earth,
no one, O Lord of the Gods, shall defeat Arjuna in battle.
The mighty-armed Daitya named Kaṃsa, as well as another, Ariṣṭa;
Keśin, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Naraka, and others likewise.
O Lord of the Gods, when these enemies have been slain, there will be a great battle;
know, O thousand-eyed one, that in that [battle] the removal of the earth's burden shall be accomplished.
Therefore, go; you ought not to feel distress on account of your son.
No enemy of Arjuna shall prevail against me.
"But for the sake of Arjuna, once the Bhārata war has ended, I shall restore all those led by Yudhiṣṭhira to Kuntī unharmed."
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the king of the gods embraced Janārdana and,
mounting the elephant Airāvata, departed once again for heaven.
Kṛṣṇa, too, accompanied by the cows and the cowherds,
returned once more to Vraja by a path purified by the glances of the gopīs.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
When Śakra had departed, the cowherds [approached] Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds.
Seeing that Govardhana mountain held up by him, they spoke with affection.
O highly fortunate one, we and the cattle have been saved by you from great danger through your deed of supporting the mountain.
"This incomparable childhood play and this loathsome state of being a cowherd, as well as your divine deeds—what is this, O Father? Let it be told."
Kāliya was subdued in the water, Pralamba was struck down, and this Govardhana was held up; our minds are filled with apprehension.
"Truly, truly, O you of immeasurable prowess, we swear by the feet of Hari that,
having beheld your heroism, we no longer consider you a mere man."
O Keśava, there is joy for the people of Vraja, including their women and children,
because of this deed of yours which is impossible even for all the gods combined.
O Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is immeasurable, even when we reflect upon our childhood, our excessive prowess, and our noble birth, they give rise to apprehension.
Are you a god, a dānava, a yakṣa, or perhaps a gandharva?
What need have we for further inquiry? You are our kinsman; homage be to you!
M1.3 ins., M1 after 8ab:
O mighty-armed one, you are for the most part either Hari or indeed Rudra himself.
Whether it be Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, or even Kubera;
Or perhaps another, the lord of all the gods, was born from the earth as Bhava.
Homage be to you, O God of gods, for that which is for our benefit.
Parāśara said:
Having remained silent for a moment, feeling a slight touch of affectionate anger at being addressed in this way by those cowherds, Kṛṣṇa also spoke, O great sage.
The Blessed One said:
"O cowherds, if no shame arises in you because of my connection with you, then I am indeed praiseworthy; what need have you for further deliberation?"
If you have affection for me, and if I am worthy of your praise,
then let your mind toward me be like that toward your own kinsman.
"I am neither a god, nor a Gandharva, nor a Yakṣa, nor a Dānava;
I have been born as your kinsman, so this should not be considered otherwise."
Parāśara said:
O highly fortunate one, having heard these words of Hari, the cowherds then departed for the forest in silence, while he remained in a state of lover’s anger.
Kṛṣṇa, however, beheld the stainless sky, the moonlight of the autumnal moon,
and likewise the blossoming night-lily that perfumed the quarters of the world.
Beholding the forest grove, which was enchanting with swarms of humming bees, he, together with the cowherd girls, set his mind upon amorous pleasure.
Without Rāma, Śauri sang very sweetly, a song most pleasing to women, with melodious words and employing various stringed instruments.
Then, hearing the delightful sound of singing, the cowherd women abandoned their dwellings and came in haste to where Madhusūdana was staying.
One cowherd girl sang very softly, following his rhythm,
while another, having fixed her attention, remembered him alone with her mind.
One girl, having cried out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!", was overcome with shame;
another, blinded by love, went to his side without any embarrassment.
A certain woman, staying inside her dwelling and seeing her elder outside,
meditated upon Govinda with her eyes closed, being entirely absorbed in him.
Thus, her store of merit was exhausted by the immense joy of that thought,
and all her sins were dissolved by the great suffering of not having attained him.
Another cowherd girl, meditating upon the source of the universe who is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman,
attained liberation through the cessation of her breath.
Surrounded by the gopīs, Govinda, eager for the delight of beginning the rāsa dance, honored the night made enchanting by the autumn moon.
And the cowherd girls, their very bodies dependent upon Kṛṣṇa’s every movement,
wandered within the interior of Vṛndāvana when Kṛṣṇa had gone to another place, gathering in groups.
With their hearts fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, they spoke this to one another: D3-5, T, G, M1, and the edition insert after 24: "With their hearts bound to Kṛṣṇa, they said this to each other."
"I am Kṛṣṇa; I go gracefully—behold my gait! said one.
Another said, "Listen to my song of Kṛṣṇa. *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 5.13.25.
In the same manner, Pūtanā was slain and the cart was overturned.
"Friends, behold the wonderful prowess of Kṛṣṇa and myself!"
Another cried out, "O wicked Kāliya, stay here! I am Kṛṣṇa!
and clapping her arms, she seized the very essence of Kṛṣṇa’s playful charm.
Another said, "O cowherds, stay here without fear;
there is no need for concern about the rain, for Govardhana has been held up by me."
M₁ inserts, while G₁ inserts after 28:
"And another friend says: 'Behold me, free from blemish!'"
He was adorned with a forest garland of various kinds, O Kṛṣṇa.
"This Dhenuka has been cast away by me; let us roam about as we please," said another cowherd girl, imitating the play of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, while engaged in various kinds of dark intrigues, those gopīs then wandered together through the delightful forest of Vṛndāvana.
Then, for those women who had taken refuge [in him], because they followed the path of Kṛṣṇa...
A conversation concerning the search for Kṛṣṇa then proceeded.
Beholding the earth, one cowherd woman, a most excellent lady among the gopīs, spoke,
her entire body bristling with horripilation and her lotus-eyes wide open.
Behold this path, O Āli, marked with lines bearing the signs of a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus;
these are the footprints of Kṛṣṇa as he moves with playful grace.
Some woman of merit, languid with intoxication, has gone along with him;
these are her footprints, both thick and sparse.
Dāmodara certainly gathered flowers here on high,
for which reason the footprints of that Great Soul are found here, each measuring only a single step.
Having sat down there, she was adorned with flowers by him—
she by whom Viṣṇu, the soul of all, had been worshipped in a previous birth.
"Behold! Having cast aside her pride, which was fostered by the honor of being bound with flowers, Nanda’s son has gone away by this very path."
Another woman, unable to keep pace in the procession due to the weight of her hips,
moved swiftly when she had to go, as her feet were placed firmly on the tips of their toes.
With her hand placed upon his outstretched hand, this friend of hers proceeds in such a way that the trail of her footsteps appears to be one whose placement is not under her own control.
By the mere touch of his hand, this woman has been insulted by the rogue;
because of her despair, it is evident from the slow steps of her departing that she has turned back.
"Surely she was told, 'Hurry,' so that she will return to your presence;
for by that Kṛṣṇa has this hurried trail of footprints been made."
"Kṛṣṇa has entered the thicket; his footprints cannot be seen here.
Turn back! He is not within the range of the moon's rays."
Then those gopīs turned back, hopeless of seeing Kṛṣṇa;
having reached the bank of the Yamunā, they sang of his deeds at that time.
Then the cowherd women beheld Kṛṣṇa, whose lotus-face was blooming, the protector of the three worlds, whose actions are effortless.
Seeing Govinda approaching, a certain woman was filled with great joy;
she cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and uttered nothing else.
A certain woman, with her tremulous eyes closed, had her mind fixed upon that devotee of the Lord.
He worshipped that Govinda, the imperishable Viṣṇu, who is the self of all.
One woman, having made her forehead-plate curved with a frown and gazing at Hari with her bee-like eyes, drank in the lotus of his face.
Upon seeing Govinda, one woman closed her eyes;
meditating on his very form, she appeared as if she had ascended to the state of yoga.
Then Mādhava brought some to submission with endearing words, others with glances and the knitting of his brows, and still others by the touch of his hand.
Together with those cowherd girls whose minds were full of devotion,
Hari, whose conduct is noble, joyfully engaged in the assemblies of the rāsa dance with great respect.
Even while forming the *rāsamaṇḍala* dance, the group of cowherd girls did not remain fixed in one place, as they never left Kṛṣṇa’s side.
Taking each gopī by the hand in the circle of the rāsa dance,
Hari caused her eyes to close at the touch of his hand.
Then the *rāsa* dance commenced, accompanied by the tinkling of moving bracelets and followed in succession by songs sung to the melodies of autumnal poetry.
Kṛṣṇa sang of the autumn moon, the moonlight, and the bed of white lotuses;
the cowherd women, however, sang only the single name of Kṛṣṇa again and again.
From the fatigue of the dance, a certain cowherd girl, speaking with her moving bracelets, placed her vine-like arm upon the shoulder of the slayer of Madhu.
A certain cowherd girl, skilled in the art of praising him with songs under the pretext of singing, embraced Madhusūdana by his shimmering arm and kissed him.
Having come into contact with the cheeks of the gopīs, Hari’s two arms attained the state of rain clouds for the sake of the crop that was the emergence of horripilation.
As soon as Kṛṣṇa began to sing the Rāsa-song with a piercingly high voice, they sang "Well done, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! with a voice twice as loud.
When he departed, the cowherd women followed him; when he turned back, they went toward him; thus the cowherd women attended upon Hari both in the opposite direction and in the same direction.
Madhusūdana sported with the cowherd girls in such a way that,
without him, even a single moment became equivalent to ten million years.
Though they were being restrained by their husbands, fathers, and brothers,
those cowherd women, fond of pleasure, took delight with Kṛṣṇa at night.
Honoring his youthful age, Madhusūdana,
whose soul is immeasurable and who has destroyed all enemies, took delight with them during the nights.
Likewise, among those husbands and those wives, as well as among all beings, He, the Lord,
exists pervading them like the wind, having the nature of the self.
Just as space, fire, earth, water,
and wind exist within all beings, so too does that Self abide, pervading everything.
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Once, at the midpoint of the evening, while Janārdana was absorbed in the Rāsa dance,
Terrifying the cow-pen with his fury, he approached unharmed.
With a luster as clear as water mixed with milk, possessing sharp horns and eyes like the sun,
he tore the surface of the earth excessively with the strikes of his hoof-tips.
Licking his lips repeatedly with his tongue with a grinding sound,
his tail lashed out in fury, and the muscles of his shoulders hardened, he stood there.
With the full expanse of his lofty hump, impossible to surpass in size,
his back covered with dung and urine, he causes distress to the cows.
With a long neck and a protruding snout, his face marked by the scars of goring trees,
that Daitya assumed the form of a bull and caused the pregnancies of cows to miscarry.
Fierce and subduing the ascetics, he who always roams through the forests.
Then, beholding him with his exceedingly terrible eyes, the cowherds and the cowherd women, overcome by great fear, cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"
Then Keśava let out a lion’s roar and made a sound by clapping his hands;
upon hearing that sound, he [the serpent] went toward the mouth of Dāmodara.
With the tip of his horn thrust forward and his gaze fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s belly,
the evil-minded bull-demon rushed toward Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the bull among the Daityas approaching, the mighty Kṛṣṇa did not move from that spot, but remained there with a playful smile of contempt.
Madhusūdana seized him as he drew near, like a crocodile;
he struck him in the flank with his knee, though he was as immovable as a mountain due to his grip on the horns.
Having shattered his pride and strength, he seized Ariṣṭa by the two horns and squeezed his throat as if it were a damp garment.
Then, having torn off one of his horns, he struck him with it;
the Daitya died instantly, vomiting blood from his mouth.
When that Daitya had been slain, the cowherds praised Janārdana,
just as the hosts of gods once praised the Thousand-eyed One when Jambha was killed.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
When Kakudmin had been slain and Ariṣṭa and Dhenuka had been struck down,
When Pralamba had been brought to his end and Mount Govardhana was held aloft.
When the serpent Kāliya was subdued, the pair of lofty trees were broken, Pūtanā was slain, and the cart was overturned; ||| ViP_5.15.2 |||
Nārada related to Kaṃsa everything exactly as it had happened in due order, including in its entirety the exchange of the embryos of Yaśodā and Devakī.
Having heard all that from Nārada, who has the vision of the gods,
the evil-minded Kaṃsa then directed his wrath toward Vasudeva.
Out of extreme anger, having reproached him in the assembly of all the Yādavas,
he censured the Yādavas and reflected upon this matter.
"As long as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are still very young children and have not yet attained full strength, they must be slain by me; once they have reached maturity, they will be invincible."
"Cāṇūra here is of great heroism, and Muṣṭika is of great strength;
through wrestling with these two, I shall cause those two arrogant ones to be slain."
"Under the pretext of the great Dhanur-maha sacrifice, I shall bring those two from Vraja;
I will strive in such a way that they both go to their destruction."
Therefore, I shall send Akrūra, the son of Śvaphalka and a bull among the Yadus,
to Gokula for the purpose of bringing those two back.
I shall also command the terrible Keśin, who wanders in Vṛndāvana;
there, that one of exceeding strength will slay them both.
The elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa will come near me and cause the slaughter of both cowherd boys, the sons of Vasudeva.
Parāśara said:
Having reflected thus, the evil-minded Kaṃsa, resolved to kill Rāma and Janārdana, spoke these words to the heroic Akrūra.
Kaṃsa said:
"O lord of charity, let my words be carried out for my pleasure:
having mounted a chariot from here, go to Nanda’s cowherd settlement."
The two sons of Vasudeva there, born from portions of Viṣṇu, have indeed arisen for my destruction; those two wicked ones are growing strong.
"My Dhanurmaha festival shall also take place here on the fourteenth day;
you must go and bring both of them for a wrestling match."
"The two wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika are skilled in hand-to-hand combat;
let all the world here witness the battle between them and these two."
The elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, urged on by his mahout,
shall slay those two wicked children, the sons of Vasudeva.
Having slain both Vasudeva and the wicked-minded Nandagopa,
I shall also kill this father of mine, the evil-minded Ugrasena.
Then I shall seize all the cattle-wealth and the property of all the wicked cowherds who desire my death.
"O Lord of Charity, without you these Yādavas are wicked toward me;
therefore, I shall subsequently strive for their destruction one by one."
"Therefore, O hero, you must go out of affection for me; with your help, I shall rule this entire kingdom, free from thorns and devoid of Yādavas."
Just as the cowherds quickly bring buffalo ghee and curd for the offering, you must speak to them in such a manner.
Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, having been thus commanded, the highly devoted Akrūra became joyful and eager, thinking, "I shall see Kṛṣṇa tomorrow."
Having said "So be it" to the king, Madhupriya then mounted a splendid chariot and departed from the city of Mathurā.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Keśin also, fierce in his strength, was dispatched by Kaṃsa’s messenger.
Desiring the death of Kṛṣṇa, he arrived at Vṛndāvana.
With his hooves scarred by the surface of the earth, shaking clouds with the toss of his mane,
and leaping across the paths of the sun and moon with heroic strides, he rushed toward the cowherds.
At the sound of his neighing, the cowherds, the Daityas' horses,
and the cowherd women, agitated by fear, went for refuge to Govinda.
Hearing their cry of "Save us! Save us! at that time, Govinda spoke these words, as deep as the roar of a water-laden cloud: *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 5.16.4.
The Blessed One said:
"Enough with this fear, cowherds! Why are you so overcome by dread?
By you, who belong to the lowly caste of cowherds, the prowess of heroes is being destroyed."
What is the use of this wicked horse, which possesses little strength, who brays and acts with arrogance, and who leaps about while being driven by the power of the Daityas?
"Come, come, you wicked one! I am Kṛṣṇa; like the wielder of the Pināka bow [Śiva] toward Pūṣan, I shall knock out all the teeth from your mouth."
Having spoken thus and slapping his arms, Govinda went toward Keśin;
and with his mouth wide open, that horse of the Daitya also rushed at him.
Then Janārdana, having extended his arm,
thrust it into the mouth of that wicked horse Keśin.
As that black arm entered Keśin’s mouth,
his teeth were shattered and fell out like fragments of white clouds.
O twice-born one, Kṛṣṇa’s arm that had entered Keśin’s body grew,
like a disease neglected until its manifestation which leads to destruction.
With his lips torn apart, he vomited copious amounts of blood mixed with foam.
The powerful Daitya, his body bathed in tears and deprived of consciousness, cried out loudly.
His two eyes became wide-open wheels, emerged, and were released from their bonds.
He struck the earth with his feet, discharging excrement and urine;
with his limbs moistened by sweat and exhausted, he then became devoid of effort.
With his mouth wide open, that most terrible asura fell, split in two by Kṛṣṇa’s arm, like a tree struck by lightning.
When Keśin was split in two, his two halves shone forth, each possessing half a foot, half a back, half a tail, half an ear, one eye, and one nostril.
Having slain Keśin, Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the joyful cowherds,
remained right there, his body unwearied, composed, and smiling.
Then, when Keśin had been slain, the cowherd women and the cowherds were filled with wonder;
they praised the lotus-eyed Lord, who was so enchanting through his affection.
Then the brahmin Nārada, situated within a cloud,
spoke, his mind overflowing with joy upon seeing Keśin slain.
Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! O Acyuta, it is by mere sport that this Keśin, the bringer of affliction to the inhabitants of heaven, has been slain by you.
"Extremely eager for battle, I have come from heaven to witness this great conflict between men and horses, the like of which has never been seen elsewhere."
O Madhusūdana, your deeds performed during your incarnations have filled my mind with wonder, and through this [account], it has attained satisfaction.
O Kṛṣṇa, even Śakra and the gods are afraid of this horse as it neighs,
its mane disheveled, looking toward the clouds.
"O Janārdana, because this evil-minded Keśin has been slain by you,
you shall therefore become renowned in the world by the name Keśava."
"May it be well with you; I shall now depart for the battle with Kaṃsa.
O slayer of Keśin, I will return with you again the day after tomorrow."
O upholder of the earth, you have brought about the removal of the earth’s burden by striking down Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, along with his followers.
In that regard, O Janārdana, many kinds of battles among the rulers of the earth were witnessed by me, as they were directed by you.
Therefore, O Govinda, I shall depart; the great task of the gods has been accomplished by you.
Honored by you, may it be well with you; I am now leaving.
When Nārada had departed, Kṛṣṇa, unsmitten by pride, entered Gokula with the cowherds,
becoming the sole vessel for the drinking-glances of the cowherd women.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: Akrūra also, having set out in a swift-moving chariot, departed.
Longing for a vision of Kṛṣṇa, he set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
And Akrūra reflected: "There is no one more fortunate than I, for I shall behold the face of the Wielder of the Discus who has descended as a partial incarnation."
Today my birth has become fruitful and my night has turned into a beautiful dawn,
since I shall behold the face of Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like the petals of a blooming lotus.
Today my eyes have become fruitful; today my words have become fruitful.
"Upon seeing Viṣṇu, there will be mutual conversation between us."
I shall behold that lotus-eyed face of Viṣṇu, which, when remembered or even merely conceived in thought, removes the sins of men.
"And from which the Vedas and all the Vedāṅgas issued forth—
that supreme abode of the gods, the mouth of the Blessed One, I shall behold."
I shall behold that Lord of the Universe, the Supreme Person, the support of all, who is worshipped by men as the Person of Sacrifice in sacrifices.
Having worshipped him with a hundred sacrifices, Indra attained the sovereignty over the immortals;
I shall behold that Keśava, who is without beginning or end.
Neither Brahmā, nor Indra, Rudra, Aśvin, Vasu, Āditya, nor the hosts of Maruts know His true nature; may that Hari touch my body.
He who is the self of all, the knower of all, the all, who dwells within all beings,
who is pervasive, imperishable, and all-encompassing— he shall speak together with me.
He who, as the unborn (aja), established the stability of the world through his forms as the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the horse, the lion, and others— he shall speak to me today.
And now the Lord of the World, the imperishable one who assumes a body by his own will, has attained human form in order to accomplish the task residing within his own heart.
He who is infinite and supports the earth situated upon his crest has descended for the sake of the world; he will address me as "Akrūra."
Salutations again and again to Him, whose māyā— consisting of fathers, sons, friends, brothers, mothers, and kinsmen— the world is unable to transcend.
Salutation to that immeasurable Self of Knowledge, by fixing whose mind within the heart the yogi crosses over the far-reaching ignorance and illusion.
He who is called Yajñapuruṣa by the performers of sacrifice, Vāsudeva by the Sātvatas, and Viṣṇu by the knowers of the Vedānta— to him I bow.
Just as this world, both existent and non-existent, is established in that Creator who is its abode, by that truth may he attain gentleness toward me.
I go for refuge to that unborn and eternal Hari, by the mere remembrance of whom a person becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness.
Parāśara said:
Thus meditating upon Viṣṇu, his mind and soul bowed down with devotion,
Akrūra reached Gokula while the sun was still shining brightly.
Then he saw Kṛṣṇa there at the cow-penning place,
standing in the midst of the calves, with the complexion of the petals of a full-blown blue lotus.
His eyes were like clearly blooming lotus petals, his chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa, his arms were long, and his broad chest was high; he had a prominent nose.
He bore a lotus-face that was the support for a playful smile,
and with his feet, he stood firmly established upon the earth, possessing high and reddish nails.
Wearing two yellow garments, adorned with wild flowers,
holding a thick blue creeper in his hand, and having a white lotus as an ear-ornament.
O twice-born one, the joy of the Yadus then beheld him who was as white as a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and who wore blue garments; and after him, he saw Balabhadra.
Tall, with long arms and shoulders, and a blossoming lotus-face,
he was like another Mount Kailāsa encircled by a garland of clouds.
O Sage, upon seeing them, that high-minded Akrūra’s lotus-like face blossomed and all his limbs were covered with horripilation.
This is that supreme abode, this is that supreme state;
it is the portion of the Blessed Vāsudeva which exists here in a twofold manner.
The pair of my eyes has attained great success here by beholding the Creator of the world;
may this body of mine also become fruitful through the grace of the Blessed One by attaining contact with his limbs.
Will this Lord of infinite forms, endowed with splendor, place his lotus-hand upon my back—
that touch of whose fingers destroys all sins and through which perfection is attained, free from the defect of decay?
By him, casting aside his wheel— which was terrifying and most fierce, garlanded with flames like fire and lightning—
he slew the lord of the Daityas and took away the collyrium from the eyes of the Daitya women.
Having offered water there as a bali-oblation, Bali, while remaining on the surface of the earth, obtained delightful enjoyments;
likewise, free from enemies, he attained immortality and the lordship of the thirty gods for the duration of a full Manvantara.
"Will he indeed make me—who am already a vessel of fault due to my association with Kaṃsa—still more defiled by sin, struck down by contempt? Fie on that birth which has been rightly cast out!"
What in this world remains unknown to him who abides in the hearts of all men— he who is composed of the essence of knowledge, a mass of stainless purity, free from defects, and ever manifest?
Therefore, with a heart bowed down by devotion, I go to the Lord of all lords,
who is an incarnate portion of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, who is without beginning, middle, or end.
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Thinking thus, that Yādava approached Govinda.
Saying "I am Akrūra," he bowed his head at the feet of Hari.
He too, having touched him with a hand marked by the signs of the banner, the thunderbolt, and the lotus,
drew him near and embraced him very firmly with affection.
Having been duly saluted by him, Balarāma and Keśava then entered his own palace, joyful and carrying him with them.
Then Akrūra, having performed the salutations and other rites with them and having eaten his meal according to custom, spoke to the two of them.
Just as Ānakadundubhi was reviled by that Kaṃsa, and just as Queen Devakī was [reviled] by the evil-minded Dānava; ||| ViP_5.18.5 |||
O Ugrasena, [tell me] how the very wicked Kaṃsa conducts himself,
and for what purpose he was dispatched by Kaṃsa.
Having heard all that in detail, the Blessed One, the slayer of Keśin, said: "O Lord of Gifts, I have understood all of this as well."
And I shall do, O illustrious one, whatever is considered appropriate in this matter;
you need not think otherwise of this—know that Kaṃsa has been slain by me.
"Tomorrow Rama and I shall go to Mathurā together with you;
the elder cowherds will also go, taking many offerings."
"O hero, let this night pass; you need not worry. Within three nights, I shall slay Kaṃsa along with his followers."
Parāśara said:
Having then given instructions to the cowherds, Akrūra,
along with Keśava and Balabhadra, slept there in the house of Nanda Gopa.
Then, at the clear dawn, the highly intelligent Kṛṣṇa and Rāma prepared to depart for Mathurā together with Akrūra.
Seeing him, the cowherd women, with tears in their eyes and bracelets slipping from their arms,
sighed deeply, afflicted by extreme grief, and spoke thus to one another:
Having reached Mathurā, how will Govinda return to Gokula?
How will he drink with his ears the honey of the artful speech of the city women?
Having found its dwelling in the drinking of the playful words of city women,
how could his heart ever again turn toward rustic cowherd girls?
By seizing Hari according to the prescribed ritual, that pitiless and evil-minded one has struck a blow at the very essence of the entire cowherd community among the cowherd women.
A smile pregnant with inner feeling, speech, a gait graceful with charm,
and even the side-long glance— these belong exceedingly to the women of the city.
This rustic Hari is bound by the fetters of their charms;
by what means, then, will he come into your presence?
"Here he is, Keśava, having mounted the chariot, proceeding toward Mathurā;
he has been deceived here by the cruel Akrūra, who is now devoid of hope."
Does this cruel man not know that we are devoted to him with love,
since he leads Hari away from here, the delight of our eyes?
"This utterly merciless Govinda is proceeding together with Rāma, having mounted his chariot; let haste be made to restrain him."
"Why do you say that it is not fitting for us to speak in the presence of our gurus?
What can the gurus do to those who have been consumed by the fire of separation?"
"Led by Nandagopa, these cowherds are prepared to depart;
not one among them makes an effort to turn Govinda back."
Today the night has dawned auspiciously for the women residing in Mathurā,
whose rows of bee-like eyes shall drink from the lotus-face of Acyuta.
Blessed are those on the path who go from here toward Kṛṣṇa unimpeded,
for as they behold him, they shall carry their own bodies covered in horripilation.
Today there will be a great festival for the eyes of the citizens of the city of Mathurā,
as they behold the limbs of Govinda.
What a fortunate dream must have been seen by those women of expansive and lovely eyes, who shall behold Adhokṣaja without any hindrance!
"Alas! Having shown this great treasure to these cowherd women, the Creator, being pitiless by nature, has plucked out their eyes."
Blessed are those on the path who behold Hari, whose form is gentle, as he proceeds.
Indeed, with unblinking eyes out of curiosity, they gaze upon him without restraint.
As Hari’s affection for us grows lax,
even the bracelets upon his wrists quickly begin to slip.
The cruel-hearted Akrūra swiftly urged on the horses;
who would not feel compassion for women in such distress?
O mighty-armed Akrūra, speak with very gentle words.
Why do you deserve to cause distress to these cowherd women?
O Lord of Men, what kind of injury have we done to you?
Or rather, O mighty-armed one, it was by the will of the Creator, or by that Kṛṣṇa, Hari.
Balabhadra certainly does not wish to restrain him, even though he is firm.
While the women were thus distressed, lamenting here and there.
As he was departing after mounting his chariot, those excellent women said this to him:
Behold this high cloud of dust from the wheels of Kṛṣṇa’s chariot;
now that Hari has moved far away, even that dust is no longer visible.
Parāśara said:
Thus, gazed upon with great affection by the cowherd women,
Keśava, together with Rāma, abandoned the region of Vraja.
Traveling by means of a chariot drawn by swift horses,
Rāma, Akrūra, and Janārdana reached the bank of the Yamunā at the time of midday.
Then Akrūra said to Kṛṣṇa, "Please remain here for a moment while I perform my daily ablutions in the waters of the Kālindī."
Having been told "So be it," that high-minded sage, having bathed and sipped water according to the rules,
O Brahmin, entered the waters of the Yamunā and meditated upon the supreme Brahman.
He beheld Balabhadra, adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods,
his body as pure as a kunda flower, and his eyes as red as the petals of a blooming lotus.
He was surrounded by great wind-eaters such as Vāsuki and Amba,
being praised by Gandharvas and adorned with a forest garland.
Wearing dark garments and adorned with a beautiful lotus as an ear-ornament,
he stood within the depths of the water, intoxicated and wearing lovely earrings.
On his lap [he saw] one dark as a rain-cloud, with large copper-colored eyes,
four arms, noble limbs, and adorned with weapons such as the discus.
Clad in two yellow garments and adorned with variegated garlands and ornaments,
he resembled a rain-cloud made beautiful by Indra’s bow and garlands of lightning.
He beheld the unassailable Kṛṣṇa, whose chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark, who was radiant with beautiful armlets and a crown, and who wore a lotus as an ear-ornament.
It was being meditated upon there by Sanandana and other stainless sages who were masters of yoga, their eyes fixed on the tips of their noses.
Having thus recognized Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, Akrūra was struck with wonder;
he thought, "How have they come here so quickly from the chariot?"
Janārdana paralyzed the speech of him who wished to speak;
then, emerging from the water, he returned once more to his chariot.
And there he beheld both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa seated upon the chariot, endowed with human bodies just as before.
And having plunged back into the water, he saw those two exactly as before,
being praised by Gandharvas, Munis, Siddhas, and great serpents.
Then, having ascertained his true nature, that lord of donors praised the infallible Lord, who consists of all knowledge.
Śakrūra said: Salutations again and again to the Supreme Self, whose form is pure existence, whose majesty is inconceivable, who is all-pervading, and whose singular nature is manifold yet one.
Salutations to you whose form is truth; salutations to you who have become the inconceivable oblation.
Salutations to the Supreme Lord, whose nature is unknowable and who transcends primordial matter.
You are the self of the elements, the self of the senses, and likewise the self of primordial matter;
you are the individual self and the supreme self—you alone abide in five forms.
Be gracious, O Soul of all, Lord composed of the perishable and the imperishable,
who art proclaimed by conceptual designations known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is inexpressible, whose purpose is inexpressible,
and whose name is inexpressible— to You I bow.
O Protector, that wherein no conceptual constructions of name, genus, and so forth exist—that is the supreme, eternal, and unchanging Brahman; you, O Unborn One, are that.
Since the apprehension of any object whatsoever does not occur apart from conceptual construction,
you are therefore praised by the names Kṛṣṇa, Acyuta, Ananta, and Viṣṇu.
O Unborn One, you are all objects through conceptual constructions; you alone are this entire world, beginning with the gods.
O Soul of the Universe, you are free from the state of modification; for there is nothing whatsoever other than you in all things.

You are Brahmā, Paśupati, Aryaman, Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, the Lord of the Thirty-three, Samīraṇa, and Agni; you are the Lord of Waters, the Lord of Wealth, and Antaka. You alone protect the world through various powers manifested as distinct entities for different purposes.
You create the universe in the form of the rays of the sun, and this entire manifold world (prapañca) consisting of the qualities (guṇas) belongs to You, O Unborn One.
To that Supreme Being, whose nature is consciousness, who is the imperishable signifier of "Being" (sat), and who is both being and non-being—to Him I bow.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva; salutations to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa;
salutations to you, Pradyumna; salutations to you, Aniruddha.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having thus praised Viṣṇu within the waters, that Yādava—
He worshipped the Lord of All with flowers and mentally created incense.
Having withdrawn his mind from all other objects and fixed it there,
he remained for a long time in the state of Brahman and then desisted from his meditative absorption.
Considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose, the high-minded one emerged from the waters of the Yamunā and returned once more to his chariot.
Then Akrūra, his eyes wide with wonder, beheld Rāma and Kṛṣṇa seated upon the chariot just as before; and Kṛṣṇa addressed him.
"Surely you have seen a marvel in the waters of the Yamunā, O Akrūra,
since you are observed with eyes wide open in wonder."
Śakrūra said:
"O Acyuta, that wonder which was seen by me there within the water,
I now behold here as well, standing before me in embodied form."
O Kṛṣṇa, I have been united with you, that Great Soul whose form this most wonderful universe is, and who are yourself the supreme marvel.
"So, O Madhusūdana, shall we go to Mathurā with this?
I am afraid of Kaṃsa; fie upon the birth of those who subsist on the food of others!"
Having said this, he urged on those horses, swift as the wind;
and by late afternoon, Akrūra had reached the city of Mathurā.
Beholding Mathurā, that Yādava said to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa:
"O you two of great prowess, go on foot; I shall enter alone by means of a chariot."
"You two must not go to the house of Vasudeva;
for it is on your account that the old man is being cast out by Kaṃsa."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, Akrūra then entered the city of Mathurā;
and Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, having entered, arrived at the royal highway.
Gazed upon with joyful eyes by women and men alike,
the two heroes proceeded with playful grace like two elephants in rut.
Seeing a washerman who was a dyer wandering about, those two of beautiful countenance begged him for some well-formed garments.
Then Kaṃsa’s washerman, his pride mounted by the favor he had received,
spoke many insulting words loudly to Rāma and Keśava.
Then, with a blow of his palm, Kṛṣṇa, out of anger, struck down the head of that wicked-minded washerman to the ground.
Then, having slain [the gardener] and taken his garments, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, clad in yellow and blue robes, went joyfully to the house of a florist.
With his pair of eyes wide open, even the garland-maker was struck with wonder;
he then thought, "To whom do these two belong, and from where have they come?"—thus [Maitreya reflected].
Seeing those two, wearing yellow and blue garments and exceedingly beautiful,
he then reflected that the two gods had arrived upon the earth.
Requested for flowers by those two, whose lotus-faces were in full bloom,
he supported himself upon the earth with his hands and touched the ground with his head.
"The two Lords, supreme in grace, have come to my home;
I am blessed, for I shall worship them," said Mālyajīvaka to them.
Then, with a joyful countenance, he began to entice them by offering them flowers at will, saying, "These are beautiful; now these."
Bowing again and again to those two supreme among men, the gardener offered beautiful,
fragrant, and stainless flowers.
Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with the garland-maker, granted him a boon:
"O blessed one, Śrī, taking refuge in you, shall never forsake you."
"O gentle one, there shall be no loss of strength for you, nor likewise any loss of wealth;
and as long as these days endure, your progeny shall not perish."
And having enjoyed vast pleasures, at the end, through my grace,
you shall attain remembrance of me and reach the divine world.
O auspicious one, your mind shall always be fixed upon the Dharma;
and for those born in your lineage, there shall be long life.
O highly fortunate one, no misfortune such as calamities shall befall one born in your lineage as long as the sun exists.
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva and honored by the flower-seller, departed from that house.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Parāśara said:
Then, on the royal highway, Kṛṣṇa [saw] a woman carrying a vessel of fragrant unguents...
He saw a hunchbacked woman approaching, in the prime of her youth.
Kṛṣṇa spoke to her playfully: "Whose unguent is this that you are carrying?
Tell me truly, O lotus-eyed one."
Desiring Hari with passion and full of affection toward him,
that hunchbacked woman, overcome by the power of seeing him, spoke these charming words.
"O beloved, why do you not know that she who was appointed by Kaṃsa is renowned as Naikavakrā for her skill in the art of anointing?"
For no ungrounded paste indeed brings pleasure to Kaṃsa;
I am truly the recipient of his abundant favor.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O lady of beautiful countenance, let this fragrant, lovely unguent, worthy of a king and suited to our bodies, be given to us."
Parāśara said:
Having heard this, the hunchbacked woman respectfully replied, "Let it be taken," and then she gave both of them unguents suitable for their bodies.
Then those two bulls among men, their limbs smeared with streaks of unguents,
shone like white and black clouds accompanied by a rainbow.
Then Śauri, who was skilled in the methods of deception, lifted her by the chin and balanced her with two fingers of his right hand.
Then Keśava pulled her with his feet and brought her to straightness;
having attained that rectitude, she became the most excellent among women.
Grasping Govinda by his garment, she spoke with playful grace, languid from the weight of her heart’s overflowing love: "Come to my house in Vraja."
Having been addressed thus by her, Śauri (Viṣṇu) looked at the face of Rāma.
Laughing, he spoke to that blameless Kubjā, who possessed many crooked features.
Having looked at her who had spoken thus, Hari, smiling, said:
"I shall come to your house," Hari said to her with a smile;
then, looking at Rāma's face, he dismissed her and laughed aloud.
With their limbs smeared with streaks of colored paste and wearing blue and yellow garments,
the two of them, adorned with wonderful garlands, then went to the bow-hall.
When the guards, questioned by those two, announced that the Āyogava was the jewel of a bow,
Kṛṣṇa suddenly seized it and drew the bow to its full extent.
Then, as he drew the bow to its full extent, it broke with force,
producing a tremendous sound by which Mathurā was filled.
Then, their bows having been broken by the guards, those two, intent on their purpose,
cut through the guard-force and emerged from the abode of the bow-makers.
Having learned the news of Akrūra’s arrival and hearing that the bow had been broken, Kaṃsa then spoke to Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika:
Kaṃsa said:
"Those two cowherd boys have arrived before you;
they must be slain in a wrestling match, for they are the takers of my life."
"O you of great strength, I have indeed been pleased by you both through that destruction in the wrestling match; I shall grant your desired wishes, for it shall not be otherwise."
Whether by right or by wrong, those two have been made my enemies by you;
they must be slain, for through their death the kingdom shall become common to you all.
Having thus instructed those two wrestlers, he then summoned the elephant-keeper and spoke loudly:
"By you, at the gate of the wrestling arena, an elephant..."
Kuvalayāpīḍa was stationed by him; those two cowherd boys were to be slain when they had reached the entrance of the arena for the wrestling match.
Having given those orders as well and seeing that all the platforms had been prepared,
Kaṃsa, whose death was imminent, awaited the rising of the sun.
Then that entire populace of the city ascended the platforms,
as did the kings with their attendants upon the royal thrones.
Kaṃsa had the assembly of wrestlers and judges positioned near the center of the arena,
while Kaṃsa himself took his place upon a lofty dais.
Platforms were likewise prepared for the women of the inner apartments,
others for the chief courtesans, and still others for the wives of the city dwellers.
The cowherds, headed by Nanda, were seated on other couches,
while Akrūra and Vasudeva were stationed at the edge of the couch.
"Among the women of Nāgarī, Devakī, longing for her son, thought:
'Even at the time of my end, I shall behold the beautiful face of my son.'"
While the musical instruments were being played, as Cāṇūra leaped about excessively, while the world was crying out "Alas! Alas!", Muṣṭika slapped his arms.
After verse 29, B2 inserts lines 4 and 9–10; 3 inserts line 5 only; D3 and T1G2.3 insert the following; and D4 continues with line 2 only after 20.31A:
"Having seen Kuvalayāpīḍa, who had terrible tusks and was most fearsome... [ViP 5.20.29*29:1]
Having played for a very long time between the marks left by the tusks of the elephant, Kṛṣṇa—
Then he seized the two tusks of the elephant with his hands.
Then he struck the elephant on the head with his left foot.
Having uprooted the left tooth with his right hand alone, he [proceeded].
He struck the charioteer, and his head split into a hundred pieces.
Balabhadra also, at that very moment, tore out his own right tooth.
In his rage, he crushed the elephant-keepers standing at his side.
He fell, struck effortlessly by that Balabhadra.
He was struck by the thunderbolt of the thousand-eyed one, like a mountain.
After line 8, the edition of Veṅkaṭeśvara inserts:
"Then, having leaped up with speed, the mighty son of Rohiṇī..."
While D₄ and T₂ insert [the following] after 29, and the edition of Veṅkaṭeśvara inserts:
"Those two heroes, Balabhadra and Janārdana, were smiling slightly. (ViP 5.20.29*30:1)
The two boys, wearing the dress of cowherds, arrived at the entrance of the arena.
Then Kuvalayāpīḍa, urged on by his mahout, [rushed forward].
He rushed forward with speed to slay the two cowherd boys.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the midst of the arena, O best of the twice-born.
Baladeva, having seen him, spoke these words:
"O illustrious one, this serpent, incited by our enemies, must indeed be slain."
Thus was he addressed, O twice-born one, by his elder brother Baladeva.
Then Mādhava, the slayer of enemy heroes, let out a lion’s roar.
Drawing one hand with the other, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, [acted].
Having violently uprooted one tusk, the elephant struck him.
Having uprooted the left tooth with his right hand alone.
He fell upon the surface of the earth like another peak of Mount Meru.
Even the Lord of all the worlds, following the play of a child, [acted thus]. (ViP 5.20.29*) 30A.
While ed. Veṅk. inserts after line 10:
Śauri whirled him about, who was equal to Airāvata in strength.
Having slain Kuvalayāpīḍa, who had been urged on by his elephant-driver,
the two of them— whose limbs were smeared with ichor and blood and whose excellent weapons were the tusks of an elephant— [stood there].
Like two lions among deer, looking about with prideful playfulness,
Balabhadra and Janārdana entered the vast arena.
Immediately thereafter, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from all the galleries, born of the people's wonder that "This is Kṛṣṇa! This is Balabhadra!"
He is the one by whom that terrible night-stalking demoness Pūtanā was slain;
he is the one by whom the cart was cast down and the twin Arjuna trees were shattered.
This is he who, as a mere child, danced upon the serpent Kāliya,
and by whom the great mountain Govardhana was held up for seven nights.
Behold this very Acyuta, by whom the wicked Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, and Keśin were slain as if in mere play by that Great-Souled One.
And here before him walks this mighty-armed Balabhadra, his elder brother,
who moves with effortless grace, bringing delight to the minds and eyes of women.
This is he who is described by the wise who perceive the meaning of the Purāṇas as Gopāla, who will lift up the submerged lineage of the Yādavas.
This is that very portion of Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings and the source of all births, who has descended to the earth as the bearer of the world's burden.
When Rāma and Kṛṣṇa had been thus described by the citizens, at that very moment—
Having entered the city, they approached, beheld by all the world.
It warmed the breast of Devakī, whose breasts were overflowing with milk due to maternal affection.
Having obtained the sight of his son’s face as if it were a great festival,
Vasudeva became like a youth again, casting off the old age that had come upon him.
With their pairs of eyes wide open, the women of the royal harem and the multitude of city women never ceased gazing at him.
B1.3 and D6 insert: "The women said," while G1 inserts:
"Thus those princesses, the queens, and the women of the city..."
And there were preeminent courtesans, maidens, and women of the city.
Those excellent women had their consciousnesses attached to the heart of the Enemy of Kaṃsa.
Then, censuring the king, they wandered about, desiring to see him.
Desiring victory for that mind, they then cried out, "Victory! (jaya).
"Friends, behold Kṛṣṇa’s face, with its exceedingly reddened eyes,
covered with droplets of perspiration born from the exertion of the elephant-fight."
Having surpassed the blooming autumn lotus sprinkled with dewdrops,
let this birth of your eyes be made fruitful.
"O beautiful lady, behold this great splendor of the child, marked with the Śrīvatsa; look at his chest, which destroys adversaries, and his pair of arms."
Do you not see this Balabhadra approaching, his face as white as a kunda flower, the moon, or a lotus stalk, and clad in blue garments?
"O friend, look at this: while Valgata and Muṣṭika, as well as Cāṇūra, are performing [their feats], Balabhadra is making them an object of ridicule."
"Friends, look! For the sake of wrestling, this Hari approaches Cāṇūra.
Are there no elders here who act with propriety?"
The lord of the earth understands nothing at all, whether it be appropriate or inappropriate.
By this [means], it is not possible for him to discern the relative strength and weakness in this matter.
And for what purpose are these ministers [appointed] as ministers in the affairs of the king?
Where is Hari, whose delicate body has just begun to reach its youth;
and where is this great asura, whose expansive body is as hard as a diamond?
"These two, in the prime of their youth, move with great grace upon the arena;
yet the Daitya wrestlers, headed by Cāṇūra, are exceedingly fierce."
This is a great transgression on the part of those who judge wrestling matches,
that a contest between a child and a strong man is overlooked by the umpires.
Parāśara said:
Thus, while the women of the city were speaking, he made the earth tremble.
After 51ab, D2 inserts:
Having heard that [the city] was besieged by the Prāṣṇikas, those two, Rāma and Keśava, [set out].
The Blessed Lord Hari leaped through the midst of the people with his loincloth tied.
And when Balabhadra too, having slapped his arms, leaped gracefully at every step, it was a marvel that the earth did not shatter.
Then Kṛṣṇa, of immeasurable prowess, fought with Cāṇūra,
while the Daitya Muṣṭika, skilled in wrestling, fought with Balabhadra.
Then Hari, together with Cāṇūra, engaged in a wrestling match,
striking with throws, fists, and blows like the falling of stakes and thunderbolts.
After verse 54, Ś₁ inserts:
"And with the striking of knees against one another, as well as by the clashing of arms."
While D5 inserts:
with knees, with blows from stones, and with heads struck together.
With dust raised by their feet and scattered about, a great battle ensued between the two.
That battle between the two was weaponless, yet exceedingly terrible and most dreadful;
it was carried out through sheer strength and vital energy in the presence of a festive assembly.
For as long as Cāṇūra fought with Hari,
he suffered a loss of vital strength more and more at every moment.
Kṛṣṇa, who is identical with the universe, also fought with him as if in mere play;
out of weariness and anger, he shook the mane of his own crest.
Seeing the exhaustion of Cāṇūra and the increasing strength of Kṛṣṇa,
Kaṃsa, overcome with rage, had the musical instruments silenced.
As soon as the drums and other musical instruments were forbidden,
numerous celestial instruments resounded in the sky.
"Victory to Govinda! Slay the Dānava Cāṇūra, O Keśava!
Thus the gods, filled with great joy, spoke as they vanished from sight.
After sporting with Cāṇūra for a long time, Madhusūdana,
making an effort to slay him, uprooted him and whirled him around.
Having whirled the Daitya wrestler a hundred times, the conqueror of enemies dashed him,
now lifeless, against the ground from the sky.
He slapped his hands upon the ground, and Cāṇūra was split into a hundred pieces;
he then turned the earth into a great mire of flowing blood.
At that time, the mighty Baladeva also fought with the Daitya wrestler Muṣṭika, just as Hari had fought with Cāṇūra.
He too, having struck him on the head and chest with his fist and his knee,
threw him down upon the surface of the earth and crushed him whose life had departed.
Kṛṣṇa once again struck the mighty Malla king Tośalaka with a blow from his left fist, felling him to the ground.
When Cāṇūra had been slain, the wrestler Muṣṭika struck down,
and the Tośalaka brought to his destruction, all the wrestlers fled in every direction.
Then both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, filled with joy, leaped about in the arena, forcibly dragging along cowherds of their own age.
Kaṃsa, his eyes red with rage, spoke loudly to the attendants:
"Let these two cowherds be forcibly driven out from this assembly by force."
"Let the wicked Nanda also be seized here with iron shackles,
and let Vasudeva too be slain with a punishment that does not spare the aged."
"Let the cowherds who are here leaping about together with Kṛṣṇa,
as well as their cows and whatever wealth they possess, be seized."
Thus commanding him, Madhusūdana laughed and,
springing up, climbed onto that couch and swiftly seized Kaṃsa.
Having pulled Kaṃsa by his hair so that his crown fell off, he threw him down upon the surface of the earth and fell upon him.
By Kṛṣṇa, who is the heavy support for the entire world, falling upon him,
the king who was the son of Ugrasena was deprived of his life.
Then, seizing the hair of the dead man, the mighty Madhusūdana dragged Kaṃsa’s body into the middle of the arena.
As he was dragged along with immense gravity,
a trench was made by Kaṃsa’s body, as if by the force of a great torrent of water.
When Kaṃsa had been seized by Kṛṣṇa, his brother Sunāman arrived in a rage,
but he was struck down with effortless ease by Balabhadra.
Then that entire arena was filled with cries of "Alas!
upon seeing the Lord of Mathurā slain by Kṛṣṇa with such contempt.
The mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva, also quickly grasped the feet of Vasudeva and Devakī.
Having raised up Janārdana, both Vasudeva and Devakī stood bowed before him,
remembering the words spoken at his birth.
Vasudeva said: Be gracious, O God, O Lord of the gods who grants boons;
likewise, O Keśava, by your grace our deliverance has been accomplished.
Since the Blessed One, having been propitiated, descended into my house for the purpose of destroying the wicked, our lineage has been purified by him.
You are within all beings, abiding in all beings;
O Soul of All, from you proceed both the past and the future.
O Acyuta, you who consist of all the gods, you are eternally worshipped through sacrifices;
you alone are the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the supreme lord of all sacrifices.
O Janārdana, you are the source of the entire world.
That this mind of mine, which conceals its true nature, should feel such affection for you—
just as Devakī feels for her own son— is an utter mockery.
Where are you, the creator of all beings, without beginning or end;
and where is this tongue of mine, a mere human, that shall say, "This is my son"?
O Lord of the World, since this entire universe has arisen from you,
by what logic could you have come into being from us without the power of Māyā?
How can he, in whom the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— is established,
be born from a human being as one who sleeps within the womb?
Therefore, be gracious, O Supreme Lord; protect the universe through your partial incarnations, for you are not merely my son.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, this entire world is deluded by you; why do you cause it to be so bewildered, O Supreme Lord, O Soul?
With a vision deluded by Māyā, I thought, "He is my son," and I experienced an intense fear of Kaṃsa;

yet you were led from here to Gokula by me who had cast off all fear. You grew up while I remained overwhelmed by great terror, O Lord; for me, there is no longer any sense of "mine-ness" regarding you.

O Lord of the worlds, you are Viṣṇu; for the sake of benefiting us, you have arrived here. Our delusion has indeed departed, as we have beheld those deeds of Rudra, the Maruts, the Aśvins, and Śatakratu, which were not previously accomplished or even perceived. ViP 5.20.92.
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: Having attained spiritual knowledge through witnessing the deeds of the Blessed Lord, those two—
But seeing Devakī and Vasudeva, Hari indeed spread forth his Vaiṣṇava Māyā once again for the sake of deluding the Yadu clan.
And he said, "O mother, O father, after a long time I, who have been longing and am terrified of Kaṃsa, have finally seen you both and Saṃkarṣaṇa."
The time that passes while one fails to honor one's mother and father becomes a useless fragment of life for virtuous people.
O dear one, for embodied beings who perform the worship of their gurus, gods, twice-born, and their mother and father,
their birth becomes fruitful.
Therefore, O father, all this that has been done in transgression must be forgiven,
for we two were under the control of others due to the power and valor of Kaṃsa.
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, both of them then bowed down to the elders of the Yadu clan in due order;
having honored them appropriately, they then paid their respects to the citizens.
Then Kaṃsa’s wives, along with his mothers, overwhelmed by misery and grief, surrounded him as he lay slain upon the ground and lamented.
Afflicted by intense remorse in many ways, Hari himself,
his eyes clouded with tears, consoled them.
Then Madhusūdana released Ugrasena from his bonds and,
though his son had been slain, consecrated him once again in his own kingdom.
Consecrated in the kingdom by Kṛṣṇa, that lion of the Yadus performed the funeral rites for his son and for the others who had been slain there.
When the funeral rites had been performed for him, Hari spoke to him as he sat upon the lion-throne:
"O Lord, command without hesitation whatever task is to be done."
"Due to the curse of Yayāti, this lineage is currently unworthy of sovereignty;
yet, while I remain as your servant, O gods, why should you issue commands through kings?"
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, he (Brahmā) remembered Vāyu, who arrived at that very moment;
and the blessed Keśava, appearing in human form, spoke to him regarding the task at hand.
"Go, O Vāyu, and say to Indra: 'Enough with your pride, O Vāsava!
Let the Sudharmā assembly hall be given by you to Ugrasena.'"
Kṛṣṇa says: "This unsurpassed jewel, worthy of a king, is called the Sudharmā assembly hall; it is fitting for the Yadus to sit within it."
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Pavana went and told everything to the Lord of Śacī; Purandara, in turn, gave the assembly hall named Sudharmā to Vāyu.
And those bulls among the Yadus enjoyed that divine assembly hall, brought by the wind and enriched with every jewel, through the protection of Govinda’s arm.
Although they had mastered all branches of knowledge and were composed of universal wisdom,
those two heroes, the best of the Yadus, demonstrated the traditional succession of disciple and teacher.
Then the two heroes, Baladeva and Janārdana, went to Sāndīpani of the Kāśya lineage, a resident of the city of Avanti, for the sake of learning weapons.
After 19c, ed. Veṅk.
inserts: ... having performed the sequence of the initiation ceremony.
... who find delight in the study of the Vedas ... // ViP_5.21.19*38:2 //
Having entered into discipleship under him, those two heroes, devoted to the conduct due to a teacher, displayed their proper behavior to all people.
O twice-born one, he studied the science of archery along with its secret doctrines and compendiums in sixty-four days and nights; that was truly marvelous.
Reflecting upon that superhuman feat of theirs, which was beyond all belief, Sāndīpani then thought that the moon and the sun themselves had arrived.
After verse 22, the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition inserts:
"And indeed, he [taught] the four Vedas with their ancillaries (sāṅga) and all the Śāstras."
Having obtained the entire collection of missiles as soon as it was mentioned, the two said,
"Choose whatever preceptor’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā) you wish to be given."
Having perceived their super-sensory deed,
that high-minded one requested back his dead son from Prabhāsa on the salt ocean.
Having said, "So be it," he set out toward the ocean together with Rāma. (ViP 5.21.24*40)
Then, having received the two who had taken up their weapons, the Great Ocean, holding a vessel of water, said:
"I have not taken away the son of Sāndīpani."
After 521.25a B1 l. 1 only, D3.4, T1, M1 insert: ...
having come by chariot to the ocean...
"O Sāgara, let the son of Sāndīpani be given back quickly."
Then, being distressed, he quickly... // ViP 5.21.25*41:3 //
O destroyer of asuras, that Daitya named Pañcajana, in the form of a conch, seized the boy within my waters.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa went into the water, slew that Pañcajana, and took from his bones that most excellent conch shell.
By whose roar the strength of the Daityas was diminished,
the splendor of the gods increased, and unrighteousness went to its destruction.
Having filled that Pāñcajanya conch and gone to the city of Yama,
Hari and the powerful Baladeva conquered Vaivasvata, the god of death.
Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the best among the strong, restored that boy— who was situated in torment— to his father, endowed with his former body.
And both Rāma and Janārdana returned once more to Mathurā, which was protected by Ugrasena, while the men and women there were filled with joy.
[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The mighty Kaṃsa married the two daughters of Jarāsaṃdha.
O Maitreya, there was also Asti and Prāpti, who were the wives of Hari, the slayer of his father.
Surrounded by a great army, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, lord of Magadha, advanced in anger to slay that Yādava.
Then, having approached Mathurā, the Lord of Magadha,
surrounded by twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs of his army, laid siege to it.
Having gone forth with small retinues, both Rāma and Janārdana,
being powerful, fought equally against his mighty soldiers.
Then, O best of sages, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa formed the highest resolve regarding the acquisition of the ancient weapons.
Immediately thereafter, O brahmin, Hari’s Śārṅga bow, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows,
and the Kaumodakī mace arrived from the sky.
And, O Brahmin, the flaming Saunanda mace, the beloved of Balabhadra, descended from the sky according to his mental desire.
Then, having defeated the lord of Magadha along with his army in battle,
both heroes, Rāma and Janārdana, entered the city.
O great sage, although that wicked Jarāsandha had been defeated,
Kṛṣṇa did not consider him truly conquered as long as he remained alive.
O best of the twice-born, Jarāsaṃdha, accompanied by his army, came once more; though he had been defeated by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, he had escaped.
Thus, the King of Magadha, who was exceedingly arrogant, fought eighteen battles with the Yadus, who were led by Kṛṣṇa.
In all these battles, Jarāsandha, though superior in strength, was defeated by the Yādavas with their small forces and fled.
That strength of the Yādavas, which was repeatedly undefeated by them,
was actually due to the majesty of the presence of the Discus-wielder, an incarnation of Viṣṇu.
That is but a play for the Lord of the universe, whose nature is the dharma of a human,
that he discharges weapons of many forms against his enemies.
For him who effects the creation and dissolution of the universe by mind alone,
what need is there for extensive effort in the destruction of his enemies?
Nevertheless, following the conduct of men, he who makes peace with the powerful and wages war against the weak acts accordingly.
Employing conciliation, bribery, and likewise sowing dissension, he inflicts punishment and sometimes even resorts to flight.
As he thus conforms to the activities of embodied human beings,
the play of that Lord of the World proceeds according to his own will.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, a brother-in-law once addressed a Brāhmaṇa named Gārgya in a gathering, calling him "impotent."
Then, in the presence of the Yadus, all the Yādavas laughed.
Then, overcome with anger, he went to the Deccan and performed austerities,
desiring a son who would bring fear to the Yadu dynasty.
Worshipping Mahādeva, he consumed iron filings;
and at the end of the twelfth year, Hara, being pleased with him, granted him a boon.
The childless Yavana king honored him,
and from his union with that woman, a son was born who resembled a bee.
Having consecrated that Kālayavana, whose chest was as hard as the tip of a thunderbolt, upon his own kingdom, the lord of the Yavanas departed for the forest.
Intoxicated by the pride of his own prowess, he questioned the powerful kings on earth; Nārada then told him about the Yādavas.
Surrounded by thousands upon thousands of millions of Mlecchas,
well-equipped with elephants, horses, and chariots, he exerted his supreme effort.
O Maitreya, filled with indignation toward the Yādavas, he set out day after day for the city of Mathurā, never halting his journey.
Kṛṣṇa also reflected: "The Yādava army has been destroyed;
the Māgadha king will now advance against me in battle."
The strength of the Magadhan has been exhausted; that powerful Kālayavana shall be his slayer.
Thus, this twofold calamity for the Yadus has arrived.
Therefore, I shall construct a fortress that will be difficult for enemies to conquer even for the Yadus;
therein, even women could fight, let alone the bulls among the Vṛṣṇis.
Whether I am intoxicated, negligent, asleep, or away on a journey,
let not my wicked enemies, who are superior in power, bring about the destruction of the Yādavas.
Having reflected thus, Govinda requested twelve yojanas of land from the great ocean; there he constructed the city of Dvārakā.
With its great gardens and massive ramparts, adorned with hundreds of lakes,
and crowded with walls and houses, it was like Indra’s city, Amarāvatī.
Having brought the inhabitants of Mathurā there, Janārdana himself went to Mathurā while Kālayavana was nearby.
When the army had encamped outside Mathurā, Govinda went out unarmed and beheld the lord of the Yavanas.
Having recognized him as Vāsudeva, that king, whose weapon was his own arms, pursued him—
he who cannot be reached even by the minds of great yogis.
Followed by him, Kṛṣṇa also entered the great cave where the immensely powerful King Mucukunda was lying asleep.
