That wicked Yavana, having entered, saw a man lying on his bed and,
thinking him to be Kṛṣṇa, struck him with his foot.
Having risen, King Mucukunda also beheld the Yavana.
As soon as he was seen by him, O Maitreya, that Yavana blazed with fire born of his wrath and was reduced to ashes in that very instant.
For he, having gone to the war between the gods and asuras and conquered the great asuras,
chose sleep as a boon from the gods, being afflicted by drowsiness for a very long time.
And it was declared by the gods: "He who shall awaken you while you are fast asleep shall instantly be reduced to ashes by the fire born from your own body."
Having thus burned that wicked one and beheld Madhusūdana,
he asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am born in the lineage of the Moon,
the son of Vasudeva, originating from the race of Yadu."
Mucukunda, for his part, recalled there the words of the aged Garga.
Having recollected and prostrated before him, Hari, the Lord of all, he said:
"O Supreme Lord, you are known; you are a portion of Viṣṇu."
Formerly, Garga declared that in the twenty-eighth yuga,
at the end of the Dvāpara age, the birth of Hari will take place in the lineage of Yadu.
There is no doubt that you have arrived as one who brings benefit to mortals.
For indeed, I am not able to withstand your exceedingly great majesty;
for your speech is more formidable than the roar of a water-laden cloud, and the earth bows down, pressed by your feet.
In the great battle between the gods and the asuras, the mighty warriors of the Daitya army could not endure my splendor; yet I cannot endure your splendor.
Whoever remembers this, his splendor has come to you for refuge.
For a single being fallen into saṃsāra, you are the supreme refuge; therefore, O destroyer of the distress of those who have sought your protection, be gracious and remove my impurity.
You are the oceans, the mountains, and the rivers; you are the forests, the earth, the sky, the wind, the waters, and fire, as well as the mind.

Intellect, the unmanifest, the vital breaths, the lord of the breaths, and likewise the person (puruṣa)— and that which is beyond the person, all-pervading, unborn, and free from conceptual construction.
Devoid of sound and the other sense-objects, undecaying, immeasurable, free from destruction,
without growth or decay— that Brahman, which is without beginning or end, you are.
From you come the immortals, along with the ancestors, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras;
from you come the siddhas and apsarases, as well as humans, animals, and birds.
All reptiles, all wild animals, and all trees [originate] from you.
Those that are gross, middling, subtle, and even subtler than the subtle; 5.23.35ab*44.
And whatever has been and whatever will be here, whether moving or stationary—
Whether it be formless or embodied, gross or exceedingly subtle—O Creator of the World, all that exists is You; there is nothing whatsoever apart from You.
O Blessed One, as I have always wandered in this wheel of saṃsāra,
overcome by the threefold suffering, I have never attained peace anywhere.
"O Lord, mistaking sufferings for pleasures, I grasped at them as if they were pools of water in a mirage; those very things have now resulted only in torment."
O Lord, [there are] sovereignty, the earth, the army, the treasury, the faction of friends, as well as sons,
the wife, the circle of servants, and the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest.
"O Imperishable One, I grasped all this with the notion that it was happiness;
yet in its ultimate transformation, O Lord, it became for me of the nature of suffering."
Even the host of gods, O Lord, having reached the celestial realm, desired assistance from me; where, then, is eternal liberation?
O Supreme Lord, without propitiating you— the source and abode of all the worlds—
who could ever attain eternal bliss?
Men whose minds are deluded by your māyā, having encountered birth, death, old age, and the like,
experience various torments and behold the face of the King of the Dead.
Consequently, O You whose true nature is unknown, men experience most terrible suffering in the hells produced by their own actions.
O Supreme Lord, I am utterly addicted to sense objects and deluded by Your illusory power; I wander within the pit of possessiveness and pride.

Thus, with my mind scorched by the exhaustion and distress of saṃsāra, I have come to you for refuge— you who are the shoreless Lord, the praiseworthy one, from whom nothing higher exists, and whose desire is fixed upon nirvāṇa, the abode of ultimate transformation.
[Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Having been thus praised at that time by the wise Mucukunda, [the Lord spoke].
The Lord Hari, the beginningless master of all beings, spoke.
Go, O Lord of Men, to the divine worlds as you desire,
with your supreme sovereignty unimpeded and augmented by my grace.
Having enjoyed divine and great pleasures, you will be born into a noble family;
by my grace, you will remember your past lives and thereafter attain liberation.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the king prostrated before the Lord, the Acyuta of the worlds,
and emerging from the mouth of the cave, he beheld men who were very small in stature.
Then, knowing that the Kali Yuga had arrived, the king went to Mount Gandhamādana, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, in order to perform austerities.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having caused that enemy's army to be destroyed by means of a stratagem,
arrived at Mathurā and seized it, resplendent with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having brought him to Dvārāvatī, he presented him to Ugrasena;
and the clan of Yadu became free from fear of defeat by enemies.
O Maitreya, Baladeva also, having laid aside all signs of agitation and longing to see his kinsmen, set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
Then the conqueror of enemies greeted the cowherds and cowherd girls with affection and great respect, just as he had done before.
He was embraced by some, and he himself embraced others;
he laughed together with some cowherds as well as with the cowherd women.
There, the cowherds spoke many pleasant words to Halāyudha,
while the cowherd girls, provoked by love, spoke with jealousy, and others spoke as well.
Other cowherd women asked:
"O beloved of the city folk, does Kṛṣṇa, whose very nature consists of flickering fragments of love, abide in happiness?"
Does he, whose friendship lasts but a moment, not mock our efforts and thereby increase the excessive pride in the good fortune of the city women?
Does Kṛṣṇa remember our sweet imitation of his singing?
Will he perhaps come even once to see his mother?
Or rather, what is the use of those words? Let another story be told, for without him we shall exist, and without us he shall exist.
Father, mother, brother, husband, and kinsmen—what have we not abandoned for his sake? For he is indeed the banner of ungratefulness.
He never remembers us anywhere with messages sweetened by conciliation.
Nevertheless, O Rāma, you must tell me the truth: does Kṛṣṇa offer any word concerning his arrival here? Do not speak falsely.
That Dāmodara, who is Govinda, now appears to us as one whose mind is attached to the women of the city; having lost his affection for us, he is difficult for us to behold.
Parāśara said:
Addressed again as "Kṛṣṇa" and "Dāmodara," the cowherd girls,
their hearts stolen by Hari, wept aloud.
The cowherd women were comforted by Rāma with Kṛṣṇa’s exceedingly charming messages, which were sweet with conciliation, full of love, and free from pride.
And as before, Rāma engaged in delightful conversations full of jesting with the cowherds, and he took his pleasure with them in the lands of Vraja.
[Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
While that high-souled one was wandering in the forest together with the cowherds,
Of Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth, who had assumed the guise of a human form.
When he had accomplished his great task and was traversing the earth,
Varuṇa spoke to Vāruṇī for the sake of his excessive enjoyment.
O auspicious one, go to the delight of that one of great luster, Ananta, for whom you, the intoxicating one, have always been desired for his enjoyment.
Thus addressed by him, Vāruṇī then made her presence known within the hollow of a kadamba tree growing in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
While wandering about, Baladeva also smelled an exquisite scent of wine and then experienced his long-standing thirst for liquor.
Then, O Maitreya, seeing a stream of liquor suddenly falling from the Kadamba tree, that wielder of the plow (Balarāma) experienced supreme joy.
And, filled with joy, he drank together with the cowherds and cowherdesses while being sung to charmingly by those skilled in song and instrumental music.
Exhausted and radiant with drops of sweat like pearls from the intense heat, he spoke to me in distress: "Come, Yamunā, I wish to bathe."
But that river, disregarding the words spoken by him as if they were those of a madman, did not come; thereupon the wielder of the plow, filled with rage, seized his plow.
Having seized her on the bank, he, overwhelmed by intoxication, dragged her along, saying:
"O sinful woman, you will not come? You will not come? Go elsewhere as you please!"
Suddenly drawn by him,
the river abandoned its course and flooded that forest where Balabhadra was staying.
Then, approaching him in bodily form with eyes agitated by terror, she said to Rāma, "Be gracious; release me, O wielder of the mace!"
He said: "O river, you despise my heroism and strength;
therefore, I shall divide you into a thousand channels with a stroke of my plow."
Parāśara said: Having been thus addressed, Balarāma, being propitiated by that river out of extreme terror,
released the Yamunā onto that flooded region of the earth.
Then, as that great-souled one had bathed, beauty came to him,
bringing a lovely blue lotus for an ear-ornament and a single earring.
For 14c–15d, Ś₂ marginally substitutes:
"Then, being entreated, the blessed Balarāma released the Yamunā."
He plunged into the water with the women, like a lordly elephant with female elephants.
Having sported as she desired, she emerged from the water wearing soiled garments.
He gave her highly precious ornaments and a garland beautiful with its radiance.
And Lakṣmī presented to him a garland of unfading lotuses sent by Varuṇa,
as well as two blue garments resembling the ocean.
Then, having placed the crest-jewel upon his head, adorned with beautiful earrings,
wearing blue garments and garlands, he shone, endowed with radiant splendor.
Thus adorned, Rāma then took his pleasure there in Vraja;
after two months had passed, he returned once more to the city of Dvārakā.
Bala married the daughter of King Raivata, named Revatī; from her were born Niśaṭha and Ulmuka.
For verses 17–19, Ś₂ substitutes:
"Having put on two blue garments and having donned a golden garland..."
Adorned with excellent ornaments, he was like the elephant of Indra.
Even today, O King, it is seen along the path drawn by the Yamunā.
Indeed, it seems to manifest the heroic power of Bala, who possesses infinite vigor.
In this way, every night passed as they took their pleasure alone in Vraja.
The mind of Rāma was captivated by the sweetness of the women of Vraja.
[Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Bhīṣmaka was the king in Kuṇḍina, in the region of Vidarbha.
Rukmī was his son, and Rukmiṇī was his excellent daughter.
Kṛṣṇa desired Rukmiṇī, and she, of the lovely smile, desired him;
yet Rukmin, out of hatred, did not give her to the wielder of the discus even though he asked for her.
And, urged by Jarāsaṃdha,
the one of vast prowess Bhīṣmaka gave Rukmiṇī to Śiśupāla along with Rukmin.
Then, for the sake of the marriage, all the kings led by Jarāsandha went to the city of Bhīṣmaka, desiring to do what was pleasing to Śiśupāla.
Kṛṣṇa also, surrounded by many Yādavas such as Balabhadra and others,
set out for Kuṇḍina to witness the marriage of the King of Cedi.
The kings who were enemies, having arrived earlier, have now entered within.
Thinking thus, Kṛṣṇa likewise prepared for them outside.
When the wedding was to take place on the following day, Hari abducted that maiden,
having placed the burden of the opposing side upon his kinsmen, headed by Rāma and others.
And then there were the illustrious Pauṇḍraka, Dantavakra, Vidūratha,
and kings such as Śiśupāla, Jarāsandha, and Śālva.
Enraged, they made a supreme effort to slay Hari,
but having come together, they were defeated by Rāma and the other bulls among the Yadus.
"I will not enter Kuṇḍina without having slain Keśava in battle";
having made this vow, Rukmin rushed toward Kṛṣṇa to kill him.
Having destroyed the army— crowded with elephants, horses, infantry,
and chariots— he was conquered and cast down upon the earth by the wielder of the discus as if in mere play.
After 10 D6, insert:
Kṛṣṇa resolved to slay Rukmin, who was intoxicated with the pride of battle.
D6 continues; meanwhile, D5 inserts after 10:
Having prostrated himself, the blessed Lord Hari was entreated by Rukmiṇī for [the gift of] Brahmā.
"I have only one brother; he must not be killed by you now."
"O Lord of Gods, restraining your anger, let the alms of your brother be given."
Having been addressed thus, he was embraced by Kṛṣṇa, the one of unwearied deeds.
At that time, Rukmī built a city named Bhojakaṭa and lived there.
Having completely defeated Rukmin,
Madhusūdana duly married Rukmiṇī, who had been obtained through the Rākṣasa form of marriage.
Then, from her was born the powerful Pradyumna, a portion of Madana;
he was indeed the one whom Śambara abducted, and he was the one who slew Śambara.
[Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
O Sage, how was the hero Pradyumna carried off by Śambara?
And how was the immensely powerful Śambara slain by Pradyumna?
Ed. Veṅk. inserts: How did he slay him who had previously been carried off by him?
O Guru, I wish to hear all of this in detail.
Parāśara said: O sage, on the sixth day after he was born, Kālaśambara carried Pradyumna away from the lying-in chamber, thinking, "He is my slayer."
Having seized him, he cast him into the fierce salt ocean,
that most terrible abode of sea-monsters filled with whirlpools produced by the surging waves.
And there, a certain fish swallowed the boy who had fallen;
yet he did not die, even though scorched by the fire within its belly.
And that fish, O twice-born one, was killed by fishermen along with other fish and presented to Śambara, the chief of the asuras.
His blameless wife, named Māyāvatī, who was the mistress of the entire household,
exercised authority over the cooks.
When the belly of the fish was torn open, there was seen a most beautiful youth,
like the first sprout of the tree of Love that had been consumed by fire.
"Who is this? How has she come to be within the belly of a fish?"—to that slender woman, thus filled with curiosity, Nārada spoke.
This son of Viṣṇu, who is responsible for the creation and destruction of the entire world, was carried away by Śambara from the maternity chamber.
Cast into the ocean, swallowed by a fish, and brought under its power—
O fair-browed one, protect this jewel among men with confidence.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, she protected that infant; from her very childhood, she was infatuated with him due to an excessive passion and his extraordinary beauty.
O Great Sage, when he was adorned with the fullness of youth, she,
who moved with the gait of an elephant, became filled with desire for him.
And Māyāvatī, blinded by passion and with her heart and eyes fixed upon him, bestowed all her illusory powers (*māyā*) upon that great-souled Pradyumna.
For 5.26.1a–5.27.13b, Ś₂ substitutes:
"Out of courtesy toward that king Bhīṣmaka, [he stayed] within his intestines. (ViP 5.27.13*52:1)
Kṛṣṇa heard of the maiden Rukmiṇī, who was renowned for her beauty.
She too heard of Kṛṣṇa, the enemy of Kaṃsa, who has lotus-like eyes.
The minds of those two possessed some indescribable excellence, refined by the essence of longing.
Rukmī, the son of Bhīṣmaka, was powerful-armed and fierce in battle.
That hero who maintains a rivalry on earth with both Bhārgava and Bhīṣma.
Proud as he was, he had always been sought after by Kṛṣṇa for his younger sister, Rukmiṇī.
Out of hatred, he did not give him [the gift], but rather remarked, "This man is a servant of Kaṃsa."
Then, at the word of Jarāsaṃdha, [he was sent] to King Śiśupāla.
Bhīṣmaka gave away that daughter, whom he had intended for his son, to him who was approved by his son.
Then Śiśupāla, the son of Vasudeva and a *vasu*, [attacked] his city.
By Kṛṣṇa and the other Vṛṣṇi heroes, who had been invited to the bridegroom’s procession.
And together with kings headed by Dantavakra and Jarāsaṃdha.
Honored by Bhīṣmaka, he departed for the wedding festival.
There, she was the moonlight for his eyes, busily engaged in worshipping Bhavānī.
Kṛṣṇa beheld Rukmiṇī, whose long eyes were like those of a black antelope.
Then, having seen her filled with longing, Vaikuṇṭha was overwhelmed by the god of love.
He suddenly carried off the daughter of Bhīṣmaka while the men looked on.
Without having slain Kṛṣṇa, who is of impure conduct and a perpetrator of wicked deeds.
I shall return to my own city, having fallen away from the vow of a hero.
Having spoken thus, the king mounted his chariot, followed by his heroes.
With the tips of his banners fluttering in the wind, he proceeded, making the quarters of the sky resound.
Seeing him approaching from afar, Rukmiṇī’s companion, seated upon his chariot, [beheld him].
Hari stood there, having turned back, with his bow drawn to his ear.
Then Śauri, having cut down all their weapons, rained down divine missiles upon them.
Nimi pierced Rukmin in the heart with sharp iron arrows.
When he had fainted and fallen, and that circle of kings had fled;
Out of compassion, Śauri protected the Rukmiṇas at the word of Rukmiṇī.
When Kṛṣṇa had gone to Dvāravatī and the Vṛṣṇis had returned.
Rukmin entered the city named Kuṇḍina without any sense of shame.
Unconquered by his adversaries, he established a city in front of him.
He reflected upon the city named Bhojakata as a place where pride would be humbled.
As if taking up the goddess of victory herself, she was like Śrī incarnate in another form.
But Kāma, who was a portion of Vāsudeva, had previously been consumed by the wrath of the Śūdra.
For the sake of obtaining a body, he once again resorted to that very same [method].
He himself was born of Vaidarbhī through the prowess of Kṛṣṇa.
The ninth [son] from his father was the horse known as Pradyumna.
Śambara, assuming the form of Time, carried off that child to an unknown place.
Having recognized him as his own enemy, he cast him into the ocean and went home.
The powerful fish swallowed it, along with others as well.
Ensnared in a great net, he was captured by those who live by fishing.
The fishermen presented him as a gift to Śambara.
The cooks, having led him quickly to the kitchen, cut him up with a sharp axe.
Having seen that child in her womb, they reported it to Māyāvatī.
Nārada related everything to her, whose mind was filled with apprehension.
The reality of the Child, his birth, and his entry into the belly of the fish.
And she was indeed the illustrious wife of Kāma, named Rati.
She awaits the rebirth of her husband’s body, which has been consumed by fire.
She was appointed by Śambara to the preparation of soup and rice.
Perceiving Kāmadeva as a child, he then felt affection for that infant.
Before long, that son of Kṛṣṇa attained full youth.
He produced a great agitation among the women as they gazed [upon him].
But as she persisted, that son of Kṛṣṇa said to the lotus-eyed woman:
"Why do you behave in such a contrary manner, casting aside your maternal nature?"
And she said to him, "You are certainly not my son;
this Kālaśambara has carried you away, the son of Viṣṇu."
Cast into the ocean, I was recovered by a fish from its belly;
yet your mother, so exceedingly affectionate, still weeps for you even today, my beloved.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the mighty Pradyumna challenged Śambara to battle; with his mind agitated by anger, he fought.
Having utterly destroyed that Daitya's army, Mādhava bypassed the seventh illusion and employed the eighth.
With that illusory power, she struck the Daitya Kālaśambara;
then, springing up together with her, she returned to her father’s house.
Seeing him fallen in the inner apartments together with Māyāvatī,
the wives of Kṛṣṇa conceived a dark suspicion regarding Kṛṣṇa.
And the faultless Rukmiṇī, her eyes filled with tears, spoke with affection:
"Blessed indeed is she whose son this is, now in the prime of youth."
"At this age, O child, if my son Pradyumna still lives,
then some fortunate mother has been graced by you."
"Or rather, from the nature of my affection for you and the appearance of your body,
it is very clear, my child, that you will become a son of Hari."
Parāśara said:
In the meantime, Nārada arrived together with Kṛṣṇa and,
gladdening her, spoke to Queen Rukmiṇī, who was staying within the inner apartments.
"O fair-browed one, here is your son who has returned after slaying Śambara;
he is the one by whom your infant was carried away from the lying-in chamber."
This virtuous Māyāvatī is the wife of this son of yours;
she is not the wife of Śambara. Hear now the reason for this.
When Manmatha had met his destruction,
she who was devoted to his manifestation assumed a form through her illusory power and deluded Śambara.
In the enjoyment of the monastery and other such pleasures, this woman with intoxicating eyes showed the Daitya beautiful forms composed of illusion.
"Kāma has descended as your son, and this Rati is his beloved;
you should have no doubt in this matter, for she is your beautiful daughter-in-law."
Then Rukmiṇī and Keśava, as well as the entire city, were filled with joy and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Seeing Rukmiṇī reunited with her son who had been lost for so long,
all the people in Dvāravatī were then struck with amazement.
[Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
§ Parāśara said:
The heroic [Vasudeva] begot Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, and Cārudeha;
Suṣeṇa, Cārugupta, and furthermore Bhadracāru.
Rukmiṇī gave birth to sons— Cāruvinda, Sucāru, and Cāru, the best among the strong— as well as a daughter named Cārumatī.
Kṛṣṇa also had seven other beautiful wives:
Kālindī, Mitravindā, Satyā, and likewise Nāgnajitī; 5.28.3.
And the goddess Jāmbavatī, Rohiṇī who could assume any form at will,
and another, the daughter of the King of Madra, Suśīlā, whose ornament was her virtuous character.
Satyabhāmā, the daughter of Satrājit, and the sweetly smiling Lakṣmaṇā—
these were the sixteen thousand other women of the wielder of the discus.
Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, was the first among all of them.
The immensely powerful Pradyumna also took the auspicious daughter of Rukmin at her svayaṃvara, and she [accepted] him, the son of Hari.
To her was born a son of great strength and prowess,
Aniruddha, a subduer of enemies who was irresistible in battle and an ocean of valor.
Keśava also chose the granddaughter of that very Rukmin;
and although Rukmin was competing with Śauri, he gave her to his grandson.
At her wedding, Rāma and the other Yādavas were present together with Hari.
Then, for the sake of their welfare, all those others who were likewise kings [did so].
They went to the city of Rukmin, O twice-born one, which is named Bhojakata.
When that marriage of the high-souled Pradyumna had been concluded, the kings headed by the King of Kaliṅga addressed these words to Rukmin: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.28.10.
Balarama, though ignorant of the dice, suffered a great calamity in the game;
why then, O one of great luster, do we not conquer his army in this gambling match?
Parāśara said:
"So be it," replied Rukmin, endowed with great strength, to those kings;
and then, together with Rāma, he engaged in a game of dice within the assembly hall.
Balarāma was defeated by Rukmin with one thousand gold coins;
on the second wager as well, another thousand was won by Rukmin.
Then Balabhadra accepted a wager of ten thousand gold coins; Rukmin, the best among those skilled in gambling, defeated him for that amount.
Then, O twice-born one, the foolish king of Kaliṅga laughed loudly, baring his teeth; and Rukmin, arrogant with pride, spoke.
"Out of ignorance, I have defeated this Baladeva at dice; blinded by the arrogance of the dice, he has needlessly insulted those who are experts in the game."
Seeing the King of Kaliṅga with his teeth bared in a grin,
and Rukmin as well uttering wicked words, Halāyudha was filled with wrath.
Then Halāyudha, his soul overcome with anger,
took up ten million gold pieces as the stake, and Rukmin likewise cast the dice for that purpose.
Baladeva defeated him and said loudly, "He has been conquered by me! Rukmin, however, cried out loudly, "By me! By me! "Enough of these false claims, O Balarāma! [he replied].
"This stake proposed by you is true; it was not approved by me.
If it has been won by you in this manner, how can it not be considered won by me?"
Parāśara said: Then, a voice resounded loudly from the sky with a deep resonance,
increasing the wrath of the high-souled Baladeva.
"Rukmin spoke falsely that he was conquered by force and by righteousness;
for even without saying anything at all, an action is accomplished through one's deeds."
Then the mighty Balarāma, rising up with eyes bloodshot with anger,
struck Rukmin with his very dice-board (aṣṭāpada).
And seizing the King of Kaliṅga as he was struggling with force, the powerful Balarāma,
enraged, broke the teeth with which he had laughed aloud.
And having dragged up a great pillar made of gold, the powerful Balarāma,
filled with wrath, struck down the other kings who were on that side.
Then, O twice-born one, when that army was enraged, the entire circle of kings cried out "Alas! and became intent on flight.
O Maitreya, having heard that Rukmin had been slain by Balarāma, Madhusūdana said nothing out of fear for Rukmiṇī and Bala.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having taken Aniruddha after his marriage was performed,
Keśava returned to Dvārakā along with the host of the Yadus.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
Parāśara said: Then, in Dvāravatī, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, [approached] Śauri...
Then, O Maitreya, he arrived riding upon the back of the intoxicated Airāvata.
Then, having entered Dvārakā and met with Hari,
he related the deeds of the Daitya Naraka.
O Madhusūdana, even while remaining in the human state, you have brought all sufferings to pacification by acting as the protector of the gods.
Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka—who was intent on the destruction of the ascetics—and likewise Keśin: all of them have been slain by you.
Kaṃsa, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Pūtanā the slayer of infants—
all these and whatever other harassers of the world existed have been brought to destruction by you.
While the three worlds are protected by the strength of your arms and your noble intellect,
the denizens of heaven attain satisfaction through the receipt of their sacrificial portions from the sacrifices you perform.
O Janārdana, you should now hear the reason for which I have come,
and having heard it, you ought to make an effort toward its remedy.
O subduer of enemies, this one named Bhauma, the lord of the city of Prāgjyotiṣa, inflicts injury upon all living beings.
O Janārdana, having abducted the daughters of the gods, siddhas, asuras, and kings, that asura indeed confined them in his own palace.
He seized the water-shedding umbrella of Varuṇa,
as well as the peak of Mount Mandara and the jewel-mountain.
O Kṛṣṇa, that Asura has carried off my mother’s two divine earrings, which distill nectar;
he desires the elephant Airāvata.
"O Govinda, this was ill-advised that I spoke to you;
let that which must be done in this matter be considered by yourself."
Parāśara said:
Having heard this and smiling, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
took Vāsava by the hand and rose from his excellent seat.
And the Lord reflected in his mind upon the eater of serpents.
Having mounted the sky-traveling Garuḍa as he had intended,
and having placed Satyabhāmā upon him, he went to the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Then, O Maitreya, Śakra also mounted the elephant Airāvata and departed for his abode in the triple heaven while the inhabitants of Dvārakā looked on.
O best of the twice-born, for a hundred yojanas all around the city of Prāgjyotiṣa, the earth was covered with the nooses of Mura, which were as sharp as razors.
Hari cut those nooses asunder by hurling his Sudarśana discus;
then Muru rose up, and Keśava struck him down.
Then Hari reduced those seven thousand sons of Mura to ashes with the fire from the edge of his discus, like so many moths.
O twice-born one, having slain Mura, Hayagrīva, and likewise Pañcajana,
the wise [Rāma] hastened toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
There, Govinda Kṛṣṇa engaged in battle with Naraka’s great army, wherein he slew the Daityas by the thousands.
The powerful wielder of the discus, the slayer of the hosts of Daityas, hurled his discus and split in two that son of Bhūmi, Naraka, who was discharging a rain of weapons and missiles.
Then, in the hell named Hate (Dveṣa), the Earth, having taken Ādi and Kuṇḍala with her, approached the Lord of the World and spoke these words: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.29.22.
O Lord, when I was rescued by you in the form of a boar,
this son, born from your touch, was then produced within me.
"This very man was given to me by you alone, and by you alone has he been struck down.
Take these two earrings and protect his lineage."
O Lord, for the sake of relieving my burden alone,
the Blessed One has come to this world with a portion of himself, his countenance gracious and serene.
You are the creator, the transformer, and the destroyer; you are the source and the dissolution of the worlds.
You are the world itself, O Acyuta; what more can be praised of you?
When the Blessed One is both the pervader and the pervaded, the action and the agent, and the effect—
then what can be praised of You, who have become the self of all beings?
Since you are the Supreme Self, the individual self, and the imperishable self of all beings, there is then no praise; for what purpose does it proceed toward you?
Be gracious, O Soul of all beings! Whatever has been done by Naraka, let that be forgiven for the sake of innocence; he was struck down as your son.
Parāśara said:
Having replied "So be it" to the Earth, O best of sages, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, took the jewels from the abode of Naraka.
O great sage, in the maidens' quarters, he of incomparable prowess beheld more than sixteen hundred maidens.
He beheld six thousand fierce elephants with four tusks each,
as well as twenty-one hundred thousand horses from Kamboja.
Govinda immediately dispatched those maidens, as well as the Nāgas and the horses, back to the city of Dvārakā by means of Naraka’s servants.
He beheld the parasol of Varuṇa as well as the mountain of jewels;
Hari placed them upon Garuḍa, the lord of birds.
And having ascended [the chariot] himself, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, Kṛṣṇa went to the abode of the three heavens to give the earrings of Aditi.
[Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Garuḍa [took] the umbrella of Varuṇa, as well as the mountain of jewels.
And carrying Hṛṣīkeśa along with his wife as if in sport, he went forth.
Then Hari, having reached the gateway to heaven, blew his conch shell;
thereupon the gods approached Janārdana, bearing vessels of respectful offerings (arghya).
Worshipped by the gods, Kṛṣṇa entered the residence of the mother of the gods,
which resembled the peak of a white cloud, and beheld Aditi.
Having bowed down to her, Janārdana gave those two excellent earrings to her along with Śakra,
and he announced to her the destruction of Naraka.
Then Aditi, the mother of the world, being pleased, composed her mind and with undistracted focus praised Hari, the creator of the worlds.
Aditi said:
Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one, who grants fearlessness to your devotees;
O eternal self, universal self, self of all beings, creator of all beings!
The director of the mind, the intellect, and the senses, consisting of the qualities,
yet transcending the three qualities, free from dualities, pure, and abiding in the hearts of all.
Completely free from all conceptual constructions such as "white" or "long," untouched by birth and the like, and devoid of states such as dreaming; ViP_5.30.8.
O Acyuta, you are the twilight, night, day, earth, sky, wind, and water;
you are fire, mind, intellect, and the source of the elements.
O Lord, you are the creator and the sovereign of the creators of creation, preservation, and destruction,
through your own forms known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The gods, yakṣas, as well as daityas, rākṣasas, siddhas, and pannagas;
the kūṣmāṇḍas and piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise human beings.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, and likewise reptiles;
Domestic animals, serpents, fish, wild beasts, and species born of the forest; 12ab Ś₂,D₇ substitute: *paśava uragā mīnā mṛgāś ca vanajātayaḥ //* 12ab*56:1*56:1*
And likewise, insects, moths, and reptiles as well.
All species of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and grasses.
Whether they be gross, middling, subtle, or even subtler than the subtle— all these various types of bodies belonging to you, which are all based upon the *pudgala*— [are such].
This is your illusion, which deludes those who do not know the supreme truth;
by it, the fool is obstructed by the perception of a self in that which is not-self.
V ins.:
"In this world, that state which arises in men [thinking] 'this is mine' regarding what is not their own," ViP 5.30.14*57.
O Lord, that sense of "I" and "mine" which arises in men here is the activity of you, Māyā, who cause the world to wander in saṃsāra.
O Lord, those men who have propitiated you by being devoted to their own duty cross over this entire illusion for the sake of self-liberation.
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as humans and animals,
are enveloped by the blinding darkness of delusion, which is the great whirlpool of Viṣṇu’s māyā.
Having propitiated you, these men desire their objects of longing and the destruction of rebirth;
O Blessed One, this very thing is your own Māyā.
Desiring a son and for the destruction of the enemy faction, I propitiated you;
it was not for the sake of liberation, for that was merely the play of Māyā.
That even from a wish-fulfilling tree, those of little merit conceive a desire for nothing more than a loincloth to cover their private parts— that fault arises from one's own defects.
Therefore, be gracious, O Imperishable One who causes the delusion of illusion for the entire world;
O Lord of Beings, destroy this ignorance which has become the very essence of knowledge.

Homage to you who hold the discus in your hand; homage to you who hold the Śārṅga bow in your hand. Homage to you, O Viṣṇu, who hold the mace in your hand; homage to you who hold the conch in your hand.
I perceive this form of yours, characterized by gross marks;
I do not know that which is beyond it. Be gracious, O Supreme Lord! (ViP 5.30.23)
Parāśara said:
Thus praised by Aditi, Viṣṇu smiled and spoke to the source of the gods:
"O Goddess, you are our mother; be gracious and become a granter of boons."
Aditi said:
"So be it, according to your wish; O tiger among men, you shall be invincible by all the gods and asuras together in the world of mortals."
Parāśara said: Immediately after that, Satyabhāmā, having bowed down to Aditi who was accompanied by Śakrāṇī, said again and again, "Be gracious."
Aditi said:
"By my grace, O fair-browed one, neither old age nor deformity shall befall you;
with faultless limbs, you shall remain so for all time."
Parāśara said:
Having received permission from Aditi, the king of the gods duly worshipped Janārdana with great reverence.
And Śacī gave a flower of the Pārijāta tree to Satyabhāmā.
Thinking her to be a mere mortal woman, she did not give [her hand], though she herself was adorned with flowers.
Then, O best of men, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, beheld the heart-stealing celestial gardens, such as Nandana and others.
And he saw [the tree], rich in fragrance, bearing clusters of blossoms,
providing coolness and delight, and adorned with copper-colored young shoots.
While the nectar was being churned,
the Lord of the World, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, produced the Pārijāta tree, which possessed a bark like that of gold.
He was highly pleased with supreme joy toward that unsurpassed king of trees.
Having seen it, O best of the twice-born, Satyabhāmā said to Govinda:
"O Kṛṣṇa, why is this tree not being taken to Dvārakā?"
"If those words of yours are true— that you are exceedingly dear to me for the sake of truth—
then let this tree be taken for the purpose of my private garden."
"Neither Jāmbavatī nor Rukmiṇī is as dear to me as you are, O Satyā"—this pleasant thing was said by you, Kṛṣṇa, many times. (ViP 5.30.34)
If this is true of you, O Govinda, and not merely a figure of speech,
then let this Pārijāta tree be the ornament of my home.
"Holding a cluster of blossoms from the pārijāta tree in my mass of hair,
may I shine in the midst of my co-wives"— this is what I desire.
Likewise, having become such-and-such, I shall produce delight for you.
She was more beautiful than those goddesses, beginning with Rukmiṇī.
By this act of yours regarding the *pārijāta* tree, I am [gratified].
O Lord Mādhava, act so that you may make me even more exalted.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Hari laughed and placed the Pārijāta tree upon Garuḍa; then the guardians of the grove spoke to him.
O Govinda, Śacī is the queen of the king of the gods;
you ought not to take away the Pārijāta tree, which is her possession.
He was born and given to the king of the gods, and he, in turn, gave him away again.
O highly fortunate one, [he spoke] out of curiosity to the queen, the goddess Śacī.
This was produced by the gods during the churning for nectar for the sake of adorning Śacī;
it is not secure, so you will not go away after taking it.
Out of folly you seek the hand of her whose very husband looks to the face of another god; for who, having taken such a man, could go home in safety?
O Kṛṣṇa, Śakra, the lord of the gods, will certainly come to his rescue;
and the immortals shall follow Śakra as he raises his thunderbolt in hand.
Therefore, O Acyuta, enough with all these gods and this conflict of yours;
the wise do not praise that karma which is bitter in its ripening.
Parāśara said:
When they had spoken thus, Satyabhāmā, becoming exceedingly angry, said to them:
"Who is Śacī regarding the Pārijāta tree, or who is Śakra, the lord of the gods?"
O gods, if this [Amṛta] has arisen during the churning for nectar as something common to all the worlds, why does Vāsava alone take it?
Just as nectar, just as the moon, and just as the fortune of the forest-guardians,
so too is the Pārijāta tree common to all the world.
Moreover, Śacī obstructs him out of great pride in her husband’s arm;
therefore, let it be told: enough with patience, for Satyā is causing Druma to be taken away.
And go quickly and tell these words of mine to Paulomī:
"Satyabhāmā says this," using words haughty with pride.
"If you are beloved by your husband, and if your husband is under your control,
then cause him to stop my husband as he carries off this tree."
I know your husband to be Śakra; I know him to be the lord of the thirty gods.
Nevertheless, as a mere mortal woman, I shall take away this Pārijāta tree from you.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, the guards went and told Śacī exactly what had been said;
and Śacī encouraged her husband, the lord of the gods.
Then, O twice-born one, Indra, surrounded by the armies of all the gods, set out for Hari in order to fight him for the sake of the *pārijāta* tree.
Then, while Śakra stood with the thunderbolt in his hand, the gods became ready for battle, equipped with excellent weapons such as iron clubs, swords, maces, and spears.
Then Govinda beheld Śakra, accompanied by his retinue of gods, standing atop the king of serpents and prepared for battle.
He made a sound like that of a conch shell, filling the quarters with its noise,
and released a multitude of arrows numbering in the tens of thousands.
Then, seeing the quarters and the sky covered with hundreds of arrows,
all the gods released their various missiles and weapons in great numbers.
Each individual weapon and missile discharged by the gods was effortlessly split into a thousand pieces by Madhusūdana, the Lord of the worlds.
Having seized the noose of the King of Waters,
the eater of serpents tore it into pieces with his beak, like the body of a young snake.
The Blessed One, the son of Devakī, caused the staff sent by Yama to fall upon the earth, shattered by the hurling of his mace.
The all-pervading Śauri reduced the palanquin of the Lord of Wealth to pieces as small as sesame seeds with his discus,
and he rendered the Sun, who was seen by his very glance, devoid of its splendor.
The fire was led away by hundreds of arrows, the Vasus were driven to the various quarters,
and the Rudras, their trident-tips shattered by the discus, were cast down upon the earth.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts were struck by the arrows propelled from the Śārṅga bow;
they were scattered in the sky like the down of the silk-cotton tree.
Even Garuḍa moved about devouring, striking, and tearing apart the gods with his beak, his two wings, and the tips of his talons.
Then, with a thousand arrows, Indra and Madhusūdana showered each other like two rain-clouds pouring down torrents of water.
In that tumultuous conflict, Garuḍa fought with Airāvata,
and Janārdana fought with Śakra and all the gods.
When all his arrows, weapons, and missiles had been cut down,
Vāsava quickly seized his thunderbolt and Kṛṣṇa took up his Sudarśana discus.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the entire three worlds raised a cry of "Alas!
upon seeing the king of the gods and Janārdana bearing the thunderbolt and the discus.
Then the Blessed Lord Hari seized the thunderbolt hurled by Indra;
likewise, he did not release his discus, and said to Śakra, "Stay!"
To the heroic lord of gods, whose vajra was lost and whose mount had been wounded by Garuḍa,
who was intent on flight, Satyabhāmā spoke.
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, flight is not fitting for you, the husband of Śacī;
Śacī herself, adorned with the full expanse of the Pārijāta garland, will attend upon you."
What kind of divine sovereignty is this for you, who do not see Śacī as she was before— resplendent with a garland of pārijāta flowers and approaching you with affection?
"Enough, Śakra! There is no need for you to depart; you ought not to feel shame.
Let this Pārijāta tree be taken away, and let the gods be free from their distress."
Due to the arrogance and pride born of her husband's status,
Śacī did not receive me with honor or hospitality when I arrived at her home.
"O Śakra, because I am a woman, my mind was not heavy [with wisdom], and I was intent on praising my own husband; therefore, I engaged in a dispute with you."
Therefore, enough with this *pārijāta* tree, which is the property of another taken from us;
for what woman would not be proud of her beauty when she possesses a husband?
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by her, O twice-born one, the king of the gods turned back;
and he said to her, "Enough, O fierce one, my friend! Cease with these excessive lamentations."
Furthermore, there is no shame for me in being conquered by him who is the creator of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the entire universe and who possesses the form of the cosmos.

O Goddess, how can there be shame for one who has been cast out by Him— the cause of the origin, dissolution, and preservation of this entire world, which is without beginning or middle, and from whom all beings shall not cease to exist?
Whose form, the source of all worlds, is subtler than an atom and is known only by those who have realized all that is to be known— and not by others—
to whom is it possible to conquer that Unborn, Uncreated Lord, the eternal one, who out of his own will appears as a mortal for the benefit of the world?
[Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said: Having been thus praised by the king of the gods, the Blessed Keśava—
Laughing with profound intent, that best of the twice-born spoke to Indra.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of the World, you are Indra, the king of the gods, while we are mortals;
therefore, you alone must forgive this offense committed by me."
"And let this Pārijāta tree be taken to its proper place;
O Śakra, it was accepted by me for the sake of making Satyabhāmā’s word true."
"And take this vajra, which was swallowed and then discharged by you;
O Śakra, it is your very own weapon for rending your enemies."
Śakra said: "O Lord, why do you delude me by saying, 'I am a mortal'?
We know you as the Blessed One, though we ourselves are not perceivers of the subtle."
O Lord, O destroyer of the Asuras, you who are who you are remain established in the activity of protecting the world; you extract the thorns of the world.
"O Kṛṣṇa, let this Pārijāta tree be taken to the city of Dvāravatī;
once you have departed from the world of mortals, it shall no longer remain upon the earth."
O God of gods, Lord of the world, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, O mighty-armed one! (D3.4, T, G1.3, M3, ed. Veṅk. insert)
O Mādhava, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, bearer of the Śārṅga bow and sword!
Parāśara said:
Having said "So be it" to the lord of the gods, Hari came to the earth,
being praised by the Siddhas and Gandharvas who followed him, as well as by the celestial rishis.
D5 inserts after verse 7, while Ś2 and D7 insert after verse 8:
"O Lord of Gods, he will himself come to Triviṣṭapa."
Then, O twice-born one, standing above Dvārakā, he blew his conch shell and inspired joy among the inhabitants of Dvārakā.
Then, having descended from Garuḍa accompanied by Satyabhāmā,
he planted the great Pārijāta tree in the pleasure garden.
Then all those Yādavas beheld him making human faces upon that tree, which possessed a superhuman physical form.
Then Kṛṣṇa seized the wealth brought by the servants, consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as the women, which were the possessions of Naraka.
The high-minded Kṛṣṇa divided [the wealth] and bestowed it upon his kinsmen.
Then, when an auspicious time had arrived, Janārdana married those maidens who had been gathered from all sides by Naraka.
O great sage, Govinda took their hands according to the prescribed rite and in accordance with dharma, one by one in separate houses, at one and the same time.
The Blessed One Madhusūdana assumed as many forms as there were sixteen thousand and one hundred women.
One by one, those maidens thought, "The Blessed Madhusūdana has taken my hand in marriage."
And during the nights, O Brahmin, Keśava Hari, the creator of the world who assumes the universal form, dwelt in the houses of all of them.
[Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
The sons of Hari born of Rukmiṇī, beginning with Pradyumna, have been described to you.
Satyabhāmā gave birth to Bhānu and Bhaimarika.
Dīptimat, Pradyumna, and the others were the sons of Rohiṇī from Hari;
and from Jāmbavatī were born Sāmba and others, who were possessed of mighty arms.
Bhadravinda and others were the sons of Nāgnajitī, all of great strength;
while Saṃgrāmajit and others were the sons born of Śaibyā.
Vṛka and others were the sons born to Mādrī, while Gātravat and other sons were obtained by Lakṣmaṇā; and Śruta and others were the sons of Kālindī.
And from his other wives, a hundred thousand and eighty thousand sons were likewise born to the wielder of the discus.
Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, was the first among them all;
from Pradyumna came Aniruddha, and from him Vajra was born.
O best of the twice-born, the mighty Aniruddha, having been obstructed in battle, married Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa and granddaughter of Bali.
There a great and terrible battle took place between Hari and Śaṅkara,
wherein the thousand arms of Bāṇa were severed by the wielder of the discus.
Maitreya said:
O Brahman, how did the battle between Hara and Kṛṣṇa occur for the sake of Uṣā?
And how did Hari bring about the destruction of Bāṇa’s arms?
O highly fortunate one, you ought to relate all of this to me;
a great curiosity has arisen in me to hear this story of Hari.
Parāśara said:
O Brahmin, having observed Pārvatī sporting with Śambhu, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, felt an intense longing for that same state.
Then Gaurī, who knows the hearts of all, said to that beautiful woman:
"Enough with this excessive distress; you too shall take delight with your husband."
When this was said, she then wondered to herself, "When [will this happen]? or "Who indeed will be my husband? To her, Pārvatī spoke once more:
"O Princess, he who shall overcome you in a dream on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha will become your husband."
Parāśara said:
On that lunar day, just as the Goddess had described in her dream, the man overcame her, and she felt passion for him there.
Then, having awakened and not seeing the man, she became anxious; and casting aside all shame, Maitreyī said to her friend, "Where have you gone?"
Bāṇa’s minister was Kumbhāṇḍa, and his daughter was Citralekhā;
she became her friend, and she asked: "Who is this person spoken of by you?"
When that friend, overcome with shame, did not tell her,
she then gained her confidence and related everything to her.
When she had understood the matter, Uṣā spoke to her again as she had been told:
"Employ that very means which was mentioned by the goddess for the attainment of that goal."
Citralekhā said:
"This matter is difficult to discern, and it cannot even be attained."
Nevertheless, some service must be rendered to you, my beloved.
Let him wait for that period of time until seven or eight days have passed.
Having spoken thus, he went into the inner apartment and then devised a stratagem.
Parāśara said: Then Citralekhā, having painted upon a canvas the principal gods, Daityas, Gandharvas, and humans, showed it to her.
Having set aside the Gandharvas, as well as the Uragas, Suras, and Asuras,
she fixed her gaze upon men, and among them, specifically upon the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis.
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, that fair-browed woman became as if paralyzed with shame;
O twice-born one, at the sight of Pradyumna, she turned her bashful gaze elsewhere.
Then, O twice-born one, as soon as her beloved son Pradyumna was seen,
that woman of exceeding gracefulness cast her shame far away.
When she said, "This is he, this is he," that lady who was traveling by means of yoga [disappeared].
After 24ab, D₃.₄.₆, T₁.₃, G₃, M₃, and ed. Veṅk. insert:
Then Citralekhā spoke to Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa.
This grandson of Kṛṣṇa, propitiated by the Goddess, shall be your husband.
He was renowned as Aniruddha, famous and pleasing to behold.
If you obtain this husband who has been attained by you, then everything will be achieved.
Formerly, the city of Dvārakā, protected by Hari, was difficult to enter.
Nevertheless, O friend, I shall bring back your husband with great effort.
This secret must not be told to anyone at all, O beloved.
I shall return before long; endure my separation.
Having thus consoled her friend Ūṣā, he then departed for Dvāravatī.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, Bāṇa also, having prostrated himself before the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva), spoke.
"O Lord, I am weary of these thousand arms without a battle."
I hope that a battle will arise which brings fruitfulness to these arms of mine; for what purpose are my arms if there is no war, but rather a mere burden?
Śaṃkara said: "O Bāṇa, when the breaking of your peacock-banner occurs,
you shall then obtain a battle that brings joy to the flesh-eating demons."
Parāśara said:
Then, having bowed to Śambhu, he returned home delighted;
and seeing that the banner had been broken, he was filled with joy and experienced an even greater surge of happiness.
At that very time, however, the excellent Apsaras Citralekhā brought Aniruddha there by the power of her yogic knowledge.
Having discovered that he was sporting with Uṣā in the midst of the maiden's inner apartments,
the guards went and reported it to the Daitya king.
Taking up an iron club, that slayer of enemy heroes struck down the army of servants commanded by that high-souled one.
When those arrows had been destroyed, Bāṇa, remaining on his chariot and intent on slaying him,
fought to the best of his ability until he was finally overcome by [Viṣṇu’s] prowess.
Then, impelled by his mantra, he fought with him through illusion;
subsequently, he bound that joy of the Yadus with the serpent-weapon (pannagāstra).
To the Yadus who were lamenting in Dvāravatī, "Where has Aniruddha gone?",
Nārada announced that he had been captured by Bāṇa.
Having heard that he had been led away to Śoṇitapura by a woman skilled in magic arts, the Yādavas gained confidence through names [of other enemies].
Then Hari, accompanied by Bala and Pradyumna, mounted Garuḍa— who arrived as soon as he was thought of— and set out for the city of Bāṇa.
Upon entering the city, there was a battle between the high-souled one and the Pramathas;
Hari led them to their destruction and proceeded to the vicinity of Bāṇa’s city.
Then the great fever of Maheśvara, three-legged and three-headed,
fought most fiercely with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow for the sake of protecting Bāṇa.
Even Baladeva, experiencing a burning sensation arising from the touch of that ash, felt exhaustion upon contact with Kṛṣṇa’s body, his eyes closing in relief.
Then, while fighting with Sahadeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
he was swiftly struck down from his dark body by the Vaiṣṇava fever.
Seeing him overwhelmed by the crushing blow from Nārāyaṇa’s arm, the divine Grandfather said, "Let him be forgiven."
Then, having said "It is forgiven," the Blessed One Madhusūdana caused that Vaiṣṇava fever to dissolve into himself alone.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Jvara prostrated himself and spoke:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Acyuta who removes the suffering of those who bow before you!
"Those men who shall remember my battle with you will be free from fever," having said this to him, the Fever departed.
Then the Blessed One, having conquered and brought those five fires to destruction,
Viṣṇu effortlessly crushed the army of the Dānavas.
Then, with his entire army, Bali’s son fought against Śaṅkara, as well as Kārttikeya and Śauri.
The battle between Hari and Śaṅkara was exceedingly terrible;
all the worlds were agitated, scorched by the rays of their missiles.
While that great battle was proceeding, the gods thought, "Surely this dissolution of the entire world has arrived."
And the gods, terrified with fear, then sought refuge in Hari.
And Śaṅkara, though entreated [for victory], accepted defeat.
With the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon, Govinda caused Śaṅkara to yawn;
thereupon the Daityas and the Pramathas fled in every direction.
Overcome by yawning, Hara sat down on the floor of the chariot;
he was unable then to fight with Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
His mount wounded by Garuḍa, oppressed by the weapon of Pradyumna,
and his spear shaken off by Kṛṣṇa’s roar of "huṃ," Guha departed.
Then, by means of a rain of arrows, he destroyed the army of the Pramathas.

When Śaṅkara had yawned and perished, when the army of the Daityas was destroyed and Guha was defeated, and when the host of the Pramathas was brought to utter ruin by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; ||| ViP_5,33.27 |||
Mounted upon a great chariot whose horses were controlled by Nandīśa,
Bāṇa arrived there to fight against Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and their forces.
The immensely powerful Balabhadra pierced Bāṇa’s army in many places with his arrows; having been struck down, they fled from him in accordance with their nature.
Bāṇa saw Balarāma drawing [his foe] with the tip of his plow and striking him down with his mace, and he saw Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the discus, overpowering Bāṇa with his own arrows.
Then there was a battle between Kṛṣṇa and Bāṇa on all sides.
Kṛṣṇa cut down with his own arrows those blazing shafts shot by Bāṇa that were capable of piercing the body's armor;
Bāṇa struck Keśava, and the wielder of the discus pierced Bāṇa in return.
O twice-born one, Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa, both supremely enraged and intent on wounding one another, discharged weapons at each other in their desire for victory.
When all his arrows were exhausted and his weapon was failing,
Hari then set his mind upon killing Bāṇa by means of a great abundance [of other means].
Then Hari, the enemy of the circle of Daityas, whose splendor was like the combined brilliance of a hundred suns, seized the Sudarśana discus.
As the enemy of Madhu was discharging that discus for the destruction of Bāṇa,
Koṭavī, a naked female spirit belonging to the Daityas' lore, appeared before Hari.
Seeing her before him, Hari closed his eyes and released the Sudarśana [discus],
aiming it at the enemy's forest of arms to cut them down.
Then, impelled by Acyuta, that [discus] gradually severed Bāṇa’s arms,
which were honored for their skill in destroying the floods of weapons hurled by the asuras.
When the forest of his arms had been severed, Madhusūdana, desiring to release that [discus] held in his hand for the destruction of Bāṇa, was recognized by the enemy of Tripura.
Having approached Govinda, the Lord of Umā spoke with conciliatory words,
beholding Bāṇa, who was raining down streams of blood from the severed staves of his arms.
Śaṅkara said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, I know you to be the Supreme Person,
the Highest Lord, the Supreme Self, without beginning or end, the Transcendent.
Among gods, animals, and humans, this play consisting of the assumption of bodies is the activity that characterizes you, the soul of all beings.
Therefore, O Lord, be gracious; protection from fear has been granted by me to this Bāṇa.
You must not make false that word which was spoken by me.
"O Imperishable One, this Daitya has grown strong through our protection; he has committed no offense against you. Since he was granted a boon by me, I therefore beg your forgiveness."
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Govinda, with a serene countenance and his anger toward the asura subsided, spoke to the trident-bearing Lord of Umā.
The Blessed One said:
"O Śaṅkara, let this Bāṇa live, for he has been granted a boon by you.
Out of respect for your word, I have withdrawn this discus."
"O Śaṅkara, that fearlessness which was granted by you has been granted by me in its entirety; you ought to perceive yourself as non-different from me."
I am he, you are that, and this world, including its gods, asuras, and humans, is also that.
There is nothing else whatsoever besides me; you ought to know this here.
Men whose selves are deluded by ignorance perceive [reality] as divided.
O Hara, they speak of a distinction and perceive a difference between us two.
"I am pleased; I shall depart. You may go, O bull-bannered one."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa proceeded to where the son of Pradyumna stood;
the serpents that bound him perished, dried up by the wind from Garuḍa’s breath.
Then, having placed Aniruddha along with his wife upon Garuḍa,
Rāma, Kārṣṇi, and Dāmodara returned to the city of Dvārakā.
Surrounded by his sons and grandsons, Janārdana took delight there.
O Brahmin, [this was done] constantly by the goddesses with the desire to cross over the burden of the earth.
[Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said: Śauri, assuming a human body, performed great deeds.
He effortlessly conquered Śakra, Śarva, and all the gods.
O highly fortunate one, let that other deed which he performed, consisting of the execution of divine exploits, be told; for my curiosity is indeed great.
Parāśara said:
O brahmin-sage, listen with respect to this as I speak of how Vārāṇasī was consumed by fire by Kṛṣṇa during his incarnation as a man.
But Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva became known as "Vāsudeva" on earth; though he was not the true one, he was addressed by people deluded by ignorance as "You have descended."
He thought, "I am Vāsudeva descended upon the surface of the earth," and with his memory thus lost, he then caused all the emblems of Viṣṇu to be made.
And he dispatched a messenger to the great-souled Kṛṣṇa,
instructing him to set aside his own insignia, such as the discus, and his own name.
O fool, having abandoned pride— especially that which consists of identifying with Vāsudeva—
seek refuge in me for the sake of your own life.
Having been addressed thus, Janārdana laughed and said to that messenger:
"I shall indeed discharge my own emblem, the discus, upon you."
And having gone there, O messenger, you must speak these words of mine to Pauṇḍraka: "The true intent of your speech has been understood; let that which is to be done be performed."
"Having taken up my insignia, I shall come to your city;
I will undoubtedly release my own wheel as your sign."
"And as for this command you previously uttered,
saying 'Come,' that too I shall fulfill for you tomorrow without delay."
"O King, having come to you for refuge, I shall act in such a way that no further fear of you will ever arise for me."
Parāśara said:
When the messenger had spoken thus and departed, Hari, remembering that [the time for battle] had arrived,
mounted Garuḍa and went swiftly to that city.
Then, having heard of Keśava’s exertion, the Lord of Kāśī,
surrounded by his entire army, arrived as a rear-guard ally.
Then, with a great force and the army of the King of Kāśī,
that Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva marched toward Keśava.
From afar, Hari saw him standing in a magnificent chariot,
holding a discus in his hand, with a mace and sword in his arms, and a lotus in his palm.
Hari beheld him wearing a garland and holding a Śārṅga bow, with a banner fashioned by Suparṇa, and the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
Seeing him wearing a crown and earrings, clad in yellow garments, and profound in his inner being, the one whose banner is Garuḍa laughed.
And he fought with his army, O twice-born one— an army powerful with elephants and horses,
and adorned with swords, spears, maces, tridents, javelins, and bows.
In an instant, he destroyed that army with enemy-shattering arrows released from his Śārṅga bow, and by the falling of maces and discuses.
Having brought the army of the King of Kāśī to destruction,
Janārdana spoke to the foolish Pauṇḍraka, who bore the insignia of his own [Viṣṇu’s] marks.
The Blessed One said:
"As for what was spoken by Pauṇḍraka to me through the mouth of his messenger— that you should 'discard your insignia'— I shall fulfill that for you."
"This discus has been released; this mace is hurled at you;
and here is Garuḍa, who is assigned to mount your banner."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, he was torn apart by the released discus;
crushed by the mace and broken by Garuḍa, he fell.
Then, while the world raised cries of "Alas!", the powerful lord of Kāśī,
remaining steadfast in his devotion to his friend, fought with Vāsudeva.
Then, having severed his head with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow,
he hurled it into the city of Kāśī, causing wonder among the people.
Having slain Pauṇḍraka and the King of Kāśī along with his followers, Śauri returned once more to Dvāravatī and rejoiced like one who has ascended to heaven.

Seeing that head fallen there in the city of the Lord of Kāśī, the people, utterly amazed, asked, "What is this? and "By whom [was it done]?"* *Note: The Sanskrit text provided for this verse is incomplete; the second half-verse (kenety atyantavismitaḥ) suggests the people were struck with wonder and inquired about the cause and the agent.*
Having learned that he had been slain by Vāsudeva, his son then,
together with the family priest, propitiated Śaṅkara.
In the great field of Avimukta, Śaṅkara was pleased by him;
he then said to that prince, "Choose a boon."
"O Blessed One, O Maheśvara, by your grace, let a *kṛtyā* arise for the sake of slaying Kṛṣṇa, the murderer of my father. ViP_5.34.31.
Parāśara said:
When it was thus declared, "So shall it be," a great Kṛtyā rose up immediately from the southern fire-altar of that very place where the fire was established.
Then, with a mouth formidable with flames and a mass of hair ablaze, the enraged Kṛtyā cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and went toward Dvāravatī.
Beholding her, O Sage, the people, their eyes trembling with terror,
went for refuge to Madhusūdana, the protector of the worlds.

Then, having understood that this [science] had been produced by the son of the King of Kāśī after he had propitiated the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), and that it was for a great purpose, the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) [acted].
"Where is this fierce Kṛtyā, with her matted locks of blazing fire, who was cast forth like a discus as a mere plaything by one addicted to dice? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.34.36)
Then the Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu swiftly pursued that Kṛtyā, who was utterly terrifying with her outpouring of flames matted together like a garland of fire.
Then the Kṛtyā of Maheśvara, shattered by the power of the discus, fled with great speed;
and he too pursued her with haste.
O best of sages, her power having been thwarted by the discus of Viṣṇu, Kṛtyā entered Vārāṇasī itself with great haste.
Then the vast army of Kāśī, as well as the force of the Pramathas,
equipped with all kinds of weapons and missiles, advanced toward the discus.
Having consumed that army by his own splendor— skilled as it was in discharging weapons and missiles— he then utterly burnt that city of Vārāṇasī, which was filled with malevolent spells (kṛtyā).
But that city, along with its mountains, servants, and citizens, including its horses, elephants, and men,
and with all its treasuries and granaries, was difficult to behold even for the gods.
The discus of Hari burned that entire city, its houses, walls, and crossroads all encircled by flames.
With its wrath undiminished and still longing for a task so easily accomplished,
that discus, flashing with brilliance, returned to the hand of Viṣṇu.
[Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Maitreya said: I desire further to hear of the wise Balabhadra.
O Brahmin, you ought to relate that heroic exploit to me so that I may hear it.
"O Blessed One, I have heard of the dragging of the Yamunā and other such deeds;
O highly fortunate one, let that which Balarāma performed next be told."
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen to the deed which was performed by Rāma—
that bearer of the earth who is Ananta, the immeasurable Śeṣa.
The hero Sāmba, son of Jāmbavatī, forcibly took the daughter of Duryodhana, who had set the time for her svayaṃvara.
Then Karna, Duryodhana, and the others, as well as Bhishma, Drona, and their followers— being of great prowess and filled with rage— bound him after he had been defeated in battle.
Having heard that, O Maitreya, all the Yādavas directed their wrath toward Duryodhana and the others, and they made a great effort to slay them.
Having restrained them, Balarāma spoke with words faltering from intoxication:
"They shall release you at my command; I alone will go to the Kauravas."
Then Baladeva, having gone to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura),
stayed in the midst of an outer grove and did not enter that city.
Perceiving that strength had returned to him, King Duryodhana and the others offered the earth,
the guest-offering (arghya), and water to Rāma.
Having duly received everything, he then said to those Kauravas:
"Ugrasena commands you: release Sāmba immediately!"
Then, O best of the twice-born, having heard those words, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others,
as well as Karṇa, Duryodhana, and their followers, were filled with rage, O most excellent of brahmins.
And all the Kauravas, led by Bāhlīka, spoke in anger,
looking upon the wielder of the mace as one born of Yadu’s lineage who was unworthy of sovereignty.
"O sir, what is this speech uttered by you, O Balabhadra?
What Yādava shall give orders to those born of the Kuru lineage?"
If Ugrasena also gives his assent to the Kauravas,
then enough with these white umbrellas, mockeries of those fit for kings.
Therefore go, O Bala, or do not; we shall release Sāmba, who acted unjustly, neither by your command nor by that of Ugrasena.
The prostration that was made by the Kukuras and Andhakas toward us, who are worthy of honor— was that merely a bow,
or was it an order issued by a servant to his master?
"You have been elevated to pride by being granted equal seats and meals;
what fault is there in your conduct that you did not look upon this with affection?"
"This honor which we have offered to you, O Balarāma, was done out of affection;
it is not appropriate for your family from our family."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, all the Kurus, firm in their resolve, said, "We will not release the son of Hari," and quickly entered the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Reeling with intoxication and the anger born from that insult,
Halāyudha rose up and struck the earth with his heel.
Then the earth was rent asunder by the heel-strikes of the Great-souled One;
he then slapped his arms, filling the quarters with the sound.
And he spoke, his eyes exceedingly copper-red and his face contorted with a frown.
"Aha! This is the arrogance of the wicked-souled Kauravas, who are devoid of substance;
for they still consider themselves our lords, born of time, by whom even today the command of Ugrasena is treated as a transgression."
The Lord of Śacī, together with the gods, shall receive his command in accordance with dharma.
Abiding by the will of Māruta, he gave a hall for the assembly of kings when [the sage] was pleased.
Ugrasena sat there in that Sudharmā hall of the Lord of Śacī.
Ugrasena occupies the Sudharmā hall; the Lord of Śacī does not.
Fie upon this satisfaction these men find in a royal throne that is the leavings of a hundred other men!
Even the king whose female attendants wear the flower-clusters of the Pārijāta tree as ornaments for their servants— he too is not a true lord of the earth for them.
Let Ugrasena, the lord of all kings, remain;
today, having rid the earth of the Kauravas, I shall depart for his city.
Today [he shall slay] Karṇa, Duryodhana, Droṇa, Bhīṣma along with Bāhlika,
Duḥśāsana and the others, as well as Bhūri and Bhūriśravas.
Having slain Somadatta, Śala, Bhīma, Arjuna together with Yudhiṣṭhira, the twin sons of Yama, and the other Kauravas, along with their horses, chariots, and elephants; ||| ViP_5.35.28 |||
Then, taking that hero Sāmba along with his wife,
I shall go to the city of Dvārakā and visit Ugrasena and my other kinsmen.
Or else, [he shall destroy] the capital of the Kauravas together with all the Kurus.
Urged by the King of the Gods for the swift removal of the burden, Ś1, Ñ1, B, D2–5.6.8 insert: "bhārāvataraṇe śīghraṃ devarājena coditaḥ."
I shall quickly cast the city named after the elephant into the Bhāgīrathī.
Parāśara said:

Having spoken thus, the wielder of the mace, his eyes reddened with intoxication, set down his plow— its handle facing downward for the purpose of dragging— and dragged it across the ramparts and the earthen embankments.
Then, seeing Hastināpura suddenly reeling, all the Kauravas, their hearts agitated, cried out in distress.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, may you forgive me, may you forgive me! Let your anger be withdrawn; be gracious, O wielder of the mace!"
O Balarāma, here is Sāmba together with his wife, returned to you;
please forgive these offenders whose power was unknown to us.
Parāśara said: Then, O bull among sages, having quickly departed from their own city, the Kauravas brought Sāmba forth together with his wife.
Having bowed to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others as they spoke pleasant words, Bala, the best among the strong, said: "I have indeed forgiven them."
Even today, O twice-born one, that city appears as if reeling;
this is the power of Rāma, characterized by his strength and heroism.
Then the Kauravas, having honored Sāmba along with Balarāma,
sent him forth accompanied by his wife and the wealth for his wedding.
[Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, listen now to [the account] of that powerful Bala.
Listen also to you regarding whatever else was performed by him.
The monkey named Dvivida, possessed of great heroism, became a friend to Narakāsura, the lord of the Asuras who was an adversary of the side of the gods.
Impelled by the King of the Gods, the powerful Kṛṣṇa slew Naraka and established a persistent enmity toward the gods.
"Therefore, I shall perform a counter-action against all the gods by destroying their sacrifices and likewise causing the destruction of the mortal world."
Then, deluded by ignorance, he destroyed sacrifices,
violated the boundaries of the righteous, and brought about the ruin of embodied beings.
The impetuous one burned down countries, cities, and the interiors of villages;
and in some places, by hurling mountains, he completely pulverized the villages and other settlements.
Having uprooted mountains, he likewise cast them into the waters of the ocean;
then, standing in the midst of the sea, he agitated the ocean once more.
O twice-born one, agitated by him,
the ocean overflows its shores with great velocity, submerging the villages and cities situated along its banks.
Assuming a great form at will,
the monkey, by rolling, wandering, and trampling, completely pulverizes the crops.
O Maitreya, by that evil-minded one, this entire world was oppressed; it became devoid of Vedic study and sacrificial invocations, and was deeply afflicted with suffering.
Once, in the Raivata garden, Halāyudha drank wine,
as did the highly fortunate Revatī and other excellent women.
Being sung to while standing in the midst of a circle of radiant women,
that best of the Yadu chiefs took his pleasure like Kubera on Mount Mandara.
Then that monkey, having approached and seized the plow of the plowman as well as his mace, held them up before him in a mocking manner.
In that very manner, the monkey laughed in the faces of those women and,
striking them with his foot, threw down their water-jars filled with drink.
Then Bala, his soul overcome with anger, rebuked him;
yet even so, he disregarded him and made a "kilakila" sound of triumph.
Then Bala rose up and seized his club in rage;
that best of monkeys also seized a formidable mountain crag.
And that best of the Yādavas shattered it into a thousand pieces with his mace as it was hurled; it fell upon the surface of the earth.
As the mace was falling, that monkey leaped over it,
approached with speed and fury, and struck him on the chest with his palm.
Then, struck on the head with a fist by Bala in his rage,
Dvivida fell down, vomiting blood, his life exhausted.
O Maitreya, as that body fell, the mountain peak shattered into a hundred pieces, as if struck by the thunderbolt of the wielder of the vajra.
Then the gods showered a rain of flowers upon Rāma, and approaching him, they praised him, saying, "Excellent! This great deed has been accomplished by you."
"O Hero, by this wicked monkey who aided the faction of the Daityas, the world was brought to ruin; by good fortune, he has now met his destruction."
Having spoken thus, the gods, together with the Guhyakas, departed joyfully for heaven.
Parāśara said:
Such were the many immeasurable deeds of the wise Baladeva, Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth.
[Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Thus Kṛṣṇa, assisted by Baladeva, performed the slaughter of the Daityas.
In the same way, he brought about the destruction of wicked kings for the sake of the world.
And the all-pervading Lord Hari, together with Phalguna, relieved the burden of the earth by the slaughter of the entire Akṣauhiṇī army.
Having relieved the earth of its burden and having slain all the kings, he departed.
The god of gods, Janārdana, manifested himself in human form.
And having performed other duties out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
O brahmin-sage, [this was done] by those led by Yudhiṣṭhira against Duryodhana.
Then the powerful one would have overlooked the dissension that had arisen among the Pāṇḍavas.
Then Kṛṣṇa instigated enmity against him who was eating the other's food.
There, having slain all the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas against one another, [they will perish].
The Lord, the sovereign and master of the worlds, attained supreme peace.
Eighteen akṣauhiṇīs were slain there, O great sage.
Under the pretext of a curse, he brought about the destruction of the Brahmins' lineage.
Having abandoned Dvārakā and relinquished his human state, Kṛṣṇa,
the self-born one who possesses all portions, re-entered his own original abode consisting of Viṣṇu.
Maitreya said: How did he destroy his own lineage under the pretext of a brahmin’s curse,
and how did Janārdana cast off his human body?
Parāśara said:
Viśvāmitra, as well as Kaṇva and the great sage Nārada.
And the sages, beginning with Durvāsas, [performed rites] at the Piṇḍāraka tīrtha, O Sage.
She was seen at the great sacred ford of Piṇḍāraka by the young princes of the Yadu clan.
Then those men, intoxicated by youth and impelled by their future destiny,
dressed Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, like a woman.
Having approached those sages, they spoke with prostrations:
"What will this woman give birth to for Babhru, who desires a son?"
Parāśara said:
Endowed with divine knowledge, they were deceived by the young boys.
The enraged sages declared, "He shall produce a pestle."
After 9cd, T3 and the edition of Veṅkaṭamādhava insert:
"The cause for the destruction of all the Yādavas, which was exceedingly powerful."
By which there shall be the destruction of the entire lineage of the Yādavas.
After verse 9, T3 inserts:
"Having pierced the surface of the triple-naveled earth, this artificial [weapon] shall become such [a thing] this very day."
Thus addressed by them, those princes related the matter exactly as it had happened:
how the club was born from the belly of Sāmba for Ugrasena.
Then Ugrasena had that mace ground into iron powder;
that powder was known as *cairaka*, and it was thrown by them into the great ocean.
O twice-born one, although the Andhakas had pulverized the iron pestle,
they were unable to crush even a single fragment of it, which remained in the shape of a *tomara* spear.
That too was thrown into the ocean and swallowed by a fish caught in a net;
when the fish was killed, a hunter took it from its belly, and old age seized him.
Although the Blessed One Madhusūdana had realized the ultimate truth,
he did not wish to alter that which was ordained by destiny.
