And a messenger dispatched by the gods, having prostrated before Keśava, spoke thus in private: "O Blessed One, I have been sent as a messenger by the gods."
Together with the Vasus, Aśvins, Maruts, Ādityas, Rudras, Sādhyas, and others, Śakra makes this request of you; O Lord, let it be heard.
For the sake of relieving the burden [of the earth], the Blessed One descended here for more than a hundred years, having been entreated by the gods of the thirty-three.
The wicked Daityas have been slain and the burden of the earth has been removed;
let the gods, having you as their protector, dwell forever in heaven.
O Lord of the World, more than a hundred years have passed since then;
now, if it pleases you, please proceed to heaven.
The gods have made this request: "If you find delight in this very place, then please remain for as long as is appropriate; your dependents must be informed."
The Blessed One said:
"O messenger, all that you have spoken, I too know.
Indeed, the destruction of the Yādavas has already been set in motion by me."
"Even now this burden of the earth has not been removed by the Yādavas who remain unslain;
having caused them to be cast down, I shall swiftly accomplish this within seven nights."
Just as I took [the earth] from the ocean and gave it to the land of Dvārakā,
so shall I withdraw the Yādavas and go to the abode of the gods.
Having cast off my human body, I am to be regarded by the lord of the gods and likewise by the deities as one who has already attained [my goal], accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Jarāsandha and others who were slain as burdens upon the earth— compared to them, even this youth of the Yadus does not fall short.
Therefore, having relieved this very great burden of the earth, I shall go for the protection of the world of the immortals; speak to them thus.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, O Maitreya, the messenger of the gods bowed to him and departed for the presence of the king of the gods by means of his divine motion.
Then the Blessed One also beheld, day and night, portents occurring on earth, in the heavens, and in the intermediate space, foreboding the destruction of the city of Dvārakā.
Seeing those [omens], he said to the Yādavas: "Behold these most terrible great portents! To pacify them, let us go to Prabhāsa without delay."
When Govinda had spoken thus and desired once more to go to heaven, G1 inserts: [text].
After the reference, Ś₁,
T₁, G₂.₃, and the edition of Veṅkaṭeśvara insert:
"When this had been spoken by Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of the Yādavas then..."
Parāśara said:
Having prostrated before Hari, Uddhava, the great devotee, spoke:
"O Blessed One, please now command me as to what I must do."
I believe that the Blessed One will annihilate this entire lineage.
O Acyuta, I perceive the omens portending the destruction of this lineage.
The Blessed One said:
"Go by means of the divine gait arising from my grace to the meritorious Badarī hermitage on Mount Gandhamādana."
On that ground purified by them at the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
"Fixing your mind on me, you shall attain perfection there through my grace;
I, however, shall go to heaven after having indeed withdrawn the lineage."
And the ocean shall submerge Dvārakā once it has been abandoned by me.
After verse 34, D3.4, T1, G2.3, M3, and ed.
Veṅk. insert:
"And this reservoir of water, out of fear of me, has abandoned my abode."
And there I shall be present, out of a desire for the welfare of my devotees.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Uddhava, with Keśava’s approval, prostrated before him and departed for the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Then, O twice-born one, all those Yādavas, having mounted swift-moving chariots, set out for Prabhāsa together with Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the others.
Having reached Prabhāsa and bathed with self-restraint, those Kukuras and Andhakas,
approved by Vāsudeva, joyfully indulged in drinking there.
As they were drinking there, through their mutual rivalry,
the fire of quarrel— fueled by harsh words— was born, bringing about their destruction.
Maitreya said:
"Let each of them eat their own [portion]; for those who are without cause, there is no quarrel."
Or was it a conflict, O best of the twice-born? You should explain that to me.
Śrī Parāśara said:
"Let him say of my food, 'It is delicious,' and of yours, 'It is not delicious.'"
Then, amidst talk of the refined and the unrefined, there arose mutual rivalry and strife.
Then, approaching one another with eyes bloodshot with rage, they—
Driven by the power of destiny, they struck one another with weapons;
and when their weapons were exhausted, they seized the nearby eraka grass.
The *erakā* grass, once grasped by them, appeared as if it were made of adamant;
with it, they struck one another in that most dreadful combat.
O twice-born one, Cāruvarman, Cāruka, Akrūra, and the others likewise struck one another with vajras in the form of eraka grass.
Hari tried to restrain the Yādavas, and they in turn tried to restrain Keśava;
yet, regarding him who had arrived as an ally, they struck one another down.
Kṛṣṇa, also enraged at them, took up a handful of *erakā* grass;
for their destruction, that handful then became an iron club.
With that [weapon], he struck down all the Yādavas who were attacking him without exception;
and others likewise, having suddenly approached, slew one another.
Then, O best of the twice-born, while Dāruka looked on, that victorious chariot of the wielder of the discus was swiftly carried across the middle of the ocean by the horses.
Having circumambulated Hari clockwise— the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the quivers, the conch, and the sword— they departed by the path of the sun.
In an instant, O great sage, there was no one among the Yādavas who was not slain, with the exception of the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa and Dāruka.
While the two of them were walking about, they saw Rāma seated at the foot of a tree,
and they beheld a great serpent emerging from his mouth.
Having emerged from his mouth, that serpent of great majesty departed for the ocean,
being honored by the Siddhas as well as by the other serpents.
Then, taking the water of honor (*argha*), the Ocean went before him;
honored by the best of the *pannagas*, he entered its waters.
Having seen Balarāma’s departure, Keśava said to Dāruka:
"Report all of this to Vasudeva and Ugrasena."
Having witnessed the departure of Balabhadra and likewise the destruction of the Yādavas,
I too, established in yoga, shall cast off this body.
And all the people residing in Dvārakā, as well as Āhuka, must be told:
"The ocean shall submerge this entire city."
Therefore, being prepared, you must await the arrival of Arjuna;
you must not remain within Dvārakā once the Pāṇḍava has departed from there.
One must go together with him alone, wherever that Kaurava goes.
And having gone, speak these words of mine to Arjuna, the son of Kuntī:
"This person, who is my own charge, must be protected by you to the best of your ability."
Thus, accompanied by Arjuna, may you take the people from Dvāravatī and depart; Vajra shall become the king of the Yadus.
Parāśara said:
Having been addressed thus, Dāruka prostrated himself before Kṛṣṇa again and again,
and after circumambulating him many times, he departed as instructed.
Having gone there, he of great intelligence acted accordingly; he brought Arjuna from Dvārakā and likewise installed Vajra as king.
The Blessed One Govinda also, having established the supreme Brahman, whose essence is Vāsudeva, within his own self, maintained it in all beings.
After verse 61, D₂.₃, T₁, G₂ marg., G₃ marg., M₁ ed., and Veṅk. insert:
"O highly fortunate one, having joined the self to the Self which is free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca),..."
And Puruṣottama lay there, sporting in the state of the Fourth (turya).
Honoring the words of the twice-born that Durvāsas had spoken,
O best of men, he became absorbed in yoga, placing one foot upon his knee.
And at that time, a hunter named Jarā arrived there,
carrying a spear with a single iron arrow remaining from a mace.
O best of the twice-born, seeing that foot in the shape of a deer from a distance, he stood nearby and pierced it in the sole with that very same lance.
Having gone there, he beheld a man bearing four arms;
having prostrated before him, he said to him again and again, "Be gracious!"
"This was done by me unknowingly, under the suspicion that it was a deer;
please forgive me. You ought not to consume me with the fire of your own sin."
Parāśara said:
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Not even the slightest fear remains for you;
go, O hunter, to heaven, the abode of the gods, by my grace."
Parāśara said:
Immediately following those words, a celestial chariot arrived;
having ascended it by her grace, the hunter departed for heaven.
When he had departed, that Blessed One, having united himself with the Self—
the immutable, inconceivable, stainless Brahman consisting of Vāsudeva— remained absorbed therein.
In that which is unborn, undecaying, imperishable, immeasurable, and the self of all,
he cast off his human body, having transcended the threefold course of existence.
[Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Arjuna, having then searched for the bodies of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, [found them].
He likewise caused the other sons to receive their consecration in due order.
The eight principal queens, headed by Rukmiṇī, who have been described,
embraced the body of Hari and entered the funeral fire.
And Revatī, O best of men, having embraced the body of Rāma,
entered the blazing fire, which was cooled by the joy of his touch.
But having heard that, Ugrasena, as well as Ānakadundubhi,
Devakī, and Rohiṇī, entered the fire.
Then Arjuna, having performed their funeral rites according to the prescribed rules,
departed, taking with him all the people as well as Vajra himself.
The thousands of wives of Kṛṣṇa departed from Dvāravatī;
and the son of Kuntī, protecting both Vajra and the people, proceeded slowly.
O Maitreya, when the mortal world was abandoned by Kṛṣṇa, the Sudharmā assembly hall and the Pārijāta tree went to heaven.
On the very day that Hari departed for heaven, abandoning the earth,
on that same day this powerful Kali, whose body is Time, descended.
The great ocean submerged that empty Dvārakā;
however, the sea did not submerge the single dwelling of the Yadu gods.
O Brahmin, even today the great ocean is not able to overstep its bounds,
because the Blessed Lord Keśava is eternally present there.
That place, endowed with the sports of Viṣṇu, is exceedingly meritorious and destroys all sins; by seeing it, one is liberated from evil.
O best of sages, Pārtha made his dwelling in the region of Pañcanada, which was well-endowed with abundant grain, for the sake of all people.
Then greed arose because of that single archer, Pārtha,
upon seeing the women being led away, their protectors— the Dasyus— having been slain.
Then those Ābhīras, performers of evil deeds whose minds were struck by greed and who were exceedingly arrogant, gathered together and took counsel.
"This lone archer Arjuna, bypassing us, carries away these women whose lords have been slain; fie on this strength of yours! (ViP 5.38.15)
Having slain Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the others, he has become arrogant; he no longer recognizes the strength of those who dwell in the villages.
"Ha! Ha! Take up your long staffs, O great ones; this man of wicked mind despises us all. What is the use of your uplifted arms? ||| ViP_5.38.17 |||
Parāśara said: Then thousands of robbers, armed with sticks and carrying stolen goods, rushed toward those people whose lord had been slain.
Then, turning back, the son of Kuntī spoke to the Ābhīras as if laughing:
"Turn back, O you who are ignorant of dharma, unless you are desirous of death!"
Disregarding his words, O Maitreya, they then seized that wealth as well as the women who were the dependents of Viṣvaksena.
Then the heroic Arjuna began to string the divine bow Gāṇḍīva, which does not age in battle, but he was unable to do so.
He made it ready with great effort, yet it became loose again;
even as he reflected upon it, the Pāṇḍava could not recall his divine weapons.
And the indignant Pārtha discharged arrows at these enemies;
those shafts shot by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva caused their very skin to split.
Even those inexhaustible arrows given by Agni came to an end while Arjuna was fighting with the cowherds at the conclusion of his worldly existence.
And the son of Kuntī reflected: "Indeed, that strength by which all the kings were conquered by me with volleys of arrows was the very strength of Kṛṣṇa."
Then, while the son of Pāṇḍu looked on, those most excellent women were carried off by the Ābhīras;
others, however, departed of their own accord out of desire.
Then, O Sage, when his arrows were exhausted, Dhanañjaya struck the bandits with the tip of his bow; but they merely laughed at his blows.
And while Pārtha was looking on, O best of sages, all those Mlecchas departed, taking with them the foremost women of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans.
Then Jiṣṇu, deeply distressed, crying out "Alas!
Alas! wept indeed, saying, "Oh, I have been released by that Blessed One!"
That bow, those weapons, that chariot, and those horses—
all were destroyed in an instant, like a gift given to one who is unlearned in the Vedas.
Oh, how exceedingly powerful is destiny, since, even in the absence of that Great-Souled One,
it bestows victory upon a base host that is devoid of any capability!
Those two arms, that fist, that position, and I myself, O Arjuna—
without that merit alone, everything has become utterly worthless.
"Arjuna’s status as Arjuna and Bhīma’s status as Bhīma were surely established by him;
otherwise, how could I have been defeated by the Ābhīras?"
Parāśara said:
Speaking thus, Jiṣṇu went to the supreme city named Mathurā;
there he installed Vajra, the joy of the Yādavas, as king.
Then Phālguna saw Vyāsa dwelling in the forest;
approaching that illustrious one, he saluted him with humility.
Beholding him as he prostrated at his feet, the Sage, looking upon Pārtha who was devoid of luster, spoke after a long time: "How is it that you have become so exceedingly like this?"
"Have you followed a woman who has no hero [to protect her], or have you committed the murder of a Brahmin?
For you are now shorn of your luster, like one suffering from the frustration of shattered firm hopes."
"O Lord, this was not given during the bright fortnight, nor in the dark fortnight; it was mixed with coarse food, grain, and wheat.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, the granter of all desires, O Master, it is because of that [food] that Your form shines in such a way."
Or perhaps those mendicants and others who came to you for alms were rejected;
or else you took pleasure in forbidden women—for that reason, you have lost your luster.
Furthermore, O Arjuna, you alone eat sweets without having given anything to the Brahmins; or have you seized the wealth of the miserable?
"O Arjuna, have you perhaps come within the range of the wind from a winnowing basket, or have you been struck by an evil eye? For otherwise, how could you be so devoid of splendor?"
"Have you been touched by water from [another's] fingernails, or perhaps sprinkled with the water from a jar?
For because of that, you are utterly lusterless, as if defeated in battle by those inferior to you."
Parāśara said: Then Pārtha, having sighed, said, "Listen, O Blessed One," and as he was thus addressed, he related his own defeat to Vyāsa exactly as it had happened.
Arjuna said:
"That strength which was ours, that splendor, that heroism, that prowess, as well as the fortune and the luster that belonged to us— Hari has departed, leaving all these behind."
O Sage, we have become as if made of straw, deprived by that other great one who speaks with a smile.
That Supreme Person, who was the personified essence of my missiles, arrows, and the Gāṇḍīva bow, has departed.
That Govinda, by whose very glance prosperity, victory, wealth, and advancement never left us— that Blessed One has departed, having abandoned us.
He by whose power Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the King of Aṅga, and others, as well as Duryodhana and his followers, were utterly consumed— that Kṛṣṇa has now abandoned the earth.
"O Father, with its youth departed and its splendor destroyed, my earth appears like one whose radiance has vanished; I am not alone in this separation from that wielder of the discus."
"By whose power Bhīṣma and the others acted like moths in the fire that was I;
without that Kṛṣṇa, I have today been defeated by mere cowherds."
That Gāṇḍīva bow, by whose power fame was attained throughout the three worlds,
has been rendered useless by those cowherds with their clubs.
O great sage, many thousands of women who had me as their protector were carried off by bandits armed with clubs, even as I was striving [to protect them].
O Kṛṣṇa, the women of Kṛṣṇa’s inner apartments, who were being led away by the Ābhīras,
were snatched back by me after I overcame their force with my staff-weapons.
"It is no wonder that I am devoid of splendor; that I still live is the marvel. Stained by the mire of insults from the low-born, O Grandfather, I am shameless."
After 5.38.53, G1, M1.3 insert:
"O great sage, there are indeed only three who partake of the name 'Kṛṣṇa'."
I, you, and the god—the omnipresent Lord—have each performed our respective duties as was appropriate.
When that mighty-armed and high-souled lord of the earth, Kṛṣṇa, [had departed].
My mind, according to its capacity, no one else knows here; I alone know it.
On the earth, this son of Devakī [played] with the food, drink, and games of his devotees.
He who has bestowed affection upon me draws my mind toward himself.
I shall either cast off this body or swallow potent poison.
Or he may throw himself from the peak of a mountain, or enter the water, O Sage.

in a month in the Dvāpara, and in a single day and night in the Kali age.
"O twice-born ones, a man attains the fruit of austerity, celibacy, recitation, and so forth; therefore it is rightly said that the Kali age is excellent. (ViP 6.2.16)
What one obtains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one obtains in the Kali age simply by chanting the praises of Keśava.
"In this Kali age, a person attains an exceedingly great excellence of dharma with very little effort; O knowers of dharma, for that reason I am pleased with the Kali. (ViP 6.2.18)
The Veda must be acquired by the twice-born through the practice of vows and offerings;
thereafter, they should perform sacrifices according to the rules with wealth obtained through their own specific duties.
For the twice-born, idle talk, idle food, and idle sacrifice lead to their downfall;
likewise, those who are self-restrained must always remain vigilant against such things.
O twice-born ones, there is a fault in their performing everything improperly; furthermore, for them, food, drink, and so forth are not obtained according to their desire.
Consequently, they are entirely dependent upon others in all their undertakings;
thus, O twice-born ones, those people conquer their own worlds only with great hardship.
"By the mere service of the twice-born, this Śūdra becomes entitled to perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
he conquers his own worlds and is therefore more blessed than that [other Śūdra]."
"O tigers among sages, because he has no restriction regarding what may or may not be eaten, nor indeed regarding what may or may not be drunk, for that reason he is called 'the Good' (Sādhu)."
Wealth always acquired by men without violating their own dharma should be bestowed upon worthy recipients and used for sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
O best of the twice-born, there is great suffering in its acquisition and in its preservation;
likewise, for men, its improper application should be known as a profound difficulty.
O best of the twice-born, by means of these and other such afflictions,
a person indeed conquers his own worlds, beginning with those of Prajāpati, in due order.
O twice-born ones, a woman who performs service to her husband through deed, thought, and speech attains residence in the same world as him.
Just as a man [attains his goal] without excessive great effort,
by that [man] the third utterance of women was accepted as "well said."
O Brahmins, I have told you this for which purpose you have come here;
ask whatever you desire, and I shall explain it clearly to you.
Parāśara said: Then those sages said, "O great sage, that which was to be asked has been explained by you exactly as it is, even though the question concerned something else."
Then, laughing, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke to those ascetics who had approached him with eyes wide open in amazement.
This question of yours was understood by me through my divine eye;
therefore, in response to your inquiry, I have spoken the words "Excellent! Excellent! to you.
For in the Kali age, dharma is indeed accomplished with very little effort by men whose every sin has been washed away by the waters of their own virtues.
O best of sages, [this is achieved] by Śūdras who are intent on serving the twice-born,
and likewise by women through the effortless service of their husbands alone.
Therefore, I consider even this triad to be most blessed;
for the twice-born, there is hardship in the accomplishment of dharma during the Kṛta and other ages.
"O twice-born ones who know the Dharma, that which was intended by you has been told by me, even though unasked; what else shall be done? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.2.37)
Parāśara said:
Then, having honored Vyāsa, they praised him again and again;
with their doubts dispelled by Vyāsa’s words, the twice-born departed as they had come.
O illustrious one, I have also told you this secret:
this is the one great virtue of the exceedingly wicked Kali age.
After verse 39, D8 inserts: "Merely by chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa, one whose bonds are released shall go to the supreme state."

And as for what I was asked by you regarding the dissolution of the worlds— both that which pertains to primordial nature (prākṛta) and that which is intermediate— I shall now describe that to you as well.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
§ Parāśara said: For all beings indeed, there is a threefold dissolution (pratisaṃcara).
It is considered to be occasional (naimittika), natural (prākṛtika), and likewise absolute (ātyantika).
Among these, the *brāhma* dissolution occurs at the end of a kalpa;
the absolute dissolution is called liberation (*mokṣa*); and the natural (*prākṛta*) dissolution occurs at the end of two parārdhas.
Maitreya said: O Blessed One, tell me the calculation of a parārdha, by which—
when doubled— it is to be understood as the period of a primary dissolution (prākṛta-pratisaṃcara).
Parāśara said:
O twice-born one, each successive place is calculated to be ten times the value of the preceding one;
thus, at the eighteenth place, it is designated as a *parārdha*.
O twice-born one, that dissolution which lasts for twice a parārdha is called the Prākṛta;
at that time, the entire manifest universe indeed goes to dissolution within its own cause, the Unmanifest.
This human blink of an eye, which is the measure of a single mātrā—
fifteen of those constitute a kāṣṭhā, and thirty kāṣṭhās likewise constitute a kalā.
A nāḍikā, by measure, consists of fifteen kalās.
By that measure, it holds twelve and a half *palas* of water;
with four gold *māṣas* [weighing] four finger-breadths, a hole is made,
and by the Māgadha standard, that is remembered as a *prastha* of water.
O best of the twice-born, two nāḍikās constitute one muhūrta;
thirty muhūrtas make up a day and night, and likewise, thirty days make a month.
Twelve months constitute a day and night in heaven;
for the enemies of the Asuras, three hundred and sixty such years constitute a year.
Twelve thousand such [cycles] are declared to be a Caturyuga;
a thousand Caturyugas, however, is said to be one day of Brahmā.
O great sage, fourteen Manus exist there during that kalpa; and at its conclusion, O Maitreya, occurs the occasional dissolution of Brahmā.
O Maitreya, listen as I describe his exceedingly fierce nature; furthermore, I shall explain to you again the dissolution of the material world.
At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, when the surface of the earth has almost entirely perished,
an exceedingly fierce drought occurs that lasts for a hundred years.
Then, O best of sages, those beings of little substance who dwell upon the earth perish entirely from being oppressed.
Then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable one who has assumed the form of Rudra,
strives to bring about the destruction of all creatures who abide within himself.
Then that Blessed Viṣṇu [entered] into the seven rays of the Sun.
After 17ab, D₂ inserts:
"Suṣupta removes affliction, and likewise Viśva as well."
Viśvadyumna, as well as Atharvan, Vasu, and Saṃyadvasu.
Standing there, O best of sages, he drinks all the waters without exception.
Having indeed drunk all the waters existing upon the earth and within living beings,
O Maitreya, he brings the entire surface of the earth to desiccation.
He brings to exhaustion all the oceans, rivers, mountains, mountain springs,
and whatever water exists within the netherworlds.
Then, by its power, those very seven rays, nourished by the intake of water, arise as the seven suns.
Then, O twice-born one, seven blazing suns appear above and below,
burning the entire triple world together with the subterranean realms of Pātāla.
O twice-born one, as the three worlds— including the expanse of mountains, rivers, and oceans— are being consumed by those blazing suns, they become entirely devoid of moisture.
Then, O twice-born one, the entire triple world becomes devoid of trees and water,
and this earth takes on an appearance resembling the back of a tortoise.
Then, having become Kālāgnirudra, Hari, the destroyer of all,
burns the netherworlds from below, produced by the breath of the serpent Śeṣa.
Having consumed all the netherworlds, that great fire reached the earth and devours the entire surface of the world.
Then, that most terrible one, consisting of great whirlpools of garlands of flames, revolves right there throughout the entire Bhuvarloka and Svarloka.
Then the entire three worlds appeared like a frying pan,
surrounded by a whirling mass of flames, with all mobile and immobile beings consumed.
Then, O great sage, those inhabitants of the two worlds who have fulfilled their duties, overcome by the heat, go to Maharloka.
Therefore, the worlds scorched by great heat go beyond that to Janaloka; seeking the highest, they do so by means of tenfold repetition.
Then, O best of sages, Janārdana, assuming the form of Rudra after having burnt the entire world,
produces clouds born from the breath of his mouth.
Then, at that time, terrible Saṃvartaka clouds, resembling herds of elephants, flashing with lightning and thundering, arise in the sky.
Some clouds were dark like blue lotuses, some resembled white water-lilies;
some were smoke-colored, some were dense, and some were yellow.
Some have the color of a donkey, others resemble lac-dye;
some are like lapis lazuli, and in some places they resemble sapphire.
Others resemble conch shells or jasmine flowers; likewise, some resemble pure collyrium, some resemble the indragopa insect, and others resemble red arsenic.
Some are like *indragopa* insects, and others likewise resemble peacocks. (ViP 6.3.34*)
Some indeed have the luster of red arsenic, while others resemble yellow orpiment.
Some thick clouds arise resembling the wings of blue jays;
some have the form of great cities, and others resemble mountains.
Others resemble gabled palaces, while some are dense masses like the earth;
with great roars and massive bodies, they fill the vault of the sky.
Raining down those great torrents, they extinguished that most terrifying fire.
O best of sages, they pacify the entire world and send down rain.
Then, with those streams resembling the trunks of elephants, they [poured] incessantly.
O Brahmin, they pacify everything that extends throughout the three worlds.
O best of sages, when the fire has been extinguished, those clouds also rain for more than a hundred years,
flooding the entire world.
Having flooded the entire earth with torrents as thick as axle-trees,
O twice-born one, they likewise flood the Bhuvarloka and the heavens above.
When the world has been turned to darkness and all things, both stationary and moving, have perished,
those great clouds rain for more than a hundred years.
Thus it is at the end of the kalpa, O best of sages; [all this] occurs in its entirety. (ViP 6.3.40*)
[This is] due to the majesty of Vāsudeva, the eternal Supreme Self.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O great sage, when the waters had reached the station of the Seven Sages (the Great Bear), they remained there.
Then this entire triple world becomes a single ocean.
Then, O Maitreya, the wind produced from the breath of Viṣṇu blows for another hundred years, destroying those clouds.
The Blessed One, who consists of all beings, is inconceivable and the creator of beings;
he is without beginning, yet the origin of the universe, having drunk up the air entirely.
Then, in that single ocean,
the Lord Hari, the primordial creator, the Blessed One, assuming the form of Brahmā, lies upon the bed of Śeṣa.
He was praised by the Siddhas, such as Sanaka and others, who had gone to Janaloka,
and was meditated upon by those seeking liberation who had gone to Brahmaloka.
The Supreme Lord, having entered into his divine yogic sleep consisting of his own creative power (māyā),
meditated upon himself under the name Vāsudeva.
Maitreya, this is called the "occasional" dissolution (pratisaṃcara);
for in that state, Hari lies down, assuming the form of Brahmā.
When the Soul of All awakens, then this world stirs;
when Acyuta rests upon the bed of Māyā, all this universe closes its eyes.
That which is a day for the Lotus-born (Brahmā), consisting of a thousand cycles of four yugas,
is held to be his night when the world has been reduced to a single ocean.
Then, having awakened at the end of the night, the Unborn One, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Brahmā, performs creation once again, as was previously described to you.
Thus, O twice-born one, this intermediate dissolution resulting from the destruction of a kalpa has been described to you; now hear further of the elemental (prākṛta) dissolution.
O Sage, when all the worlds and all the nether regions had been completely cleansed by the contact of fire resulting from a lack of rain, [the earth was purified].

When that process of reabsorption has commenced— brought about by the will of Kṛṣṇa— the dissolution of all modifications, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), takes place.
The waters indeed first swallow up the quality of the earth, which consists of smell;
once its smell has been taken away, the earth is then prepared for dissolution.
When the subtle element of smell has perished, the earth becomes of the nature of water;
then the waters increase, becoming impetuous and loud-sounding.
Filling this entire universe, they remain and move about,
pervading those various worlds on all sides with their surging waves of water.
After verse 16, D4.5,T2.3,G2.3 insert:
"O best of the twice-born, this entire world became completely pervaded."
That quality which belongs to the waters is consumed by light;
consequently, those waters perish through the dissolution of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra).
Then the waters, their essence having been withdrawn, indeed reach the realm of light;
for when the water is in the state of fire, it is enveloped on all sides by heat.
And that fire, pervading everywhere, likewise takes up that water;
then this entire world is gradually filled with flames.
When that [world] is enveloped by rays of light extending sideways, upwards, and downwards,
the wind devours even the supreme form of the luminaries, the source of light.
Then, when that fire, which is the self of all, has dissolved and become wind,
and the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra) has perished, the fire is deprived of its form.
Then the light subsides and the great wind blows violently;
the world is then without light, and the fire has come to rest within the wind.
Then, having reached its source, that wind, manifesting its own origin,
vibrated violently upward, downward, and across the ten directions.
Then space swallows the quality of wind, which is touch;
consequently, wind subsides, and space remains unobstructed.
Formless, without taste or touch, odorless, and not possessing material form,
that exceedingly great [Brahman] shines forth, filling everything.
That circular void is space, characterized by sound;
that space, consisting of mere sound, stands pervading everything.
Then the Bhūtādi (the principle of egoity) again devours its quality, sound;
for when the elements and the senses have simultaneously merged into the Bhūtādi,
this Bhūtādi is known as being of the nature of self-conceit and characterized by darkness (tamas).
Furthermore, the Great One, characterized by the intellect (buddhi), indeed devours the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
The Earth is vast and great, extending to the limits of the world, both within and without.
Thus, O Great Sage, these seven primary natures indeed enter into one another in succession during the process of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
By him this entire egg is enveloped, which dissolves into the waters—
along with its seven continents and oceans, its seven worlds, and its mountains.
That which is the obstruction of water is indeed consumed by light;
light goes to dissolution in wind, and the wind goes into space.
Space, in turn, devours the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and the Great One (mahat) likewise devours that;
O twice-born one, primordial nature (prakṛti) devours the Great One along with these [preceding principles].
O Great Sage, that state in which the qualities (guṇas) are in equilibrium— neither excessive nor deficient—
is called Prakṛti, the Cause, Pradhāna, and the Supreme Source.
Thus, this entire primordial nature, consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
O Maitreya, dissolves into that unmanifest state which is its own essential form.
The person (puruṣa) is one, pure, imperishable, eternal, and all-pervading;
yet he too, O Maitreya, is a portion of the Supreme Self who exists within all beings.
There, in the Lord of All, where there are no conceptual constructions of name, genus, and so forth—
in that which is to be known as consisting of pure existence, whose nature is consciousness, and who is the Supreme Self— there exist no such notions.
That is Brahman, that is the supreme abode, and he is the Supreme Self and the Lord;
he is Viṣṇu, this entire universe, from whom the ascetic does not return.
The primordial nature (prakṛti), which I have described as having the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
and the person (puruṣa)— both of these dissolve into the Supreme Self.
And the Supreme Self, the support of all, the Supreme Lord,
is celebrated by the name Viṣṇu in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas.
Vedic action is twofold: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to liberation;
by both of these, He whose form is everything is worshipped by men.
For he, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice, the Supreme Person, is indeed worshipped by men through the paths of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas as they proceed in sacrifice.
When the path has ceased, Viṣṇu— who is the self of knowledge, who is worshipped through the yoga of knowledge, and whose very form is knowledge— bestows the fruit of liberation upon the yogis.
Whatever object whatsoever is denoted by short, long, or protracted vowels,
and that which is beyond the range of speech— all that is the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Manifest he is, and unmanifest he is; he alone is the imperishable Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, the Self of the universe, Hari who assumes all forms.

Within that [unmanifest], O Maitreya, primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, is completely dissolved; and the person (puruṣa) likewise dissolves into the all-pervading, unobstructed Self.
O Maitreya, that period of time consisting of two parārdhas which I have described to you is said to be one day of Viṣṇu, the Lord.
O great sage, when the manifest has dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise primordial nature has dissolved into the Puruṣa,
another night remains there, equal in duration to that [day].
For that eternal Supreme Self, there is neither day nor night;
nevertheless, O twice-born one, this conventional designation is applied to that Lord.
Thus, O Maitreya, this dissolution of the primary elements has been described to you;
now, O Brahmin, learn of the absolute re-absorption.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
O Maitreya, having understood the threefold suffering—beginning with that which is internal—the wise man [should seek liberation].
One whose knowledge and dispassion have arisen attains ultimate dissolution.
The internal [suffering] is indeed twofold: physical and likewise mental.
The physical is divided into many varieties; listen now to that.
By various means, such as diseases of the head, catarrh, fever, colic, fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, asthma, swelling, vomiting, and so forth; (ViP 6.5.3)
Likewise, the suffering born of the body is divided into those known as eye-disease, dysentery, leprosy, and bodily ailments; you should now hear about that which is mental.
It is born from desire, anger, fear, hatred, greed, delusion, and despondency;
likewise, it arises from grief, envy, humiliation, jealousy, and malice.
"O best of the twice-born, even mental distress is of many kinds;
through such various distinctions as these, distress is indeed known as internal (ādhyātmika)."
For human beings, afflictions caused by other beings (ādhibhautika) are produced by wild animals, birds, humans, and the like, as well as by piśācas, uragas, rākṣasas, reptiles, and so forth.

O best of sages, suffering arising from conception, birth, old age, ignorance, death, and likewise from hell, is divided into thousands of varieties.
Within the womb, the creature of delicate body is enveloped by much impurity,
wrapped in the fetal membrane, with the collection of its back and neck bones bent.
Due to his mother’s consumption of food that was excessively bitter, pungent, sharp, hot, and salty,
and because she drank too much, his pains increased exceedingly.
He is no longer the master of his own limbs for such acts as extending or contracting them;
lying in the great mire of excrement and urine, he is tormented in every way.
Then, breathless yet conscious, remembering hundreds of previous births,
he remains in the womb in extreme suffering, bound by his own karma.
Being born with a face defiled by feces, blood, urine, and semen,
his skeletal frame is tormented by the *prājāpatya* wind.
Indeed, turned head-downwards by the powerful winds of birth,
the distressed one emerges from the mother's womb through great sufferings.
Having fallen into a great swoon and being touched by the external air,
O best of sages, he experiences a loss of consciousness upon being born.
With his limbs as if pierced by thorns and torn apart by saws,
he fell upon the earth like a worm from a putrid sore.
Incapable even of scratching himself and powerless even to turn over,
he receives bathing, drinking, food, and so forth only through the will of others.
Lying upon a bed of impurity, even while being bitten by insects, gadflies, and the like,
he is not at all capable of warding them off.
One encounters many sufferings of birth immediately following birth,
as well as those pertaining to other beings and so forth, during the state of childhood.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, with a deluded inner organ, a man does not know: whence he comes, who he is, where he is going, or what his true nature is.
By what bond am I bound? What is the cause and what is not the cause? What is to be done and what is not to be done? What is to be spoken and what is not to be spoken? ||| ViP_6.5.22 |||
"What is non-dharma and what indeed is dharma? In what does it abide, or how? What is to be done and what is not to be done? Or what possesses virtue and what possesses fault? (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.5.23)
Thus, great suffering born of ignorance is experienced by men who are like beasts, deluded, devoted solely to their genitals and bellies.
Ignorance is a state of darkness (tamas); it causes the failure to engage in the commencement of actions. Therefore, O twice-born one, the neglect of duties occurs among those who are ignorant.
The great seers have declared that hell is the fruit resulting from the neglect of one's duties;
therefore, for the ignorant, there is supreme suffering both in this world and in the next.
And a man whose body is worn out by old age, with limbs slackened, with loose and decayed teeth, and covered with wrinkles, sinews, and veins; (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.5.27)
With his eyes lost at a distance, with stars appearing within his sky-like mouth,
with clusters of hair emerging from the openings of his nostrils, his body was trembling.
With the entire collection of bones in his back clearly visible and bent,
his digestive fire extinguished, he took little food and remained inactive.
His movements—walking, rising, lying down, and sitting—become difficult;
his hearing and sight grow dim, and his mouth becomes fouled by trickling saliva.
With all his faculties no longer under his control and facing death,
he is unable to remember at that very moment even all the things he had previously experienced.
When the sentence was uttered but once, he experienced great exhaustion;
he suffered from insomnia brought on by heavy breathing, coughing, and great exertion.
The aged man is raised up by one person and likewise laid down by another;
he has been reduced to a state of humiliation for his servants, himself, sons, and wife.
With all his purity exhausted, longing for pleasure and food,
he became an object of ridicule even to his own attendants, having lost all interest in his kinsmen.
As if remembering his own actions in another birth,
he sighs deeply and is greatly tormented as he recalls his youth.
Having indeed experienced such sufferings as these in old age,
hear now also of those sufferings which one encounters at death.
Then the man’s neck, feet, and hands become slack; he is overcome by trembling, repeatedly experiences exhaustion, is helpless, and occasionally possesses fragments of consciousness.
Agitated by an excessive sense of "mine" regarding gold, grain, sons, wife, servants, houses, and so forth, he thinks, "How will these endure? (ViP 6.5.38)
With great diseases that pierce the vital points, as cruel as saws and as fierce as the arrows of Death, his skeletal joints are being torn asunder.
With his eyes rolling and his hands and feet flailing repeatedly,
his palate and lips parched, he gasped with a wheezing sound.
His throat was obstructed by floods of humors, he was oppressed by the upward-moving breath (udāna),
pervaded by great heat, and likewise afflicted by thirst and hunger.
Afflicted by the servants of Yama, he undergoes departure from his body due to his afflictions;
and thereafter, through suffering, he assumes a body of torment.
These and other terrible sufferings await men at the time of death;
now hear of those which are experienced by deceased persons in hell.
The seizing by the nooses and other instruments of Yama’s servants, the flogging with rods,
the sight of Yama himself, and the vision of the terrifying path.

O twice-born one, those unbearable torments which exist in each individual hell— terrifying with pits of glowing embers, sand, fire, machines, weapons, and the like— [are experienced by those who have committed evil deeds].
Of those being split with saws, blown in a crucible, hewn with axes, and even buried in the ground; (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.5.46)
While being impaled upon pikes, cast into the mouths of tigers, devoured by vultures, and preyed upon by leopards; ||| ViP_6.5.47 |||
They are boiled in the midst of oil, they are made to rot in a mire of alkaline sludge;
they are cast down from great heights and hurled by mechanical catapults.
O Brahmin, there is no known limit to the number of sufferings arising from sinful causes that are experienced by those in hell.
O best of the twice-born, it is not only in hell that there is a succession of sufferings;
even in heaven, for one who fears falling and whose merit is subject to decay, there is no true peace.
Furthermore, a man comes to be in the womb and is born again;
he dissolves back into the womb once more, and even as he is being born, he goes to his end.
One dies as soon as born; death is certain whether in childhood, in youth, having reached middle age, or in old age.
As long as it lives, it remains overwhelmed by various kinds of sufferings,
like a cotton seed amidst the mass of fibers that are the cause of the thread.
In the loss of wealth, as well as in its acquisition and preservation, men experience manifold sufferings; likewise, so it is when their cherished desires fail.
Whatever object arises, Maitreya, that brings pleasure to men,
that very thing becomes the seed of the tree of suffering.
Through wife, sons, friends, wealth, houses, fields, riches, and the like,
men do not experience such abundant happiness as that which is found in [this] bliss.
Thus, for those whose minds are scorched by the heat of the sun of the suffering of saṃsāra,
where else can there be happiness for human beings except in the shade of the tree of liberation?
Therefore, this threefold mass of suffering, which arises for the wise in the states of conception, birth, old age, and so forth, [is to be understood].*ViP_6.5.58*
The attainment of the Blessed One, characterized solely by the state of bliss consisting of unsurpassed and extraordinary delight, is considered the singular, absolute, and eternal medicine.
Therefore, wise men should exert effort to attain that;
O Great Sage, it has been taught that both knowledge and action are the means for attaining it.
Thus, knowledge is said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment;
the former consists of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), while the latter is born of discernment and is the Supreme Brahman.
Ignorance is like blinding darkness, while that which arises from the senses is like a lamp;
O brahmin sage, that knowledge born of discernment is like the sun.
O best of sages, listen now as I relate here, in this context, that very meaning of the Vedas which Manu also spoke after recollecting it.
Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman.
"Two sciences indeed are to be known," so says the Atharvaṇa Śruti;
by the higher one there is the attainment of the Imperishable, while the lower consists of the Ṛgveda and the others.
The wise indeed behold Him— the all-pervading, omnipresent, eternal source of beings, who is without cause, who pervades all yet is not pervaded by anything.
That is Brahman, that is the supreme abode, that is to be meditated upon by those desiring liberation;
it is the subtle, supreme station of Viṣṇu, proclaimed by the words of the Vedas.
That very nature which is to be expressed by the word "Bhagavat" is the essential form of the Supreme Self;
the word "Bhagavat" is the designator of that primordial, imperishable Being.
Thus, that knowledge by which the true reality of the matter thus described is known in its essence is supreme; it is other than that which consists of the three Vedas.
O twice-born one, although that Brahman is beyond the range of words,
the term "Bhagavat" is applied to its worship in a figurative sense.
O Maitreya, the word "Bhagavat" applies to the Supreme Brahman, which is pure, known as the Great Sovereignty (Mahāvibhūti), and the cause of all causes.

O Sage, the letter *bha* is endowed with two meanings: it signifies "one who supports" (*saṃbharta*) and likewise "a supporter" (*bhartṛ*). Similarly, the meaning of the letter *ga* is "one who leads," "one who causes to go," and "the creator" (*sraṣṭṛ*).
The term *bhaga* is said to denote the sixfold totality of sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion.
Beings dwell there within that Self of beings, who is the Self of all;
and he dwells in all beings without exception; therefore, he is the imperishable one whose meaning is expressed by the syllable *va*.
Thus, O best of beings, this great sound "Bhagavān" belongs to Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman; it applies to no other.
In this context, this word is accompanied by a technical definition denoting an object worthy of worship;
it is not used figuratively, for elsewhere it is indeed used figuratively.
He who knows the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings,
and who knows both knowledge and ignorance— he is to be called Bhagavān.
Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor— in their entirety,
and devoid of all qualities and attributes subject to abandonment— these are what is denoted by the word "Bhagavat."
All beings dwell there within the Supreme Self, and that Universal Self dwells within all beings; therefore, he is remembered as Vāsudeva.
In former times, when questioned by Khāṇḍikya Janaka, Keśidhvaja gave a true explanation of the names of the infinite Vāsudeva.
Since he dwells within all beings and they dwell within him,
Vāsudeva is therefore the Lord, the creator and ordainer of the worlds.
Regarding verse 82, B2 substitutes:

"He who dwells eternally within all beings, and in whom all beings reside—the Creator, the Ordainer, and the Supreme Lord—he is Vāsudeva; there is no other superior to him. B1 inserts this after verse 82.

O Sage, he has transcended the primordial nature of all beings, their transformations, and the defects arising from the qualities; having passed beyond all veils, he is the soul of all, by whom that which exists within the intermediate spaces of the worlds is pervaded.

For he consists of all auspicious qualities; having veiled the creation of beings with a mere fraction of his own power, he assumes whatever vast body he desires at will, having accomplished the welfare of the entire world.
He is the singular mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, and his own heroic power and capacity;
he is the supreme among the supreme, the Lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist.
He is the Lord, consisting of both the individual and the collective, whose nature is unmanifest and yet manifest;
the sovereign of all, the seer of all, the knower of all, possessing all powers, he is known as the Supreme Lord.

That by which something is perceived—whether it be seen or understood—as being free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single nature, is knowledge; everything other than that is said to be ignorance.
Having heard [this], he who turns his face away from the speaker’s mouth has lived a hundred births in vain.
It should be known as equal to a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and superior to a hundred [visits to] Kurukṣetra.
The life of one who is averse to knowledge is fruitless.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Parāśara said:
That Supreme Person is perceived through the study of the Vedas and self-restraint.
Brahman is the cause for attaining that [state], and it is recited as "That Thou Art" (Tat Tvam Asi).
One should practice yoga through the study of sacred texts, and one should perform the study of sacred texts through yoga;
through the perfection of both the study of sacred texts and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed.
For the purpose of seeing that [Brahman], sacred study is one eye and yoga is the other;
he who has become Brahman cannot be seen with the physical eye of flesh.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, I desire to know that yoga; please describe it, so that once it is known, I may behold the Supreme Lord, the support of all.
Parāśara said:
Just as Keśidhvaja formerly explained Yoga to the high-souled Janaka, the son of Khaṇḍikya, so shall I describe it to you.
Maitreya said: O Brahmin, who was Khāṇḍikya, and who was Keśidhvaja?
And how did their conversation, which concerned the connection with Yoga, take place?
Parāśara said:
Janaka was indeed Dharmadhvaja; his son was Amitadhvaja, and there was also a king named Kṛtadhvaja who was ever devoted to the supreme self.
O twice-born one, Kṛtadhvaja’s son was the famous Keśidhvaja;
and the son of Amitadhvaja was Khāṇḍikya-Janaka.
On the path of ritual action, Khāṇḍikya was skilled on this earth;
Keśidhvaja also became exceedingly proficient in the knowledge of the Self.
Both of them were indeed desirous of conquering one another;
Khāṇḍikya was deposed from his own kingdom by Keśidhvaja.
Then, accompanied by his domestic priest and ministers, he was expelled from the kingdom due to his meager resources and became a wanderer in the difficult forests.
Relying upon knowledge and established in the science of Brahman, he too performed very many sacrifices in order to cross over death by means of wisdom.
O best among those who know yoga, once while he was engaged in a sacrifice,
a fierce tiger killed his Dharmadhenu in the lonely forest.
Then the king, having learned that the cow had been killed by the tiger, asked the officiating priests, "What expiation is prescribed for this? (ViP 6.6.14)
They said, "We do not know; let Kaśeru be asked.
Thus addressed by him, Kaśeru replied to the descendant of Bhṛgu, "So be it."
"Ask Śunaka, O Indra among kings; I do not know, but he will know.
Having gone there, he questioned him, and he too said, "Listen, O Sage, to what I shall say."
Neither Kaśeru, nor I, nor anyone else on earth now knows this,
except for your single enemy Khāṇḍikya, who was defeated by you.
And he said to him: "O Sage, I am going now to question my own enemy;
for the sacrifice has already been secured by me, even if he should slay me."
"If that enemy of mine, when questioned, declares the expiation,
then the sacrifice will proceed without flaw, O best of sages."
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, the king, wearing a black antelope skin, mounted his chariot and went to the forest where the high-minded Khāṇḍikya resided.
Beholding his enemy approaching, Khāṇḍikya,
his eyes copper-red with rage and having strung his bow, spoke:
Śāṇḍilya said:
"By binding on this black antelope skin as armor, you intend to slay us;
yet, wearing the black antelope skin, you believe that he will not strike me."
