I shall kill you; you shall not escape from me alive. You are an assassin, O evil-minded one, and an enemy who has seized my kingdom.
Keśidhvaja said:
"O Khāṇḍikya, I have come to you to ask about a doubt;
it was not to kill you that I considered this, so either release your anger or discharge your arrow."
Parāśara said:
Then the high-minded Khāṇḍikya deliberated in private with all his ministers and priests.
The ministers said to him: "This enemy, having fallen into our power, must be slain;
for once he is killed, the entire earth will come under your control."
And Khaṇḍikya said to them all, "It is even so, there is no doubt;
once he is slain, the entire earth shall come under my control."
"Victory in the next world is his, and the entire earth is mine;
if I do not kill him, victory in this world is mine, but the earth belongs to him."
I do not think that the earth could be greater than the conquest of the worlds. (ViP 6.6.29*11)
Victory over the next world is infinite, whereas victory over the earth is but for a very short time;
therefore, I will not kill him. Whatever he asks, that I shall tell him.
Parāśara said:
Then Khāṇḍikya Janaka approached his enemy and said:
"Ask whatever you wish to ask; I shall tell you all of it."
Then, O twice-born one, having related everything exactly as it had happened— the slaughter of the Dharmadhenu— he asked about the expiation pertaining to that act.
And he explained to Keśidhvaja, O twice-born one,
that expiation which is prescribed there in its entirety and according to the proper rule.
Having understood the matter and being permitted by that very high-souled one,
he approached the sacrificial ground and performed all the rites in their proper sequence.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites in due order and having bathed in the concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha),
the king, feeling that he had accomplished his purpose, then reflected.
All the officiating priests were honored by me, and the members of the assembly were respected;
likewise, the multitude of supplicants was provided by me with their desired wealth.
I have performed every action here in this world according to what was appropriate;
nevertheless, why is my mind still as if its task remains unaccomplished?
While reflecting thus, that lord of the earth remembered:
"I have indeed not yet given the teacher’s fee to Khāṇḍikya."
Then, O Maitreya, that king Khāṇḍikya mounted his chariot once more and proceeded further to where Durgagahana was situated.
Khaṇḍikya also, seeing him approaching again, stood with weapon raised, his mind set on killing him; the king spoke to him once more.
"O Khāṇḍikya, I have not come to do you harm; do not be angry.
Know that I have come to provide the payment for my preceptor."
"The sacrifice has been successfully performed by me through your instruction;
as such, I wish to give you a gift—choose a teacher’s fee."
Parāśara said:
Once again, that king deliberated with his ministers, desiring to perform a heavy act of atonement: "What should he be entreated to do? ||| ViP_6.6.43 |||
The ministers said to him: "Let this entire kingdom be requested;
for a kingdom is sought by capable men without having their soldiers wearied."
Laughing, that high-minded King Khaṇḍikya said to them:
"How could a short-lived sovereignty over the earth be desired by those such as I?"
"So it is, O ministers who accomplish worldly ends!
But what is the ultimate truth here? How is it that you are not discerning in this matter?"
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, he approached King Keśidhvaja and said to him,
"Will you certainly give me the teacher's fee?"
Having been told "So be it" by him, Khāṇḍikya then said to him:
"You are one who is discerning regarding the supreme truth of the knowledge of the inner self."
"If you would grant me the price for my preceptor,
then declare that deed which is sufficient for the pacification of my afflictions."
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Keśidhvaja said:
"Why did you not request from me my kingdom, which is free from all thorns?"
Nothing else is more dear to Kṣatriyas than the acquisition of a kingdom.
Śāṇḍilya said:
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas: the protection of their subjects and the execution of those who oppose their own kingdom through a righteous war.
After verse 3, G2 inserts:
"That which is the protection of subjects, and that which is the subduing of adversaries to one's own kingdom."
Since you have carried me away while I was powerless, no fault lies with me;
for even this ignorance, when abandoned without due order, leads only to bondage.
"This desire of mine for sovereignty is for the sake of obtaining the enjoyment of my birth;
it is not born of the faults of others, but follows only the path of dharma."
Begging is not for those born of the kṣatriya lineage; this is the view of the virtuous regarding dharma.
After 6ab, G1 inserts:
"There exists nothing other than yoga that brings about the exhaustion of the experience of birth."
O illustrious one, O best among those who know yoga, [teach] me the yoga of Brahman.
You have understood the meaning of the treatises on yoga within this lineage of Nimi.
Therefore, this kingdom which you have requested is not for you, as it is encompassed by ignorance.
The ignorant, whose minds are captivated by the sense of "mine," covet sovereignty;
those like me do not, for they are intoxicated by the great draught of the pride of "I."
Parāśara said:
Then King Keśidhvaja, greatly delighted, said "Excellent! to Khāṇḍikya-Janaka and affectionately spoke these words: "Listen to my speech."
"Desiring indeed to cross over death through ignorance, I perform kingship and various sacrifices, as well as the depletion of merit through enjoyments."
Thus, by good fortune, this mind of yours has attained the sovereignty of discernment;
now listen, O delighter of your lineage, to the true nature of ignorance as well.
The notion of a self in what is not-self, and the thought of "mine" in what is not one's own—
this twofold state is the seed from which the tree of ignorance arises.
Enveloped by the darkness of delusion within this body composed of the five elements, the embodied soul of poor intellect loudly forms the thought: "I am this. (ViP 6.7.12)
When the self stands apart from ether, air, fire, water, and earth,
who can produce a sense of "self" within this body?
For what wise person would think "this is mine" regarding houses, fields, and so forth— which are merely for the enjoyment of the physical body— when the Self is actually bodiless?
And thus, regarding sons and grandsons produced from that body, what wise man would exercise ownership over this non-self physical frame?
A human being performs every action for the sake of the enjoyment of the body;
yet when that body is other than the person, then that [action] leads to bondage.
After verse 16, Ś₂ and D₇ insert: "If indeed that which is inside this body were to become outside,"
Taking up a staff, this world would ward off dogs and crows.
Just as a house made of clay is indeed plastered with clay and water,
so too this earthly body exists by being plastered with clay and water.
If the body, which consists of the five elements, is nourished by enjoyments that consist of the five elements,
then why does a person feel pride on this account?
Traversing the path of saṃsāra through many thousands of births,
he has undergone the fatigue of delusion, shrouded by the dust of latent impressions (vāsanā).
When that dust of his is washed away by the hot water of knowledge,
then the fatigue of delusion of this traveler on the path of saṃsāra comes to rest.
When the exhaustion of delusion has come to rest,
the person whose inner organ is composed attains supreme Nirvana, which is unsurpassed and unassailable.
This self consists entirely of nirvāṇa; it is composed of knowledge and is stainless.
Suffering, ignorance, and impurities are properties of primordial nature (prakṛti), but they do not belong to the self.
O Sage, although water has no contact with fire, it nevertheless produces properties such as the intensification of sound through its contact with the cooking pot.

In the same way, the Self, through attachment to primordial nature (prakṛti), is defiled by egoism and other such traits, and thus partakes in the qualities of nature; for it is indeed distinct from them and immutable.
Thus, I have explained to you this seed of ignorance;
there is nothing other than yoga that brings about the destruction of the afflictions.
Śāṇḍilya said:
"O highly fortunate one, best among those who know yoga, tell me that yoga; for you have mastered the meaning of the treatises on yoga within this lineage of Nimi."
Keśidhvaja said:
O Khāṇḍikya, listen as I describe the true nature of yoga,
established in which the sage, having attained absorption into Brahman, does not fall away.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
it is attached to sense objects in bondage, and likewise free from sense objects in liberation.
Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, the sage whose self is consciousness should,
by means of that mind, contemplate the Supreme Lord who has become Brahman for the sake of liberation.
O Sage, that [power] leads this meditator on Brahman to his own essential nature by means of its own capacity,
just as a magnet attracts iron that is susceptible to transformation.
The union of that distinguished movement of the mind, which depends upon one's own effort, with Brahman is designated as *yoga*.
Thus, he whose yoga consists in the discernment of qualities endowed with absolute distinction is indeed called a seeker of liberation, a yogin.
After verse 32, Ś₂ and D₇ insert:
"There is indeed but one [cause] for bondage and liberation; there is no second whatsoever."
The path that leads to the eastern ocean does not go to the western one.
Due to the activity of attachment, the intellect would not be possible in its prior arising.
Thus, through this means, Dharma is established; it is not the cause in other doctrines.
The yogi who is engaged in yoga is first called "one who is practicing" (yuñjāna);
but when his samādhi is perfected, he is one who has attained the realization of the Supreme Brahman.
Even if his mind is defiled by the fault of obstacles,
liberation from his previous state arises for him through practice over successive births.
But the yogin who has perfected samādhi, having burned away the accumulation of karma by the fire of yoga, attains liberation in that very birth before long.
Leading his own mind toward fitness, the desireless yogin should practice celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness.
One who has restrained the self should perform sacred study, purity, contentment, and austerity,
and likewise direct the mind toward the supreme Brahman.
These five restraints (yamas) along with the five observances (niyamas) have been proclaimed;
when performed with desire, they grant distinguished fruits, but for those free from desire, they bestow liberation.
Having occupied a single seat, such as the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana) and others, the disciplined ascetic, endowed with virtues,
should practice yoga through those known as restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
That by which one brings the vital air called *prāṇa* under control through practice is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*; it is both with seed (*sabīja*) and without seed (*abīja*).
When the two breaths, prāṇa and apāna, mutually overcome one another,
that third [breath] arises through the twofold suppression of those two by means of saṃyama.
O best of the twice-born, for that yogin who possesses an object of focus and practices, gross form is known to be the object of focus for the Infinite (Ananta).
Restraining the senses that are attached to sound and other objects, the knower of yoga,
devoted to withdrawal (pratyāhāra), should make them follow the lead of the mind.
By that means, supreme mastery over the extremely restless senses is born; for one who has not mastered them, the yogi does not accomplish yoga.
Having brought the vital breaths under control through *prāṇāyāma* and the senses through *pratyāhāra*,
one should then cause the mind to abide in a virtuous object of focus.
Śāṇḍilya said:
"O highly fortunate one, tell me that auspicious support of the mind,
by resting upon which it destroys the entire arising of defects."
Keśidhvaja said: "O King, Brahman is the support of the mind; it is twofold by its very nature:
manifest and unmanifest, as well as supreme and non-supreme."
O King, understand that this entire universe consists of three kinds of manifestation:
that called Brahman, that known as karma, and likewise that which is of the nature of both.
For the cultivation of existence (bhāvabhāvanā) is threefold: one consists of the nature of karma, another consists of the nature of Brahman, and likewise another consists of both natures.
Sanandana and the others were endowed with the contemplation of the state of Brahman;
others, from the gods down to the moving and stationary beings, were endowed with the contemplation of karma.
And among those such as Hiraṇyagarbha, who are endowed with both authority and awakening, there exists a twofold cultivation of being consisting of the nature of Brahmā and his functions.
O King, as long as all the specialized knowledges and activities remain unexhausted,
this entire universe and that which is beyond it appear divided by the vision of those who perceive duality.
That knowledge which is designated as Brahman is that in which all distinctions have subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of words, and to be realized by the self.
And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu— the formless, unborn,
and imperishable Supreme Self— characterized by being the opposite of the nature of the universe.
Since it is not possible for one engaged in yoga to contemplate that [subtle form], O King,
one should therefore contemplate the gross form of Hari, which is the object of the entire universe.
The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsava, and Prajāpati;
the Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, the suns, the stars, and the planets.
The Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Daityas, and all other divine species;
humans, animals, mountains, oceans, rivers, and trees.
O King, all beings without exception, as well as the causes of beings—
everything from primordial matter (pradhāna) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa), consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious— [are his].
Whether one-footed, two-footed, many-footed, or footless—
this embodied form of Hari consists of the threefold nature of creative contemplation.
All this— the entire universe, this world of moving and non-moving beings—
is endowed with the power of Viṣṇu, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
And because of that reality, the emanations of power (śakti-vikṣepa) of the All-pervading Lord are designated as his commands (ājñā).
The supreme power of Viṣṇu is said to be one, while that called the individual soul (kṣetrajña) is the other;
ignorance, known as karma, is intended as the third power.
O King, by that [avidyā], the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña-śakti) is enveloped;
thus it undergoes all the continuous torments of saṃsāra.
And because it is concealed by that [power], O King, the power known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is perceived in all beings according to its varying degrees.
In non-living beings it is very slight; in stationary beings it is greater than that;
in reptiles it is greater still, and in birds it is even more powerful than those.
From birds come wild animals; by their power, domestic animals are superior to them;
and from domestic animals come human beings, who are distinguished by their power over men.
O King, from them also [arose] the deities such as the Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas.
From all the gods, Śakra [received it]; from him, Prajāpati;
and from him, Hiraṇyagarbha, who was characterized by the Power (Śakti) of the Supreme Person.
O King, all these forms without exception are his own forms,
since they are joined with his power just as [all things] are joined with space.
O Great-minded One, the second form of Viṣṇu is that which is to be meditated upon by yogis;
it is the formless aspect of Brahman, which is called "Being" (sat) by the wise.
O King, that form in which all these powers are established is indeed the form of the universal nature; it is another, great form of Hari.
O Lord of Men, by His own sport He brings forth all forms consisting of His various powers, endowed with the activities of gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the immeasurable one is not born of karma; it is all-pervading and characterized by being unimpeded.
O King, that form of the Universal-formed One should be meditated upon by one engaged in yoga for the sake of purifying the self and for the destruction of all sins.
Just as fire with its flames raised up burns dry grass when aided by the wind,
so does Viṣṇu, abiding within the mind, burn away all the impurities of yogins.
Therefore, one should establish the mind there, in that support of all powers; that indeed should be known as pure dhāraṇā.
O King, that is the auspicious substratum of the all-pervading mind, which is likewise the Self; transcending the cultivation of the three states of existence, it leads to liberation for yogins.
But others, O tiger among men, who are the supports of the mind—
those beginning with the gods— are all impure, for they have their origin in karma.
The embodied form of the Blessed One, which is free from desire for any support—
this indeed is declared to be *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is fixed.
O lord of men, hear now what kind of embodied form of Hari should be meditated upon; for concentration (dhāraṇā) is not possible without a support.
With a serene and beautiful face, eyes resembling lotus petals,
lovely cheeks, and a radiant, broad forehead-plate.
With beautiful ear-ornaments placed as far as his even ears, with a neck like a conch shell, and a broad chest marked with the Śrīvatsa; ViP_6,7.81.
With an abdomen marked by three folds and a sunken navel,
he should be Viṣṇu with eight long arms, or else with four arms.
One should meditate upon him who has become Brahman, with his thighs and shanks standing evenly, his lotus-like feet and hands well-placed, and clad in pure yellow garments.
Adorned with a crown, beautiful armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
He was endowed with the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, the sword, the discus, and a rosary of beads.
And [he is] with hands granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with hand-rings.
The yogi, having composed his own mind, should contemplate, becoming absorbed in that.

O King, this concentration (*dhāraṇā*) becomes firm right there when it does not depart from the mind— whether one is walking, standing, or performing other actions according to one's will; then one should consider it perfected.
Then the wise man should meditate on the form of the Blessed One as tranquil, devoid of the conch, mace, discus, Śārṅga bow, and other [weapons], and holding a rosary.
When that concentration has likewise become stable,
one should then meditate upon [the deity] as being devoid of ornaments such as crowns and armlets.
Then the wise one should indeed contemplate that deity with his mind as consisting of a single limb; thereafter, he should become intent upon the meditation on the whole composed of those limbs.
And that mental continuum, having that as its object and free from longing for anything else,
O King, is accomplished through those first six factors of dhyāna.
That very apprehension of its own nature, free from conceptual construction,
which is to be accomplished by the mind through meditation— that is designated as *samādhi*.
O King, consciousness is that which attains the supreme Brahman as its object;
likewise, the Self is that which is to be attained once all mental constructions have been utterly destroyed.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has knowledge as its instrument;
by that instrument, having accomplished the task of liberation for him, it ceases once its duty is fulfilled.
Having attained the state of being that [very essence], he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
and any difference of his would be caused by ignorance.
When the ignorance that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction,
who will create the non-existent distinction between the Self and Brahman?
"Thus, O Khāṇḍikya, since you have questioned me, this yoga has been explained by me to you both in brief and in detail; what else shall be done for you?"
Śāṇḍilya said: "Now that the true essence of yoga has been explained, everything has indeed been accomplished for me;
for by your instruction, the impurity of my mind has been entirely destroyed."
O Lord of Men, that which I have stated— that "mine" is unreal and not otherwise— cannot be explained even by those who are experts in what is to be known.
"This is I" and "this is mine"—such is this ignorance; by means of it, worldly convention proceeds.
But the ultimate truth is ineffable; it is not within the range of words.
Therefore, depart for your own welfare; all this has been done by you for me, since the imperishable Yoga that grants liberation was proclaimed by Keśidhvaja.
Parāśara said: O Brahmin,
having been honored by that Khāṇḍikya according to his merit,
King Keśidhvaja then returned to his city.
Khāṇḍikya also, having made his son the king for the sake of attaining yoga,
went to the forest with his mind fully devoted to Govinda.
Having found exclusive delight therein and being purified by virtues such as self-restraint (yama),
the king attained absorption into the stainless Brahman known as Viṣṇu.
Keśidhvaja also, intent on the exhaustion of his own karma for the sake of liberation,
enjoyed sense objects and performed actions without attachment.

Then, O twice-born one, having exhausted his sins through the enjoyment of non-virtuous things, he became stainless and attained perfection, the fruit of which is the ultimate destruction of all torment.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Parāśara said:
Thus has this third dissolution been fully described.
It is absolute liberation, which is absorption into the eternal Brahman.
Primary creation, secondary creation, the lineages, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the accounts of the dynasties— these have all been narrated by me to you.
This Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa indeed destroys all sins;
it is superior to all scriptures and provides the means for attaining the goals of human existence.
O Maitreya, that imperishable [truth] has been declared to you exactly as it is, since you are a devoted listener;
whatever else remains to be said, ask that now and I shall tell it to you.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, O Sage, everything that you were asked by me has been told;
I have heard this with devotion, and there is nothing else remaining for me to ask.
All doubts have been severed and the mind has been rendered pure;
through your grace, I have understood the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of all things.
O Guru, you have fully understood the fourfold aggregate, the threefold power,
and the threefold cultivation of states of being in their entirety.
"O twice-born one, by your grace I have understood that there is no need for other objects of knowledge;
I have realized how this entire world is not distinct from Viṣṇu."
I have achieved my purpose and am free from doubt through your grace, O Great Sage,
since the duties of the social classes and other dharmas have been understood by me in their entirety.
I have understood all karma—both that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to liberation.
Be gracious, O best of Brahmins; there is nothing else remaining for me to ask.
O Guru, whatever effort I have made in engaging you in this discourse, please forgive it; for among the virtuous, there is no distinction between a son and a disciple.
Parāśara said:
This Purāṇa, which I have related to you, is equal to the Vedas;
when it is heard, the heap of sins arising from all defects is destroyed.
Primary creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the complete history of the dynasties have all been recounted by me here to you.
In this regard, the gods, as well as the Daityas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas,
Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and likewise the Apsarases, are described.
Sages whose selves are cultivated and who are endowed with austerity are thus described;
likewise, among men of the four castes, those men are distinguished by their conduct.
The holy regions of the earth, the sacred rivers and oceans, the most meritorious mountains, and the deeds of the wise; ViP_6.8.16.
The duties of the castes and other such dharmas, as well as all the branches of the Vedas in their entirety—
by the mere hearing of which one is immediately liberated from all sins.
He who is the imperishable cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the world—
that Lord Hari is said to be all beings and the self of all.
Even when his name is uttered involuntarily, one is released from all sins.
After 19ab, insert:
Having heard from that Vyāsa this [account] which destroys the sins of you all...
A person is instantly liberated, like deer terrified by a lion.
After verse 19, B1 D6 insert:
"All this has been told by me in seven thousand [verses]."
O Maitreya, the chanting of the Name with devotion is the unsurpassed dissolution of all sins, just as fire is for metals.
The extremely fierce impurity of the Kali age brings suffering to men in the hells.
After 21ab, Ś₂ and D₇ insert:
"Indeed, the remembrance of Hari alone, through devotion, is the supreme destroyer of that [suffering]."
Therefore, O Brahmin, there is nothing whatsoever that remains [as a fixed entity] which must be sought elsewhere.
Upon remembering it even once, one immediately attains dissolution [into that state].
By Hiraṇyagarbha, Indra, Rudra, the Ādityas, the Aśvins, and Vāyu;
by the Pāvakas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and other such gods.
By yakṣas, rākṣasas, and uragas; by siddhas, daityas, gandharvas, and dānavas;
likewise by apsarases, as well as by all the stars, lunar mansions, and planets.
Likewise by the seven ṛṣis, by the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇya), and by the lords of those hearths;
likewise by humans beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, and similarly by domestic animals and wild beasts.
With reptiles and birds, with trees such as the *palāśa*, with forests, mountains, oceans, rivers, and the netherworlds (pātāla), along with the earth and other elements; ||| ViP_6.8.25 |||
O twice-born one, this entire cosmic egg, together with its sound and other qualities, is like a minute atom compared to Him; O best of the twice-born, it is composed of that very essence.
He is all, the all-knowing, possessing every form yet devoid of material form;
the Blessed One Viṣṇu is celebrated here as the destroyer of sins.
After verse 27, Ñ₁ V₁ B insert:
"That is auspicious, that is a means of securing well-being, that is pure, and unsurpassed."
O best of sages, having heard this, one obtains in its entirety that very fruit which one indeed attains when bathing at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the horse sacrifice.
A man who observes a fast at Prayāga, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and Arbuda obtains that same merit simply by hearing this.
O Brahmin, that fruit consisting of great merit which one obtains through a year of well-performed Agnihotra sacrifices is attained by him from hearing this but once.
Having bathed in the waters of the Yamunā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha and having beheld Hari in Mathurā, one attains the supreme goal.
One obtains that fruit perfectly through chanting with concentrated devotion.
Therefore, one who possesses good renown should listen to this with reverence. (ViP 6.8.32ab*22)
O brahmin-sage, with your mind offered to Keśava, [listen to] this Purāṇa.
O best of sages, a man who bathes in the waters of the Yamunā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, having observed a fast, [attains the highest state].
Having properly worshipped Acyuta with a concentrated mind in Mathurā,
one obtains the complete fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Then, observing the supernatural power of others who had been raised up by their own kinsmen,
the fathers and grandfathers of those others reportedly said this:
"Will one born in our family, having fasted and bathed in the waters of the Kālindī, worship Govinda in Mathurā?"
"In the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭhāmūla, by this very [rite],
may we too attain supreme prosperity, having been delivered by those born of our own lineage."
In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped Janārdana,
one born of a noble family shall offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the Yamunā.
At that time, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa there with a concentrated mind and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors, he bathed in the waters of the Yamunā.
Whatever merit a man gains by delivering his ancestors,
a devoted person obtains that same merit by hearing this chapter of the Purāṇa.
This is the unsurpassed protection for those who fear saṃsāra;
it destroys bad dreams for men and eradicates all that is evil.
After verse 41, the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition inserts:
"And may there be auspiciousness among all auspicious things, which bestows the attainment of sons."
In ancient times, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] spoke this to Ṛbhu;
Ṛbhu spoke it to Priyavrata, and he in turn told it to Bhāguri.
Bhāguri taught it to Stambhamitra, and he in turn told it to Dadhīca; he told it to Sārasvata, and Bhṛgu received it from Sārasvata as well.
Bhṛgu spoke it to Purukutsa, and he in turn spoke it to Narmadā;
Narmadā spoke it to the nāga Dhṛtarāṣṭra and to Apūraṇa.
And those two spoke it to Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas, O twice-born one;
Vāsuki spoke it to his son, and Vatsa indeed to Aśvatara.
And he spoke to Kambala, and he indeed to Elāpatra.
Then the sage Vedaśiras reached Pātāla;
having obtained all of this, he indeed gave it to Pramati.
It was given by Pramati to the wise Jātūkarṇa,
and it was likewise spoken by Jātūkarṇa to others who were endowed with merit.
"By virtue of the boon granted by Pulastya, this has come to my memory as well;
thus, O Maitreya, I have related this to you exactly as it is."
You too shall speak this to Chinīka at the end of the Kali age.
Thus, this supreme secret, which destroys the impurities of the Kali age—
any man who hears it, O twice-born one, is liberated from all sins.
He who hears this day after day has performed a collective praise of the immortals for the sake of the ancestors, yakṣas, and humans.
After verse 52, D₂ inserts:
"O Brahmin, having heard this entire great Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa..."
O best of the twice-born, one should worship the reciter there, who is equal to Vyāsa himself.
And one should give gold and cows according to one's ability, provided they are not wandering about.
O Brahmin, when the reciter is honored, Keśava is thereby honored.
Having heard ten chapters of this [work], one undoubtedly obtains that merit born from the gift of a tawny cow, which is extremely difficult to attain. (ViP 6.8.53)
But that person who hears this entire [account], fixing Acyuta in their mind—He who is everything, consisting of all things, the support of all worlds, and whose refuge is the Self;

He who is knowledge, the object of knowledge, infinite, without beginning, and the benefactor of all the immortals—he attains, without a doubt, the complete fruit which is obtained from the horse-sacrifice.

In which [text] the Blessed One—the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, who consists of the knowledge of Brahman, the infallible Lord of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire world—is present in the beginning, the middle, and the end;
hearing that, reciting it with devotion, and retaining it, a person attains Hari, the supreme purifier, the absolute perfection in all the worlds, for whom there is no equal.

When the mind is fixed upon Him, one does not go to hell; even heaven is an obstacle when He is the object of contemplation; and for one whose self and mind are absorbed in Him, even the world of Brahmā seems insignificant.
Since He, the Imperishable One, bestows liberation upon men of pure intellect when He dwells within their hearts, what wonder is there that sin dissolves away when Acyuta is glorified?

Those who know the sacrifice constantly worship with sacrifices the Lord of Sacrifice, the one composed of Brahman whom the performers of action and the men of knowledge meditate upon as the supreme beyond both the higher and the lower;
having attained whom, one is not born, does not die, does not increase nor diminish, and who is neither non-existent nor existent—what more than that can be heard of Hari? Listen!

He who, assuming the form of the ancestors, partakes of the *kavya* offered according to the rules, and as the Lord, the beginningless and endless Blessed One, partakes of the *havya* in his divine state—known by the names *svāhā* and *svadhā*;
in whom, the Brahman that is the abode of all powers, the measures of those who pride themselves on their logic do not suffice for finality; he, Hari, has entered our ears and destroys our impurity.

I bow to that Supreme Person, the Lord worthy of praise, who has no end and no origin; who, being devoid of transformation, knows no increase; and who never undergoes diminution—He who is the non-conceptual Reality.

I bow forever to that eternal and imperishable Puruṣa, who alone, though pure, appears as if impure through the distinctions of various bodily forms; who experiences that which is favorable to him in many ways; who is endowed with knowledge; and who is the creator of the manifestations of all the principles (tattvas).
I bow to that which consists of the unity of the regulation of the activity of knowledge, which is capable of bestowing experience upon the person, which is composed of the three qualities (guṇas),
which is unmanifest, which is the cause of the contemplation of worldly existence, which exists as its own essential nature, and which is eternally ageless.
After verse 61, Ś₁ inserts:
*Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva.* ViP 6.8.61*25:1.
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; homage to you, O creator of the universe!
Homage be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa.

I am forever bowed to the Manifested One, who consists of the arrangement of ether, air, fire, water, and earth; who is capable of bringing forth the objects of enjoyment such as sound and the rest; who assists the person through all the sense organs; and who is both manifest and subtle-pure.
May that Lord Hari, whose manifold and eternal form consists of both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the supreme self (parātman),
bestow upon all men that perfection which is free from birth, old age, and the like.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
